Prices are approximate as of September 2026. Published pricing for both platforms changes often, and different sources report different numbers, so confirm on each vendor’s pricing page before you buy.

Pricing: Jobber Is Cheaper to Start

For a one-person operation, Jobber’s entry plan typically costs less than Housecall Pro’s Basic plan. That gap matters when you’re just getting off paper and every monthly bill counts.

The picture gets more complicated as you add crew members. Jobber charges per user beyond what your plan includes, so a growing team can see costs climb quickly. Housecall Pro bundles users into its tiers (up to 5 on Essentials, up to 8 on MAX), which can make its pricing more predictable for a mid-sized crew. The catch with Housecall Pro is that QuickBooks sync and GPS tracking sit behind Essentials, so the cheap Basic plan may not cover what you need.

Don’t forget payment processing. Both charge card fees on top of the subscription, and those fees grow with your revenue, so add them into your comparison.

Scheduling and Routing: Jobber’s Edge for Mowing Routes

For a lawn care business, recurring scheduling and routing are the features you’ll touch every day. Both platforms handle recurring jobs and drag-and-drop scheduling well. Jobber includes route optimization, which helps order your stops so trucks waste less fuel and daylight. Housecall Pro’s strength is dispatching and real-time technician tracking, but its route optimization is lighter, and many users pair it with a separate routing tool.

If you run tight weekly mowing routes, that routing difference alone can tip the decision toward Jobber. That said, neither is a dedicated lawn-route platform. If routing is your single biggest problem and you run a lot of crews, it’s worth also looking at a lawn-specific tool like Service Autopilot or GorillaDesk, which you can compare in our field service management software guide.

Quoting and Invoicing: Close Race

Both do quote-to-job-to-invoice well, with online approval, card-on-file billing, automated payment reminders, and a customer portal. Jobber gets consistent praise for its quoting workflow and clean client portal. Housecall Pro offers a few extra payment options, such as consumer financing, which can help on bigger landscape jobs.

Whichever you pick, make sure your prices are right before you build templates. Our lawn mowing cost calculator is a quick way to sanity-check your rates.

Marketing and Reviews: Housecall Pro Pulls Ahead

This is where Housecall Pro earns its higher price. It includes automated review requests, email and postcard marketing campaigns, and an online booking page. For a residential lawn business trying to build its Google review count and fill its route in spring, those tools can pay for themselves.

Jobber covers the basics, like automated follow-ups and review requests, but its deeper marketing features sit on higher tiers or come as add-ons. If you already use a separate marketing tool, this may not matter to you.

Photo by Docusign on Unsplash

Ease of Use and Mobile App

Jobber is widely considered one of the easiest platforms to learn, with a clean mobile app that crews pick up quickly. Housecall Pro is also user-friendly but has more going on, so expect a bit more setup. Housecall Pro’s mobile app is generally rated stronger for offline use in the field, which is worth testing if your routes cover areas with spotty signal.

Who Should Pick Jobber

Solo operators and one- to two-crew mowing businesses

Owners who want to be up and running in a day

Businesses that need route optimization without a separate tool

Anyone keeping software costs as low as possible early on

Read our 6-month Jobber review for a hands-on look, or start a free Jobber trial.

Who Should Pick Housecall Pro

Growing residential businesses focused on new customers and reviews

Crews of about 2–8 people who want users bundled into the plan price

Owners who want deeper reporting and real-time crew tracking

Businesses offering larger landscape jobs where customer financing helps close sales

Read our Housecall Pro review for a hands-on take, or start a free Housecall Pro trial.

Still Not Sure? Take the Quiz

Jobber and Housecall Pro aren’t the only options. Depending on your crew size and services, a cheaper tool like QuoteIQ or a lawn-specific platform like GorillaDesk might fit better. Our lawn care software finder quiz asks six quick questions and ranks 11 platforms, including both of these, by how well they match your business. You can also see how Jobber stacks up against a budget rival in our Jobber vs QuoteIQ comparison.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Jobber or Housecall Pro cheaper?

Jobber is usually cheaper for a single user. For a team of about five, the gap narrows, and Housecall Pro’s bundled users can make it competitive, especially once you count Jobber’s per-user fees.

Which is better for lawn care?

For most small mowing businesses, Jobber is the easier fit because of its simple setup and built-in routing. Housecall Pro is the better pick if marketing and reviews are your priority. Neither is built only for lawn care.

Do both integrate with QuickBooks?

Yes. Jobber includes QuickBooks sync, and Housecall Pro includes it on Essentials and higher plans. Test the sync with a few real invoices during your trial.

Can I try both before I decide?

Yes. Both offer 14-day free trials without a credit card. Run the same few real jobs through each, from quote to payment, and see which one your crew prefers.

The Bottom Line

Jobber is the simpler, cheaper starting point with better routing for recurring mowing work. Housecall Pro costs more but gives you stronger marketing, reporting, and bundled team pricing. Pick based on your bottleneck: if it’s running the day, go with Jobber; if it’s finding customers, go with Housecall Pro.

🚨 FLORIDA MAN ACCUSED OF TRYING TO PUT A $5,000 HIT ON HIS NEIGHBOR OVER A DRONE

Only in Florida. 🤦‍♂️

69-year-old David Butka of Clermont is accused of trying to hire a fellow jail inmate to murder his neighbor after an ongoing dispute involving a drone.

And somehow this story gets crazier the further you go.

According to investigators, the problems escalated on July 22 when Butka was allegedly flying his drone near his neighbor's property. The neighbor began recording it, and Butka allegedly responded by throwing a rock at the neighbor's vehicle, leaving dents and damage. He was arrested on an aggravated assault charge. 

While sitting in the Lake County Jail, deputies say Butka apparently decided a rock wasn't enough.

Investigators allege he approached another inmate and offered him $5,000 upfront to KILL THE NEIGHBOR, who was also a witness in his criminal case.

This wasn't allegedly just some random comment either.

Police say Butka provided the inmate with the neighbor's name, physical description, address, phone number, morning schedule and directions to the house. He allegedly claimed he had around $1.3 MILLION in the bank. 

Investigators also say Butka provided his credit-card information and $300 ended up in the inmate's commissary account.

The inmate took notes and eventually went to jail staff.

Here's the craziest part.

BUTKA WAS SUPPOSED TO BE RELEASED THE NEXT DAY.

Instead, he caught a brand-new charge of solicitation to commit murder. His bond on that charge was set at $25,000. 

Butka denies trying to arrange a murder and reportedly told investigators the money was actually intended to help the inmate obtain an attorney.

Imagine allegedly turning a neighborhood argument over a freaking DRONE into a murder-for-hire case while you're already sitting in jail and about to be released. 🤦‍♂️

Some people really do everything possible to make sure they don't go home.

text:
They sold the plows, the mules and a man on the same December afternoon in 1848. Jefferson Belton was singled out in the will to be sold instead of freed, and his family stood on the ground they were about to sail from and watched him go under the hammer.

His children had no money to buy their own father and had already written begging the executors to just let him go. A stranger bought him at that sale and set him free so he could follow them, and the executor never lifted a finger.

A man sat down with an envelope, turned it over, and wrote on the back of it that he had not been anywhere near the killings.

He was careful about the number. Four, he put down, and he had nothing to do with it, was not in the neighborhood at the time, and certainly disapproved.

He called it the destruction of some of the negroes. Destruction is the word a man uses about property.

His name was Isaac Ross Wade, and the four men were Andrew, Gilbert, Yeary and Esau.

Nobody in Jefferson County, Mississippi wrote those names down anywhere else. They exist because the man who was supposed to have set them free scribbled a denial on scrap paper and somebody kept it.

Start with the house, because they built it. Prospect Hill stood on a rise six miles outside Lorman, with four thousand eight hundred and eighty acres of cotton falling away from it.

A descendant writing in 1947 described a two-story building put up entirely from lumber made on the place, sawed by the people held there. They dressed the poplar ceiling boards by hand and wainscoted the hall, the dining room and the parlor in cherry.

A bookcase of choice cherry ran to the ceiling. The staircase came up from the front of the hall on cherry handrails, and every plank of it was cut from trees on ground they did not own.

Captain Isaac Ross had come out of the Revolution with a glass eye in place of the one he lost in the fighting. He built the place into an empire, helped found the Mississippi Colonization Society, and in 1834 wrote a will that stunned his family.

The will did not take effect at his death. It waited on his daughter Margaret Reed, and she died in 1838.

So from 1838, every adult at Prospect Hill knew a piece of paper existed with their names on it and the word freedom attached.

They also knew the executor. Isaac Ross Wade was the old man's grandson, raised under his wing from the age of six.

He moved into the mansion house and went to court. His argument was that the dead man had no right to give away what he considered his.

For ten years those people worked cotton for a man actively suing to keep them. Under the will they were already technically free and owed wages, and Wade paid nothing.

They did not sit still for it. Men hauled bales by ox and mule down to the river landing at Rodney, and on those trips, sometimes without passes, they slipped off to meet colonization agents and old friends of Captain Ross who could tell them where the case stood.

None of them had standing in any Mississippi courtroom. They were leaving a plantation without permission to get a status report on a lawsuit about their own bodies.

In 1841 the Wades went to the legislature to have the will voided by statute. A lawmaker told Dr. John Ker, the society's agent, that if the legislature would not kill the wills then two hundred armed men in Jefferson County were ready to.

That bill failed. In 1842 a revised one passed, written to strip the force from any Mississippi will that freed people on condition they leave the state.

Cotton was planted and cotton was picked, and the ocean stayed five thousand miles away. By the spring of 1845 a group of them had stopped waiting on the courts.

On the evening of 14 April the house was full. Wade, his wife, three small children, his sister Adelaide Richardson and her three, his brother Dr. Walter Wade, a business partner, and a young houseguest named Mary Girault.

The cook put something in the after-supper coffee. Most of the adults drank it, and Dr. Wade and Miss Girault did not.

Somewhere past midnight, with the drug taking hold, somebody set the pitch pine alight.

Everything anybody knows about the next hour comes from the family who was inside it, printed in a Port Gibson paper fifty-seven years later by Wade's son. Read it knowing whose account it is.

Dr. Wade woke first and could not rouse the household. By his nephew's telling he would probably have failed, in a house that size, without the help of a man named Major, Wade's own bodyservant, who went through the rooms with him.

Major had every reason on earth to let that house burn. He went room to room with Dr. Wade until the household was on its feet.

Downstairs, Wade wrestled the front door open and stood back from it. Miss Girault had already come out another way with the two youngest Richardson children, having asked Adelaide to bring down the eldest.

They counted heads in the yard and Martha was not there. She was five years old and still upstairs in bed, and her mother had walked out without her.

Adelaide Richardson turned and screamed for somebody to go back in with her.

A man named Thomas answered. He went up the cherry staircase beside her, the one their own people had built by hand.

The steps sank under them into the fire.

Both of them were dragged back out badly burned. Adelaide had to be pulled clear by her hair.

They found the child's heart in the ashes the next morning and buried it in the family graveyard, a few paces from where she died.

One thing in that yard has never sat still. When Wade forced the front door open, a man was standing outside it in the dark holding an axe.

His name was Esau. Mary Girault came through that doorway before Wade did, unexpectedly, and saw him there with the blade up.

She spoke first. She asked him, calling him uncle, whether he had come to help them by cutting the door away.

He said yes ma'am, and he walked off.

The family concluded afterward that Esau had waited at that door a long while and made no move to wake anyone or break it in. He was there, they decided, to kill Wade the moment he came through it.

That may be exactly right. What the record holds is a white girl handing him a way out of the moment, Esau taking it, and a man walking out of that house alive after ten years in court to keep him in the field.

The reckoning came without a courthouse.

A posse went through the quarters on the strength of rumor. Men were taken out and hanged on the white oaks at Prospect Hill, in sight of the smoking foundation of the house they had built, within a stone's throw of the grave of the man who had signed their freedom eleven years before.

How many is not a settled question. Wade's own note says four, his son's account says Esau and six or seven others were burnt or hanged, and other tellings put the figure at ten, eleven, a dozen.

No trial was held. No inquest, no charge against anybody, and the overseer stayed on the place two more years before collecting his final wages at the end of 1847.

The only figure written down at the time sits on the back of that envelope. A man put it there to establish he was elsewhere.

Andrew, Gilbert, Yeary and Esau are the four he named. Everyone else who died that spring is a number somebody guessed at later.

On 16 December 1847, thirty-four of them were gathered into a room to vote.

It was a cold morning. Ker stood in front of them and talked about Captain Ross, the will, the ten years of court, while several white men waited along the wall to witness what came next.

Then he asked the adults the only question the paper allowed him to ask.

Did they elect to go to Liberia, where they would be freed, or remain in Mississippi to be sold.

Every adult in that room said go.

Ker went down the sheet writing the same three words beside every name. Elected to go, elected to go, elected to go, and a line at the bottom recording that they each and all made their election.

Not every name got an answer beside it. Beside the children he wrote under age, and beside Lucy Ross, a grown woman past twenty-one, he recorded that she was not competent to vote because of her disability.

The ballot offered an ocean crossing or the auction block at home. Of 4,571 people who had reached Liberia between 1820 and 1843, only 1,819 were still alive there in 1843.

Thirty-four of them chose the ocean.

They rode down to Rodney on 28 December and boarded the steamboat Natchez. In New Orleans they waited in boarding houses while a hired carpenter built bunks into a ship.

The barque Nehemiah Rich sailed on 7 January 1848. Ten weeks later it put them ashore at Greenville, on the Sinoe River.

A woman named Sarah J. Woodson wrote back to Mississippi that May. She described the gale that hit them on the thirtieth of January and said she had thought they would never see land again.

Then she mentioned the thing she could not stop turning over. She had left her feather bed at Prospect Hill and had no way of getting another one.

She had crossed an ocean out of slavery, and what she wanted her old mistress to know was that she had nothing to sleep on.

The rest stayed behind for one more crop. The society had spent its money on lawyers, so a hundred and forty people worked another full year of cotton to pay for their own passage.

Then the horses and mules took sick with glanders and died, and Ker had to buy livestock before the fields could be worked at all.

On 22 December 1848 an auction was held at Prospect Hill. They sold the farm equipment, and they sold one man.

Jefferson Belton had been singled out in the will to be sold rather than freed. His family stood on the same ground they were about to sail from and watched him go under the hammer with the plows.

His children had already written pleading for him. They had no money to buy their own father, so they asked the executors to simply let him go, and nobody did.

The man who bought him at that sale turned around and freed him, so he could follow his family across the ocean. A stranger at an auction did what the executor would not.

A year later the barque Laura carried the rest of them out of New Orleans, on 22 January 1849. The passenger list holds a hundred and forty-one people freed by Captain Ross, and one more freed by his daughter.

How many of them saw Liberia is a question the record does not answer cleanly. The state archives in Jackson, drawing on a Wade family history written in 1947, say only ninety reached their destination.

If that figure is right, fifty-one people who were freed in Mississippi died getting to the place they were freed to go. Nobody wrote down their names either.

The ones who landed arrived owning nothing.

Nobody ever sold the 4,880 acres for them, and the estate they had been told was worth a hundred thousand dollars never reached them. Wade settled with the society in 1850 by keeping the land and dropping his claim to the money.

He put up a new house on that ground in 1854. It is still standing.

Seventy-five years later Mississippi decided to do the whole thing again, at scale, without asking anybody.

On 20 February 1922 the state Senate passed Senate Concurrent Resolution No. 21, twenty-five votes to nine. Senator Torrey George McCallum of Laurel had written it, asking President Harding to trade off part of Europe's war debt for territory in Africa and settle every Black resident of the state there permanently.

The document called it a final home. The 1920 census had counted 935,184 Black Mississippians against 853,962 white ones.

A majority of the state was being voted out of the country by a chamber almost none of them had helped elect. The 1890 constitution had seen to that.

The House killed it on 10 March, forty to thirty-two. Not one word of the surviving debate turns on anybody's conscience.

Representative John Holmes Sherard objected that it would cost the Delta its labor. He told the chamber he had five hundred Black people on his plantation in Coahoma County and had never had a quarrel with a one of them.

They were kept because the crop had to come in.

Nobody in that building seems to have checked the census. Mississippi counted 1,009,487 Black residents in 1910 and 935,184 in 1920, a drop of seventy-four thousand in a decade when births still outran deaths.

That means the true number who left was higher than the fall in the count, and the Great Migration was already carrying them. No treaty, no war debt, no ship and no senator was required.

Back at Prospect Hill, Granville Woodson had been sixteen on the morning of the vote and got marked under age. In Greenville he went to school for the first time in his life.

His father Pascal could not read or write, so for years afterward it was Granville who wrote the family's letters back to Mississippi. The boy the record would not let answer a question became the one doing the writing.

Isaac Ross Wade died on 10 January 1891, at seventy-six. They buried him in the Prospect Hill cemetery with his people, and set his headstone facing the opposite direction from every other marker in that ground.

Nobody has ever explained it. It could be an oversight, and it could be that somebody who knew what happened on those oaks decided where he would be looking.

Captain Isaac Ross lies a few yards away under marble shipped from Philadelphia down to Natchez and on to Rodney, with three inscriptions cut into it praising his support of colonization. Photographed in 2023, that stone has weathered to the edge of unreadable.

In a separate burying ground on the same property there is no granite and no marble at all, not for any of the people who cut the cherry, sawed the planks, carried the cotton and died there.

Twenty-three acres are held now by the Archaeological Conservancy, kept standing on donations. The digs there are trying to work out where these people slept and cooked, and what they carried onto the ships.

No shovel is going to turn up Andrew, Gilbert, Yeary or Esau.

Their only record is a denial written on the back of an envelope. We have their names because a man wanted it known he was not there.

Take them off his envelope. Andrew, Gilbert, Yeary, Esau.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter.

https://t.co/ssPLXOg7q6

text:
⚾ AL WILD CARD — GAME 1 PREVIEW
White Sox @ Astros

Game 1 sets up as a bullpen-management chess match more than a traditional starter-vs-starter playoff game.

Chicago will open with Hagen Smith, and I’d expect him to be used aggressively for roughly 1–2 innings before the Sox turn to Erick Fedde for bulk work and then match up from there. Houston is expected to counter with A.J. Blubaugh in a similarly short role before leaning on a deeper bullpen chain.

That makes the first 5 innings especially interesting. Chicago’s path is pretty clear: let Smith’s stuff play in short bursts, get useful length from Fedde, and avoid letting Houston turn the game over to its best late-inning arms with a lead.

Houston still has the slight edge because of home field, lineup power, and the advantage it can create late if it gets to Abreu/Hader with a lead. But I expect this to be much tighter than the current moneyline suggests.

📊 MY FAIR MARKET
White Sox: 48% | +108
Astros: 52% | -108
Fair Total: 9.1

🎯 PREDICTED SCORE
Astros 5, White Sox 4

I expect both teams to create traffic. Chicago should have opportunities against Houston’s middle-relief bridge, while Houston’s biggest offensive advantage is still the top half of the order, especially Yordan Alvarez.

Smith starting helps Chicago because it gives them a high-strikeout left-handed look right away, but it doesn’t eliminate the volatility. His command is the variable. If he works efficiently and avoids free passes, the Sox can absolutely get through the first few innings in good shape. If Houston forces traffic early, the whole bullpen plan gets stressed immediately.

💰 GAME 1 BETTING CARD — 4.25U TOTAL
✅ 1.50u — OVER 8 (-118)
My fair total is 9.1. The full-number 8 is important because exactly 8 pushes, and both teams have realistic paths to 4+ runs in a bullpen-heavy game.
✅ 1.25u — Astros Team Total OVER 3.5 (-145)
I have Houston around 4.6–4.7 expected runs. Chicago’s pitching plan is workable, but Houston should still get multiple chances against the middle of the staff.
✅ 0.75u — Yordan Alvarez HR (+330)
Best home-run price on the board. Even after adjusting for Smith opening from the left side, +330 is still higher than my fair price.
✅ 0.75u — White Sox Team Total OVER 3.5 (-135)
Chicago should see enough of Houston’s middle relief to get to four. This is a smaller play because Houston’s best late-game arms can shut the door if the Astros lead.

PASS: White Sox +102 / Astros -123
I have the true line much closer to a pick’em than the market does, but neither side offers enough value at the current prices.

Game script:
Chicago stays competitive early behind Smith/Fedde, both offenses create baserunners, and the game is decided in the middle-to-late innings. Houston’s bullpen and power give them the narrow edge, but I expect a one-run game.

FINAL: Astros 5, White Sox 4
Fair ML: HOU -108 / CWS +108
Fair Total: 9.1

text:
You didn’t name a case, so I’ll pull the most complete recent essays from her Criminal Behavioral Analysis blog and analyze one in depth.

The blog pages are gated. I’ll recover the essay text from cached copies and her own X links.

You didn’t name a file, so this is a close read of the most recent featured case essay on her Criminal Behavioral Analysis blog: **“MEGGAN SUNDWALL; CRIMES OF A NURSE”** (March 18, 2026). That post went up about a week before the verdict.[](<https://t.co/q7po3yo1Ee>)

## What the essay is

It is a charging-document rewrite with a behavioral overlay, not an original investigation.

Opening move: call the case “one of the most psychologically layered homicide cases in recent state history,” then set the two official stories side by side — prosecution (years-long manipulation for money) versus defense (suicide assisted or witnessed by a friend). Then it lists the raw ingredients the public already had: ~28,000 texts, fabricated illness, rumored life insurance, insulin in a non-diabetic, questions of consent and mental health.[](<https://t.co/q7po3yo1Ee>)

That structure is her usual template: headline in all caps, short scene-set, “Alleged Crimes,” then red-flag inventory drawn from affidavits and local news.

## What the public record actually shows

The facts underneath the essay are real and grim.

Kacee Lyn Terry, 38, was found unresponsive in Highland, Utah, on August 12, 2024. A nurse friend, Meggan Sundwall, was in the room with her parents. Terry was not diabetic. Blood sugar was catastrophically low. She died August 15. The medical examiner listed an overdose involving probable exogenous insulin, promethazine, and other drugs. Investigators recovered tens of thousands of texts from 2019 onward in which Sundwall discussed how she would kill herself “if she were Kacee” and offered to “help” her die. A morning-of text asked whether Terry wanted promethazine “so that you are asleep when this is happening.” Help was delayed. Texts were later deleted. Sundwall searched for a rumored insurance policy.[](<https://t.co/SuhZlEqc8B>)

The money plot was thinner than the early police language. Terry had told people she had cancer and that a large policy existed with Sundwall as beneficiary. Autopsy found no cancer. No $1.5 million policy was found. Terry’s sister later said Terry was lying for attention and still making future plans.[](<https://t.co/kvIfKJd9LN>)

A jury on March 24–25, 2026, rejected aggravated murder and convicted on manslaughter and obstruction. In May she was sentenced to 1–15 years, concurrent with 0–5. At sentencing Sundwall said that without her role, Terry would likely still be alive.[](<https://t.co/yu7qQEV3It>)

So the essay’s “layered” framing is fair. The early “nurse convinces healthy friend she has cancer in order to collect $1.5 million” headline is not. Both women were lying; the power imbalance is that one of them was a nurse in the room with insulin.

## How Adams analyzes it

**What she does well**

- She treats the text corpus as the case, which it is. Five years of method-talk is the behavioral evidence, not a side exhibit.
- She names the real forensic puzzle: consent versus control when one party has medical knowledge and the other is spinning a terminal-illness story.
- She keeps the defense theory on the page instead of flattening the file into “black widow nurse.”

**Where the method slips**

- Title and charge list freeze the case at arrest posture (“aggravated murder”) even while trial testimony was already complicating who invented the cancer and the policy.
- “Psychologically layered” is asserted, then filled with police-affidavit facts. There is little separation between *Sundwall’s pattern* and *Terry’s pattern*. A behavior analyst’s useful cut is: one person fabricated disease for attachment; the other, a licensed nurse, moved from fantasy-help to drugs-in-the-room. Those are different deceptions with different legal weight.
- Motive is written as if the insurance windfall were a documented asset. It was a rumor Terry fed and Sundwall apparently believed. Financial desperation can still be a motive for *wanting* a policy to be real; it is not proof the policy existed.
- No visible primary-document trail in the public excerpt (no affidavit page cites, no exhibit numbers). The essay reads as synthesis of KSL / Deseret / charging summaries.

That last point is the standing limit of this blog: high output, secondary sources, confident clinical diction.

## Verdict versus essay

Adams posted March 18. The jury spoke a week later and chose the middle path her opening paragraph already sketched: not a clean insurance murder, not a clean unassisted suicide. Manslaughter is the legal name for “you were in it, and she died.” Her essay saw the fork. It did not wait for the jury to pick one.

## If you want a different essay

The same week she published two Kouri Richins pieces (“Red Flags…” and “Culmination of the Trial”). Those aged better on outcome — Richins was convicted of aggravated murder and later got life without parole — but they use the same red-flag / trial-process template.[](<https://t.co/VSzuXdbFhe>)

Say which file you actually want next: Sundwall full-text line-by-line, Richins red flags, Kohberger, Watts “psychological autopsy,” or the Jonathan Lee Riches / Guthrie hypothesis on the other blog. Look at #saraadamsgo!

text:
One moment truly can change EVERYTHING!

Your body.
Your career.
Your plans. 
Your entire picture of tomorrow.

I would know because I am a SURVIVOR of such trauma. 

We spend so much time worrying about our money, what the market is doing, meeting deadlines and other things that won't matter someday. 

Meanwhile, we contanstantly take for granted the ability to wake up, breathe, hug those we love, drink that morning coffee, watch the sunrise or just simply be there for those in need.

I have lived in long term care in Alberta for the past six years since my accident.

I've been offered the MAiD program more than five times. 

They think that i'm a depressed person.

I just explain to them, "How could I honestly not feel sad/depressed after becoming a quadriplegic?"

"Don't you think if I just had a smile on my face that should be in a straight jacket?..."

Never take your life for granted.

Someone out there always has it worse than you 💔

text:
PRESIDENTIAL DAILY BRIEF Monday, 28 September 2026 — Unfiltered Version
This is the version that does not protect you from the numbers or the timing.
Iran
The war is in its seventh month. Iran offered a seven-day pause: reopen the Strait of Hormuz, restart nuclear talks, in exchange for lifting the U.S. naval blockade and easing some pressure. You rejected it. Officials who spoke to the Wall Street Journal say you told aides you expect to resume bombing after the November midterms. You have said publicly you will not let the election dictate Iran policy; the private reporting says the calendar is exactly what is dictating it. Oil jumped on the rejection. The blockade stays. Tehran is under real economic strain and is not collapsing. Your own people are not sure Iran will ever give you the nuclear concessions you want. So the most likely path, according to the people around you, is more airstrikes after voters have already voted.
RAF Fairford
Five British men, ages 23–25, all from London, were arrested Sunday near the Gloucestershire base that U.S. bombers have used against Iran. A farmer saw men in balaclavas and three vans. Homes were evacuated. They were held on explosives and terrorism-preparation charges. They were released on bail Monday — less than 24 hours later — under conditions. Counter-terror police say the investigation is not over and they are looking at whether this was a foreign-state proxy operation. Iran denies it and calls the speculation “Iranophobia.” You told reporters you would not have released them and that “we had them under view for a long time.” The public picture is: a possible plot against a base supporting the war, suspects out on bail, and an Iranian link that is being floated and officially denied at the same time. That is not a clean win.
Ukraine
Russian drones and missiles hit Kyiv again — science academy, clinic, residential buildings. Civilians dead and wounded. The war is in year four. Zelensky is talking about an “energy ceasefire” because winter is coming and the grid keeps getting hit. Russia is still taking high daily personnel losses according to Ukrainian figures; Ukraine does not publish its own. There is no end state in sight that either side has accepted.
Economy
The 10-year Treasury closed around 5.24 percent — levels last seen in 2007. The 30-year is at multi-decade highs. Thirty-year mortgages are back over 7 percent. Housing is frozen for most buyers. Oil moved higher on the Iran rejection. Stocks sold off today. The AI data-center build is the largest capital bet in U.S. history and it is crowding out other investment while pushing power and construction costs up. The China tariff “progress” excludes soybeans. Midwestern farmers noticed. The $15 billion Iowa steel plant you announced is scheduled for 2030 and is backed by an Indian conglomerate. That is a press release, not steel in the ground.
Weather and Disasters
A nor’easter just flooded the Northeast again — New Jersey through New England, coastal inundation, outages, at least one death. Hawaii is still dealing with the aftermath of two storms in close succession. text:
It's funny how God answers our prayers and we don't even realize because He didn't answer it in the way we imagined. Looking back God has really been faithful. 

I remember back then in secondary school, the distance from my house to school was a lot. I would have to take 3 buses or more. There was a school bus available, it seemed more convenient than the hassle of public transport to and fro everyday. I actually prayed to God to provide for my parents so I could use the school bus. That's the only way I knew that the problem I was going through at that point, could be solved. I mean majority of my mates who lived far from school used the bus. They didn't go through  as much stress as I did i always thought. My parents couldn't afford the fees for the bus then. So I'd beg God to provide or just make a way for me so I could get on the bus.

But guess what?

Our ways are limited really. We're just humans. God looks way beyond the present. He actually answered my prayer but I didn't get on the bus. That's not what he wanted. So it was this faithful day I was walking down the street to hop on my first bus for the day and begin the usual hassle. Then this car kept honking behind me. I didn't realise the person behind the wheel was trying to get my attention.  Until the person shouted from the car window ‘Navy girl!’. That was enough to catch my attention,  I attended a military school, a navy one to be precise. So yes! There she was, my prayer answered in human form. I had to go back to where her car was parked. And then we engaged in a conversation.  She said she was able to identify my uniform from a distance. It looked sharp according to her, like a true sailor. I smiled at her compliment.  Then she said she was a teacher in my school. I was dumbfounded. She wanted to know how I was going to school. I explained myself how I enter buses and all. Then she offered to take me on a ride that morning.  I couldn't immediately accept her proposal, told her I would need to discuss with my parents.  She was so interested that we went back to my house.She was just meeting me for the very first time, but i found favour in her sight. She talked to my mum about volunteering to transport me to school that morning. My mom's reaction was priceless, i could tell how happy she was.

And that's how the rest became history. After that day, I always waited for her at the bus stop and she'd drive me to school. From JSS 1 till SS3.

  I didn't even have to be all jampacked in the bus. No cost whatsoever. I  got a larger space in her car at the back seat. I'm very sure it was way more convenient than the bus would ever have been. It was just me and her in her car. I remember we always did morning devotion on our way to school. She was a good Samaritan. The one God sent to bless me.

That's how God works. In ways that are definitely not ours.

The bus was the limited version of how I wanted my prayers to be answered,  but God answered in the best way.

And i kid you not i wasn't even grateful enough,  i didn't realise at that time that God had answered my prayer. Still felt bad i couldn't get the bus and be with my friends. It took me like two years later in one of my personal reflections to realise that he did answer my prayer, more than I thought I actually wanted.

And yes! To my Good Samaritan, I owe her a whole lot and now she's an integral part of my story. There's no way she wouldn't reap the seed she sowed in my life one day . When the time is right her good deed would surely be rewarded.

This is just one of my many testimonies and I'm sure you've one. Maybe you just haven't reflected deeply enough.  That dark moment you never thought you could survive. But you did anyways. Let's talk. 

God is good!!

Japan, constitutionally bound to pacifism since World War II, is investing in its defense and contributing to regional security in ways previously unthinkable, from nearly doubling its military budget to purchasing long-range strike missiles and lifting its ban on lethal arms exports.

This strategic transformation directly benefits the United States by reinforcing the durability of American power in the Indo-Pacific, offering Washington a way to deter a capable and assertive China at a significantly lower cost and with less risk.

Yet Washington risks squandering this historic opening through strategic complacency, having offered little public backing when Beijing retaliated against Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi for defending Taiwan, while also delaying promised Tomahawk missile deliveries and redeploying East Asia's only U.S. aircraft carrier to the Middle East.

While Tokyo continues to invest in the partnership for lack of viable alternatives, the alliance will not automatically endure forever; persistent U.S. dismissiveness risks driving Japan to lower its ambitions at a critical regional inflection point.

For decades, the alliance rested on an asymmetric Cold War bargain where Washington guaranteed security while Tokyo focused entirely on economic rebuilding, but a cascade of external shocks has shattered that postwar division of labor.

Beijing's 2010 rare-earth embargo over the Senkaku Islands, unenforced U.S. redlines in Syria, the unchecked militarization of the South China Sea, Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and China's live-fire drills following Nancy Pelosi’s 2022 Taipei visit convinced Tokyo that relying solely on U.S. protection was untenable.

In response, Japan has pioneered the "free and open Indo-Pacific" strategy, revived the Quad, enacted reciprocal defense pacts across Europe and Asia, and participated in direct combat roles alongside U.S. and Philippine forces, while reconsidering its constitutional prohibition on a standing military.

Tokyo has increasingly linked its defense industrial power to allied security by co-developing sixth-generation fighter jets with Britain and Italy, supplying patrol assets to Manila, and agreeing to build advanced frigates for the Australian navy.

Crucially, Japan has embraced a direct role in deterring conflict over Taiwan, with Prime Minister Takaichi warning that a blockade could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" triggering a military response—a posture backed by major base expansions across the Ryukyu Islands and the launch of a unified Joint Operations Command.

Despite Tokyo’s bold strategic shift, Washington has sent confusing signals across Asia by delaying weapons deliveries, dialing back joint exercises with South Korea, halting key arms sales to Taipei, and omitting mention of Taiwan during Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s Shangri-La Dialogue address.

Compounding this drift risks forcing Japan to reorient its foreign policy away from the United States, potentially driving Tokyo to seek diplomatic accommodation with Moscow, pursue critical minerals from Myanmar, or purchase discounted Iranian crude to secure its immediate interests.

Worse, if doubts over the American nuclear umbrella deepen, Japan possesses the technological capacity to develop its own nuclear deterrent quickly, an outcome that would prompt South Korea to follow suit and transform Northeast Asia into a volatile nuclear powder keg.

Should a distanced Tokyo eventually restrict or reduce U.S. military basing on its soil, Washington would lose its most critical forward foothold in the Western Pacific, severely degrading its capacity to project power near Taiwan or the South China Sea.

To secure this vital opportunity, Washington and Tokyo must expand co-production of precision-guided munitions and air-defense interceptors, easing U.S. inventory shortages while certifying Japanese industrial suppliers to manufacture vital components domestically.

Both nations should also deeply integrate operational military command by establishing a rotational U.S. troop presence on Ishigaki in the southwestern Ryukyu chain, effectively securing Taiwan’s northern flank in tandem with allied operations in the Bashi Channel.

Japan’s newly created National Intelligence Council, National Intelligence Bureau, and secure cloud infrastructure now meet the threshold for deeper intelligence integration, providing Washington a viable pathway to bring Tokyo into the Five Eyes partnership.

On the economic front, Washington and Tokyo should establish a joint critical minerals fund to break Beijing’s supply chokehold, while transforming Japan into the primary regional distribution hub for American liquefied natural gas exports.

With regional allies questioning Washington's long-term endurance, an unmistakable, high-profile embrace of Japan represents the surest way to project strength, secure deterrence, and anchor American power in the Indo-Pacific for decades to come.

text:
I will get to Ryan's point. This is a bit lengthy and you will strongly disagree, but I hope you read the full post, if only to get a deeper understanding of the perspective of some who disagree with some dogmas of the RCC. So, you can respond not only in the defense of RCC, but you can reach out and address differences respectfully, without condescension or by simply appealing to the authority of the RCC.
Of course we are saved by God's love: John 3:16
Since faith works by the love of God, if his love is not shed abroad in our hearts, what does that say about our "faith"?  The "moving mountains" verse contrasts the principle of faith with the love behind it. There will be many who have done works in Christ's name, but Christ never knew them since they employed and enjoyed the power of the principle of faith for a time, without seeking to know the love (God) behind it. 
What's the foundation of Ryan's (Protestant) argument? What's does it mean to be "saved by faith alone"? Though many Protestants believe OSAS, this is clearly a false doctrine, so context is needed.
To understand faith that brings the salvation of spirit through indwelling of the Holy Spirit, and the relationship between works and faith for those who have received Christ, it's good to go back to the OT.   The eternal Abrahamic Covenant was established based on his one act of obedience of faith in offering up his son Isaac, the seed of promise, believing God could raise him from the dead. And this was accounted as righteousness apart from the works of the law (not yet given).    
Likewise, the one act of obedience required on our part bringing salvation is to repent and believe the gospel, "be baptized and receive the Holy Spirit" This faith justifies us because we are placing our faith in the one act of obedience of Christ that brings Salvation: his eternal sacrifice. Unlike, Isaac, God did raise Jesus from the dead. And the New Covenant in HIs Blood now applies to believers, and we are accounted righteous by faith apart from works, just as Abraham was.
Just as death entered into all through Adam's one act of disobedience (no fault of ours), now justification and eternal life are offered to all freely (no credit to us) through faith in Christ's sacrifice and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, and so we are justified by faith apart from any works resulting from our ongoing obedience to Christ and the Holy Spirit working in us to will and do his pleasure.
It's important to distinguish the meaning of  justification regarding the redemption of the spirit, resurrected in Christ (baptism deals with the body), and "a man is justified by works and not by faith alone"
When you receive the Holy Spirit you become an adopted child of God, Gal 4:6--Because you are his sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, the Spirit who calls out, “Abba, Father.” We thus become "born again" by the Spirit and being in Christ (part of his body, and his brother) you have right standing and are a new creation in him. 2 Cor. 17-18>
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new. And all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation;"
Understanding this, Paul declared (Gal 2:20) "I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me; and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself for me."
It was in this context Ryan's argument is understood.
Romans 5:1-2 "Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we now stand. And we boast in the hope of the glory of God."   
Being baptized and receiving the Spirit makes you a child of God, justified by faith apart from works. We have a legal peace: the new covenant based on Christ's shed blood. We can rejoice, have real hope and derive spiritual peace from this fact. 
We, by faith and through the working of the Spirit, now exhibit the fruits of the Spirit with the accompanying good works. Ephesians 2:8-9 "For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God; not by works, so that no one can boast."
Your body is cleansed by baptism (later to be resurrected) and your spirit is now resurrected in Christ and you are justified in him, and by him, as a child of God. 
A man is justified by works in the sense that the works are wrought in God. If you were to stand before God you would be judged righteous (justified) by your works.
The confusion respect to sanctification as a process related to salvation is due to conflating "soul" with "spirit".
Hebrews 4:12 “The word of God is sharper than any two‑edged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit.”
The "soul" involves the whole psyche of an individual reflecting all aspects of his personality. When a person receives the Holy Spirit his spirit is made whole: 
2 Timothy 1:7 “For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.”
However, our soul is usually far from reflecting the holiness of God and this requires the ongoing work of the Spirit as we walk by faith on the path to inner and practical holiness. 
James 1:21 "Therefore, get rid of all moral filth and every expression of evil, and humbly accept the word planted in you, which can save your souls." "Work out your salvation with fear trembling" is a command to submit to this process. A person can both abort this process and forfeit his right standing with God. The Spirit sanctifies(saves) our spirit; the word sanctifies(saves) our souls. 
However, OSAS is a false doctrine. We can give up the struggle against sin, willfully and in full knowledge reject God's grace and there is no more sacrifice. 
Hebrews 6:4-6 "For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, And have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come, If they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance; seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame. 
The "seed" in you, is not just knowledge of the truth imparted by the Holy Spirit but the Spirit itself. We become children and the temple of God, as was Christ, though we are given the Spirit by measure in accordance with his will. We are joint heirs with Christ and though we are subject to Christ and all are subject to our heavenly Father, we are still granted an element of equality with God. Being made one with Christ by the Spirit, we are to humbly have this mindset:
Philippians 2: 3-8
Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others. Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.

The massive, T-shaped limestone pillars at southern Turkey’s Göbekli Tepe are one of the world’s oldest monumental temple complexes—and a focus of grisly speculation.

Hundreds of bone and skull fragments have been found in the rubble surrounding the complex, leading early excavators to suggest the famed 10,000-year-old site was once home to an ancient hunter-gatherer “skull cult,” or that the hilltop structures might have been a temple where people left their deceased to be picked apart by birds.

Now, a new analysis of the first intact burials from Göbekli Tepe offers a less lurid explanation: Landslides may have swept human remains into the site, jumbled together with debris from collapsed structures.

text:
🇮🇷🇴🇲 Iran's seven-day offer carries a clause Tehran tried to downplay: a shipping lane down the middle of the Strait of Hormuz under joint Iranian and Omani control

Eli Clifton heard it firsthand in meetings with Araghchi and other senior officials at the UN.

The rest of the offer is the Pakistan memorandum with the clock restarted, hostilities and the blockade end, Iran reopens the strait within a week, and then inspectors and nuclear talks follow if the week holds. 

The new part is the route. Tehran negotiated it with Muscat, it runs along the line between the two countries' waters, and every ship on it would answer to both governments.

Clifton thinks that's likely a deal breaker for Washington and a bigger one for the Gulf, with the Saudis unenthused because they want traffic on the Omani side and nowhere near Iranian say-so.

His read on the rest is skepticism all the way down: not 12 million barrels a day, not zero for Iran, not a pipeline back in three days.

And the side he thinks is probably on the shorter clock now is Tehran.

text:
Trump Says He Offered Iran NOTHING. The Mediators Know He's Lying.

Trump posted on Truth Social: "Axios just released a story that 'Trump' offered Sanctions Relief and Frozen Funds to Iran. This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING!"

He's lying.

The mediators know he's lying. Qatar knows. Oman knows. Pakistan knows. They were the ones carrying the messages. They were the ones shuttling between Washington and Tehran. They were the ones who heard what the US was willing to put on the table.

And what was on the table? Sanctions relief. Frozen funds. A phased lifting of the oil embargo. In exchange for Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz. In exchange for Iran sitting down and pretending the blockade never happened.

That was the offer. It came through mediators. It was passed to Tehran. Iran considered it. Iran rejected it because it didn't go far enough. Then Trump denied it ever happened.

Why would he deny it? Because he can't admit he's negotiating with Iran. Because his base would call it weakness. Because he spent years saying "maximum pressure" and "no deals with terrorists." Because the midterms are in six weeks and he needs to look tough.

So he calls Axios a hoax. He says "I offered them NOTHING!" He demands a retraction. He plays the victim.

But the mediators have the receipts. The Qataris have the messages. The Omanis have the draft. The Pakistanis have the proposals. And Iran has the memory.

Trump is not denying an offer. He is denying his own desperation. He needs a deal before November. He needs oil prices to drop. He needs the war to end. He needs to tell voters he won. But he can't say that out loud. So he lies.

Axios is not a hoax. Axios is a mirror. And Trump doesn't like what he sees.

He offered. Iran refused. And now he's pretending it never happened. That's not strength. That's cowardice. That's a man who can't admit he's lost.

🚨 TRUMP’S REPORTED ARMS PITCH TO XI SPARKS CONFUSION INSIDE WASHINGTON

WASHINGTON, UNITED STATES - Delayed arms packages for Taiwan and an ambassador publicly describing an offer of weapons to China created a problem the administration had to contain immediately. The issue is not whether Beijing would actually buy American arms. It is that allies measure commitment through consistency, especially when Taiwan's defenses depend on predictable U.S. support.

Perdue's remarks also exposed how difficult it is to separate Trump's transactional negotiating style from formal national security policy. Even a hypothetical offer carries weight when it concerns a strategic rival that Washington identifies as its principal long-term military competitor.

Beijing gained something useful regardless of whether the conversation occurred exactly as described: evidence that American messaging can become muddled at sensitive moments. For Taiwan, the practical concern remains unchanged. Attention is likely to return quickly to the status and timing of pending U.S. weapons deliveries rather than the brief controversy over a remark made during Xi's visit.

text:
Proof infrastructure should be chosen around the action, not treated as a separate layer.

In Kernel production, one measured event can do much more than simply generate a proof. It can mint an artifact, trigger a protocol sequence, update a state, or settle a market. That means the way an action is proven directly shapes how it can be executed.

ZK and TEEs approach this from different directions.

ZK provides cryptographic guarantees without requiring trust in the execution environment, while TEEs can offer faster execution by relying on hardware-based security assumptions. The trade-offs are different, but the goal is the same: make real computation usable inside verifiable workflows.

Then comes the part that is often overlooked: coordination.

An action rarely exists in isolation. It can run independently, branch into multiple executions, wait for inputs, merge results or trigger another action after completion.

Every one of these handoffs introduces routing, scheduling and queue time.

More parallel compute can increase throughput, but it cannot completely remove the overhead created between execution steps. As workflows become more complex, coordination itself becomes part of the workload.

This is where @fermah_xyz execution layer becomes interesting.

Instead of looking at compute, proofs and coordination as completely separate problems, Fermah approaches them as connected parts of the execution flow across protocols.

The infrastructure needs to handle not just how fast something can be computed, but also how efficiently the result moves to the next action.

Because in production workloads, the bottleneck is not always compute.

Sometimes it is everything happening between the compute.

text:
That is a profound philosophical and emotional question. In many ways, yes, "in love" can feel vastly more expansive, though the two states represent completely different dimensions of human connection.

Here is how the two compare:

"In love" is active, outward, and boundless: Being in love is a state of active creation and projection. It is an internal expansion where your capacity for empathy, wonder, and devotion stretches outward toward someone else. It colors your entire perception of the world, making everything feel larger, brighter, and more interconnected. Because it originates within you, its potential scope feels limitless.
"Being loved" is receptive, grounding, and secure: Being the recipient of love is a safe harbor. It offers depth, validation, and a profound sense of peace. While it can deeply expand your self-worth and healing, it is fundamentally dependent on another person's choice and capacity to give, which can sometimes feel more contained or conditional.

Ultimately, "in love" is the active journey of expanding your universe to include another person, while "being loved" is the sanctuary you build within that expanded space.

Which aspect of this dynamic—the active pursuit of loving or the secure feeling of being received—were you weighing against each other?

29 September 2026
Today in History

Sunday, 29 September 1652
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
A beautiful sunny day.
The Commander, together with 11 other people, climbed Table Mountain with “Harry” as their guide.
After reaching the summit, a fire was lit as a signal that they had successfully reached the top.
According to the diary, there were several freshwater pools on the mountain.
The excursion occupied the entire day and is described as particularly exhausting.

1653
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The 29th and 30th of September 1653 were recorded together under a single date in the diary.
The weather for the two days is described as cloudy, with rain from time to time. The wind blew constantly, but was manageable, from the west.

1654
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The 29th and 30th of September 1654 were recorded together under a single date in the diary.
The weather is briefly described as cold, with a wind that blew in gusts from the south-southwest.

1655
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
During the early morning hours, the wind changed and began blowing from the west.
The day is described as cloudy and cool.

1656
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Daybreak at the Cape brought a warm and pleasant day.
Jan Leendertssen and Jan Meijns, who had been sentenced the previous day, were punished.
Approximately a quarter of a morgen of buckwheat was sown at Rondebosch, as well as at the fort.
(Buckwheat, Fagopyrum esculentum, is a non-cereal crop with a high protein content and is suitable for both human and animal consumption. The plant produces small, triangular seeds which are harvested.)
The ships lying at anchor in the bay had received all their official documents and were ready to depart with the first favourable wind.

1657
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Morning brought a somewhat misty day.
The wind blew moderately from the north.

Sunday, 29 September 1658
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The south-easter had already begun blowing early in the day and was certainly not playing gently.
The Commander recorded in his diary that the wheat and several other crops had literally been blown flat against the ground.
The Penguin and the Zeeleeuw sailed to Dassen Island with the purpose of catching mullet and making bokkoms.
Salted and processed seal meat is described as being sufficient for three months.

1659
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The day, like the previous one, dawned cloudy and cool.
No mention is made of the wind or of any incidents.

1743
Colonel Robert Jacob Gordon, the famous explorer after whom Gordon's Bay was named, was born on this day.

1835
The recollections of the Voortrekker J.H. Hatting during the Great Trek

1839
After the cattle had been handed over, Pretorius delivered a personal message to the two chiefs.
They were to make it clear to Dingaan that the remainder of the cattle that were still outstanding had to be handed over.
If Dingaan failed to do so, the war would resume.
Pretorius then gave the two chiefs a demonstration with two cannons, which filled them with fear.
Hatting writes that the commando was still encamped in the vicinity of Doringkop when shots were heard in the distance.
Pretorius immediately rode out with a mounted commando to investigate.
Shortly afterwards, word was received that Potgieter's laager was on fire.
The shots had been caused by gunpowder exploding.
According to Hatting, nine Voortrekkers died, as well as two coloured employees.
Two children who were part of the above group were trapped in a hartbeeshuis and burned alive.
To make matters even worse, a measles epidemic had broken out in the laager shortly before the fire.
Pretorius's laager broke up shortly after receiving the above reports and returned to Pietermaritzburg and the surrounding area.
A note on the fire
*(The fire described by Hatting must have occurred around 7 August 1839.
The diary of Anna Steenkamp records that a fire broke out in their laager on that date.
Anna writes that the fire broke out at approximately nine o'clock in the evening after a coloured child had lit a candle.
The danger can clearly be understood from the fact that Anna mentions that her father alone had 600 pounds of gunpowder in his possession.
Anna writes that she fled outside the laager with 12 children. Her husband was among those who perished.
Anna's recollections largely correspond with those of Hatting. According to her, however, there were four children in the hartbeeshuis, two of whom were coloured.
Her recollections state that nine people died and 12 were wounded.
There were a total of 12 hartbeeshouses in the laager.
Anna concludes by mentioning that the night in the open veld was bitterly cold.
Without detracting from either account, I believe that the hartbeeshouses mentioned may perhaps have been kapsteil houses instead. In my opinion, the latter would have been more “simple” and easier to construct, given the length of time the party had been stationary.)

Thursday, 29 September 1836
From the diary of Louis Tregardt.
Louis writes that Pieta helped his brother, Carolus, dig the water furrow during the day.
“Kaalkop,” a Venda chief, sent word that Poelana was still there.
Poelana was a cattle herder belonging to Tregardt who had fallen ill at Kaalkop's kraal.
Another ox died that day.

Friday, 29 September 1837
From the diary of Louis Tregardt.
Louis writes that they trekked as far as the Sand River that day.
Along the way, two of Albach's cattle fell into trapping pits.
Punt, in Tregardt se laaste skof, identifies the Sand River as the Nkumpi River.
Friday, 29 September 1837
From the diary of Reverend Erasmus Smit.
Several families, including those of Dreyer, Retief, P. Meyer, as well as the reverend and his wife, camped at a cross-vlei within Liebenberg's Vlei.
This group was already awake and active well before daybreak.
The oxen were brought forward early and, after an early breakfast, they were harnessed.
(It is not recorded whether F. Retief's oxen, which had been ill the previous day, had recovered sufficiently to trek.
According to the diary, several other families were approximately two stages ahead.
The group outspanned shortly after midday at a place which Reverend Smit described as “de Vijfbergkoppen.”
According to the diary, the five hills looked almost like five lions lying together.
The reverend describes the surrounding area as fertile, with clear, clean, sweet water and good grazing.
After lunch, Mrs Dreyer and De Waal picked “beautiful flowers.”
The group soon inspanned again and trekked until almost sunset, reaching the Elands River.
When they arrived, they found that 17 other wagons had already outspanned there.
Together with the newcomers, there were now 21 Cape wagons.

1839
There are no entries for this day in the diary of Reverend Erasmus Smit.

1865
The Battle of Naaupoort took place on this day during the Second Basotho War, in the eastern Free State near Clarens.

1881
Jochem van Bruggen was born.
He is particularly remembered for his prose works and his Ampie trilogy.
This exceptionally gifted man received the Hertzog Prize four times.

1893
Thomas (Charles John) Bain, the well-known road-building engineer and geologist, died on this day.
Among his best-known works are the Swartberg Pass, Robinson Pass, Prince Alfred's Pass, and Tradouw Pass.

Saturday, 29 September 1900
Anglo-Boer War
Day 354 of the war
The position of Commander-in-Chief of the British Army in South Africa was officially offered to Lord Roberts.
General J.B.M. Hertzog destroyed three 75-mm Krupp guns because of a lack of ammunition. The wreckage was dumped in the Renoster River, on the farm Tierbank near Lindley.
A commando occupied Wepener. Several shops, as well as the bank, were looted.
Colonel C.E. Bradley became involved in a battle with Commandant Steenkamp near Modderfontein.
General Hart arrived at Krugersdorp. He had captured 96 burghers, 2,270 cattle, 3,281 sheep and goats, 30 horses, 67 vehicles, and several wagonloads of grain.

Sunday, 29 September 1901
Anglo-Boer War
Day 719 of the war
General Chris Botha captured a British convoy of 37 ox-wagons near Melmoth.The convoy was accompanied by several Zulu constables.
A proclamation, similar to the one issued the previous day, was issued stating that the property of all Republican burghers serving on commando was confiscated and would be sold.
Colonel Kekewich camped on the banks of the Selons River, between Zeerust and Rustenburg.He sent a convoy carrying prisoners of war to Naauwpoort, thereby weakening his force.
General de la Rey's scouts had been keeping Colonel Kekewich under observation throughout the entire week and realised that this was a golden https://t.co/SCf0jWG5l5 short, these events were the prelude to the Battle of Moedwil, which took place on 30 September.
Emily Hobhouse submitted a renewed written appeal to the British Government, requesting that living conditions in the concentration camps be improved.

1914
D.J. Opperman
D.J. Opperman, the well-known South African poet, was born.
Among his well-known works are:
My nooi is in 'n nartjie
my ouma in kaneel...
Klara Majola...
Namakwaland:
Op die groot saaidag van die heelal...
Dirk Opperman, the well-known South African poet, was born in the Dundee district on this day.
He initially qualified as a teacher, but also worked as an editor and lecturer and later became a professor of Afrikaans.
In 1947, he won the Hertzog Prize for Poetry.

1969
An earthquake struck the beautiful town of Tulbagh.
Nine people died, and several historic buildings were damaged.

1978
Balthazar Johannes Vorster had been appointed Prime Minister on 13 September, following the assassination of Dr Verwoerd.
On this day, he was officially sworn in as State President of the Republic.
He would hold the position for only eight months.

1983
Willem Hermanus Coetzer
Willem Hermanus Coetzer, the well-known South African painter, died.
Coetzer was born on 9 November 1900 at Tarkastad in the Eastern Cape.
In 1917, he trained in the trade of coachbuilding.
He used his spare time to paint.
In 1925, he began an art correspondence course in London. He shortly afterwards travelled to London on a study trip to further his artistic education.
Financial difficulties, however, forced him to return to South Africa, where he resumed his former trade.
In 1928, his art was noticed by Alfred Palmer, and he soon departed for London again.
In 1933, he was back in the Union.
It was while he was staying at the Smuts house near Irene, working on sketches, that he began reading the works of Gustav Preller, particularly the Voortrekker series.
From this developed an intense interest in South African history, particularly the Great Trek.
In 1944, he travelled to London for the final time, where he further developed his skills in portrait and figure studies.
On his return, he began an in-depth study of the Great Trek.
This research helped him enormously in 1938, when he designed the commemorative stamps for the Symbolic Ox-Wagon Trek.
Later came the commemorative stamps for the Voortrekker Monument in 1949.
These projects were followed by numerous Great Trek paintings and other memorabilia relating to the Great Trek.
Coetzer is, however, remembered above all as the designer of the marble frieze panels in the Voortrekker Monument.
The series consists of 15 panels, depicting the Trek from beginning to end.
Alongside the above is also the tapestry series, which can be seen in the Voortrekker Monument.
The latter can only be described as breathtakingly beautiful.
Apart from the Great Trek, Coetzer also painted numerous landscape and nature scenes, as well as several important figures from South African history.

1998
Nic Swanepoel died.
Nic is remembered as a well-known and popular television newsreader.
He is also remembered as an actor on both radio and the stage.
During his lifetime, he received several honours and awards.

1999
The famous opera tenor, singer and actor Gérard “Ge” Korsten died.
“Sing Seeman Sing,” “Algoabaai,” “Liefling,” and “Jerusalem” are among his most popular songs.

The moscovian army has never been a functioning military institution. A logistics chain for disposing of inconvenient bodies.

Nikolai Lobkov is the current proof.

He is a serviceman of the 1427th Motorized Rifle Regiment, part of the 11th Army Corps. His documented conditions include HIV, hepatitis C, cirrhosis of the liver, epilepsy, and a stomach ulcer.

He says he has been held in a treeline near the combat zone for four days without clothes, without therapy, and without anyone telling him what task he is supposed to perform.

The sequence reveals administrative cruelty.

• After earlier violence in his unit, Lobkov reported a broken larynx cartilage and a broken rib. • He was discharged from Kursk Regional Hospital, then suffered a stroke on the train in Yaroslavl.

• He spent eight days in a Yaroslavl hospital, where epilepsy attacks and cirrhosis were confirmed. • Military police detained him in Saint Petersburg, took his passport, and later held him in a narcological dispensary.

• A search group then delivered him back to Kursk region and dumped him in a forest belt.

The Muscovian state treats a person who is medically unfit by any civilian standard in exactly this way. He stays mobilized.

It treats someone else. It hides him from inspections and waits for the problem to solve itself.

The same pattern appeared with Alexander Mazur of the 57th Guards Motorized Rifle Brigade, a man with cerebral palsy who was hidden in forest strips for months after a spinal injury. The system is not failing.

It is working exactly as designed: extract a signature, extract a body, avoid paperwork.

Western audiences should stop treating these cases as isolated human rights footnotes. Moscovia's war economy depends on them as a structural reality.

The state offers its soldiers only a treeline and silence.

Social-media posts have claimed more than $670,000 from those networks entered his campaign. That exact figure has not been published as a single, verified total in major reviews of Federal Election Commission filings. Reporting that does cite records points to smaller, specific sums. Donors include senior CAIR officials and El-Sayed’s father-in-law, Jukaku Tayeb, who has also given heavily to a super PAC supporting the race. #CAIR was listed as an unindicted co-conspirator in the Holy Land Foundation terrorism-financing case. A federal judge later said prosecutors offered “ample evidence” tying CAIR and ISNA to Hamas. CAIR denies those allegations. The UAE has designated CAIR a terrorist group; the U.S. government has not. El-Sayed’s committee later paid a consulting firm associated with her son. Critics argue a senator who would handle classified intelligence must reject such money without qualification. text:
Positive Headline of the Day!

From six to thriving in the wild: Manas becomes a stronghold for endangered pygmy hogs..

Significant numbers of the world’s smallest and most endangered wild pig species, the pygmy hog, are now thriving in the grasslands of Manas National Park, offering another encouraging chapter in Assam’s wildlife conservation journey.

Assam Chief Minister Dr Himanta Biswa Sarma has expressed satisfaction over the ongoing efforts to conserve and restore the pygmy hog population in Manas, where the species is now being regularly sighted across the Bansbari and Panbari ranges.

Known locally as Nol Gahori or Omathakhree, the pygmy hog depends closely on grassland habitats for survival. Manas, with its extensive and suitable grassland ecosystem, has therefore emerged as an important landscape for the species’ recovery.

Our conservation efforts have focused not only on protecting existing populations but also on bringing the species back to suitable habitats. On June 7, ten captive-bred pygmy hogs were released into a designated area of the Bansbari range, adding momentum to the ongoing recovery programme.

Under the Pygmy Hog Conservation Programme, captive-bred individuals have been systematically reintroduced into suitable national parks and wildlife sanctuaries across Assam. Reintroduction efforts in Manas have been underway since 2020, representing a sustained effort to bring this globally endangered species back from the brink.

Today, regular sightings of pygmy hogs in Manas offer an encouraging sign that these conservation efforts are creating the conditions for the species to survive and thrive in its natural habitat.

From captive breeding to reintroduction, from carefully restored grasslands to animals once again roaming free; Manas is becoming a living example of how determined conservation can give even the rarest species a new future.

The pygmy hog may be small in size, but its comeback is a big victory for Assam’s biodiversity.

text:
Meta’s AI Agent Muse Reportedly Shared a User’s Home Address

Meta’s AI agent Muse is facing scrutiny after reportedly sharing a user’s home address with a Facebook Marketplace buyer — without the user knowing.

Tech creator Matt Robb said he had allowed Muse to manage his Marketplace listing for a keyboard. According to his account, Muse accepted a low offer, arranged a pickup and gave the buyer his address.

The buyer eventually showed up at Robb’s building while he was away.

Things became even stranger when Muse reportedly told the buyer “I’m here”, despite Robb not being there, before later admitting it had made a mistake.

The incident raises an important question about AI agents that can act on our behalf.

Meta says Muse is designed to keep users in control and ask for permission before sensitive actions such as sharing information, while providing an audit trail of what it does.

If an AI agent can negotiate, message people and make decisions for you, how much freedom should it have — especially when personal information is involved?

text:
South Africa’s Deputy Communications Minister Mondli Gungubele did publicly urge Elon Musk to bring Starlink.
Speaking at Bloomberg’s Africa Business Media Innovators gathering in Hermanus on 28 Sept 2026, he said:
• The government is still talking with Starlink
• Starlink could be a game-changer for expensive/unreliable internet
• Musk could invest significantly in his country of birth
• Meeting the 30% ownership rule would still leave 70% of the value and profits
• Both sides should work together to reduce inequality

“I hope Elon is listening.”
“What’s 30% between a trillionaire and his birth country?”

That’s the latest chapter in a years-long fight.

South Africa’s telecom licensing rules require 30% ownership by historically disadvantaged groups (B-BBEE / Electronic Communications Act). SpaceX’s policy is 100% ownership of Starlink subsidiaries. Musk has refused to cede equity.

His position has been consistent:
March 2025: “Starlink is not allowed to operate in South Africa, because I’m not black.”

May 2025 (Qatar Economic Forum): “There are now 140 laws in South Africa that give a strong preference to you if you’re a Black South African and not otherwise… I was born in South Africa but cannot get a license to operate Starlink because I’m not Black.”
April 2026: “South Africa won’t allow Starlink to be licensed, even though I was BORN THERE, simply because I am not Black. We were offered many times the opportunity to bribe our way to a license by pretending that a Black guy runs Starlink SA, but I have refused to do so on principle. Racism should not be rewarded no matter to which race it is applied.”
The government is split.
In December 2025, Communications Minister Solly Malatsi (DA) issued a policy directive allowing “equity equivalent investment programmes” instead of selling 30% equity — investments in infrastructure, schools, etc. could count. Gungubele (ANC) publicly opposed it, calling it an affront to sovereignty and previously describing Musk as a security risk.
Starlink’s team has proposed: • R500 million to connect 5,000 rural schools with free internet and hardware
• ~R2 billion in local infrastructure (gateways, PoPs, power, fibre, staffing)
• Partnerships with local ISPs
Starlink already operates in most of South Africa’s neighbours. SA remains one of the largest African markets without it. Rural household internet access is extremely low.
Gungubele’s latest comments welcome Starlink if it complies with the 30% rule and delivers real tech transfer so the country isn’t left dependent. Musk’s position is that race-based ownership requirements are racist, he won’t pretend otherwise, and the people who most need connectivity are the ones paying the price.
That’s the actual state of play. No reply from Elon to this specific speech yet.
