There is a part hiding inside your microwave oven that was never meant to be understood, only to be obeyed.

Engineers call it a transformer. Scrap dealers call it free money. Anyone who has ever put a meter on the right wire calls it something they can't repeat in public.

Here is the secret: it doesn't matter how many volts it makes. What matters is what happens when you stop asking for volts and start demanding amps.

Because volts are the thing that scare you.

Amps are the thing that melt steel.

This is a long one. Do not skim it. By the last line you will never look at a wall socket, a phone charger, a power line, or a car battery the same way again.

And then you'll scroll back up and watch that video a second time with completely different eyes.

Let's go.

1. THE BIGGEST LIE YOU WERE TOLD ABOUT ELECTRICITY

Somewhere around age eight, someone taught you that voltage is the dangerous one.

Yellow signs. A skull. A lightning bolt. "DANGER: 10,000 VOLTS."

Nobody has ever hung a sign that says "DANGER: 10,000 AMPS." And that is strange, because volts do not do the work.

Volts are pressure. Volts are potential. Volts are a promise.

Amps are delivery.

Volts are the size of the loan. Amps are how much money actually changes hands.

A doorknob spark on a dry winter day can be several thousand volts, sometimes more than ten thousand. It has never destroyed anything but your mood, because almost no charge moves. The promise was huge and the delivery was a rounding error.

Now flip it.

A car battery is a humble 12 volts. Touch both terminals with your fingers and you will feel nothing at all. Lay a steel wrench across them and that wrench can turn red, weld itself to the post, and throw molten droplets across the garage. Same battery. Same 12 volts. Wildly different ending.

Voltage decides whether current can get through something. Current decides what it does to that thing on the way.

Read that twice. Almost every electrical myth you believe dies right there.

2. THE ONE EQUATION THAT RUNS THE PHYSICAL WORLD

If you only remember one line from this entire post, make it this one:

Heat equals current squared, times resistance.

Engineers write it as P = I^2 x R. Say it out loud: I squared R.

Not current times resistance. Current SQUARED.

That little exponent is the most important exponent in electrical engineering, and it is a trap for human intuition, because we think in straight lines and nature does not.

Take a scrap of conductor with a resistance of just one milliohm. One thousandth of an ohm. Basically nothing. A stub of thick wire, a slightly loose clamp, a smudge of oxide on a joint.

At 10 amps it dissipates one tenth of a watt. You can't feel it.

At 100 amps it dissipates 10 watts. Warm to the touch, like a phone left in the sun.

At 1,000 amps it dissipates 1,000 watts. That is a kitchen space heater, concentrated in a spot the size of your thumb.

At 10,000 amps it dissipates 100,000 watts. One hundred kilowatts. The output of a small industrial furnace, crammed into a piece of metal you could hide in a fist.

The resistance never changed. The material never changed. The only thing that changed was the current, and the heat went up not ten times per step, but one hundred times.

Ten times the current. One hundred times the fire.

That is why a wire that carries a hair dryer is boring, and the same wire carrying a thousand times more is a blowtorch with no fuel.

Nothing here needs fuel. Electricity is simply refusing to squeeze through a narrow place quietly.

And if you think that's dramatic, wait until you see how high the numbers actually go.

3. THE AMP LADDER (EVERY RUNG IS WORSE THAN THE LAST)

Let's climb. Hold on to something.

RUNG 1: 0.001 amps (one milliamp)
You can just barely feel it. A faint tingle. Your nervous system files it under "weird."

RUNG 2: 0.01 amps (ten milliamps)
The muscles in your hand can clamp shut around the source. You do not decide to let go. Your arm has stopped taking orders. This is why the scariest thing about small currents is not the pain. It is the loss of a vote.

RUNG 3: 0.1 amps (a tenth of an amp)
Across the chest, for long enough, this is in the range where a heart loses its rhythm. One tenth of one amp. About the current of a small 12 watt bulb. Your entire life is sitting on a margin that thin.

RUNG 4: 15 amps
The breaker in your wall. A kettle, a toaster, a hair dryer all live here. On a 120 volt circuit that is 1,800 watts, enough to boil a liter of water in about three minutes. It is also the ceiling of what your house wiring will tolerate for long before it starts complaining with heat.

RUNG 5: 300 amps
Your car starter motor, cranking a cold engine. Your whole life you have turned a key and asked a small metal cylinder for more current than the main breaker of many homes is even rated to pass. You did it half asleep, holding coffee.

RUNG 6: 10,000 amps
Welcome to the industrial world. Resistance spot welding, the technique that fuses the thin steel panels of a car body, pushes thousands to tens of thousands of amps through a contact patch for a fraction of a second. A modern car carries thousands of those welds. Each one was a tiny, controlled, deliberate lightning strike.

RUNG 7: 11,850 amps
The nominal current in the superconducting magnets that steer protons around the Large Hadron Collider, held at 1.9 kelvin. That is colder than deep space. Not a coincidence. We will come back to that.

RUNG 8: 30,000 amps
A typical lightning stroke. The strong ones climb past 200,000. The air along the channel briefly reaches roughly 30,000 kelvin, about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun, and the thunder you hear is the air itself being blown outward faster than the speed of sound.

RUNG 9: 100,000 amps
The electrodes of an electric arc furnace, the machine that recycles scrap steel by lighting an arc between graphite rods as thick as a barrel and the metal itself. The arc runs at temperatures far above the melting point of anything it touches. Steel does not resist. It just becomes a liquid you can pour.

RUNG 10: 500,000 amps
A single cell in a modern aluminum smelter, running around the clock at just four or five volts. Four volts. Less than a laptop charger, at a current that adds up to roughly two megawatts per cell. Rows of these cells form a line up to about a kilometer long, and it never turns off, because switching it off can freeze the metal inside and wreck the whole plant.

RUNG 11: about 1,000,000 amps
The electromagnetic railgun, an experimental weapon that uses a pulse of current on the order of a million amps to accelerate a projectile to several times the speed of sound with no gunpowder at all. The forces involved are so violent that the rails themselves get eroded by the very thing that launches the shell.

RUNG 12: 26,000,000 amps
The Z Machine at Sandia National Laboratories in New Mexico. For roughly a hundred billionths of a second, it slams tens of millions of amps into a target the size of a spool of thread. Metal wires do not melt. They turn into plasma and get crushed by their own magnetic field. Researchers there have reported temperatures in the billions of degrees.

Look at the pattern on that ladder.

On the working rungs, volts barely move. A smelter cell runs on less voltage than a laptop charger. A spot welder runs on a handful of volts. A car starter runs on twelve.

The headline number, every single time, is the amps.

That should bother you. It bothers everyone who realizes it. Because the natural next question is:

How do you even make that much current from a wall socket?

Keep reading. The answer is an idea so simple it will feel like cheating.

4. THE ONLY HONEST TRICK IN ELECTRICAL ENGINEERING

Energy cannot be created. Everyone agrees on that. It is the one rule the universe never bends.

But energy can be traded. And the cleanest trade ever invented is two coils of wire wrapped around a lump of iron.

That is a transformer. It has no moving parts. No software. No fuel. It just sits there humming, and it does something that sounds illegal.

It trades pressure for flow.

Power is volts times amps. Put 120 volts and 10 amps into one side and you are feeding it 1,200 watts. A good transformer hands almost all of that back out the other side, but you choose the shape of it.

Step the voltage up by ten, and the current drops by ten.

Step the voltage down by ten, and the current rises by ten.

Step it down by a hundred, and 10 amps becomes, in an ideal world, 1,000 amps.

The rule is stunningly simple. The ratio of the voltages is the ratio of the turns of wire. The ratio of the currents is the exact opposite. That's it. That is the whole law.

A transformer is a gearbox for electricity. Low gear gives you brute force. High gear gives you speed and reach. You never get free power out of it. You only get to decide what kind of power you receive.

And here is the part almost nobody says out loud:

Big power hides in small voltages just as easily as it hides in big ones. It is the same watts wearing a different outfit.

The appliance that heats your lunch has to make thousands of volts, because that is what its tube demands. But the iron inside it does not care which direction you shift the gears. It was built to climb. Ask it to descend, and the same slab that produced a whisper of current at four figures of volts will hand you a shout of current at almost no volts at all.

That is the loophole. That is why a scrap part from a dumpster is, physically, a cousin of the machines on the ladder above.

Which brings us to the strangest fact in this whole post.

5. WHY ONE VOLT CAN BE MORE DANGEROUS THAN A THOUSAND

You cannot shock yourself on a couple of volts. Your skin's resistance is far too high. The pressure isn't there to push a meaningful current through you.

So the low-voltage, high-current world feels safe in the way a sleeping dog feels safe.

It is not a shock hazard. It is a heat hazard. And heat is indifferent to whether you feel a tingle.

Every mechanic, jeweler, and electrician has heard the same warning: take off your ring. A metal ring that bridges a battery or a heavy bus bar can heat up in seconds. There are real injuries, some terrible, from people who touched a "harmless" 12 volts with one careless piece of jewelry.

Your senses were tuned by evolution to fear the tall thing, the loud thing, the thing that crackles. The quiet thing that just makes metal glow slipped through the filter.

This is why the most respected experts in this world never eyeball anything. They measure. They measure current. They measure temperature. They measure everything, because their instincts have taught them that instinct is exactly the wrong tool here.

The louder the display, the more important it is to remember what you are actually looking at.

6. HEAT LIVES WHERE RESISTANCE LIVES

Here is a riddle that gets more interesting the longer you stare at it.

An incandescent light bulb is plugged into the wall by a cord. The exact same current flows through the cord and through the filament. The cord stays cool. The filament reaches roughly 2,700 degrees Celsius.

Same current. Wildly different outcomes.

The difference is resistance. The current is the same everywhere in a simple loop, but the heat is made only where the path is narrow, thin, dirty, or loose.

So the rule is:

Current is the force. Resistance is the location.

Put a thousand amps through a fat copper bar and nothing much happens. Put the same thousand amps through a spot where two pieces of metal barely touch, and that tiny contact patch turns into the hottest place in the room.

This is not only how welders work. It is how electrical fires start in houses. A slightly loose screw on a terminal. A corroded contact. A plug that isn't fully seated. Nothing dramatic. Just a little extra resistance, doing its I squared R in the dark, for months.

It is why the modern fast chargers for electric cars use heavy cables with liquid coolant running through them. Push several hundred amps through a plug for twenty minutes and copper needs to be cooled or it will cook itself. The newest megawatt chargers for electric trucks target currents up to about 3,000 amps.

Every high-current engineer has the same obsession: find the narrowest point in the loop, because that is where the energy will go to die.

Hold that thought. It applies to more than wires.

7. THE WAR THAT WAS DECIDED BY AN EXPONENT

In the 1880s, the world argued about how to deliver electricity to cities. One camp backed direct current. The other backed alternating current. The public version of the story is a feud between famous men.

The real version is a spreadsheet.

Wires waste energy as heat. That waste is I squared R. To send power a long way, you have two options: use fat, expensive wires, or cut the current.

You cut the current by raising the voltage. Send the same power at 100 times the voltage and the current falls to one hundredth. Because loss scales with the square, the waste falls to one ten-thousandth.

One hundred times the voltage. Ten thousand times less loss.

But in the 1880s there was no easy way to change the voltage of direct current. Alternating current had a superpower: the transformer. Hungarian engineers at the Ganz works showed a practical closed-core design in 1885, and William Stanley built one of the first commercial systems in Massachusetts in 1886.

The transformer decided the winner. Not charisma. Not marketing. A lump of iron and two coils.

Today the biggest lines on Earth run at 765,000 volts and beyond, so that a few hundred amps can move a colossal amount of power across a continent. China operates a line at plus and minus 1,100,000 volts that spans more than 3,000 kilometers and moves on the order of 12 gigawatts.

And at the end of that journey, a substation steps the voltage back down, and the current climbs back up, and it flows into your house at a level that will not cook the walls.

The entire electrical grid is one long argument between volts and amps, refereed by transformers.

The same object that keeps a city lit for a century can, in a very different form, produce a current that vaporizes metal.

That is not a contradiction. That is the same law, run in the other direction.

8. WHEN RESISTANCE DISAPPEARS

Now for the wildest twist in the entire story.

If heat is I squared R, then what happens when R goes to zero?

In 1911, the physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes cooled mercury to about 4 kelvin and watched its electrical resistance vanish. Not shrink. Vanish. He had discovered superconductivity.

With no resistance, there is no I squared R. With no I squared R, there is no heat. And with no heat, you can push absurd currents through a wire, forever.

That is the trick behind the magnets in an MRI machine and in the Large Hadron Collider. Currents of hundreds to thousands of amps, with no meaningful loss, in cables cooled to temperatures colder than the void between galaxies.

Physicists have set current flowing in a closed superconducting loop and then watched it for years without measuring any decay. Their calculations put the lifetime of that current at more than 100,000 years.

A current that outlives every civilization that has ever measured it.

So the story of amps is a story with two poles.

At one end, a normal metal, where current meets resistance and turns into fire.

At the other, a superconductor, where current meets nothing and stays alive indefinitely.

Everything else, every wire, every appliance, every motor, every power plant, lives in between, negotiating.

9. YOUR ENTIRE ROOM WAS ELECTROCUTED INTO EXISTENCE

Look around you.

The aluminum in your phone, your window frames, your soda can: made by pushing enormous direct currents through molten salts. Producing a single kilogram takes on the order of 13 to 15 kilowatt-hours. Across the world, aluminum production consumes roughly three percent of all the electricity generated on the planet.

The steel in the nearest building: a large share of it was melted by an arc furnace.

The copper in the walls: refined by electrolysis, one electrode at a time.

The chlorine that keeps water safe to drink: made by passing current through brine.

Modern civilization is not only powered by electricity. It is manufactured by it.

And the entire stack rests on one number nobody puts on a warning sign.

Not volts.

Amps.

And here is a number to make it land.

An average lightning stroke carries around 30,000 amps and lasts a few millionths of a second. One cell in an aluminum smelter carries roughly sixteen times that, quietly, without a pause, for years. The sky does it once and makes headlines. A factory does it every second of every day and nobody notices.

The most extreme currents on Earth are not in storms. They are in buildings you drive past on the highway.

10. WHAT HAPPENS WHEN YOU KEEP PUSHING

There is a phenomenon so old that people discovered it before they understood it.

In 1774, the English experimenter Edward Nairne discharged a battery of Leyden jars through a thin wire and watched the wire vanish. Not glow. Not soften. Vanish, in a flash of light and a small bang.

Physicists now call it the electrical explosion of wire. It happens when current rises so fast and so high that the metal heats past melting, past boiling, and turns into plasma before it can even move.

There are three regimes, and they map neatly onto how nature responds when you turn up the current:

Low current: the metal warms. Nothing interesting happens.

High current: the metal glows. It softens. It fails at its weakest point.

Extreme current: the metal doesn't fail. It stops being metal.

That last line is the thing to sit with. Materials are not fixed. Steel isn't steel, copper isn't copper. They are what they are at a given energy density, and above that threshold they turn into something else entirely.

Every material has a current at which it stops being itself.

Which raises a question that has nothing to do with electricity.

What is yours?

11. THE PART WHERE I TELL YOU NOT TO BE AN IDIOT

Everything above is physics. It is beautiful, and it is true. It is also the reason this subject has a body count.

The people who work with this kind of energy for a living do not look like daredevils. They look like accountants. They wear the right gear. They lock out the power. They measure twice, then measure again. They treat the boring checklist as the actual product.

Mains-powered iron and copper does not give second chances. Neither do the capacitors that sometimes sit next to it, holding charge long after the plug is pulled. The difference between a pro and a casualty is almost never courage. It is procedure.

If a clip of someone casually doing something outrageous with electricity makes you think "I could do that," the correct reaction is to go and learn the physics first. Study I squared R. Study insulation. Study what a fuse actually protects. Learn the difference between the thing that looks scary and the thing that is scary.

Watch it. Learn from it. Respect it. Do not copy it.

The person who makes it look easy has usually spent years making it boring.

12. THE RULES OF AMPS

Print these. Tape them above your desk.

1. Volts are the promise. Amps are the delivery.

2. Heat is current squared, times resistance. Never forget the square.

3. Double the current and you quadruple the heat. Ten times the current, a hundred times the heat.

4. Current is decided by the load, not by the source. A source only says what it can offer. The circuit decides what it takes.

5. A transformer does not create power. It trades voltage for current, and current for voltage.

6. Lower the voltage by a factor, and the available current rises by the same factor.

7. Low voltage is not the same as low danger. It just moves the danger from your nerves to your skin and your jewelry.

8. Heat concentrates where the path is narrowest, dirtiest, or loosest.

9. The fastest way to start a fire is a connection that is almost good enough.

10. The grid runs on high voltage so that the wires can stay cool.

11. Resistance is the enemy of efficiency and the friend of every heater ever built.

12. Superconductors are what happens when you cheat resistance and pay in cold.

13. Every material has a current where it stops behaving like itself.

14. Never trust your instincts around energy. Trust your meter.

15. If the number on the display frightens you, that is not a bug. It is the point of the display.

13. WHY YOU CANNOT LOOK AWAY

There is a reason a clip like the one above stops your thumb mid-scroll.

Human beings are wired to notice hidden forces becoming visible. Wind you can only see when it bends a tree. Gravity you can only see when something falls. Electricity you can never see at all, until the moment it makes metal do something metal was not supposed to do.

Nothing in your evolutionary history prepared you for a force that is completely silent right up until it isn't. So when it finally shows itself, your brain treats it like a magic trick, and refuses to let go until it understands the trick.

That is the pull. It is the same pull that drew Nairne to his Leyden jars, Kamerlingh Onnes to his cold mercury, and every engineer who ever leaned closer to a scope and said "wait, what?"

Curiosity is not a distraction from serious work. It is where serious work starts.

This is also why the best explanations never begin with the equation. They begin with the moment your jaw drops. The equation is what you reach for afterwards, once you are desperate to know why it happened at all.
And now you know enough to be dangerous in the only good sense of the word: dangerous to your own ignorance.

14. THE MOST DANGEROUS THING IN YOUR KITCHEN IS BORING

Think about how strange this all is.

You own a box that is, by any reasonable definition, an industrial energy device. It sits next to the bread. It has a pretty digital clock. A child can operate it.

Inside is a lump of iron and copper that is physically a relative of the machines that melt scrap steel and smelt the metal in your phone. The only thing separating the two is how it is wired and how hard it is asked to work.

That is the deepest lesson of amps. The world is full of ordinary objects holding extraordinary potential, and what decides which one you get is not the object.

It is the circuit you build around it.

15. WHAT TO CARRY OUT OF HERE

If this post melted your brain a little, here is the compressed version:

Volts push. Amps do.
Heat scales with the square of the current.
Transformers trade pressure for flow.
Low voltage does not mean low danger.
Energy lands where the path is narrowest.
The number on the meter never lies. Only your instincts do.
Every material has a breaking current.
And the most powerful things are usually the quietest ones, right up until they are not.

16. NOW GO BACK TO THE TOP

Scroll up. Press play again.

Sound on.

The first time, you watched a spectacle.

This time, you know about I squared R, about the gearbox made of iron, about the narrowest point in the loop and the number that decides where all that energy has to go.

Do not watch the light. Watch the place it comes from.

You will see what most of the internet will never see: not a stunt, but a law of physics doing exactly what it always does, at a scale your intuition was never built for.

Then tell me in the replies:

What is the largest current you have ever seen on a meter? What surprised you? And what number in your own life have you been ignoring because it is quiet?

If this post taught you one thing you did not know an hour ago, repost it. Somebody in your feed is about to say "it's only twelve volts," and they deserve to hear the rest.

Follow for more posts where a boring object turns out to be a monster in disguise.

Volts get the warning signs.

Amps get the last word.

DEEP-VALUE LEN5, FIVE TO WATCH: INTUITIVE SURGICAL $ISRG HAS ERASED ITS JULY SLIDE. THE PROOF ARRIVES IN OCTOBER:

Intuitive Surgical ISRG at $414.79, +$9.61 / +2.37% on Monday, closed at its highest price since July 8 - above the $402.33 it closed at on July 16, the afternoon it reported a strong quarter and the day before its stock fell 14%. Of the five names the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5 is watching here, it is the only one whose price has stopped waiting for evidence.

The other four show what this Len5 is finding right now, and it is not wreckage. All five lead their fields - surgical robots, salvage car auctions, U.S. banking, payroll, and the software community banks run on - and each has been marked down on one specific fear. On each company's latest full year or quarter, four earn more per share than a year earlier; the fifth, Copart, earns 2.5% less. Their stocks sit 8% to 41% under their highs of the past year. So far the prices have moved much further than the profits.

Intuitive makes the da Vinci surgical robot and the instruments surgeons use in each operation on it; 85% of its sales repeat - instruments, service and leases - rather than coming from one-time machine sales. This Len5 picked it as a debt-free leader that an event knocked down harder than the business deserved: $8.6B of cash and investments, no debt, and a stock that fell about 45% from its $603.88 peak on January 7 to $328.57 on July 23.

The July 16 report, quarter to June 30:
- Revenue $2.89B, +19%
- Procedures +16%; U.S. da Vinci +12%, international +20%
- 468 da Vinci systems placed vs 395 a year earlier; 267 in the U.S., +24%
- Profit $2.29 a share vs $1.81, +27%
- First-half free cash flow - cash left after running the business and paying for equipment - $1.76B

What the market sold was the outlook. Intuitive held its 2026 forecast for da Vinci procedure growth at 13.5% to 15.5% rather than raising it, and named the drags: changes to Affordable Care Act premium subsidies that may be leading some patients to put off surgery, bariatric operations down high single digits as weight-loss drugs spread, and a tougher China. Six days later, Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) at $271.95, +$0.73 / +0.27% on Monday, won FDA authorization for Ottava, a surgical robot built into the operating table, cleared for ten general-surgery procedures from gallbladder removal to gastric bypass and launching with select U.S. hospitals. J&J sits on this same Len5, for a drug-and-device franchise whose value holds up even after counting all of its debt.

Intuitive is up 24.9% from its July 23 close of $332.02. Monday's gain came as the 10-year Treasury yield - what the U.S. government pays to borrow for ten years - closed at 5.24%, up 0.06 point, the kind of day that usually hits richly priced stocks hardest. The strongest fact against it is that price: about 46 times its last year of profit, with much of the July discount already spent.

J&J reports October 13, its first quarterly report since Ottava was cleared. Intuitive reports October 20 after the close; analysts expect $2.54 a share. The number that decides it is U.S. da Vinci procedure growth, 12% last quarter. What would knock Intuitive off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: U.S. procedure growth slowing again while U.S. system placements fall - the sign hospitals are waiting to compare robots, not waiting on insurance. Verdict: the business came through July intact, and the stock has priced that in before the first evidence on the rival arrives.

The Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5 hunts a sound business priced below a cautious estimate of what it is worth - or one an event has knocked down harder than the business deserves.

- Copart (CPRT) at $27.22, -$0.37 / -1.34% on Monday. It runs online auctions for wrecked and totaled cars, mostly for insurers. The Len5 picked it for its yard network, hard to copy because few places will zone land for acres of wrecked cars. Its special situation lands tomorrow: Copart's $10.50-a-share cash offer for ACV Auctions (ACVA) at $10.46, +$0.00 / +0.00% on Monday, an online dealer-to-dealer used-car marketplace, expires one minute after 11:59pm ET Wednesday unless extended, and needs a majority of ACV's shares tendered plus U.S. antitrust clearance. ACV is on none of the six Len5 watchlists; its price simply tracks the offer. September 10, year to July 31: profit $1.55 a share, -2.5%; $4.5B of cash and securities, no debt; $1.6B of buybacks. U.S. insurance volume fell 7.5% in the quarter, but would have risen 2.3% without one insurer it lost. About 18 times profit, 41% under its October 2025 high of $45.89. What would knock Copart off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: U.S. insurance volume falling even with that lost customer set aside, in the report tentatively due November 19. Verdict: priced like a shrinking business after losing one account.

- JPMorgan Chase (JPM) at $336.59, -$6.47 / -1.89% on Monday. The largest U.S. bank: checking accounts, credit cards, business loans, dealmaking and trading. The Len5 picked it as a top-quality lender valued on its earnings with one-time gains taken out. On that basis, July 14: $6.14 a share, leaving out $1.56 a share of one-time investment gains, vs $4.96 a year earlier, +24%; net interest income - what it earns on loans minus what it pays depositors - $25.6B, +10%; trading revenue $12.1B, +35%; dealmaking fees $3.3B, +30%. It paid $4.0B of dividends and bought back $6.2B of stock in the quarter, and the dividend rises to $1.65 from $1.50 for holders of record October 6. The stock fell 3.4% on September 22, a day 24/7 Wall St. tied bank selling to the 10-year near 5% and a nearly flat yield curve - little gap between short- and long-term rates, which squeezes what a bank earns borrowing short and lending long. It fell another 1.9% Monday. About 15 times its cleaned-up profit, 8% under its August 13 high. What would knock JPMorgan off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: trading and dealmaking falling back hard on October 13, proof the $6.14 was a peak rather than a base; analysts expect $5.88. Verdict: a bank earning 24% more per share than a year ago, marked down for the rate climate around it.

- Automatic Data Processing (ADP) at $261.80, -$1.87 / -0.71% on Monday. It runs payroll and HR for businesses from one-person shops to multinationals. The Len5 picked it as the dominant payroll processor, valued even after charging for its software spending and the stock it pays employees. July 29, fiscal year to June: revenue $21.9B, +7%; adjusted profit - leaving out one-time items - $11.12 a share, +11%; $4.7B returned in dividends and buybacks. Higher rates quietly help: ADP holds client payroll money before paying it out - $40.4B on average last year, earning 3.4% - and expects about 3.7% this year, lifting that interest income to $1.54B-$1.56B from $1.36B. The fear is hiring: pays per control, the number of workers on each U.S. client's payroll, grew 1% last year and is planned at 0% to 1%. About 24 times profit, 11% under the $294.35 high it set a year ago today. What would knock ADP off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: pays per control shrinking in the October 28 report, where analysts expect $2.77 a share. Verdict: a steady compounder with one line, client interest, that the rate climb is paying for.

- Jack Henry & Associates (JKHY) at $147.82, +$0.03 / +0.02% on Monday. The Missouri company runs the core systems - deposits, loans, the ledger - for community banks and credit unions, and moving off one takes a bank years. The Len5 picked it as a sticky franchise priced below what its current earnings support. August 18, fiscal year to June: revenue $2.54B, +7%; profit $6.98 a share, +12%; a record 58 banks and credit unions won from rivals, 14 of them with more than $1B of assets. The soft spot is the last quarter: $1.57 a share vs $1.75 a year earlier, -10%, on higher staff and research spending. It bought back $448M of stock in the year at an average $152, above today's price. Its plan for fiscal 2027 is $7.33-$7.38 a share - about 20 times at today's price, 24% under its January high of $193.39. What would knock Jack Henry off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: a second straight quarter of shrinking profit in the report tentatively due November 3. Verdict: a record year of client wins, priced as if the soft quarter were the trend.

Four of these five still carry their fear in the price. Intuitive has already set its fear down, three weeks before hospitals give their first real answer on the rival robot - which makes it the one name here where the stock, not the company, has something to prove.

Not investment advice.

Elon Musk is criticizing New York’s voting rules after his mother, Maye Musk, said a woman at a polling place angrily knocked away the ID she offered while voting.

Maye Musk, the 78-year-old model, dietitian, and author, was responding to a list of the 14 states that still refuse to require voter ID at the polls. Those states, as conservatives have noted for years, reliably deliver Democratic wins.

“Definitely New York,” she wrote. “When I voted and showed my ID, the woman was angry and hit it away.”

Definitely New York. When I voted and showed my ID, the woman was angry and hit it away. https://t.co/NXK0Op7iMC— Maye Musk (@mayemusk) September 27, 2026

That is not a first for Maye. During the 2024 cycle she said early voting in New York City required no ID at all and that workers “won’t even look at your ID.” Later she described being told to sign a form, stuff it in an envelope, and drop it in a box while the worker “refused to see my ID.”

After his mother, Maye Musk, described being met with hostility when she tried to show identification at a New York polling place, the X owner dropped a charge that Democrats in the country’s two largest blue states have spent years pretending is “disinformation.”

In New York and California, they have made it illegal for officials to ask for or for you to show your voter ID!They made election fraud mandatory. https://t.co/mxvjfv7DDq— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) September 27, 2026

Don’t take Musk’s word for it. Take Letitia James.

The New York Attorney General’s official voting-resources page states, in black and white, that voters “are never required to present photo identification to cast an in-person ballot” and instructs New Yorkers: “If you see or hear of anyone improperly requesting voter identification, contact OAG.” Read it here.

Poll-worker guidance tracks the same line: do not ask for ID unless the voter file is already flagged. Signature matching is the substitute. No photo. No citizenship check at the table. Just a scribble.

That is why a poll worker would get angry at a woman holding out a government ID. The training says don’t look. The AG’s office says report the person who asks.

California is even more aggressive. In 2024, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill 1174, which bars cities and counties from requiring identification at the polls, a direct strike at Huntington Beach after voters there passed their own ID rule. Courts later killed the local measure. Sacramento made sure no charter city could close the barn door.

As The Gateway Pundit reported last month, California still lets applicants register online with no driver’s license and no Social Security number. The state’s own acceptable-ID list for the rare first-time voter who actually gets asked includes a gym card, an insurance card, or a credit card.

You can vote for governor with a Planet Fitness membership. You cannot cash a paycheck with one.

The hypocrisy is not subtle.

According to Fox News, New York City demanded two photos, two original IDs, and a Social Security card from emergency snow shovelers last winter, the same city that tells election inspectors not to look at a voter’s license.

As The Gateway Pundit reported in August, Socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani floated ID requirements for his government grocery stores so people wouldn’t resell discounted food. President Trump’s response was the obvious one: they will check your papers to buy milk, but not to choose the people who run the country.

Need a beer? ID. Board a plane? ID. Pick up a prescription? ID. Decide who controls the House in November? In New York and California, that is treated like a poll tax.

text:
After the release of Step 5 Preview, @StepFun_ai  co-founder Yibo Zhu took a closer look at an idea the team has been exploring over the past few months: can training also benefit from “PD separation”?

He shared his answer on Zhihu: KV-Invariant Transformer Expansion for Efficient Agentic LLM Scaling—a firsthand technical deep dive into a potential new path for scaling agentic LLMs.

🔗 https://t.co/bkqAUul3yr

The core challenge is optimizing three things at once: model quality, training cost, and inference cost.

MoE is a classic example of this “three-way win.” But approaches such as Upcycling and YOCO often trade off one dimension against another: scaling them to recover model quality can increase training or inference costs.

KITE combines scaling with upcycling, while keeping KV computation invariant.

First, a smaller prefiller is trained to generate the KV cache. The model is then expanded with decoder-side components that reuse this KV and continue pretraining. Because these added components do not affect KV computation, the model can scale up to recover quality without proportionally increasing prefill cost.

This is particularly relevant in the Agent era, where long-context workloads can make prefill a major part of inference cost.

Using a simple Step Scale Transformer (SST), the paper demonstrates a three-way gain over a proportionally scaled classical Transformer baseline: better model quality, lower training cost, and lower inference cost.

KITE is ultimately a broader principle of KV-invariant scaling, rather than a single architecture. Better prefiller/decoder designs, KV usage strategies, and scaling laws remain open questions.

If agentic workloads continue to be prefill-heavy, KITE could offer an interesting path toward more efficient LLM scaling.

KITE has not yet been applied to Step 5, but similar ideas may eventually appear in StepFun’s mainline models.

text:
Good morning X!! 😎☕️🫡

📢Let's fix this headline:
What's 30% between a trillionaire and the @MYANC's usual connected Mafia cadres?

https://t.co/CWNnOA7eXu

Deputy Communications Minister Mondli Gungubele (@MondliGungubel_) spoke at @Bloomberg's Africa Business Media Innovators event in Hermanus on September 28, 2026.

The line that became the @TimesLIVE headline: @Starlink is welcome to improve connectivity, if @elonmusk "walks with us" on transformation - meaning the 30% historically disadvantaged / Black ownership rule for a telecoms license.

"What's 30% between a trillionaire and his birth country?" He also said he hoped Elon was listening, and that 30% is small next to the 70% Musk would still keep.

THAT is the official pitch!!
The policy reality is however narrower and A LOT uglier!!

South Africa's Electronic Communications Act / @ICASA_org licensing still treats equity transfer as the gold standard for a network license. Other sectors already allow Equity Equivalent Investment Programmes (EEIPs) - @Microsoft, @IBM, AWS, @Dell and banks have used them for years.

Starlink's public offer is not "nothing": about R500m to put free hardware and service into 5,000 rural schools (~2.4 million learners), plus roughly R2bn in ground stations, PoPs, power, fibre and local staffing, plus reseller work for local ISPs. They refuse to sell 30% of the operating company (and RIGHTFULLY SO, I might add) because Starlink is a global constellation they will not fragment.

Musk has also said he was offered the classic workaround: pretend a Black partner runs Starlink SA. He called that a bribe-by-fronting and refused.

https://t.co/M8K0CV09Aq

Two competing South African stories are colliding though:
1. Gungubele / ANC transformation line: ownership share = redress; foreign tech without a local slice is "dependence."
2. Malatsi / EEIP line (GNU tension): connect schools and build infrastructure instead of handing equity to a politically connected few.

BEE's stated aim is to (supposedly) undo apartheid exclusion.

But let's look at hard facts:
After three decades the pattern critics keep documenting is:
* elite capture,
* fronting, and
* a policy that raises the price of investment...
... while the mass of Black South Africans still face extreme unemployment and a digital divide SA Connect has not closed.

Demanding 30% of a satellite network from a Pretoria-born founder is not "walking together" and never has been... that's just the ANC's go-to slogan which they have coined the last 32-very-unproductive-years!!

It is treating connectivity for rural kids as a bargaining chip for ownership that usually does not reach those kids anyway.

ELECTIONS

See which incumbents have the biggest cash advantage in the tightest U.S. House races

PUBLISHED FRI, SEP 25 2026

Luke Fountain@LUKE_FOUNTAIN25  Gabriel Cortés@GABECORTES

KEY POINTS

•In 11 of 19 incumbent-versus-challenger competitive U.S. House races analyzed by CNBC, one candidate had at least twice as much cash on hand --- and every one was the incumbent.

•The districts with the biggest gaps include Michigan’s 7th, Colorado’s 8th and California’s 22nd, where Republican incumbents held several times the cash of their Democratic challengers.

•Six challengers did outraise incumbents in available cash, but none held a 2-to-1 advantage, underscoring how much stronger the largest incumbent cash cushions are.

The most competitive races for control of the House of Representatives in the 2026 midterm election may be toss-ups on the political map. But in the most fiercely contested districts, one candidate often holds a massive financial edge.

In 11 of the 19 incumbent-versus-challenger matchups rated as “toss ups” by The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, a clear financial divide emerged: One campaign had at least twice as much money available as the other, according to Federal Election Commission data compiled by OpenSecrets, a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization that tracks money in politics. In every one of those races, the incumbent held that commanding lead.

The latest uniform quarterly reports covered activity through June 30, though some candidates have since filed additional reports tied to their states’ primary calendars. CNBC used figures from the most recent FEC reporting period available for each candidate as of Sept. 18.

The pattern cuts across party lines, but it matters especially for Republicans because the GOP is defending most of the seats at the center of the House battlefield. The Cook Report currently rates 21 House races as toss-ups, including 16 Republican-held seats and five Democratic-held seats.

In Michigan’s 7th District, Republican Rep. Tom Barrett had about $2.9 million on hand compared with roughly $383,000 for Democratic challenger William Lawrence --- a more than 7-to-1 advantage.

MI-07Republican Rep. Gabe Evans had about $3.9 million available in Colorado’s 8th District compared with roughly $601,000 for Democratic challenger Manny Rutinel. And in California’s 22nd District, Republican Rep. David Valadao held about $3.4 million, nearly six times the roughly $572,000 held by Democratic challenger Randy Villegas.

CO-08

Democratic incumbents have built large cushions of their own. Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur had about $3.5 million on hand in Ohio’s 9th District, more than seven times the amount available to Republican challenger Derek Merrin. Democratic Reps. Jared Moskowitz of Florida and Texas’s Vicente Gonzalez also held more than three times as much cash as their Republican opponents.

FL-2

$5

But incumbency does not guarantee the advantage.

Democratic challengers had more cash than Republican incumbents in both Iowa toss-up races and two of Pennsylvania’s three.

Christina Bohannan had about $5.4 million on hand compared with roughly $4.7 million for Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa’s 1st District.

IA-01In Pennsylvania’s 10th District, Democrat Janelle Stelson had nearly $4.5 million available compared with about $2.8 million for Republican Rep. Scott Perry.

Paige Cognetti also led Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan in Pennsylvania’s 8th District, while Democrat Elaine Luria held a narrow cash advantage over Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans, who defeated Luria in 2022, in Virginia’s 2nd District.

PA-08

Rep. Rob Bresnahan

Still, the challenger advantages were generally much smaller. Among the 21 races CNBC analyzed, six challengers led incumbents in cash, but none had twice as much money as the sitting https://t.co/pDiaASKv0G contrast, 11 incumbents held at least a 2-to-1 advantage.

Cash on hand offers a different view than top-line fundraising because it shows what campaigns still have available after spending as Election Day approaches. It also captures only part of the money flowing into these contests. 

Super PACs and other groups can independently spend to support or oppose candidates without those dollars flowing through the candidates’ campaign accounts, under federal campaign finance rules.

text:
99.99% IMPOSSIBLE: THE SAILBOAT STORY THAT CANNOT BE NORD STREAM

Filmmaker Moritz Enders, director of the documentary "Nord Stream Die Sprengung", sat down on Gegen den Strom and tore into the official Andromeda account. A few Ukrainians sail out of Rostock, clip a peg on their noses, dive eighty meters with hundreds of kilos of explosives, and blow the most important piece of German energy infrastructure since 1945. That is the story we are told to swallow. Enders’ question is simpler: how stupid do they think we are?

THE STORY WE ARE SUPPOSED TO BELIEVE
➡️ A charter yacht leaves Rostock, crosses another border with special underwater charges, gets flashed on Rügen, plants a Ukrainian flag, and parks over the pipes.
➡️ The crew then completes four professional dives in the dark, in the cold, against current, at one of the deepest points in the Baltic.
➡️ German prosecutors still treat this amateur-sailboat plot as the working explanation.

WHY ENDERS SAYS THE MATH BREAKS
➡️ “Every detail by itself is almost impossible. Combined, it is probably 99.99 percent impossible.”
➡️ Eighty meters is not aqua-aerobics. You need decompression stops or a chamber. Bottles empty fast. Currents eat the rest.
➡️ A military journalist told him the job needed at least ten hours. A drifting sailboat cannot hold station. A proper anchor chain at that depth would run about 240 meters. Kill the transponder and a yacht lingering exactly over the pipeline still looks wrong.

THE CLUES THAT DO NOT FIT A SECRET CREW
➡️ They took the long way. Kołobrzeg in Poland sits far closer to the blast sites than Rostock.
➡️ Investigators later found explosives on the kitchen table. 
➡️ The yacht went back to its owners in days. A real forensic sweep would take weeks. Sweden recovered material and locked it away. If the match were clean, he asks, why not publish it?

THE MILITARY READ
➡️ After the film he spoke with military journalists and people around the Bundeswehr. Their shared conclusion: this was a planned commando operation, prepared in peace, not a drinking trip with a nose clip.
➡️ He takes Seymour Hersh’s account seriously: BALTOPS in June 2022 as cover, charges placed by professionals, later ignition discussed as a sonar buoy from a Poseidon P-8 flying with its transponder off.
➡️ Other officers told him remote acoustic ignition is too failure-prone. They would plant timed charges from underwater demolition teams, mini-subs, or robots — gear that also solves the decompression problem Germany, he was told, does not even have at that depth.

WHO COULD — AND WHO WANTED TO
➡️ Once you accept a military operation, Enders says the live question is no longer the nose clip. It is who had the capability and who had the interest.
➡️ Hersh and former CIA analyst Ray McGovern, whom he interviewed, point to a tight National Security Council circle: Jake Sullivan as the driver, Antony Blinken and Joe Biden signing off, combat swimmers trained in Florida, possible Norwegian deep-water help from the oil patch.
➡️ He does not claim every Hersh detail is locked. He does claim the official yacht story is too thin to carry the heaviest attack on German infrastructure in eight decades.

THE PHOTO THAT WILL NOT AGE WELL
➡️ On the eve of the Ukraine war, Biden stood next to Olaf Scholz and said that if Russia invaded, there would be no Nord Stream.
➡️ Scholz smiled in English about always pulling together with America’s friends. Enders calls the scene a tragedy of sovereignty: the economic foundation of German industry being announced dead while the chancellor stands there like a pregnant squirrel.
➡️ Did Scholz know, cover, or help shade the aftermath? Enders will not pretend to know. He will say German authorities show almost no will to find out. Sweden, Denmark, and Germany, investigative journalist Dirk Pohlmann says in the film, already know enough to know they do not want to know more.

THE BOTTOM LINE
Enders is not asking the public to convict a country from a cinema seat. He is asking why the only story on offer requires four impossible dives, kitchen-table explosives, and a yacht returned before the lab work was done — while the states that could settle it look away. The blast was real. The cover story, on his evidence, is not.

For it is written,

to be given a Queen who understands the soul of her King is to be given a sacred paradise, a love torn from the pages of an ancient manuscript and breathed into human form.

But understand what it may have cost her to still know how to love you.

There are women whose love was so sacred that lesser men did not know what to do with it.

So they wounded it.

They locked her away and called the cage love. 

They abused the softness they could not comprehend, tormented the heart that continued offering tenderness, and tried to break what they could never become worthy enough to receive.

Year after year, she prayed for escape.

And God heard her.

He saw the doors close behind her in darkness entrapped by men before.

He heard the cries swallowed by walls.

He counted every tear shed in places where nobody came to save her.

He watched a Queen be torn to shreds because men encountered something beautiful and, instead of kneeling before its sacredness, tried to possess it.

Yet they could not destroy the holiest thing about her.

Her ability to love.

Think of the miracle in that.

To be offered genuine love from a woman who has every reason to distrust it is like being handed the rarest jewel from universes beyond Earth, something darkness touched repeatedly and still could not corrupt.

So if God places such a woman beside you, do not become another man she must survive.

Love her.

Nurture what was neglected.

Respect what was violated.

Protect what others imprisoned without ever believing you own it.

And never mistake the depth of her devotion for weakness.

Because when a woman like this finally finds a King who does not punish her for loving deeply, she does not need to be forced into surrender.

She gives freely what other men spent years trying to steal.

And that is one of God's most beautiful forms of justice..

the men who imprisoned her could never possess her soul,
while the man who finally sets her heart free 
will be trusted with the paradise they spent years trying to destroy.

She was never difficult to love.

She was sacred in the hands of men who did not know how to hold holy things. 🙏🤍

text:
Denver’s best touchdown came from a coverage mismatch.

Bo Nix briefly answered Kansas City through design and execution. The broadcast highlighted Denver’s touchdown pass as a clear example: using Waddle from the backfield created a weakness in Kansas City’s zone coverage, and Nix found the opening for a score.

That response came after Denver’s opening drive ended with rookie Delain’s interception. Nix and his receivers showed enough to stabilize the Broncos temporarily, while the backfield alignment gave the quarterback a clearer opportunity against the defense’s coverage responsibilities.

The sequence offers a specific explanation for Denver’s success. The Broncos were not without answers; they found one by using formation and movement to create a favorable zone matchup. The play showed how scheme could help Nix attack a defense that had already disrupted him, provided the execution remained clean.

Denver struggled to reproduce that success. Kansas City’s pressure later forced a Nix fumble recovered by Chris Jones, and the Broncos were stopped on nine straight third downs. Turnovers, protection breakdowns and failed conversions undermined the flashes Nix produced.

The practical lesson is to preserve the creativity while improving consistency. Waddle’s backfield usage gave Denver a way to stress zone coverage, but the offense needed cleaner execution and better ball security to turn that idea into sustained drives. The touchdown was a useful blueprint, not a complete solution.

Brent headed for 17% rise in September.

 Oil prices rose for a second ‌successive session on Tuesday as lingering concern over Middle East supply disruption brought about by the US-Israeli war on Iran outweighed signs of recovering crude exports from the region.

Brent crude futures for November rose 19 cents, or 0.2%, to $105.47 a ​barrel at 0844 GMT, while the more actively traded Brent December contract rose 11 cents to $97.94 ​a barrel. Meanwhile, US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $92.82, up 22 cents.

November-loading Brent ⁠and WTI are headed for monthly gains of around 17% and 8%, respectively.

Crude exports from major Middle Eastern producers climbed to 12.8 million barrels a day ​in September, the highest since February, preliminary figures from data provider Kpler showed on Monday, helped by ​increased shipments from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

US and Iranian officials spoke separately with mediators in a renewed effort ‌to ⁠end seven months of war, officials of both countries said.
But US President Donald Trump said he has offered Iran nothing to end the war, rejecting media reports that cited US officials saying he was willing to ease sanctions and release frozen funds for "concrete" steps regarding Iran's nuclear programme.

Meanwhile, the US is considering regulatory relief to ​allow broader sales of red-dyed ​diesel to help ⁠lower prices, people familiar with discussions told Reuters. The proposal emerged as a leading alternative to a diesel export ban.

US crude oil ​and gasoline inventories were expected to have fallen last week, while distillate stockpiles were likely unchanged, a preliminary Reuters poll showed on Monday."

text:
I’VE BEEN ASKING THE WRONG QUESTION.

For almost 20 months, I’ve been trying to understand where Mark Carney actually wants to take Canada.

And I don’t think the question is:

WHY CAN’T CARNEY GET A U.S. DEAL?

I think it’s:

DOES HE ACTUALLY WANT ONE?

⸻

During the election, Canadians were told we would negotiate a new economic and security relationship with the United States.

Diversification was part of the plan too.

Fair enough.

WE WERE SUPPOSED TO DO BOTH.

Then Canada reportedly got close to a U.S. deal.

And walked.

Carney later said:

“Diversifying trade abroad is not our Plan B. It has been our Plan A from the start.”

That sentence changed the way I looked at everything.

⸻

Because now look around.

🇲🇽 Mexico kept negotiating.

🇨🇳 China just found areas where it can reduce trade barriers with Washington despite enormous strategic disagreements.

🇪🇺 Canada is pursuing a much deeper relationship with Europe.

And Canada?

Still no U.S. deal.

⸻

Maybe there’s a perfectly reasonable explanation.

GOOD.

SHOW US.

What changed?
What was offered?
What did Canada reject?

Because I’m no longer convinced this is simply about getting a better agreement.

I think Carney may be trying to reduce Canada’s structural dependence on the United States and move us toward much deeper economic, political and security integration with Europe and other global institutions.

Maybe he believes that makes Canada stronger.

That doesn’t automatically make it wrong.

BUT CANADIANS SHOULD KNOW THAT’S THE PLAN.

⸻

Diversification?

Absolutely.

More customers is good business.

But weakening our most important economic relationship while rebuilding around another geopolitical model is something very different.

Especially when Europe itself is wrestling with economic stagnation, energy costs, industrial competition, migration pressures and political fragmentation.

STOP ROMANTICIZING THE EU.

It has problems too.

⸻

So show Canadians the destination.

Show us what we gain.

Show us what we lose.

And show us the American deal we apparently couldn’t sign.

Because this isn’t Mark Carney’s economy to redesign.

IT’S OURS.

⸻

Clarity is Courage:

China didn’t create my suspicion.

It just made it harder to dismiss.

🍪🍪 Share My Cookies:

Don’t share this because you agree with me.

Share it because Canadians deserve enough information to decide for themselves.

⸻

🇺🇸 TRUMP JUST RESET AMERICA’S FUEL-ECONOMY RULES. THE BACKDOOR "EV MANDATE" IS CRIPPLED.

The Trump administration has finalized its new “Freedom Means Affordable Cars” CAFE standards—and there’s a lot more to this story than EVs.

Under the final rule, NHTSA projects fleetwide fuel economy will reach about 34.9 MPG by model year 2031, up from 30.1 MPG for model year 2024. 

According to DOT/NHTSA’s analysis, the new standards are projected to:

🚘 Lower the average new-vehicle price by about $1,300
💰 Save consumers roughly $138 BILLION over five years
🇺🇸 Give automakers greater flexibility to build the vehicles consumers actually want
🛡️ Prevent more than 300,000 serious injuries and save roughly 1,900 lives, based on NHTSA’s projection that lower prices will help more Americans replace older vehicles with newer, safer ones. 

There’s another major change that isn’t getting much attention: NHTSA is eliminating CAFE credit trading beginning with model year 2028. The administration argues this will stop traditional automakers from having to purchase compliance credits and instead encourage fuel-saving technology across their own fleets. 

Ford CEO Jim Farley previously called the change a “victory for affordability and common sense,” saying Ford expects greater ability to offer affordable versions of popular models and introduce lower-priced vehicles built in America. 

Here's the important distinction: this doesn't eliminate fuel-economy standards. It changes how aggressive those standards are and gives manufacturers more flexibility in meeting them.

The administration calls the previous system a “backdoor EV mandate.” Critics argue less-stringent standards could mean Americans ultimately buy more gasoline.

So here’s the question for Cowboys and Cowgirls:

🇺🇸 Should Washington keep pushing automakers toward increasingly aggressive fuel-economy targets—or should manufacturers build what Americans want and let consumers decide what belongs in their driveway?

text:
Iran's IRGC Publishes 26-Page Open Letter To Directly to AMERICANS

I read the entire letter. It is FAR more extensive than the excerpts circulating online.

The IRGC DIRECTLY addresses American citizens, students, academics and journalists, laying out its view of the war, decades of U.S.-Iran hostility and what it believes Americans should do next.

Key points:
• IRAN CLAIMS VICTORY: The letter argues the U.S. and Israel failed to achieve their objectives despite vastly greater military spending. It points to Iran's control of the Strait of Hormuz, continued weapons production, national unity and damage inflicted on U.S. regional bases.

• WHY IRAN DID NOT BREAK: The IRGC says Iran's strength ultimately comes not from missiles or drones, but from Quranic principles, national unity and religious leadership. It devotes several pages to Karbala and the Shia principle of resisting oppression regardless of the cost.

• "DEATH TO AMERICA SLOGAN": The IRGC says the slogan targets America's ruling political establishment, NOT ordinary Americans. It argues that Iranians and Americans are both victims of the same political elite.

• 73 YEARS OF HOSTILITY: The letter traces the conflict from the 1953 coup through the Shah, the Iran-Iraq War, sanctions, Flight 655, the killing of Qasem Soleimani, the 2025 war, the January 2026 unrest and the current war.

• IRGC TERRORISM DESIGNATION: The Guards argue Washington designated the IRGC a terrorist organization because it repeatedly blocked U.S. attempts to weaken or overthrow the Islamic Republic.

• NUCLEAR PROGRAM: The letter calls allegations that Iran is pursuing nuclear weapons one of Washington's biggest lies. It notes that U.S. officials have claimed for 25 YEARS that Iran was only "weeks or months" away from building a bomb, yet Iran still has no nuclear weapon.

• ISRAEL: The IRGC argues U.S. support for Israel has damaged America's interests, reputation and finances, while American taxpayers continue funding Israeli military operations.

• AMERICAN DECLINE: The letter blames foreign wars, military spending, national debt, deindustrialization and poor leadership for weakening the U.S. It contrasts this with China's continued advances while Washington spends enormous resources fighting wars abroad.

• CLOSE THE BASES: The letter urges Americans to demand the closure of roughly 800 U.S. overseas military bases, bring American troops home, end aid to Israel and redirect that money toward science, advanced manufacturing and domestic prosperity.

• CHANGE U.S. LEADERSHIP: Americans are urged to use their votes to remove politicians the letter describes as corrupt and dishonest. It specifically mocks politicians who think they can buy Americans' votes with a $5,000 payment.

• THE WARNING: The IRGC warns that continuing the war could trigger broader political and economic backlash against U.S. interests around the world.

• THE OFFER: Despite its attacks on the U.S. government, the letter tells Americans:
"We can live together in peaceful coexistence."

text:
AT 1:35AM ET, OIL TOPPED AND STOCK FUTURES BOTTOMED IN THE SAME FIVE MINUTES. EUROPE OPENED AFTER THE TURN:

Two hours into Europe's Tuesday, London, Frankfurt and Paris are trading on the calm side of an overnight reversal. The FTSE 100 (UK) is at 10,715, +29.93 pts / +0.28% so far in Tuesday's session, trading now. The DAX (Germany) is at 25,445, +70.43 pts / +0.28%. The CAC 40 (France) is at 8,087.21, +8.73 pts / +0.11%. The Euro Stoxx 50, the euro area's big-company benchmark, is at 6,342.69, +41.41 / +0.66%.

The verdict for the U.S. open: the overnight oil scare has already come and gone, and U.S. stock futures are back at Monday's close. What has not moved is the 10-year Treasury yield, the borrowing cost that did most of Monday's damage. It sits at 5.243%, right where Monday left it.

The turn came in one five-minute window, 1:35am ET:
- U.S. crude (WTI) for November topped at $94.74 a barrel, +$2.14 / +2.3% from Monday's settlement
- S&P 500 futures bottomed at 7,716, -30.75 / -0.40%
- Nasdaq 100 futures bottomed at 30,372.25, -194.00 / -0.63%
- Tokyo's Nikkei 225 hit its low of the day, 64,699.49, -1,178 pts / -1.79%

Everything has run the other way since. U.S. crude is back at $92.79, +$0.19 / +0.21%. Brent, the international benchmark, for November delivery, is at $105.41, +$0.13 / +0.12% since Monday's settlement, after touching $107.87. The S&P contract is 32 points off its low; the Nasdaq contract, 251. Nobody was hiding, either: gold is at $4,171.90 an ounce, +$3.50 / +0.08%.

No single headline explains the turn, but the timing lines up with one. Around 1:30am ET, wire reports citing Iranian state media quoted Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying Tehran expects a formal U.S. answer today, through Qatari mediators, to its plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Iran wants frozen funds released, oil sanctions lifted and the U.S. naval blockade of its ports ended within days. Oil also has a physical reason to cool: Middle East crude exports are back to just under 80% of pre-war levels, the most since the war began in February, per tanker tracker Kpler. The strait is still far from normal: about 10.6M barrels a day Saturday vs 17.1M pre-war.

This is the second overnight oil spike in two days to fade within hours. U.S. crude, same November contract:
- Friday's settlement: $92.41
- Monday's early high, after President Trump rejected Iran's offer over the weekend: $96.54
- Monday's settlement: $92.60
- Tuesday's overnight high: $94.74
- Now: $92.79
Two scares, and crude sits 38 cents above Friday.

Asia handed Europe a smaller loss than its morning promised. Tokyo rallied about 780 points off that 1:35am low in its last hour and closed at 65,481, -396 pts / -0.60%. About 300 of those points were not selling but Tuesday's ex-dividend markdown, when new buyers stop getting the upcoming payout, by the estimate of Nihon Keizai Shimbun, Japan's main business newspaper. The Hang Seng (Hong Kong) closed at 24,523.57, -118.94 / -0.48%, with the Hang Seng Tech Index at 4,249.62, -46.38 / -1.08% - the city's big internet and technology names falling about twice as fast. The Shanghai Composite closed at 3,830.45, +6.83 / +0.18%.

Europe's bond market shows how much oil is setting the tone. At 3am ET, Spain's statistics office, INE, put September inflation at 4.9% from a year earlier vs 4.6% expected and 4.3% in August; core, which leaves out energy and fresh food, rose to 3.1% from 2.9%. A hot number like that usually pushes borrowing costs up. Instead they fell. The UK's 10-year gilt yield - what Britain's government pays to borrow for ten years - is 5.395%, down 3.1 basis points (hundredths of a percentage point). Germany's 10-year is 3.625%, down 1.9. With crude sliding, bond traders looked past a hot Spanish print.

The U.S. bond market did not follow. The 10-year Treasury yield - what the U.S. government pays to borrow for ten years, and the rate mortgages and business loans are priced from - is up 0.1 basis point from Monday's close, after ranging from 5.219% to 5.264% overnight. The 2-year, the maturity most tied to what the Federal Reserve does next, is 4.945%, up 2.1 basis points. The Fed, which raised rates September 16, meets again October 27-28; overnight, Australia's central bank raised its own for the fourth time this year, to 4.60%. A higher 10-year makes far-off profit worth less today, which is why technology stocks fell hardest Monday.

U.S. futures - contracts that trade overnight and point to where the big indexes may open - since Monday's close:
- S&P 500 futures at 7,748.00, +1.25 / +0.02%
- Nasdaq 100 futures at 30,623.25, +57.00 / +0.19%
- Dow futures at 51,783.00, -54.00 / -0.10%
- Russell 2000 futures, which track smaller U.S. companies, at 2,839.00, -1.10 / -0.04%
Overnight trading is thin, and moves this small often shrink or reverse by the 9:30am ET opening bell.

What decides whether the calm holds:
- The U.S. answer to Iran, due today by Tehran's account. Monday evening Trump posted "I offered them NOTHING!", answering an Axios report that he was open to sanctions relief. A flat no would show whether the overnight fade was relief or a pause.
- 10am ET: the Bureau of Labor Statistics' JOLTS count of August job openings, 7.23M expected vs 7.27M in July, and the Conference Board's September household survey of consumer confidence, 90.1 expected vs 89.4 in August. Slower hiring and gloomier households would argue against a second Fed increase.
- The 10-year against 5.24%.

The 9:30am bell inherits both halves of the night: an oil scare that has now drained away twice within hours, and a 5.24% 10-year that neither fade has moved. A no from Washington today could revive the first. The 10am data is today's first real chance to move the second.

text:
Baby brain IS real, scientists say | Daily Mail

From lost keys to forgotten shopping lists, ‘pregnancy brain’ has long been dismissed as an old wives' tale.

But scientists have now identified a hormonal brain circuit that appears to make expectant mothers more forgetful during late pregnancy.

As part of a study, researchers from Baylor College of Medicine in Texas exposed mice to pregnancy-level concentrations of oestrogen.

They discovered that these high hormone levels disrupted a specific brain circuit involved in memory formation.

Elevated oestrogen appeared to overstimulate neurons in the hypothalamus, which then interfered with activity in the hippocampus, a key memory centre.

When the researchers switched off this pathway, memory problems disappeared – suggesting it plays a direct role in the phenomenon known as ‘mumnesia’.

‘We worked with mouse models designed to mimic the sustained, high blood-oestrogen levels of pregnancy,’ senior author Dr Zheng Sun said.

‘These models showed that elevated oestrogen caused reversible memory impairment without affecting mood or motivation, suggesting a specific cognitive effect.’

The team then tested pregnant women and found that memory performance declined in late pregnancy and was linked to higher levels of circulating oestrogen.

Importantly, the effects appeared to be temporary and specific to certain memory tasks, rather than a sign of broader cognitive decline.

Senior author Dr Xianghua Zhuang said: ‘Mumnesia is real, it has a defined biological basis and is temporary.

‘We hope this work validates what many women have described anecdotally for years.’

The researchers said their findings, published in the journal Science Bulletin, offer the first biological explanation of how exposure to high levels of oestrogen can temporarily impair memory.

They said the discovery could eventually help doctors reassure women experiencing ‘pregnancy brain’, and may even lead to treatments that prevent memory lapses without affecting the hormone's other important roles in the body.

So how did Indians end up in the Russian army?

Although some Indians deliberately signed up for the army, most of them were recruited through trafficking networks and recruitment agents who made false promises about jobs in Russia.

Some were targeted through social media and promised jobs as army helpers, drivers, cooks, cleaners or security guards, while others were offered easy pathways to Europe. 

They were encouraged to travel to Russia for these jobs, but after arriving, some found themselves enlisted in the Russian army.

Their passports were taken away, they were forced to sign contracts in Russian, and they were eventually sent to the battlefield.

text:
U.S. Army Long-Range Precision Fires, Forward Posture Around Iran, and Effective Strike Volume Inside Iranian Territory

For years, U.S. bases in the Middle East have symbolized Washington’s security and military relationships with Arab states. They have also been central to the depth of America’s defensive posture across the Middle East and the Indian Ocean. In the 40-day war, those bases became among the Islamic Republic’s first targets and suffered extensive damage. Once that vulnerability became clear, some analysts argued that the bases need structural change or modest geographic standoff, and that the current architecture cannot meet new threats. Others go beyond the technical debate and argue, on political grounds, that the United States should leave these bases altogether.

During the 40-day war, the United States tried to sustain its volume of fire inside Iran by relying on more mobile and relatively safer assets: aircraft carriers, missile-armed surface ships, aircraft staged at bases farther from Iran’s borders, and air and missile defenses. Ground-launched Army ballistic missiles provided a further, if partial, boost against targets in southern Iran. Some sources claim the U.S. Army fired more than 1,300 short-range ballistic missiles into southern Iran. Overall, the absence of forces immediately adjacent to Iranian territory complicated tanker support and made it harder to increase the weight of attacks. Even so, the forces that remained comparatively safer and still operational around Iran were the Army’s missile and drone launchers. Keeping those systems in action is easier than sustaining air platforms that depend on concentrated airfields, because launchers can be dispersed across terrain. That advantage, however, still requires dedicated protection and specific operating practices. The recent war also showed that IRGC has serious access to Chinese and Russian satellite intelligence, which can leave these ground units exposed as well.

The U.S. Army now has an extensive program to diversify its long-range precision fires, one that would markedly expand its ability to strike all of Iran, or at least most of it. The service is slated to field a mix of advanced and low-cost ground-launched missiles and one-way attack drones, covering a wide set of munitions at much greater scale. The range runs from high-end, expensive systems such as the Dark Eagle hypersonic missile, with a reported reach of 2,700 to 3,500 kilometers, to cheaper hypersonic weapons such as Blackbeard, with a range of about 800 kilometers. Through the Typhon system, the Army can also employ the Tomahawk cruise missile. The real center of gravity in the Army’s bid to increase volume, however, is the mass production of low-cost munitions weapons that could give land forces a substantial share of the long-range strike capacity now concentrated in the Navy and Air Force.
The key to that outcome is the ability to fire from close to Iranian territory. Greater volume depends on making these weapons smaller and cheaper, and that logic only holds if the fires are launched from shorter range. Given the current state of Iran’s air defenses, a family of low-cost systems could likely remain effective across much of the country, including LUCAS one-way attack drones, the Barracuda-500M cruise missile with a range of about 900 kilometers, and the Anthem missile, etc.
One point should not be overlooked: the distinctive value of the Army’s high-speed launchers. Rapid fires after the immediate acquisition of targeting data would allow its ballistic and hypersonic systems to displace quickly and strike time-sensitive targets, like mobile missile launchers and etc. The same process is usually slower with fighters and cruise missiles. Even a fighter carrying hypersonic weapons would take longer, unless it were already airborne and in the operational cycle.

In sum, keeping U.S. Army forces around Iran would offer two important advantages: a sharp increase in strike volume and the ability to deliver immediate fires. With the capabilities now approaching the force, southern Iran would no longer be the only part of the country within reach of Army missiles and one-way attack drones. All, or at least most, of Iranian territory as far as Tehran could fall under the Army’s long-range fires. As the Army becomes a serious long-range strike actor, it will take on a share of America’s precision-fire volume, with significant operational effects. That is already visible in Ukraine, where Russian one-way attack drones and ballistic missiles alone account for a large part of Russia’s deep-strike campaign. For that reason, the U.S. military presence around Iran is not merely a political question. It has serious technical implications. ones American planners are likely to weigh.

END

text:
استراتژی آتش دوربرد دقیق نیروی زمینی آمریکا، استقرار در اطراف ایران و حجم آتش موثر روی خاک ایران

پایگاه‌های آمریکا در خاورمیانه سالها نماد روابط امنیتی-نظامی ایالات متحده با کشورهای عربی بوده‌اند. این پایگاه‌ها نقش مهمی در عمق بخشی به راهبرد دفاعی آمریکا در خاورمیانه و اقیانوس هند ایفا می‌کنند. در جنگ 40 روزه، این پایگاه‌ها به یکی از نخستین اهداف حملات جمهوری اسلامی تبدیل شدند و خسارت‌های زیادی دیدند. با آشکار شدن این آسیب‌پذیری، برخی کارشناسان معتقدند پایگاه‌ها به تغییرات ساختاری یا کمی فاصله‌گیری نیاز دارند و ساختار فعلی را پاسخگوی تهدیدهای نوین نمی‌دانند. برخی دیگر، فراتر از نگاه فنی و از زاویه سیاسی، بر این باورند که آمریکا باید این پایگاه‌ها را به کلی ترک کند.

در جنگ 40 روزه، آمریکا کوشید با تکیه بر توان متحرک و امن‌تر ناوهای هواپیمابر، شناورهای موشک‌انداز، استقرار بخشی از هواگردها در پایگاه‌های دور از مرزهای ایران و اتکا به پدافند، حجم آتش خود را در خاک ایران حفظ کند. این تلاش با موشک‌های بالستیک زمین‌پرتاب نیروی زمینی آمریکا برای مناطق جنوبی ایران نسبتا تقویت میشد. برخی منابع مدعی‌اند نیروی زمینی آمریکا بیش از 1300 موشک بالستیک کوتاه‌برد به مناطق جنوبی ایران شلیک کرده است. در مجموع، نبود استقرار در مجاورت خاک ایران موضوع سوخترسان‌ها و افزایش حجم حملات را پیچیده‌تر میکند. با این حال، نیرویی که توانست نسبتا امن‌تر در اطراف ایران فعال بماند، پرتابگرهای موشکی و پهپادی نیروی زمینی آمریکا بود. عملیاتی نگه داشتن این سامانه‌ها، به‌دلیل امکان گسترش آن‌ها روی زمین، بهتر از سامانه‌های هوایی است که به فرودگاه‌های متمرکز وابسته‌اند. البته این کار حفاظت و اصول خاصی می‌طلبد. جنگ اخیر نشان داد سپاه پاسداران به اطلاعات ماهواره‌ای چین و روسیه دسترسی جدی دارد و همین امر می‌تواند این نیروها نیز را آسیب‌پذیر کند.

نیروی زمینی آمریکا برنامه بسیار گسترده‌ای برای تنوع بخشی به آتش دوربرد دقیق خود دارد. برنامه‌ای که توان ضربه به تمام خاک ایران، یا دست‌کم بخش عمده آن، را به‌طرز چشمگیری افزایش می‌دهد. قرار است این نیرو به انواع سامانه‌های موشکی و پهپادی زمین‌پرتابِ پیشرفته و ارزان قیمت مجهز شود و طیف وسیعی از تسلیحات را در حجمی بسیار بزرگ در اختیار بگیرد. از سامانه‌های پیشرفته و گران‌قیمتی مانند موشک هایپرسونیک دوربرد Dark Eagle با برد 2700 تا 3500km تا سلاح هایپرسونیک ارزان‌قیمت Blackbeard با برد 800km. نیروی زمینی آمریکا با سامانه تایفون قابلیت به کارگیری موشک کروز Tomahawk را نیز دارد. با این حال، قلب افزایش حجم آتش ارتش آمریکا بر توسعه انبوه تسلیحات ارزان‌قیمت استوار است. تسلیحاتی که می‌توانند نیروی زمینی را به درصد خوبی از توان فعلی آتش دوربرد نیروی دریایی و نیروی هوایی برسانند.

کلید این موفقیت آن است که نیروی زمینی آمریکا بتواند این تسلیحات را از نزدیک خاک ایران شلیک کند. بهبود حجم آتش بر کوچک‌سازی و ارزان‌سازی این سلاح‌ها بنا شده و این منطق با آتش هرچه نزدیک‌تر معنا پیدا می‌کند. با توجه به وضعیت پدافندی آسمان ایران، احتمالا طیفی از سامانه‌های ارزان‌قیمت می‌تواند روی بخش عمده خاک ایران کارآمد باشد، از جمله پهپادهای انتحاری LUCAS، موشک کروز Barracuda-500M با برد 900km  و موشک Anthem...

نکته‌ای که نباید از نظر دور داشت، نقش ویژه پرتابگرهای پرسرعت نیروی زمینی آمریکاست. امکان آتش سریع پس از کسب فوری اطلاعات به سامانه‌های موشکی و هایپرسونیک این نیرو اجازه می‌دهد با استقرار سریع، روی هدف فوری آتش پرسرعت ایجاد کنند(مانند هدف قراردادن لانچرهای موشکی). همین فرآیند با جنگنده‌ها و موشک‌های کروز معمولا طولانی‌تر است. حتی اگر جنگنده به سلاح هایپرسونیک مجهز باشد، مگر آنکه از پیش در حال عملیاتی بوده باشند.

در مجموع، حفظ استقرار نیروهای زمینی آمریکا در اطراف ایران امکان مهمی فراهم می‌کند: هم افزایش چشمگیر حجم آتش و هم آتش فوری. با امکاناتی خواهد آمد، دیگر تنها جنوب ایران هدف موشک‌ها و پهپادهای انتحاری نیروی زمینی آمریکا نخواهد بود، بلکه همه یا عمده خاک ایران تا تهران می‌تواند زیر ضربه بلندبرد این نیرو قرار گیرد. نیروی زمینی آمریکا با تبدیل شدن به بازیگری جدی در حملات بردبلند، بخشی از حجم آتش دوربرد دقیق آمریکا را در آینده به دست خواهد آورد و این امر آثار عملیاتی جدی خواهد داشت. چنانکه امروز پهپادهای انتحاری و موشک‌های بالستیک روسیه به تنهایی بار بخش بزرگی از آتش دوربرد روسیه به عمق خاک اوکراین را بر عهده دارند. از این رو، استقرار نیروهای آمریکا در اطراف ایران صرفاً موضوعی سیاسی نیست و ابعاد فنی جدی دارد، ابعادی که احتمالا آمریکایی‌ها به آن فکر خواهند کرد.
