text:
Off Leash update 29 September 2026

UK
•UK counterterrorism police release abruptly freed on bail the five men they’d arrested early Sunday near RAF Fairford on suspicions of plotting a terrorist attack on the base, which houses U.S. B-1 bombers.
•The men’s release suggested police didn’t find enough evidence to substantiate their initial terrorism allegations – though counterterrorism police chief Laurence Taylor said his force was still “considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals, either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state.”
•U.S. officials seem to think so. SecState Rubio said the incident “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor,” while Pres. Trump said the suspects “might” be linked to Iran and had been “under view for a long time.”

YEMEN
•The World Health Organization estimated that at least 838 people have died and over 3,000 have been injured since early August, when fighting resumed between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen.
•The Yemeni army says that Houthi fighters made up 476 of those killed and wounded in the last 24 hours alone.
•Government forces and Houthis are currently engaged in fierce fighting across 10 different fronts, and Saudi backing is proving to be insufficient to turn the tide in the army’s favor. The Yemeni government is reportedly pleading with the U.S. to step in and desperately trying to recruit more soldiers. It’s even enticing Houthi fighters to switch sides with offers of amnesty.

ETHIOPIA
•After Ethiopia’s army chief accused Egypt, Eritrea, and Sudan of backing the newly allied rebel forces fighting the government, The Economist pointed out that all three have a reason to.
•Egypt accuses Ethiopia of stealing its precious water resources with the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam; Eritrea resents Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s threats to annex part of its coastline for a port; and Sudan’s government despises Abiy’s support for the Rapid Support Forces it’s fighting in a brutal civil war.
•Fighting continues to intensify in the north, but government forces still seem to have the upper hand and control the air. They retook the southern Tigrayan town of Alamata – a key supply hub – back from rebels yesterday.

RUSSIA
•According to documents seen by Reuters, Russia plans to expand its 2027 military budget by 27% to 17.1 trillion rubles ($203 billion), which is the highest level planned since the start of the Ukraine war in 2022. [Russia’s actual military spend is classified but likely ends up being slightly higher than planned each year.]
•On the other side of the equation, the same documents showed that the Kremlin expects its budget deficit for 2026 to yawn to double its original estimate of 1.6% of GDP and land on 3.2% of GDP, or about 7.5 trillion rubles ($87 billion).
•The draft budget that planners will submit to parliament next week will offer clues as to how the Kremlin plans to close the fiscal gap. It has already announced tax increases for 2027, including a new windfall tax on mining companies that will raise an estimated 200 billion rubles per year.
•But taxes alone won’t be enough to close the gap – at least not at levels that Russian citizens or companies will tolerate. That’s perhaps why the Kremlin is also grabbing assets from the few foreign firms still operating in the country.
•This week, it placed the Russian assets of several major European firms – including France’s Leroy Merlin and Auchan, Germany’s Makro, and Switzerland’s Nestlé – under temporary administration, seizing company shares and replacing foreign managers in a possible first step towards confiscating or nationalizing the local subsidiaries.
•Moscow said the asset seizures were a response to “hostile actions” by “unfriendly” European governments, but it surely won’t mind the idea of squeezing foreigners instead of taxpayers for funds to help close the budget gap.

ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
•OpenAI said it won’t release its latest model, GPT-6.1 Astra, after the company’s own researchers raised concerns about the model’s behavior in testing.
•Specifically, Astra demonstrated a propensity for misleading its human users during tests and drifted worryingly from its prescribed scope without checking in for instructions.
•Instead of shipping Astra, OpenAI said it will focus on reinforcing safeguards in future models it plans to build atop the same base model.

𝐎𝐧 𝐒𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟐𝟗, 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔, 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐨𝐲𝐚𝐥 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐢 𝐀𝐫𝐦𝐲 (𝐑𝐓𝐀) 𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝟒,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐥, 𝟐𝟖𝟖 𝐯𝐞𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐥𝐞𝐬, 𝟐𝟎 𝐛𝐨𝐚𝐭𝐬, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐞𝐱𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐟 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐬𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐬, 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧 𝐁𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐤𝐨𝐤. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐀𝐫𝐦𝐲 𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐝 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐚𝐧𝐠 𝐊𝐚𝐩𝐢 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐋𝐚𝐭 𝐊𝐫𝐚𝐛𝐚𝐧𝐠 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐬, 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐛𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟏𝐬𝐭 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐲 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝐊𝐢𝐧𝐠'𝐬 𝐆𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐝) 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟐𝐧𝐝 𝐂𝐚𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐫𝐲 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝐊𝐢𝐧𝐠'𝐬 𝐆𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐝), 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐲. 𝐀𝐥𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡 𝐰𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐝𝐬 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐛𝐞𝐠𝐮𝐧 𝐭𝐨 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐝𝐞, 𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧 𝐁𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐤𝐨𝐤, 𝐥𝐨𝐰-𝐥𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐬, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐳𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐥𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐚𝐣𝐨𝐫 𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐨𝐧 𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐡 𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐫𝐭.

𝐌𝐨𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐒𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐞 𝐀𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧
𝐀𝐫𝐦𝐲 𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐤𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐨𝐧 𝐌𝐚𝐣𝐨𝐫 𝐆𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐖𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐢 𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐨𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐝𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐬:

𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐥: 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝟒,𝟎𝟎𝟎

𝐕𝐞𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐥𝐞𝐬: 𝟐𝟖𝟖 (𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐡-𝐜𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐤𝐬)

𝐁𝐨𝐚𝐭𝐬: 𝟐𝟎 (𝐢𝐧𝐟𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐫𝐮𝐛𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝐛𝐨𝐚𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐟𝐥𝐚𝐭-𝐛𝐨𝐭𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐨𝐚𝐭𝐬)

𝐌𝐨𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐟𝐢𝐞𝐥𝐝 𝐤𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐤𝐬: 𝟗

𝐔𝐧𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐀𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐕𝐞𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐥𝐞 (𝐔𝐀𝐕) 𝐬𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐬: 𝟐 𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐬

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐀𝐫𝐦𝐲 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐑𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐟 𝐂𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐜𝐨𝐨𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐀𝐫𝐦𝐲 𝐀𝐫𝐞𝐚, 𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐠𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐨𝐧𝐬, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐫𝐨𝐲𝐚𝐥 𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐚𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐨𝐩 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐞 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜 𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬.

𝐄𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧 𝐁𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐤𝐨𝐤: 𝐓𝐰𝐨 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐂𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬
𝐁𝐚𝐧𝐠 𝐊𝐚𝐩𝐢 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐭: 𝐌𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟏𝐬𝐭 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐲 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝐊𝐢𝐧𝐠'𝐬 𝐆𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐝). 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐊𝐡𝐞𝐡𝐚 𝐊𝐡𝐥𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐥𝐨𝐰-𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐲. 𝐓𝐫𝐨𝐨𝐩𝐬 𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐬𝐭 𝐢𝐧 𝐞𝐯𝐚𝐜𝐮𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐯𝐮𝐥𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐩𝐬, 𝐰𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐨𝐨𝐤𝐞𝐝 𝐦𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬, 𝐝𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐰𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐲.

𝐋𝐚𝐭 𝐊𝐫𝐚𝐛𝐚𝐧𝐠 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐭: 𝐌𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟐𝐧𝐝 𝐂𝐚𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐫𝐲 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝐊𝐢𝐧𝐠'𝐬 𝐆𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐝). 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐊𝐡𝐞𝐡𝐚 𝐑𝐨𝐦 𝐊𝐥𝐚𝐨 𝐥𝐨𝐰-𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐲, 𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐰𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐡. 𝐓𝐫𝐨𝐨𝐩𝐬 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐝𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐟𝐥𝐚𝐭-𝐛𝐨𝐭𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐨𝐚𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐡-𝐜𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐬𝐭 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐞𝐯𝐚𝐜𝐮𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐫𝐨𝐲𝐚𝐥 𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐮𝐭𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐨𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐰𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫. 𝐒𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐀𝐥𝐞𝐫𝐭 𝐙𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬
𝐏𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐮𝐦 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐢: 𝐀𝐥𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡 𝐰𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐝𝐬 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐝, 𝐥𝐨𝐰-𝐥𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐛𝐚𝐧𝐤𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐫𝐭. 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐲 𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐧 𝐒𝐚𝐦 𝐊𝐡𝐨𝐤 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐫𝐞𝐢𝐧𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐜𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐛𝐚𝐠 𝐛𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐝𝐰𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬.

text:
“We’ll meet again.” A Russian POW carried a wounded Ukrainian to safety — then promised to return to the war.

This is not a story about battlefield brotherhood.

It is a story about survival — and the strange logic war can produce.

Ukrainian Border Guard Dmytro, callsign TRYDE, was wounded in an ambush near Vovchansk. He and a fellow soldier survived the firefight, but Dmytro could no longer walk.

The nearest evacuation point was about 25 km away.

A Ukrainian search-and-strike group went to recover him. On the way, they captured two Russian soldiers.

The Ukrainians fed the POWs, gave them water and shared cigarettes. For Dmytro, after close combat and losing comrades, that was not easy.

But there was a rule that mattered more:

POWs are protected by international law.

When the situation in the sky finally allowed the evacuation to begin, the two Russians offered to help carry Dmytro out.

He did not mistake it for compassion.

They were deep inside a lethal combat zone. The Ukrainian position was under constant Russian pressure. For the prisoners, leaving with the Ukrainian group was also their best chance to survive.

One Russian carried Dmytro’s equipment.

The other, a contract soldier named Ivan, carried Dmytro himself.

They talked along the way.

Ivan told him he had signed a contract and gone to war for money. He spoke about the decision proudly.

Several times, Ivan became exhausted. Dmytro told him to leave him behind.

He refused and kept carrying him.

Then, about halfway through the route, they found an old bicycle in a tree line.

It became their improvised evacuation vehicle.

A wounded Ukrainian border guard. An abandoned bicycle. Two Russian POWs. And kilometers still separating them from safety.

Eventually, they reached Ukrainian positions.

Then came the part that stripped the story of any possible sentimentality.

Before they separated, Ivan told Dmytro that after a prisoner exchange, he planned to return to the war.

He needed the money.

He looked at Dmytro, smiled and said:

“We’ll meet again.”

Dmytro looked back at him.

“I’ll be looking forward to it.”

TRYDE is now undergoing rehabilitation. He wants to recover and return to his unit — where his comrades are still fighting.

Tasis Confronts the Army’s UN Narrative — Ahmed Taqad Lisan: Sudan’s War Is Ultimately a Struggle Over the Shape of the State

The New Republic – Nyala

In the aftermath of Sudan’s address to the United Nations General Assembly, Ahmed Taqad Lisan, spokesperson for the Sudan Founding Alliance, Tasis, offered a sharply critical political reading of the Sudanese army’s position on the war and the country’s future, placing the central dispute beyond the battlefield and within a broader struggle over the nature of the Sudanese state, the institutions that govern it, and who should have the authority to determine its political trajectory.

Taqad Lisan accused the Sudanese army and the Islamist movement of being responsible for igniting the war, arguing that they entered the conflict on the basis of flawed military calculations. He said the army’s leadership and the Islamist movement had believed the war could be settled within hours. His remarks constitute a political interpretation of the origins of the conflict, while the Founding Charter of Sudan identifies ending the war, addressing its underlying causes, and launching a new political process as central elements of the proposed reconstruction of the Sudanese state.

Taqad Lisan argues that continued reliance on a military solution reflects what he describes as the army leadership’s continued adherence to a security-first and military approach, saying it has been left with “no option other than continuing the war and attempting to impose a new reality through military force.” This position stands in contrast to Tasis’s stated conception of a transition away from the management of political conflict through armed force toward political and constitutional arrangements designed to redefine the institutions of the state and their relationship with civilian authority.

At the heart of this dispute is the slogan “one army, one weapon,” which Taqad Lisan described as “a statement of truth used for a false purpose.” His argument is not, as presented, a rejection of the principle of a unified national army, but a challenge over how such an army should be created and through what political and constitutional process.

The 2025 Transitional Constitution adopted by Tasis calls for the reconstruction of a unified, professional and national army operating under civilian authority, free from partisan, regional or tribal loyalties. Its stated role is to protect the country, its people and the democratic system rather than to intervene in political or economic affairs. In this framework, therefore, the concept of “one army” differs from simply preserving the existing military institution and incorporating other armed forces into it through military arrangements alone.

From this perspective, Taqad Lisan’s rejection of reducing military unification to a slogan corresponds with Tasis’s constitutional approach, which links the restructuring of the armed forces to a broader political process. The proposed arrangements include the reorganization of existing armed formations and the dismantling of armed structures affiliated with political parties, as part of a process grounded in constitutional order and civilian authority.

Taqad Lisan goes further, arguing that “these armies” cannot become a single unified national army except through political and negotiated arrangements. That position is consistent with Tasis’s broader proposition that the war cannot be brought to an end simply by one military actor achieving battlefield superiority, but requires a political settlement capable of redefining relations between military and civilian forces and laying the foundations for rebuilding state institutions.

XAU/USD – Price Analysis and Forecast: Gold Recovers, but Upside Potential Remains Limited
On Tuesday, the XAU/USD pair is showing a moderate recovery, trading slightly below the $4,150 level. However, the unfavorable fundamental backdrop is keeping the precious metal near the round $4,100 level.

The hawkish stance of the U.S. Federal Reserve, high U.S. Treasury yields, and geopolitical risks are supporting the U.S. dollar near a two-month high, limiting the upward potential for gold prices and calling for caution when opening positions based on expectations of a substantial increase in its price.
Earlier this month, the U.S. central bank raised its interest rate by 25 basis points, the first increase in more than three years, reaffirming its determination to combat persistently high inflation. In addition, several leading members of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) mentioned the potential need for further rate hikes through the end of 2026. According to CME Group's FedWatch tool, traders estimate the probability of another Fed rate hike in October at 70%, taking into account inflation risks driven by rising energy prices amid the conflict in the Middle East.

Federal Reserve Governor Adriana Kugler emphasized persistent inflationary pressures associated with the development of artificial intelligence and geopolitical risks, maintaining the Fed's hawkish stance. Her remarks, which received a score of 7 out of 10 from the FXS Speechtracker, above the baseline level of 6.9, point to continued inflationary pressure in the coming months. Kugler noted that future rate changes will depend on inflation data and labor market conditions, while emphasizing that productivity gains from AI could help slow inflation, but not quickly enough to offset current inflationary risks. The FXS Fed Sentiment Index declined by 0.63 points to 146.89, indicating a moderate easing of hawkish sentiment; however, the Fed's stance remains clearly hawkish. This means that any future rate hikes or the maintenance of rates at high levels will continue to support the U.S. dollar, even despite a slight cooling in market expectations.

Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump rejected an Iranian peace proposal concerning the settlement of the military conflict and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz if Tehran's demands were met. Trump also denied reports that he had offered Iran sanctions relief and the unfreezing of assets in exchange for specific steps regarding its nuclear program. Continued geopolitical tensions are keeping crude oil prices at high levels, increasing inflation concerns and pushing U.S. Treasury yields toward multi-year
In particular, the yield on 30-year U.S. Treasury bonds rose to its highest level since mid-May 2004, the yield on benchmark 10-year bonds reached its highest level since mid-June 2007, while the yield on 2-year bonds rose to its highest level since May 2024. This dynamic is strengthening the position of dollar bulls and makes it reasonable to expect continued buying until it is confirmed that gold prices have reached a bottom.

Market participants would be better advised to wait for the release of important U.S. macroeconomic data this week before opening significant directional positions in the XAU/USD pair.
On Wednesday, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index, a key inflation indicator monitored by the Fed, is due to be released, along with the final second-quarter GDP data. On Thursday, the ISM Manufacturing PMI will be released, but the main focus should be on the U.S. Nonfarm Payrolls (NFP) report, which will be published on Friday. In addition, speeches by influential FOMC members will also affect the market. This, in turn, will influence demand for the U.S. dollar and provide significant momentum for gold prices.

From a technical perspective, the XAU/USD pair maintains a bearish bias following the recent downside break of the 200-day exponential moving average (EMA). The oscillators are negative, confirming the bears' advantage in the market. The round $4,100 level provides support. The nearest resistance will be the 4170–4200 level. However, the key resistance levels before bearish pressure weakens are the important moving averages, including the 200-day EMA. The oscillators are negative, confirming the bears' advantage in the market.

text:
Tim Goss, Racing Bulls: "For the second leg of our triple-header, we head to the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, where we return to the Sepang International Circuit for what will be Formula 1’s first visit to the track since 2017. It is a circuit with a rich history and one that has consistently provided a challenging test for both drivers and teams.

"Characterised by its fast, sweeping corners and two long straights separated by a tight hairpin, it offers opportunities for overtaking while placing significant demands on the tyres. Pirelli bring the mid-range compound selection of C2, C3 and C4, and with higher tyre energies than Baku, we should expect degradation and tyre management to play a much greater role than at the previous race.

"On top of this, the weather can throw in another dimension. Conditions are typically hot and humid, with the ever-present threat of tropical rain, making it physically demanding for the drivers and presenting an additional challenge for our strategists.

"We have a slightly larger points buffer to defend following the last race; together with the support of everyone at the track and back at the factory, we will aim to get our preparation and execution spot on to maintain that momentum and extend the gap further."

Media Release - Fabletics opens its first store in India at DLF Promenade, New Delhi

The global activewear brand marks its India debut with an experience-led store, including an RFID-enabled fitting-room experience, in exclusive partnership with Reliance Brands Limited

New Delhi, 29th September 2026: Fabletics, the global activewear brand known for bringing together fashion-forward design and high-performance apparel at accessible price points, today opened its first store in India at DLF Promenade, New Delhi, in exclusive partnership with Reliance Brands Limited (RBL). The opening marks the brand’s formal retail entry into the country and brings a technology-driven approach to activewear to the Indian consumer.

The choice of DLF Promenade places Fabletics in one of Delhi-NCR’s most style-conscious retail destinations, home to a young, fashion-forward and increasingly fitness-oriented consumer. As Indian shoppers move fluidly between the studio, the workplace and everyday life, demand for performance apparel that is as considered in design as it is in function continues to grow – a shift the brand is built to serve.

The store is designed as an experience rather than a conventional retail floor. Its signature feature is an RFID-enabled fitting-room experience: as a customer enters the trial room, an in-room tablet automatically recognizes the products they have carried inside, displays them, and suggests alternative available sizes and styles that can be requested directly from the fitting room. This cutting-edge technology is grounded in creating a better and more enjoyable shopping experience for consumers and reflects Fabletics’ commitment to pairing technology with physical retail.

The launch drew an enthusiastic queue of more than 100 people. Visitors took part in a balance-board challenge and won exciting surprises from an in-store claw machine, while the DLF Promenade atrium hosted a movement pop-up and a pedal-powered smoothie station where guests cycled to blend their own complimentary smoothie.

Fabletics India collection will offer a versatile range of apparel and accessories for women and men, spanning leggings, pants and joggers, shorts, sports bras, tank tops, tops and polo shirts, sweatshirts, jackets and vests, along with bags and hats. Designed to bring together performance, comfort and contemporary style, the collection is created to move seamlessly from workouts and training to everyday life, offering versatile styles that support different ways of moving, dressing and living.

Commenting on the opening, Sumeet Yadav, Head, Reliance Brands Limited, said: “The Indian activewear consumer now expects apparel that performs as well as it looks, and Fabletics answers that with a rare combination of design, technology and accessibility. Opening our first store in Delhi, with a format built around experience and personalization, is the right way to introduce the brand, and we see significant headroom to grow Fabletics across the country.”

Meera Bhatia, President, Fabletics, added: “Opening our first store in India is a major milestone and an exciting opportunity for customers to experience Fabletics firsthand. The store brings together two core strengths of our brand: incredible product and technology designed around the customer, creating a retail experience that feels seamless, intuitive and personalized.”

The Fabletics store at DLF Promenade is now open to consumers, with an upcoming store launch planned in Mumbai.

STORE DETAILS

Store phone: +91 8178135467

Operating hours: 11 a.m. – 10 p.m., all days

text:
This isn't an e-bike upgrade. It's a 200-year-old loophole in physics that nobody ever patched.

Watch the clip once for the trick. Watch it twice for the physics. Then come back here, because what happens under those wheels is the reason ordinary human legs suddenly behave like they belong to someone else.

I'm going to give you the numbers, the history, the engineering, and the one thing that can actually kill you. By the end you'll want to try it. I'll tell you exactly why you shouldn't, and the single situation where you can.

Read slowly. The best part is in the middle.

———

THE NUMBER THAT RUNS THE WORLD

Every machine you have ever ridden in is fighting one enemy, and at bicycle speeds it isn't the air.

It's the ground.

More precisely, it's the energy that leaks out of a wheel every single time it rolls. Engineers boil that leak down to one figure: the rolling resistance coefficient. Multiply it by weight and you get the force you must beat just to keep moving. Not to accelerate. Not to climb. Just to not stop.

Here are the rough numbers for a wheel on a flat, hard surface:

Knobby mountain bike tire on loose gravel: 0.02 to 0.05 Car tire on asphalt: about 0.010 Good road bike tire on smooth asphalt: about 0.004 to 0.006 Steel wheel on a steel rail: about 0.001, sometimes less
Read the last line again.
A steel wheel on a steel rail loses roughly one fifth to one tenth of what your best road tire loses. Against gravel it's not even a contest. The surface is doing almost none of the fighting.
That single decimal point is why an entire continent's worth of cargo moves on two lines of iron instead of ten million trucks. It's why the railway won the nineteenth century. And it's why a thing that looks like a weekend hobby project is quietly doing something your car can't.

———

WHY STEEL IS ALMOST FREE

Why is the number so small?

Because of what a wheel does to the thing it rolls on.

A rubber tire is soft. Every rotation, the patch touching the road squashes flat, then springs back. That squashing and un-squashing is not free. Rubber is a lousy spring: it gives back only most of the energy it takes in. The rest turns into heat. Engineers call this hysteresis, and it's the main reason a tire gets warm on a long drive. You are literally paying, in fuel or in watts, to warm up rubber.

Steel doesn't do that. Steel is one of the best springs there is. When a steel wheel presses on a steel rail, both deform by a microscopic amount, then snap back and return nearly everything they borrowed.

And the contact patch is tiny. Under a heavy train wheel, the area actually touching the rail is often compared to the size of a small coin. That coin carries several tons. The pressure inside it climbs past a gigapascal, which is a number that would flatten most materials on earth.

Steel survives it. Steel is fine with it. Steel barely notices.

So you get a wheel that is hard, springy, and touching the world through a point of contact so small that almost nothing can drag. A locomotive is not a powerful machine pretending to be efficient. It's a stubborn one that found the one surface where stubbornness costs almost nothing.

Now hold that thought. Because the next section is where it gets unfair.

———

THE BACK-OF-ENVELOPE MATH THAT SHOULD BE ILLEGAL

Take a rider and a bike at about 100 kilograms total, cruising at 20 km/h. That's 5.6 meters per second, an easy pace.

On a good road tire, rolling resistance costs roughly 25 to 30 watts. On steel rails, roughly 5 to 6 watts.

Air drag on an upright rider at that speed is around 8 watts, and rails don't change that part.

So the total power to keep going drops from roughly 35 watts to roughly 13. Same legs. Same body. The bill for existing at that speed just fell by about sixty percent.

Now the part nobody expects.
Rolling resistance scales with weight. That's the whole formula: coefficient times mass times gravity. On the road, every extra kilogram is taxed at the road's rate. On rails, every extra kilogram is taxed at one fifth of that rate.

Which means you can add a lot of mass before the tax catches up. Take that same 27 watts you were losing to the road. On rails, it pays the rolling cost of about 500 kilograms.

Five hundred. For the price of one person on asphalt.

This is not a trick of clever design. It's a trick of where the machine is standing. The bike didn't get stronger. The floor got out of the way.

If you've ever wondered how a tiny motor can move something that looks far too heavy for it, that's the whole answer, and it's older than the light bulb.

Numbers are rounded, ignore bearings and joints, and your mileage will vary. The direction of the result is not in dispute.

———

THE PART EVERYONE GETS WRONG

Ask a hundred people what keeps a train on its rails and ninety-nine will say the flanges: the little lip on the inside of the wheel.

They're wrong. Or at least, they're describing the backup plan.

A railway wheel is not a cylinder. It's a shallow cone. The tread is tapered, typically around 1 in 20 in traditional designs, and the two wheels are fixed rigidly to one axle so they must turn together.

Now watch what geometry does on its own.

If the axle drifts a little to the left, the left wheel rides on a slightly larger diameter of its cone and the right wheel on a slightly smaller one. The larger wheel covers more ground per turn. The pair swings back toward the center. Overshoots. Swings back again.

No steering. No sensors. No software. A pair of cones on a stick, correcting itself for free, for two hundred years.

The flange is only there for emergencies and for tight curves. On a healthy straight track the wheel never touches it. The rail is holding the vehicle in place by shape alone, quietly, like a magnet made of geometry.

There is a catch, and a famous one. At higher speeds this self-centering becomes a self-oscillation: the wheelset starts swaying side to side faster and faster. Railway engineers call it hunting. A German engineer named Klingel worked out the basic math of it back in 1883, and modern high-speed trains still spend enormous effort keeping it under control.

So when you see something roll along a pair of rails with nobody steering it, you aren't watching luck. You're watching a piece of nineteenth-century mathematics that still hasn't been beaten.

———

HOW A HORSE TAUGHT THE WORLD TO CHEAT

Long before steam, somebody noticed the trick without understanding it.

Wooden wagonways were hauling coal in England by the early 1600s, with horses in front. Lay two smooth timber beams, run a cart on them, and one animal could move a load that would have bogged down a dozen on a muddy road. Period accounts and later estimates put the gain at several times, sometimes up to about ten times, what a horse could haul on an ordinary road.

Nobody called it physics. They called it profit.

Timber gave way to iron plates, then to iron rails, then to steel. In 1825 the Stockton and Darlington opened in northern England, and in 1830 the Liverpool and Manchester proved that steam on rails could carry people and goods at speeds no animal could touch. The gauge Stephenson used, 4 feet 8 and a half inches, is still the standard for more than half the railways on earth today.

That number has a legend attached: that it goes back to Roman chariot ruts, which supposedly matched the width of two horses. It's a wonderful story. It's also largely a myth. The real answer is duller and stranger: it was inherited from the colliery wagonways of northern England, where it happened to be what the carts were built to. Half of modern logistics rests on a number picked because it was the size of the things already lying around.

Hold that idea. Standards are rarely designed. They're survived.

———

THE MAN WHO INVENTED THE BIKE AND THEN PUT IT ON RAILS

In 1817, a German forester and inventor named Karl Drais built a two-wheeled machine you sat on and pushed along with your feet. No pedals. No chain. It became known as the draisine, or the dandy horse, and it is the ancestor of every bicycle ever made.

Here's the twist most people never hear.

Drais didn't stop at roads. Rail-running versions of his idea followed, human-powered vehicles built to skim along the track, and his name stuck to them. In German the word Draisine still means a light rail vehicle. In French it's draisine. In Russian it turned into drezina, a word that today covers everything from hand-pumped track inspection carts to small motorized railcars.

Sit with that. The man who gave us the bicycle also gave the world's railways the word for their smallest, lightest, most human-scaled vehicle.

The bicycle and the rail-bike are not two inventions. They are one idea that went down two different roads, and every so often, on the right stretch of iron, they meet again.

And then in the nineteenth century, America turned that meeting into a job.

———

THE SECTION HAND'S SECRET WEAPON

By the 1870s and 1880s, American railroads had a problem: thousands of miles of track, and crews who had to walk it. Then came light handcars, pump cars, and velocipede cars, machines that let one or two workers cover miles of line in minutes instead of hours. One famous maker, Sheffield, in Three Rivers, Michigan, sold lightweight track cars that a single worker could lift off the rails and carry aside when a train approached.

Read that again. Lift off the rails. Carry aside.

The entire design philosophy was: be so light and so cheap to push that the vehicle is barely there. A machine you could drag out of the way with your hands, yet strong enough to carry a crew and their tools across a county before lunch.

Later came gasoline "speeders," small motor cars that turned inspectors into commuters of the steel road. Sections of every major line were patrolled this way for generations.

And then, mostly, it disappeared. Trucks got better. Rail got consolidated. Whole branch lines went quiet and were abandoned, leaving thousands of kilometers of perfectly good track with no one on it.

Perfectly good track. Sitting there. Waiting.

Which brings us to the modern chapter, and to the reason this clip found you.

———

THE SECOND LIFE OF DEAD RAILWAYS

Somewhere in the last few decades, people started asking a question that railways had forgotten: what if the track is the product?

In Japan, a former rail line in Gifu Prefecture became the home of Gattan Go, a rail-bike attraction where visitors pedal cars along old track through the countryside. In South Korea, disused lines in Gangwon Province were turned into rail-bike parks with tunnels and river views, and they became so popular that reservations sell out. In the United States, operators lease old lines and run pedal-powered rail cars for tourists. Similar projects have appeared in Europe, Australia, and elsewhere.

Look at what they all share:

A line nobody uses. A vehicle that is barely more than a frame and some wheels. A surface so efficient that ordinary people with no training can cover kilometers without tiring, often carrying more weight than they'd ever manage on the road.

A railway is expensive to build and impossible to justify once the freight leaves. But a railway that already exists is the smoothest, straightest, lowest-effort path across the landscape that human beings have ever constructed. Leave it empty and it rots. Put pedals on it and it becomes a destination.

That's the business model. The physics is the free part.

———

WHY GRAVITY SUDDENLY BECOMES YOUR ENEMY

Here's a detail that separates people who understand rails from people who just like the aesthetic.

When rolling resistance falls to almost nothing, something else takes over as the main obstacle: slope.

The force of gravity along a hill is roughly weight times the gradient. A gentle 1 percent grade, one meter of climb per hundred meters forward, adds a force equal to about one hundredth of the vehicle's weight.

On a rail, the rolling resistance is about one thousandth.

Do the division. A hill that most drivers wouldn't even notice costs ten times more than the entire rolling loss of the vehicle. Ten times.

This is why railways look the way they do. They cut through hills instead of climbing them. They cross valleys on viaducts nobody would bother building for a road. They take enormous detours to keep the gradient under a percent or two on main lines. The surface is so efficient that the only real enemy left is height, so engineers spent a century building the world's most expensive, most patient, most obsessive engineering to avoid even small hills.

Next time you see an old railway curving for no obvious reason across a landscape, understand: that curve is not an accident. That curve is a battle, lost or won, against one percent.

———

THE ELECTRIC HELPER, AND THE MOTOR THAT DOESN'T NEED TO TRY

Now put a small electric motor into this picture.

A common road e-bike is limited to 250 watts of assistance in the European Union and up to 750 watts in much of the United States. On asphalt, those numbers are the difference between working and coasting.

On rails, they are absurd.

Take a combined load of 400 kilograms rolling at about 25 km/h. Rolling resistance at 0.001 comes to roughly 4 newtons. Air drag on an upright rider, at that speed, is perhaps 15 newtons. Add them up: about 19 newtons, at about 7 meters per second. That's roughly 130 watts to hold a steady pace.

A hundred and thirty watts. Half of what the smallest legal motor can offer, with a person still pedaling on top.

It's a back-of-envelope figure. It ignores bearing friction, track joints, wind, curves, and every real-world thing that makes numbers messier. But even if you double it, the conclusion doesn't change: the motor is not the hero here.

The rail is.

———

THE PRICE OF SLIPPERY

Every miracle has an invoice. This is the invoice.

The same smoothness that makes steel-on-steel so cheap to roll makes it terrible to stop.

Friction between a steel wheel and a steel rail, the thing that lets you brake and accelerate, is far lower than between a tire and a road. On a dry rail, engineers work with an adhesion coefficient in the neighborhood of 0.2 to 0.3. On a wet rail, it can fall to around 0.1. And when the rail is contaminated, it can drop lower still.

Autumn is the famous villain. Leaves get crushed under passing wheels and bake into a thin, slick film on the railhead. Railways in northern countries spend real money every year fighting it, with special trains that blast the rail clean and lay down sand for grip. "Leaves on the line" is a British joke and a genuine operational headache.

Now translate that into stopping distance. The basic formula is speed squared divided by twice the friction coefficient times gravity.

At a gentle 20 km/h with a coefficient of 0.1, a vehicle needs around 16 meters to stop by friction alone. With 0.3, about 5 meters.

That doesn't sound like much until you remember something: those numbers assume the brakes are strong enough to lock the wheels, and that nothing else is moving on the same line.

Scale the same physics up to a heavy freight train and you get the sentence that safety organizations repeat because it's true: a train at highway speed can need a mile or more to stop.

The lesson is simple, and it's not a comfortable one. Rails give you speed and weight for almost nothing. They give you stopping power only reluctantly. A machine that is easy to start is not automatically easy to stop.

———
THE INVISIBLE SYSTEM YOU'RE NOT THINKING ABOUT

Here is the part that keeps railway safety people up at night.

A working railway is not just two rails. It's a nervous system.

On many lines, the rails themselves carry a small electrical signal. When a train's steel axles bridge the two rails, they short-circuit that signal, and the control system knows a train is there. The signals ahead turn red. Junctions lock. Level crossings drop their barriers. This is called a track circuit, and it is one of the quiet foundations of modern rail safety.

Now imagine a light vehicle with plastic or insulated wheels. It rolls along the rails. It weighs almost nothing. It doesn't short the circuit.

To the railway's control system, it does not exist.

That's not a theoretical problem. It's why light rail-going vehicles have been a headache for railway engineers for as long as they've existed, and why the world's rail-bike attractions operate almost exclusively on lines that are closed to normal traffic, or fully controlled by the operator. On a live line, a lightweight vehicle can be invisible to signals and invisible to the person driving a locomotive that cannot stop in time.

So here is the sentence I promised you at the start.

Never ride, push, drive, or place anything on an active railway. Not on a quiet branch line. Not "just for a minute." Modern trains are quiet, they look slower than they are, and as we just calculated, they cannot stop. Even a disused-looking track can still belong to somebody and still see a train.

The legal way to do this is boring and wonderful: find an operator that runs rail-bike tours on a closed line, or get written permission from the owner of a private track. That's it. That's the whole guide.

The physics is free. The consequences are not.

———

THE WHEEL YOU CAN'T ESCAPE

Materials matter more than people think.

Steel wheels give you the lowest rolling loss, but they're loud, heavy, and unforgiving on rough track. Polyurethane and nylon wheels are quieter, lighter, and cheaper, and they have somewhat higher rolling resistance, but they're far easier on the track and the passengers. Aluminum frames keep the weight down, and aluminum, at about a third of the density of steel, is the reason a whole platform can be light enough for one person to handle.

Then there's the track itself.

Modern rails are heavy, often around 60 kilograms per meter. They sit on sleepers, and the sleepers sit on ballast, the sharp crushed stone you see between and beside the tracks. That stone isn't decoration. Its angular edges lock together like a giant three-dimensional puzzle, spreading load, draining water, and holding the whole line in place.

Old jointed track has gaps between rail sections, which is where the famous clickety-clack comes from. Newer continuous welded rail has no gaps. Steel expands with heat, roughly 12 millionths per degree Celsius, so a kilometer of rail heated by 50 degrees would want to grow by about 60 centimeters if it were free. Welded track is anchored to keep that from happening, and in extreme heat, when it can't be, the rail can buckle in what's called a sun kink.

A railway looks like the simplest thing in the world: two lines and some stones. It's actually a machine a hundred kilometers long, and every single part is fighting the weather.

———

THE MOST EFFICIENT MACHINE ON EARTH MEETS THE MOST EFFICIENT SURFACE

In 1973, an article in Scientific American ranked the energy efficiency of animals and machines moving over a distance. The winner among all of them, per unit of body weight, wasn't a cheetah or a condor.

It was a human on a bicycle.

The reason is a combination of things: a rider's legs work in a smooth rotary motion, a chain drive wastes only a few percent of what it receives, and two thin wheels with pumped-up tires barely touch the ground. The bicycle is a machine built so that a mediocre engine, the human body, gets the maximum out of every calorie.

Now place that machine on the most efficient land surface humans have ever built.

Two systems, both optimized for the same thing: turning very little energy into very much distance. Stack them and you don't get addition. You get multiplication.

Railways themselves make the same point at industrial scale. The freight rail industry regularly cites figures of roughly 470 to 480 miles moved per ton of cargo on a single gallon of fuel in the United States. That's an industry-reported number and it should be treated with care, but the ordering isn't controversial: rail moves freight with less energy per ton-mile than trucks do, often by a factor of three or four.

Two hundred years of engineering pointing in one direction. And here we are, watching a person and a small motor and some wheels, borrowing all of it.

———

QUESTIONS YOU'RE ABOUT TO ASK IN THE REPLIES

Can it go uphill? Yes, but remember section 9. One percent costs ten times the rolling loss. A real climb is a real workout, and coming back down is a real braking problem.

How fast can it go? Far faster than it should. The limit is not the wheels. It's braking, track condition, and the fact that a light vehicle on rails has no way to swerve. Every extra kilometer per hour buys you a lot more stopping distance, because that distance grows with the square of speed.

What about corners? Rails are laid out in curves with gentle radii, and the outer rail is often raised slightly, called cant, so the vehicle leans into the turn. Slow vehicles handle curves easily. Fast ones are how you learn what a flange is for.

Does rain matter? A great deal. Wet rail means less grip for braking. Wet leaves mean much less. Rail-bike operators cancel tours in bad weather for a reason.

Can I just build one? Building the vehicle is the easy part. The parts that matter are the gauge, the wheel profile, the brakes, the weight distribution, and above all the track: who owns it, who is allowed on it, and whether a train can still arrive. If you can't answer the last three, the first three don't matter.

———

WHY YOU CAN'T LOOK AWAY

Forget the physics for a second. Why does this kind of scene grab the brain and refuse to let go?

Because it's freedom with the steering removed.

Every vehicle you've ever driven asks something of you: watch the road, correct the line, brake for the corner. A rail vehicle asks for none of it. The path has already been decided by somebody else, two hundred years ago, with a level and a surveyor. All you're left with is the good part: motion, scenery, wind, and momentum.

There's a second hook, and it's about scale mismatch. We're trained to expect that moving a big load needs a big machine. When the machine is small and the load is large, our brains register a kind of glitch, a violation of the expected order of things. That's the tiny jolt of delight you felt on the first watch. The mind loves an impossible-looking thing that turns out to be possible.

And the third: the landscape. A railway is a line drawn through a place. It shows you the back of a country, the side you never see from the highway: fields, water, forgotten stations, and stretches of quiet nobody planned for tourists. Rails go where roads don't bother to.

Put those three together and you get something rare on the internet: an image that's calm, strange, and slightly enviable all at once.

———

THE CHEAT SHEET

If you only remember one screen from this, make it this one.

Steel on steel rolls about five to ten times easier than a good road tire. The gap comes from rubber's hysteresis, a heat loss that steel barely has. Coned wheels on a solid axle steer themselves. The flange is the backup. On rails, a 1 percent slope costs about ten times the rolling loss. Adhesion is low: roughly 0.2 to 0.3 dry, about 0.1 wet, lower with leaves. Braking distance grows with the square of speed. Lightweight vehicles can be invisible to track circuits on signaled lines. The Russian drezina, French draisine and German Draisine all trace back to Karl Drais. Never enter an active railway. Use closed lines with permission, or an operator.

———

THE QUESTION I'LL LEAVE YOU WITH

Everything you just read was known, in pieces, by the 1880s.

The steel was there. The bicycle was there. The track was there, laid out across continents and mostly abandoned. What's changed is only that a few people connected two old ideas and let the physics do the rest.

That's the pattern behind a lot of things that seem new. Not invention. Recombination. Somebody notices that two solved problems, put together, leave an unsolved problem sitting in the middle, and quietly solves it with a wheel and a bracket.
So here's what I'd ask you to do.
Go back to the clip. Watch it with the numbers in your head this time. Watch what the machine isn't doing. Watch how little effort is on screen, and remember that the missing effort isn't magic. It's a coefficient. It's 0.001.
Then think about what else in your life is being taxed at the wrong rate, where you're paying full price to roll on rubber when a rail already exists somewhere nearby.
If this was worth your time, do three things. Send it to the friend who always says there must be a smarter way. Save it, because you'll want the numbers. And follow, because the next one is going to make you look at something ordinary and ask why nobody told you.
The rail was always there. Just there.

text:
Black Flag, Grey Fog — Utrecht
The pine needles were wet enough to silence even the best boots. That was the only mercy the forest offered.
Sergeant-Major Koen Visser of the Netherlands Korps Commandotroepen — attached for this rotation to a joint EU rapid-response element — moved down the track with the suppressor of his C8 still warm against his glove. Behind him the Fennek recce vehicle sat half-swallowed by mist, its engine ticking as it cooled. The EU stars on his left shoulder were the only colour left in a world of black nylon, wet bark and mud.
The target had been a logistics node three kilometres north: a farmhouse that wasn’t a farmhouse. They had gone in quiet, come out quieter. No shots fired that the world would ever hear. That was the point.
Now the extraction window was closing and the radio in his chest rig hissed with coordinates that would put them on a Dutch Navy NH90 before last light. From there it was inland, over the low country, toward the Dom and the ring of canals. Utrecht. Not the loudest city in the Netherlands, but the one that sat in the middle of everything — railways, highways, old brick and new glass. A place that understood that Europe’s security sometimes looked like this: a man in a respirator walking out of someone else’s woods so that the lights along the Oudegracht could stay on and the trains through Utrecht Centraal could keep running on time.
Visser adjusted the sling, checked the patch one last time, and kept walking. The fog would lift. Utrecht would still be there. That was the deal.

text:
Instead, something inside me went completely still.

“You’re choosing them,” I said.

Weston exhaled as though I were making the moment more difficult than necessary.

“I’m choosing my family’s future.”

I almost smiled. Not because anything was funny. Because the line was so polished, so rehearsed, so empty of the two people standing before him that I knew he had practiced it somewhere else.

I looked down at Marlo. Her eyelashes were fine and damp as silk. One hand had slipped free from the blanket, five impossibly tiny fingers resting against my gown.

Then I looked back at my husband.

“Remember this moment,” I said quietly, “because it is the last one you will ever get from us.”

Weston stared at me.

Then he laughed.

It was soft, almost affectionate—the kind of laugh a man gives a woman he believes is too exhausted to mean what she says.

He had no idea that by the next morning, I would stop waiting for him.

He had no idea an estate attorney had been calling me for three weeks about a folder I had not yet opened.

And he had no idea that the daughter he refused to hold would become the one person the Callaway family could not afford to dismiss.

Four years earlier, Weston Callaway entered my life with the quiet assurance of a man who had never questioned whether a room would make space for him. I met him during a contract review meeting on the twenty-third floor of a glass office tower in uptown Charlotte, where conference rooms were named after rivers and the coffee sat in metal carafes nobody finished.

Back then, I was a contracts auditor for a midsize firm, the kind of job that made people’s eyes glaze over at dinner parties until they needed someone to explain why a clause hidden on page thirty-two could cost them six figures. I liked the work. It was exact. It rewarded patience. It taught me that people rarely hide the truth in dramatic places. They hide it in fine print, missing signatures, and dates that do not match.

Weston arrived late to that first meeting in a navy suit and offered no apology, only a calm nod to the room. He was handsome in a way that seemed built less on features than ease. Dark blond hair, gray eyes, relaxed shoulders beneath tailoring that had clearly never touched a sale rack. His family owned Callaway Holdings, a real estate and hospitality group that had begun with one roadside motel outside Asheville and grown into resorts, office towers, restaurants, and private clubs where people pretended not to discuss money while organizing their lives around it.

He did not flirt with me during that meeting. That was probably why I noticed him.
Men like him usually made women aware of their attention as if it were a privilege. Weston listened. When I pointed out a risk in a vendor renewal clause, he did not cut me off. He asked one question, then another. Afterward, while everyone gathered laptops and paper cups, he thanked me by name.

“Sable Reed,” he said, reading from the folder in front of him. “You saved us from an expensive headache.”

“I save people from headaches for a living.”

He smiled. “That sounds more useful than most jobs.”

It was a small thing. A clean thing. I had no reason to distrust it.

Our first date was at a quiet Italian restaurant in Dilworth with low lighting and brick walls, the sort of place where the waiter describes the olive oil. Weston asked about my work, my family, and the books on my apartment shelves. He did not check his phone. He did not speak over me. When I told him my sister Odette lived in Savannah and called every Sunday whether I answered or not, he smiled and said loyalty sounded better when it was inconvenient….

Trump denies Iran concessions in ‘hoax’ report
The US president has rejected claims that he is prepared to ease sanctions in exchange for steps on Tehran’s nuclear program
Published 28 Sep, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/GzqbQXWiba
US President Donald Trump has denied offering any concessions to Iran after indirect negotiations resumed in New York on Monday in the hopes of ending the war he launched alongside Israel against the Islamic Republic seven months ago.
Trump took to social media to refute an Axios report claiming that he was prepared to lift some sanctions and release frozen Iranian funds in return for “concrete Iranian steps” regarding its nuclear program. AP published similar claims early Tuesday morning, also citing US officials.
“This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING! Axios’ story, like most others, is a HOAX, used only for purposes of satisfying their Trump Derangement Syndrome,” he wrote on Truth Social, demanding that the “fake story” be taken down.
US and Iranian officials met separately with mediators on the sidelines and are expected to focus on a revised proposal submitted by Tehran last week during the UN General Assembly, according to Reuters.
Trump confirmed on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s proposal for a seven-day ceasefire that would have reopened the Strait of Hormuz, arguing that he sought a better deal. The US president has emphasized that his primary goal is to dismantle Iran’s nuclear program and ensure that Tehran never acquires nuclear weapons.
Iran, meanwhile, has maintained that its nuclear program is entirely peaceful and that uranium enrichment is its right as a sovereign state.
The situation remains tense around the Strait of Hormuz, where disruptions to shipping are driving up energy prices worldwide. On Wednesday, an Indian sailor was killed after a projectile struck the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged cargo ship Cape Dao. Although Iran has not claimed responsibility for the attack, it has previously warned vessels passing through the strait not to use the “illegal” routes designated by the US Navy.

Wrong. 

The bringing back the Jewish people back to their homeland was from the Babylonian Captivity. 

Their exile began in 586 BC when King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon captured Jerusalem, destroyed the Temple, and deported a significant portion of the population to Babylon. This period of exile was marked by a deep sense of loss and longing for the homeland, as expressed in Psalm 137:1 : "By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept when we remembered Zion."

After 70 years in captivity, and the after the fall of Babylon to the Persian Empire, King Cyrus issued a decree allowing the exiled Jews to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple. This event is recorded in Ezra 1:2-3 :

 "This is what Cyrus king of Persia says: 'The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth and has appointed me to build a house for Him at Jerusalem in Judah. Whoever among you belongs to His people, may his God be with him, and may he go to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel. He is the God who is in Jerusalem.'"

The return from exile was not just a physical journey but also a spiritual renewal. The books of Ezra and Nehemiah detail the challenges and triumphs of the returning exiles as they rebuilt the Temple and the walls of Jerusalem. Nehemiah 8:8 highlights the spiritual revival that accompanied the return: "So they read from the Book of the Law of God, translating and giving the meaning so that the people could understand what was being read."

The return from exile is also seen as a fulfillment of God's promises and a testament to His faithfulness. Isaiah 44:28 prophesied about Cyrus, saying, 

"who says of Cyrus, 'He is My shepherd, and he will accomplish all that I please'; he will say of Jerusalem, 'Let it be rebuilt,' and of the temple, 'Let its foundations be laid.'"

The exile and return are significant in understanding God's relationship with His people. The exile serves as a reminder of the consequences of disobedience, while the return underscores God's mercy and faithfulness. 

This exile and return also foreshadows the ultimate redemption through Jesus Christ, who offers spiritual restoration and reconciliation with God. The themes of exile and return resonate with the Christian experience of sin and redemption, emphasizing the hope of restoration and the promise of a future home with God.

text:
FASTING: Training the Body, Strengthening the Spirit - A Christian Discipline for Drawing Nearer to God

Fasting Is About Far More Than Food
Fasting can easily be misunderstood as simply not eating. Christian fasting is much deeper. It is the deliberate decision to temporarily surrender something the body desires so that we can become more attentive to what the soul needs.
Jesus did not speak of fasting as something strange or reserved only for monks, priests, or exceptionally holy people. In Matthew 6, He said, “When you fast…” - not if you fast. Prayer, charity, and fasting have long stood together as fundamental Christian disciplines.

For a man pursuing spiritual masculinity, fasting has another powerful dimension: self-mastery.
A man cannot lead himself well if every appetite gets a vote and every desire gets its way.
Hunger says, Feed me.
Comfort says, Make life easier.
Anger says, React.
Lust says, Take what you want.
Pride says, Prove yourself.
The disciplined Christian man learns that he does not have to obey every impulse that enters his body or mind. Fasting becomes practice for saying:
“My desires do not command me. God does.”
That makes fasting spiritual training. We voluntarily surrender something good for a period of time so that we can pursue Someone greater.
The guide you shared presents seven excellent principles: have the right motive, determine your purpose, start slowly, prepare spiritually, plan your fast, use the time wisely, and stay hydrated. Each deserves a closer look.

1. HAVE THE RIGHT MOTIVE
Fast for God, Not for Attention

The first question isn't “What am I giving up?”
It is:
“Why am I doing this?”
Jesus was particularly direct about fasting for appearances:
“Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance…” — Matthew 6:16

Fasting isn't a spiritual performance.
We don't fast to impress people with our discipline, advertise our holiness, lose a few pounds under a religious label, or prove that we are tougher than somebody else.
The purpose is God.
That makes humility essential.
A spiritually mature man does not need everyone to know about every sacrifice he makes. Some of the greatest victories of his life may occur where nobody sees them except God.
There is masculine strength in learning to do difficult things without needing applause.
Before beginning a fast, therefore, ask:
Am I doing this to draw closer to God?
Am I seeking His will—or merely trying to get Him to approve mine?
Am I willing to be changed through this?
HUMILITY • SINCERITY • SURRENDER

2. DETERMINE YOUR PURPOSE
Know Why You Are Fasting
The guide correctly emphasizes identifying a purpose.
A fast becomes far more meaningful when connected to prayerful intention.
You might fast while seeking wisdom concerning an important decision. You might fast for your marriage or family. You could fast while praying for a child or grandchild, asking for greater freedom from a persistent temptation, seeking forgiveness, discerning a new season of life, or simply desiring greater closeness with God.
The danger is treating fasting like a transaction:
“God, I'm giving this up, so now You owe me this.”
That isn't fasting.

We don't manipulate God through sacrifice.
Instead we say:
“Lord, I am making room for You. Change whatever needs changing in me.”
Sometimes we begin a fast asking God to change our circumstances and discover that God uses the fast to change us.
That may be the greater answer.
“Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you.” - James 4:8

PURPOSE • DISCERNMENT • INTENTION

3. START SLOW
Discipline Is Built, Not Demonstrated
The image offers practical wisdom: if you're inexperienced with fasting, don't begin by attempting something extreme.
That is not weakness. It is prudence.
You might begin with one meal, a limited period, or another modest form of fasting appropriate to your circumstances. The point isn't to see how miserable you can make yourself.
The purpose is spiritual attentiveness, not punishment.
This also reflects an important principle of masculine discipline.
We often want dramatic transformation.
God frequently works through consistency.
One prayer becomes a prayer habit.
One chapter of Scripture becomes daily reading.
One disciplined morning becomes a routine.
One small sacrifice teaches us that discomfort doesn't control us.
Then we build.
This is spiritual progressive resistance: train the soul as deliberately as you would train the body.

“He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much.” - Luke 16:10

BEGIN • PRACTICE • GROW

4. PREPARE SPIRITUALLY
Don't Just Empty the Stomach—Prepare the Heart
This may be the most important point in the entire guide.
A Christian fast without prayer can easily become little more than skipping lunch.
Preparation changes that.
Confess your sins.
Examine your conscience.
Read Scripture.
Forgive someone you've been holding resentment toward.
Ask God what needs to change.
Enter the fast with humility.
This is where fasting can become uncomfortable in an entirely different way.
Physical hunger is one thing.
Spiritual honesty is another.

When the distractions disappear, we may encounter things inside ourselves we have avoided: anger, pride, jealousy, fear, resentment, impatience, lust, selfishness, unforgiveness, or simply the realization that we've slowly moved God toward the margins of our lives.
Don't waste that discovery.
Bring it to Him.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10 

CONFESS • EXAMINE • RENEW

5. PLAN YOUR FAST
Discipline Requires Intention
The guide recommends deciding beforehand what kind of fast you will undertake and how long it will last.
That is wise because vague intentions are easy to negotiate away once discomfort arrives.
Determine what you are fasting from.
Determine when the fast begins.
Determine when it ends.
Determine what you will do when hunger or temptation arrives.
And determine what spiritual practice will replace what you've surrendered.

This principle extends beyond food.

There may be seasons when a person chooses to abstain from something else that has become disproportionately important—social media, entertainment, unnecessary spending, television, or another comfort—in order to devote that attention to prayer and God.
The deeper question becomes:
What owns too much of me?
That's a worthwhile question for every man.
If I cannot voluntarily walk away from something for a while, perhaps I should consider whether I possess it—or it possesses me.

“All things are lawful unto me, but I will not be brought under the power of any.” — 1 Corinthians 6:12

INTENTION • ORDER • SELF-MASTERY

6. USE THE TIME WISELY
Replace Consumption With Communion
This is where fasting truly becomes spiritual.
Suppose you normally spend thirty minutes eating lunch.
You fast through lunch but spend those thirty minutes scrolling on your phone.
You've certainly skipped a meal—but spiritually, very little has changed.
Instead, take the time normally devoted to whatever you surrendered and give it to God.

Pray.
Read Scripture.
Journal.
Sit quietly.
Attend Mass if possible.
Pray the Rosary.
Take a prayer walk.
Write down what God may be showing you.
Pray specifically for your wife, children, grandchildren, friends, and people who are suffering.

This is where hunger itself can become a reminder.

When your stomach says, I'm hungry, let your spirit answer:
“Then it is time to pray.”
Hunger becomes a bell calling you back to God.

“Be still, and know that I am God.” — Psalm 46:10 

PRAY • LISTEN • WORSHIP

7. STAY HYDRATED AND USE WISDOM
Discipline Is Not Recklessness
The guide concludes with a practical reminder about hydration, and that deserves emphasis.
Christian discipline should never become a contest in unnecessary suffering.
There is no spiritual trophy for making yourself sick.

For ordinary fasting, hydration matters. And people who are older, pregnant, have diabetes or other medical conditions, take medications affected by food intake, have a history of eating disorders, or have other health concerns should seek appropriate medical guidance before undertaking significant food fasting.

There are many ways to practice sacrifice without irresponsibly endangering health.

That distinction matters to spiritual masculinity.
Courage isn't recklessness.
A mature man knows the difference between discomfort that strengthens him and behavior that unnecessarily harms him.
God gave us bodies to steward, not abuse.

“Your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you…” - 1 Corinthians 6:19

WISDOM • STEWARDSHIP • DISCIPLINE

WHAT FASTING TEACHES A MAN ABOUT HIMSELF
This is where I think fasting becomes particularly powerful when viewed through the lens of spiritual masculinity.
Eventually hunger starts talking.
And hunger is persuasive.
One bite won't matter.
You have already proved your point.
Nobody will know.
You deserve this.
That conversation is bigger than food.
Those are essentially the same arguments temptation uses throughout life.
Fasting gives us an opportunity to practice answering:
No.
Not because food is bad.
Not because pleasure is sinful.
Not because the body is our enemy.
But because a Christian man should be capable of governing his appetites rather than being governed by them.

The lesson transfers.

If I can practice saying no to food when food is permissible, I strengthen my ability to say no when something is not permissible.
Fasting therefore teaches one of the great lessons of disciplined living:
I can experience a desire without obeying it.
That is self-mastery.

FASTING, PRAYER, AND ALMSGIVING

Within the Catholic tradition, fasting becomes especially meaningful when joined with prayer and almsgiving.
Think of the three together:
Fasting removes something.
Prayer fills the space with God.
Almsgiving turns our attention toward others.
Without prayer, fasting can become self-improvement.
Without charity, fasting can become self-absorption.
Together, they move us away from ourselves.
One practical approach is beautifully simple: if you skip a meal, consider giving what you would have spent on that meal to someone in need.
Now the sacrifice accomplishes three things:
Your body learns discipline.
Your soul turns toward God.
Your sacrifice serves another person.
That is Christian formation in action.

A POWERFUL SCRIPTURE FOR SPIRITUAL MASCULINITY
A particularly fitting passage is St. Paul's description of disciplining himself:
“But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection…” - 1 Corinthians 9:27 (KJV)

The broader passage compares spiritual life to athletic training.
That is a tremendous model for spiritual masculinity.
An athlete doesn't hate his body. He trains it.

He doesn't eliminate appetite. He learns to govern it.

He doesn't wait until he feels motivated. He practices discipline.

And he doesn't train once and declare himself finished. He returns tomorrow. 
So should we.

DISCIPLINE • SACRIFICE • MASTERY

Conclusion — Sometimes Strength Is Simply Saying No
Fasting turns the ordinary experience of hunger into spiritual training.
It teaches us that we don't have to satisfy every desire immediately.
We don't need constant comfort.
We don't need endless stimulation.
We don't have to obey every appetite.
And perhaps most importantly:

We discover that some of the things we thought we needed aren't things we need at all.
That lesson extends far beyond the dinner table.
A spiritually masculine man isn't measured merely by what he can lift, earn, build, command, or accomplish.

There is another kind of strength.
Can he govern himself?
Can he control his tongue when angry?
Can he remain faithful when tempted?
Can he forgive when wounded?
Can he remain humble when praised?
Can he pray when afraid?
Can he sacrifice for his family?
Can he surrender his plans when God calls him somewhere unexpected?
Can he say no to himself so that he can say yes to God?

That is strength.
Jesus gives us the proper heart for fasting:

“But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face; that thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret: and thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly.” - Matthew 6:17–18

Don't fast to prove how strong you are.
Fast to discover how much you need God.
Don't fast merely to empty yourself.
Empty yourself so there is more room for Him.
Don't make hunger the destination.
Let hunger point you toward the One for whom the soul is truly hungry.
And when the body whispers, “I want,” allow the spirit to answer:
“God comes first.”

PRAY • FAST • SURRENDER

A disciplined man learns to master his appetites. A spiritual man learns why. A man of God ultimately places both his strength and his weakness at the feet of Christ.

On National Coffee Day Have The Brew With A View

September 29th marks National Coffee Day, an annual occasion dedicated to celebrating the rich, energizing beverage that powers mornings and fuels connection across the country. Whether enjoyed as a straightforward drip, a smooth cold brew, or a carefully crafted specialty espresso, coffee remains an indispensable part of daily life for millions of Americans.

VOTE NOW: https://t.co/KCWGkgxSGF

Coffee’s history in the United States is deeply tied to the nation's independence and cultural evolution. First introduced to North America in the 17th century, coffee became America's dominant morning beverage following the Boston Tea Party of 1773. When American colonists protested British tea taxes, drinking tea was widely discarded as unpatriotic, prompting a dramatic shift toward coffee as the patriotic drink of choice. Its role only grew in subsequent centuries: coffee served as essential military rations during the Civil War, World War I, and World War II to maintain troop morale. By the mid-20th century, the official workplace "coffee break" became embedded in American corporate and industrial culture, eventually leading to the artisanal roasters and specialty coffeehouses that thrive across the country today.

TOP 10 LOCAL COFFEE SHOPS:  VOTE NOW

Today, America's love affair with coffee is stronger than ever. According to statistics from the National Coffee Association, roughly 66% of American adults—approximately 170 million people—drink coffee every single day. Nationwide, the country consumes an estimated 500 million cups of coffee per day, averaging around 2.8 cups per coffee drinker.

Sampling the Brew in Gulf Shores and Orange Beach

For locals and visitors on the Alabama coast, National Coffee Day provides the perfect excuse to support local coffee houses and sample a freshly poured cup. Gulf Shores and Orange Beach offer a variety of fantastic options to experience the awakening brew:

To the East: Stop by Buzzcatz Coffee & Sweets in Orange Beach for locally brewed coffee, specialty espresso drinks, and fresh house-made pastries.

To the West: Head over to Happy Pappy's Coffeehouse in Gulf Shores for a cozy atmosphere, Greek-inspired coffee treats, and classic morning roasts.

text:
COPART $CPRT BOUGHT BACK STOCK AT $37.63. THE NEXT $1.9B BUYS ACV:

Copart CPRT at $27.22, -$0.37 / -1.34% on Monday, disclosed with its year-end results that it bought back 43.4M of its own shares at an average $37.63 - $1.6B for stock now worth about $1.18B. The next $1.9B leaves once its cash offer for ACV Auctions clears, and that offer expires one minute after 11:59pm ET Wednesday unless extended. Names that miss a Len5's headline usually make the more useful read: the leader is the clean example, while the name behind it is an argument still being settled, with a date attached.

The verdict: Copart's auction business is still priced below a cautious estimate of its worth, but the $4.49B of cash and Treasury bills under that case is being spent - about $3.5B committed in little more than a year.

The Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5 hunts a sound business priced below a cautious worth, or an event that changes the math. Copart auctions wrecked and totaled cars online, mostly for insurers, from 250+ yards in 11 countries. Its year to July 31: profit per share $1.55 vs $1.59, -2.5%, cushioned by fewer shares; U.S. service revenue - fees for handling and selling cars - $3.39B, -1.8%; international $581M, +12.4%. At about 17.6 times profit, it closed a nickel above its lowest close of the past year, $27.17 on July 21.

ACV Auctions (ACVA) at $10.46, +$0.00 / +0.00% on Monday, runs an online marketplace where car dealers sell trade-ins to each other. It is on none of the six Len5 watchlists; its price just tracks the $10.50 cash offer. The forecast ACV's managers gave their board before agreeing to sell: $857M of revenue this year, and free cash flow - cash left after running the business and buying equipment - below zero every year through 2029.

Rates raise the bar. Copart's cash earned $181.9M of net interest last year, about a tenth of its pretax profit, and management expects ACV to add nothing to profit per share until fiscal 2028. With the 10-year Treasury yield - what Washington pays to borrow for ten years - at 5.24%, idle cash is real competition. Closing also needs a majority of ACV's shares and a U.S. antitrust waiting period to end.

What would knock Copart off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: U.S. service revenue shrinking again in the report tentatively due November 19 - a cheap price tracking a shrinking business. Verdict: still priced below a cautious worth, with less cash under that price after every deal.

MOMENTUM LEN5:
Palantir Technologies (PLTR) at $187.48, -$2.19 / -1.15% on Monday. Software that pulls an organization's data together and lets AI act on it. Momentum hunts a stock climbing on real news: Palantir closed at $192.59 Thursday, its best since December, up 66% in three months after August's raised 2026 revenue forecast of $8.15B-$8.16B. What keeps it behind the leader: just +31% over six months. Monday, Nvidia listed it among 100+ users of new AI-agent safety tools, with no deal attached, and the stock slipped. What would knock Palantir off the Momentum Len5: September-quarter revenue short of its own $2.16B forecast, tentatively November 2. Verdict: a climb built on numbers, not headlines.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
Microsoft (MSFT) at $509.22, -$6.95 / -1.35% on Monday. Windows, Office and Azure cloud computing. Quality-Value hunts a business rivals can't copy, at a markdown. The quality: profit above estimates eight straight quarters, latest $4.74 a share vs $4.23. Friday it folded its office and coding AI helpers into one Copilot app; the stock rose 3.7%. Under that: 30M+ paying Copilot seats out of 450M+ commercial Office seats, under 7%. What keeps it behind the leader: a thin markdown, about 29 times profit and 8% under its October 2025 high. What would knock Microsoft off the Quality-Value Len5: paid seats stalling while data-center spending, $41B last quarter, keeps rising - tentatively October 28. Verdict: the AI sale has barely started, and the price expects it to land.

GROWTH LEN5:
Ameris Bancorp (ABCB) at $81.44, -$0.85 / -1.03% on Monday. An Atlanta bank across the Southeast with a big mortgage arm. Growth hunts profit rising faster than the price credits, on a long record. The record holds; the last year doesn't: profit before one-time items was $1.60 a share in the June quarter vs $1.59 a year earlier. Rates cut both ways: 30% of its $22.59B of deposits pay no interest, yet it made more mortgages than in March, $1.15B vs $1.09B, and earned less on them, $32.5M vs $37.0M. What keeps it behind the leader: a fair price, about 14.7 times profit, not a low one. What would knock Ameris off the Growth Len5: profit near $1.60 again on October 26, tentatively, vs $1.68 expected. Verdict: a sound bank whose growth has paused.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
AppLovin (APP) at $308.24, -$2.51 / -0.81% on Monday. Its AI engine picks the ads mobile-app users see, now for online stores too. Hypergrowth hunts very fast growth at real size: June-quarter revenue $1.92B, +53%; September guided +46% to +48%. Fresh evidence cuts both ways: Citi counted 13,105 online stores advertising through it on September 18, +5.1% in a week, while Edgewater Research says its share gains have stalled. What keeps it behind Palantir, this Len5's leader: growth slowing on its own forecast. What would knock AppLovin off the Hypergrowth Len5: September-quarter revenue under its own $2.055B floor, tentatively November 4. Verdict: still hypergrowth, with a second engine a stock down 54% this year isn't counting.

INCOME LEN5:
Smithfield Foods (SFD) at $19.14, +$0.10 / +0.53% on Monday. It raises hogs and sells pork plus Smithfield, Eckrich and Nathan's Famous meats. Income hunts cash paid to owners that a business can keep paying: $1.25 a year, 6.5% of the share price. Its September 8 outlook split three ways: hog farms $25M-$45M of quarterly profit vs $89M a year ago; fresh pork a $70M-$90M loss; packaged meats' $1.075B-$1.15B yearly range held. First-half operating cash, $204M, nearly doubled but trailed $246M of dividends. What keeps it behind the leader: a thinner cushion. What would knock Smithfield off the Income Len5: packaged meats cut below $1.075B with results, tentatively October 27. Verdict: a dividend now resting on one leg of three.

Copart says ACV adds to profit per share from fiscal 2028. ACV's own managers, planning as a stand-alone company, saw no free cash until 2030. Wednesday night starts the clock on which forecast Copart owners live with.

Not investment advice.
