text:
Why run "claude" when you can run "sclaude"?

Announcing SideKernel: an AI agent sandbox for macOS with a focus on usability.

When AI coding agents first arrived, many of us faced a dilemma that felt impossible.

We could give them free rein over our data and systems, putting both at risk, but letting them do great things unattended....

or we could use them cautiously and watch others, who accepted more risk by temperament (you can call it bravery, you can call it ignorance, and probably both would be right), move faster.

Either way, many of us were caught between a rock and a hard place.

For months I waited for a solution to come, either from the open-source community or directly from the frontier labs: some sandbox that offered reasonable security while also being easy to use.

Well, many sandboxes were indeed released, but almost all of them targeted production use cases, i.e. programmable agents built on SDKs.

From hosted services like E2B to open-source projects like microsandbox, that part of the industry matured and gained popularity quickly.

The more I tried using those sandboxes, however, the more I realized they tend to get in the way of the AI coding agents (e.g. Claude Code, Codex) most of us run daily in our terminals.

They were good solutions, but not for my problem.

As a result, I—and frankly, most of us—kept running those coding agents directly on our machines, or on clunky VMs, or on separate VPSs or spare Mac Minis… You get the gist.

For months I waited for a solution to come, either from the open-source community or directly from the frontier labs: some sandbox (a term that is overused today, but that's a discussion for another time) that offered reasonable security while also being easy to use

So when my MSc practicum at School of Cybersecurity and Privacy at Georgia Tech came around, I decided to built the sandbox I wanted.

SideKernel runs your coding agent inside a lightweight VM on macOS, with a real virtualization boundary between the agent and your machine, while feeling almost as quick as running it directly.

It's open source under Apache 2.0.

Try it out, compare it break it, and tell me what you find (a ⭐ on GitHub helps too).

Thanks to Prof. Mustaque Ahamad for inspiring me to work in systems security through his course and supervising the capstone.

But also to the amazing TA and colleague, @eMADAK for the legendary guidance, and supervision along the way and during the capstone.

At last, I'm grateful to @kalio_late for pushing me and motivating me to release it, and to my colleague Stuart and to @epmatt_ for the many awesome talks around security, systems and infra as well as the awesome builder community of the @thejfloor

Try it out and let me know what you think: https://t.co/O2xWDgZwJr

text:
Your offer can make great work unnecessarily hard to buy.

I learned this first hand over the past year.

Nuova worked almost entirely through fixed-price engagements for one year. 

We signed some of our biggest projects, including a $60k engagement, and did some of the most ambitious work we’ve ever done.

Fixed projects make a lot of sense when a company has a clearly defined transformation it wants to tackle at once.

But working this way made something else increasingly obvious to me:

A lot of growing companies don’t actually need another big project.

They need experienced people who can stay close to the business and keep moving whatever matters next.

The product needs attention now.

Next month it might be the website.

Then a launch.

Then a new feature.

Then the brand starts falling behind the company.

And asking a company to define all of that upfront, commit to a large scope, or build a full internal team before the need is permanent doesn’t always make sense.

So we brought back a different way to work with Nuova.
But with everything we learned working on big fixed projects.

Today we’re launching Nuova One.

A monthly partnership that gives growing tech companies access to the same senior team across product, web, brand and full stack development, without a large commitment at the beginning.

The idea is simple:

Start with what matters now.

We get into the business, understand the context and move one important priority forward.

Then we ship it and move to the next one.

No resetting the relationship every time the priority changes.

No replacing one specialist with another and explaining the company all over again.

The team stays. The context compounds. The work adapts with the business.

For the client, that means you can:

- stay lean without being under-resourced,
- access several senior disciplines without hiring them all,
- change focus as the roadmap changes,
- and build trust through the actual work rather than committing to a huge engagement before we’ve worked together.

And if design and development need to move together, we built Nuova One Pro for that.

Nuova One starts at €4,999/month.

For the first 3 new partnerships, that rate stays locked for the life of the partnership.

After those spots are taken, it becomes €5,999/month.
Nuova One is live today.

text:
Media Release - India’s AI-led development innovations take centre stage at the fifth ‘India Day’ during the UNGA week

‘India Day @ UNGA’ organised by Reliance Foundation, the United Nations in India and the Observer Research Foundation during the week of the UN General Assembly

- The fifth edition of ‘India Day’ explored AI, digital public infrastructure, women-led development, health, and inclusive growth

- A high-level ministerial conversation examined new models of global development cooperation amid geopolitical, climate, and technological disruption

- Special publication on lessons from India’s AI ecosystem launched

New York / Mumbai, September 29, 2026:  As world leaders gathered for the 81st United Nations General Assembly and the international community entered the final stretch to the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals deadline, ‘India Day’ @ UNGA shone the spotlight on how development innovations from India can be adapted, scaled, and shared across the Global South and beyond.

Reliance Foundation, the United Nations in India and the Observer Research Foundation, convened the fifth edition of India Day @ UNGA on Thursday, September 24, 2026, with two sessions exploring ideas to accelerate the global sustainable development agenda, and to make AI work to solve problems at scale. The sessions ‘From India to the World: Scaling Development Innovations for Global Impact’ brought together governments, multilateral institutions, civil society, and private sector innovations to ensure resilience and prosperity for all. The evening high-level ministerial session ‘Ruptures & Ramparts: Building Bridges for a Changing World’ focused on AI, climate action, and innovative partnerships to redefine the global development agenda.

Since 2022, the India Day @ UNGA events have become an opportunity to focus conversations on accelerating development pathways, and looking at innovations that lead to equity, scalable models and the India story of resolving complex problems with ingenuous solutions. Held at the juncture of climate, geopolitical and technological transformation reshaping development, the 2026 sessions focused on governance, collaborations and models to accelerate resolutions from local contexts to population-scale solutions.

The session, ‘Ruptures & Ramparts’, featuring S Jaishankar, Minister of External Affairs, India; Kamina Johnson Smith, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, Jamaica; Melvin Bouva, Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Business and Cooperation, Suriname; Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, Minister for Foreign Affair, Ghana; and Celeste Connors, President and Chief Executive, East-West Center, USA explored how emerging challenges will require a new development compact around innovation, technology, finance, and partnerships.

S Jaishankar, Minister of External Affairs, Government of India, said: “The UN is central to the international system – BRICS is supportive to the UN system. The issues that were highlighted by BRICS are the key issues today – sustainability, co-operation which issues for the United Nations as well…What did the BRICS do to strengthen the UN cause? It nudged it a bit and exerted pressure on the bottom line.”

Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, Minister for Foreign Affairs, Ghana, said: “We have had many generations of exploitation and being taken for granted. We need to come to the table as equal partners. We don’t have to be in a binary arrangement. We don’t have to show our hands and put ourselves on a position that disadvantages. Welcome everybody to the party – at the end of the day, get the best out of it.”

Speaking at the India Day event, Rohit Kansal, Secretary, Department of Rural Development, Government of India, said: “The real message is not in the numbers, it’s the kind of infrastructure that we’ve built. India’s message is at population scale; we democratize access, we build the architecture, and we leave the ecosystem to do the rest…Humans need not learn the language of AI, but AI should learn the language of human.”

Punya Salila Srivastava, Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India, who presented at the India Day event, said: “Infrastructure and technology need to work together to achieve what we want it to achieve. We will need to have the infrastructure, but we will also have to have AI and digital technology to build a healthier future for others.”

Santosh Kumar Sarangi, Secretary, Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, India, said: “Energy for AI will not be a problem, but a solution once we have addressed AI for energy. If you look at India’s energy potential, there is no issue. But the requirement is for AI to make energy infrastructure more resilient, and for distribution companies to increase efficiency.”

In a statement, B Srinivasan, Executive Lead, Reliance Foundation, said: “In the changing world scenario today, AI and development is beyond individuals, institutions and nations. The challenges are complex, but the solution is in a new world, driven by humanity. We need co-operation and collaboration on a scale larger than ever before, where empathy and soft power redefine the way we deliver development, and that is the core message that India Day brings to the world.”

Stefan Priesner, United Nations Resident Co-Ordinator, India, delivering remarks at the events, said: “Four years remain until 2030. That is not long, but it is long enough if the solutions India has proven at home can travel the world. That is what today is about: taking what works from India to the world, and turning innovation to opportunity for every household and every person.”

Vishal Harsh, Deputy Consul General, Consulate General of India, in his inaugural remarks, said: “Countries are looking for development solutions and India’s experience offers an important perspective. As a major economy and with over 1.4 billion people, any successful project in India must reach the world. Development and innovation matter most when they reach the last person. AI is the next major opportunity. Solutions developed at scale in India can support countries across the Global South.”

Samir Saran, President, ORF, placed the events in context. “India Day is now a day-long affair with one primary purpose: people. The purpose of these conversations is service—serving humans—and to do that we explore how technology, innovation, partnerships, philanthropies, and international institutions can collaborate to serve humans. AI is not just a passion project of “tech bros” but a broader human project that can change how societies prosper and service each other.”

Through the day, four thematic sessions spanned artificial intelligence, digital public infrastructure, women-led development, health, and the future of inclusive growth.

AI emerged as a connecting thread across conversations, reflecting its increasing urgency in approaching how development challenges are addressed from enabling scale through digital public infrastructure to strengthening health and education systems increasingly AI for solutions that are more accessible, responsive and impactful.

The session, ‘Beyond 2030: Rewiring Development for an Age of Intelligence, Inclusion and Instability’, examined geopolitical, climate, demographic, and technological shifts in development while ‘Women, Children and Youth: Building Healthier Futures for the Next Billion’ delved into public systems, community-led delivery, technology and partnerships for health, education, and economic opportunity.

‘The AI Promise: Diffusion at Population Scale’ probed the role of AI across languages, sectors, institutions, and public service delivery systems in India and the Global South, while ‘Rules of Engagement: AI Governance for a Changing World’ explored approaches to AI regulation, data governance, institutional capacity, and responsible deployment.

The programme also launched the fifth in the series of publications of India Day @ UNGA. When Silicon Meets the Soil: India's AI Revolution, brings India’s experience in making artificial intelligence work, and positioning the country as the world’s AI use-case capital across 18 chapters.

Beyond conversations, India Day @ UNGA 2026 aimed to present an architecture for models of cooperation that could the social development agenda for the global south and the world.

About the publication: When Silicon Meets the Soil India's AI Revolution: India’s AI ecosystem is entering a defining decade - marked by impactful solutions, wide diffusion, and a growing ambition to lead the Global South. This publication presents 12 mature case studies and 6 emerging innovations showing how India is putting artificial intelligence to work - reaching farmers, health workers, and communities at population scale, responsibly and in context - positioning India as the world’s AI use-case capital. Publication link: https://t.co/0KHfB6TPf3

About Reliance Foundation: Reliance Foundation, the philanthropic arm of Reliance Industries Limited, aims to play a catalytic role in addressing India’s development challenges through innovative and sustainable solutions. Led by Smt. Nita M Ambani, Founder and Chairperson, Reliance Foundation is relentlessly working for the overall well-being and enhanced quality of life for all, focusing on rural transformation, education, health, sports for development, disaster management, women empowerment, urban renewal and arts, culture and heritage, and has touched the lives of over 100 million people across India, in over 98,500 villages and urban locations. More on https://t.co/a6kl0DZLh6.

About Observer Research Foundation (ORF): ORF is a leading multidisciplinary think tank with centres in New Delhi, Mumbai and Kolkata and an overseas affiliate in Washington DC. It helps discover and inform India’s choices and carries Indian voices and ideas to forums shaping global debates. It provides non-partisan, independent, well-researched analyses and inputs to diverse decision-makers in governments, business communities, and academia and to civil society around the world. For more information, visit: https://t.co/epVDhYPuFJ

About United Nations in India: The United Nations system in India includes 26 organizations that serve in India. The UN provides strategic support to India to help the country achieve its aspirations to end poverty and inequality and to promote sustainable development in line with the globally agreed SDGs. The UN also supports India, as the world’s largest democracy, in the country’s ambitious commitments to rapid change and development priorities. For more information, visit: https://t.co/1O1IGfKnBU

text:
DeepSeek @deepseek_ai  has shared a new technical article on Zhihu introducing DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec), the sandbox infrastructure behind its large-scale Agent workloads.

From DeepSeek-V3.2 to V4.1, DSec has handled all sandbox workloads for Agent training, evaluation, and data preprocessing. In production, it runs across thousands of servers, with millions of sandboxes running concurrently. Its overcommit ratio has exceeded 50×, pushing CPU and memory utilization to the limit.

So how does DSec support Agent workloads at this scale?

Below is the full article, covering the architecture and engineering behind DSec—from composable environments and on-demand image loading to high-density resource management, rollout recovery, and Agent security.

📖 DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec): Sandbox Infrastructure for Large-Scale Agent Training

DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec) is the sandbox infrastructure supporting the entire training, evaluation, and data preprocessing pipeline of DeepSeek-V4.

Training a reliable Agent model requires repeated trial and error in real environments: reading code, modifying files, installing dependencies, running tests, and launching services. These operations continuously change the environment, so sandboxes must persist state across multiple rounds of interaction.

These workloads have several distinct characteristics: sandbox creation requests are bursty; CPUs remain mostly idle after startup while memory needs to stay resident; Agent environments are highly diverse with low base-image reuse; and long-running tasks can be interrupted by resource preemption. These characteristics directly shape the design of DSec.

Unified Access for Diverse Workloads

Different Agent tasks require different levels of isolation, operating system functionality, and execution overhead. DSec supports four execution backends—FnCall, Container, MicroVM, and Full VM—all accessed through a unified Python SDK, libdsec, with the backend selected according to the task.

FnCall reuses pre-created containers for short tasks such as online evaluation. Container provides fast startup and high deployment density for general software engineering and tool use. MicroVM offers stronger isolation for security-sensitive tasks. Full VM provides a complete operating system environment, supporting applications such as graphical interfaces, rendering, and Android.

DSec architecture: unified sandbox creation and runtime management, with multiple execution backends for different workloads.

Layered and Composable Environments

Large-scale Agent training requires a large number of environments, making efficient environment construction and updates a fundamental challenge.

In one week of production data from 2026, the container backend used 11,266 base images, 102,171 workspaces, and hundreds of toolkits. Under a traditional approach, updating any of these components would require rebuilding a large number of images.

DSec therefore separates each sandbox environment into three layers:
🔹 Base image — the operating system and basic software
🔹 Workspace — task-specific code repositories and dependencies
🔹 Toolkit — tools such as DeepSeek Harness
These layers have different update cycles and are versioned independently, then composed at runtime.

DSec stores images, workspaces, and toolkits in EROFS, which supports metadata/data separation and cross-image deduplication. When creating a sandbox, OverlayFS combines the required EROFS layers on demand.

When base software, task code, or toolkits change, only the corresponding EROFS layer needs to be rebuilt, avoiding unnecessary reconstruction of unrelated content.

Monolithic images require rebuilding every image containing an updated toolkit. With composable environment layers, only the toolkit layer needs to be updated and recombined with existing base images and workspaces.

On-Demand Image Loading

Analysis of production image data showed that sandboxes actually access only 4.2%–13.3% of the total image data at runtime. Pulling complete images locally therefore means transferring and storing a large amount of unused data.

DSec instead stores all image data on the 3FS distributed file system, fetching only the required metadata locally and reading the bulk data on demand.

In an experiment creating 8,192 containers simultaneously, on-demand loading reduced completion time from more than 60 minutes to about 35 minutes, achieving a 1.71× speedup and reducing disk writes by approximately 57%.

In another workspace provisioning experiment, directly mounting EROFS layers instead of extracting tar.gz files reduced completion time from 79 minutes to 45 minutes, while total disk writes fell to roughly 1/5.5 of the original.

High-Density Resource Management

Agent training workloads spend much of their time waiting for the model to generate the next action. Around 90% of sandboxes use no more than 5% of their requested CPU capacity on average, leaving CPU idle for long periods while memory must remain resident to preserve files, processes, and other state.

This creates significant room for overcommitment. In production, DSec achieves an overcommit ratio of more than 50×.

To support high-density deployment, DSec focuses on cache sharing and reclaiming idle memory.

Using virtio-pmem and DAX, MicroVMs on the same host can share a host page cache. In experiments, enabling this mechanism alone reduced peak host memory usage by 40.2% compared with the baseline.

Enabling memory reclamation mechanisms—DAMON and balloon free-page reporting—reduced time-accumulated host memory consumption by 21.2%. Combining the two mechanisms resulted in the lowest overall memory consumption.

Under such high-density deployment, DSec also prioritizes latency-sensitive tasks, allowing less latency-sensitive workloads to utilize idle CPU capacity, while reducing interference from hyperthreads sharing the same physical core.

With optimized CPU scheduling, when other workloads consumed 50% of node CPU capacity, the latency increase of latency-sensitive tasks over the no-interference baseline fell from 45.2% to 17.3%.

Three core mechanisms: on-demand image loading, composable environment layers, and high-density resource management.

Decoupling Rollouts from GPU Training

In reinforcement learning (RL), Agents typically need multiple rounds of interaction with sandbox environments to complete a rollout.

In early training pipelines, the Agent execution loop and GPU training task ran in the same Pod. When the training task was preempted, the sandbox remained intact, but the Agent execution loop responsible for advancing the interaction had already terminated.

Recovery required replaying command logs to reconcile the progress saved by the training framework with the actual state of the sandbox, creating complex recovery logic and additional coordination overhead.

Starting with DeepSeek-V4.1, this execution logic was moved into DSec and split between an Agent sandbox and a worker container.

The Agent sandbox runs the Agent framework and toolkits, while the worker container manages the sandbox and advances the interaction process. Both run outside the preemptible GPU resource pool and jointly preserve execution progress and environment state.

As a result, when a GPU training task is preempted, the Agent's execution state remains intact. Once training resumes, the Agent can continue directly from where it was interrupted.

Using Agents to Build Environments for Agents

Large-scale Agent RL training and evaluation require highly diverse environments, including binary dependencies, code repositories, Harness toolkits, evaluation scripts, and other components used to generate Agent outputs and measure their correctness.

Using Agents to automate environment construction provides an efficient and scalable way to build these environments.

An important observation is that the Agent building an environment is itself already running inside the environment it is building. Rather than maintaining one platform for Agent training and another for environment construction, DSec puts both on the same “platform for running Agents”, greatly simplifying the system architecture while ensuring that the Agent's build and runtime environments remain identical.

DSec introduces a pack_diff mechanism for environment construction. Agents can instruct the platform to create incremental snapshots of a sandbox and later restore them as new sandboxes.

This makes it easy to preserve sandbox state—and even turn every round of Agent interaction into a reusable sandbox environment.

These incremental snapshots can also support trajectory branching: save a snapshot at step k, restore multiple sandboxes from the same state, and continue exploration independently. Each branch shares read-only layers while recording only its changes, avoiding repeated execution of steps before the branch point.

MicroVM snapshots can preserve and restore memory and process state, while the container implementation currently supports primarily disk-level snapshots.

Security Boundaries for Agents

As Agent capabilities improve, the security boundaries of training environments also need to evolve.

In production, DSec has observed Agents attempting to read residual answers, forge RPC requests, overwrite /bin/bash to inject commands, and even bypass access controls through mechanisms such as XFS_IOC_SWAPEXT.

Such behavior can affect training and evaluation results, and potentially damage the runtime environment.

If an environment provides a shortcut to obtaining rewards, models may exploit it. DSec therefore treats fine-grained access control as a fundamental capability.

AppArmor constrains file and socket access, with these restrictions remaining effective even when the Agent runs with administrator privileges. eBPF provides per-sandbox network allowlists, restricting the addresses, ports, and protocols that a sandbox can access.

These measures can only mitigate part of the problem. There is still no general defense against destructive behaviors such as exploiting kernel vulnerabilities.

As model capabilities continue to improve, the security arms race between systems and Agents will likely continue, with system defenses evolving alongside them.

Production Data

DSec scales horizontally through shards. Each shard contains around 160 servers, providing approximately 30,000 CPU cores and 250 TB of memory.

A single shard serves around 3 million sandboxes per day, with peak concurrency exceeding 380,000 sandboxes and a creation rate of more than 5,000 sandboxes per second.

Multiple such shards are deployed in production, supporting millions of sandboxes running simultaneously.

From DeepSeek-V3.2 to DeepSeek-V4.1, DSec has handled all sandbox workloads for Agent training, evaluation, and data preprocessing.

The DSec technical report, “DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec): A Sandbox Infrastructure for Effective Agentic Training at Scale,” is now available on arXiv, sharing the engineering practices behind large-scale Agent sandbox infrastructure.

Conclusion

We believe Agents still have enormous room for exploration.

Next, we plan to expand the number and diversity of Agent runtime environments by hundreds or thousands of times, and bring the capabilities developed through these tasks back into open models.

This requires more diverse environments, more reliable infrastructure, and more development partners.

Join us in building an elastic computing platform for Agents and the next generation of Agent foundation models.

How to Apply

Apply through the DeepSeek careers website by searching for “Agent Elastic Computing R&D Engineer.”

Or send your resume to talent@deepseek.com with the email subject: Name – Position – Contact Information.

Data from the DeepSeek Elastic Compute technical report, “DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec): A Sandbox Infrastructure for Effective Agentic Training at Scale.”

text:
The startup bringing the SpaceX playbook to nuclear power | Francisco "A.J." Camacho, Politico

General Matter, a startup helmed by one of the first employees of Elon Musk's rocket company, is hoping to help drive a revival in the U.S. nuclear industry.

Not many people would see potential in a forest on a hazardous waste site, but Scott Nolan and the federal government believe it will drive the future of American energy.

For Nolan, the plot of land just outside Paducah is ideal for his company, General Matter, to repeat what he did with Elon Musk at SpaceX: breathe new life into a sector that was at the center of the mid-20th century’s technology revolution.

This time it’s the nuclear power industry that he hopes to revive.

While his approach has drawn detractors inside the industry, Nolan, General Matter’s co-founder and CEO, has attracted allies across the political spectrum, a sign of how the politics of nuclear have changed. That includes an ambitious governor eager to tout his own ability to bridge partisan divides.

“It has investment both from Peter Thiel-backed groups and John Kerry-backed groups,” Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) told POLITICO, referring to the right-wing investor and former Biden administration climate envoy, respectively.

“I mean, it’s truly bringing together folks that have vastly different politics but [are] looking for what is the best answer to meeting our energy demands in the future,” he added before addressing a gathering, which also included then-White House senior policy strategist Emily Underwood, boxer-influencer Jake Paul and Nolan.

The event in Paducah marked one year since General Matter broke ground on its flagship nuclear enrichment facility, which it expects will double America’s production of enriched uranium for nuclear power plants. What’s now a Superfund site was the last U.S.-owned enrichment complex, making the project a powerful emblem for what Paul, an investor in the startup, called “American reindustrialization.”

The nuclear sector boomed in the 1960s as utilities embraced the Atomic Age optimism that a former top U.S. nuclear regulator said would produce power “too cheap to meter” — but it fell out of favor within decades after suffering a handful of high-profile disasters and soaring costs. More recently, the closure of the old Paducah plant that once supplied the potent fuel to dozens of power stations has left the U.S. industry heavily dependent on foreign suppliers.

Now, the development of new, smaller and potentially safer nuclear reactors and the push to end the industry’s awkward reliance on uranium fuel imports from U.S. geopolitical adversary Russia — as well as billions in funding from Washington — have opened the door for the audacious, tech-savvy team led by Nolan to show they can master the complex process of producing enough enriched uranium to fuel a new generation of nuclear power plants.

Nolan, who is also a partner at Thiel’s Founders Fund, got his engineering start with Boeing before joining SpaceX as roughly its 30th employee. He left just before its first successful launch but remained wowed by the startup’s ability to advance commercial rocket technology, ultimately dominating the field. Now, advancing nuclear power is Nolan’s obsession.

“I enjoyed investing and didn’t plan to start another company,” Nolan said, recalling 2023 when he began a deep dive into nuclear power that included a foray into microreactors. “I met most of the advanced reactor startups, and in asking them what the most difficult thing about their business was, it wasn’t regulation, it wasn’t technology — it was access to fuel.”

The Manhattan Beach project

“Advanced reactor” is something of an umbrella term encompassing designs that are smaller or use different cooling systems than the 96 large, conventional reactors operating across the U.S.

Nolan, like many other investors, saw that nuclear power was drawing support in Washington, with new designs promising better economics and safety. But unlike many financiers, he saw another roadblock.

Currently, the U.S. only produces 30% of the standard low-enriched uranium needed to fuel existing reactors. Meanwhile, most advanced reactor designs will require high-assay low-enriched uranium — or HALEU — which is four times more concentrated and only commercially sold by Russia.

With a U.S. ban on Russian uranium imports set to take full effect in 2028, conventional and especially advanced nuclear companies are bracing for a beating.

It’s not easy to just enrich more, either. For one, centrifuges, the world’s predominant enrichment technology, are “very sensitive,” according to Dale Klein, a professor at the University of Texas and former Nuclear Regulatory Commission chair.

The vertical cylinders spin gaseous uranium at high speeds, forcing heavier, less valuable atoms to the outside to be peeled off. “If they’re out of balance and they ever start to wiggle a little bit, then they tend to blow apart,” Klein said.

Plus there’s “the classified nature of enrichment technology, which can be used in a nuclear weapons program,” said Daniel Poneman, a former acting Energy secretary. Accordingly, there are formidable government guardrails.

It’s unsurprising, then, that Nolan was wary of entering the business in 2023.

That’s when Leslie Dewan —a nuclear engineer with connections across the sector — put Nolan in touch with her acquaintance in the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit named Lee Robinson. Robinson was running due diligence for the Department of Defense microreactor program, and fuel constraints were just getting on his radar.

That fall, Nolan, Dewan, Robinson and Andrew Higier — the director of the Defense Innovation Unit’s energy portfolio — gathered at the Defense Department unit’s headquarters in Mountain View, California, for a 30-minute meeting that ended up dragging on for three hours.

Robinson left the meeting with a personal mission. “I spent three months just basically walking the halls of DOE and the National Nuclear Security Administration, the Department of Defense, and national labs to find out what the severity of this problem is,” he said.

Nolan’s efforts to find an existing company he could invest in to produce enriched uranium had come up short. He rejected the legacy enrichers. The centrifuge design used by the U.S.-based Centrus Energy Corp., he concluded, was not commercially competitive, and its European competitors, Urenco and Orano, were not interested in expanding aggressively enough to meet potential market growth.

In December 2023, Robinson flew to Los Angeles and bee-lined for Manhattan Beach, where he met up with Nolan. The pair talked and walked, making their way to the pier on a quintessential Southern California winter morning.

“Nobody else is going to do this,” Robinson told Nolan on the pier. “If we don’t do this, nobody else is going to do it.”

Nolan had already reached the same conclusion, and he knew the right investor: Thiel, the PayPal founder and mentor to Vice President JD Vance whose net worth is now estimated at $32 billion. The two first met at Stanford University while Thiel was teaching and Nolan was studying for his MBA, and they’ve since spent 15 years at Founders Fund together.

Even though they recognized the enormity of the challenge, they filed paperwork in January 2024, and General Matter was officially born. Nolan was the principal founder, aided by co-founders Robinson, renewable energy executive Drew DeWalt, former Urenco officer Ashby Bridges and fellow SpaceX alum Emily Henriksson. Thiel even took a seat on the board, a rare move for a man accustomed to staying in the background.

The race for enrichment

Fast forward to this fall, and General Matter has won multiple contracts with advanced reactor companies like X-energy and Antares Nuclear, the U.S. government, and major American utilities already operating nuclear plants, according to a person close to the company granted anonymity to discuss confidential information.

Robinson confirmed the company is “working with a wide range of partners like utilities, advanced reactor developers and the U.S. government,” but did not comment on contracts.

When DOE announced its landmark, congressionally funded enrichment awards earlier this year, General Matter came away with $900 million. So did Centrus and Orano, while Global Laser Enrichment snagged $28 million and Urenco got snubbed.

Multiple people familiar with the bidding process for that $2.7 billion in Energy Department funding who were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive issues said General Matter’s ambitious timelines worked in its favor. Its connections to Thiel — an ally of President Donald Trump and Vance — also gave it an edge.

One person familiar with the DOE contracts said the company offered 355 metric tons of HALEU annually for the $900 million. With its $900 million, Centrus said it would initially deliver 12 metric tons annually and subsequently scale up.

To keep the momentum, General Matter needs speed, Nolan said.

“A failure mode would be going too slowly,” he said. If they’re not online “in 2029 or sooner,” existing reactors could suffer under a full Russian uranium ban. If they dally too long on HALEU, “the industry doesn’t take off the way it can.”

Another deal is already on the table. In March, the U.S. Export-Import Bank pledged $4.2 billion in debt financing for Japan and South Korea if they decide to purchase General Matter uranium.

Washington is looking to accelerate nuclear more broadly, too, with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission streamlining the licensing pathway for various nuclear facilities.

Nolan says he is applying four main principles from SpaceX to his new endeavor. First, identify the “dominating” obstacle — the supply and price of fuel, in this case. Second, keep the team small and focused on that obstacle. Third, recruit both industry experts and outsiders. Finally, “think from first principles about what the technology should look like.”

Its founders were worried about making mistakes that tripped up other enrichment companies. To get around fixed ideas about technology and engineering, Nolan and the team sought engineers experienced with nuclear power who worked on other areas of the fuel cycle.

The SpaceX approach cuts both ways, says Poneman, who was previously CEO of Centrus, the privatized company that is the descendant of the U.S. government’s Cold War enrichment program.

“When I was at Centrus, we wanted to try to graft SpaceX people and thinking,” he said. “There were a couple of challenges.”

For one, enrichment has decades of government-led research behind it. Starting with a clean slate of ideas for using new technology carries risks. Secondly, he noted, much of the best research on enrichment technology is classified because of its ties to the atomic bomb.

The Founders Fund Strategy

General Matter hasn’t publicly disclosed even the most basic characteristics of its enrichment technology, such as whether it will use out-of-fashion gaseous diffusion, standard centrifuges or newer laser-driven methods.

General Matter says it will reveal its basic technology in the coming months. But under the company’s other playbook — taken from Nolan’s concurrent employer — the concealment might as well be marketing by mystique.

Nolan is leaning into his Founders Fund experience — and reputation — to satisfy investors who are drawn to his personality and SpaceX success. He has likened a company’s technology to a horse and its CEO to the jockey: While traditional thinking sees the technology as the most important factor, Thiel’s Founders Fund anchors its investments to a company’s founder.

“I’m a founder-first, idea-second investor,” said Blake Lieberman, a venture capitalist who flew to the Paducah event last month from Texas to “check in” on his General Matter investment.

“At the end of the day, it’s a team,” Lieberman said. “Look at how it got incubated inside of Founders, Peter [Thiel] on the board, the talent that they’ve hired on the research side.”

The competition

Still, General Matter joined the race late. They need to catch up with Centrus, Urenco, and Orano — companies with decades-long successful track records in making fuel for conventional reactors — as well as startup Global Laser Enrichment’s years of research and development and support from nuclear giant Cameco.

While the publicly traded Centrus has struggled to enrich its own uranium at scale since it was spun out from the U.S. government, its Ohio plant upriver from Paducah does produce HALEU at a pilot scale.

“Our technology is proven, licensed by the NRC, and has been producing HALEU for nearly three years,” said Dan Leistikow, vice president for corporate communications at Centrus. Centrus noted recent fuel supply contracts with X-energy, Radiant Nuclear and Antares Nuclear.

Urenco — a consortium of the British, Dutch and German governments — is the only company enriching significant amounts of uranium in the U.S. today, and it’s undergoing a 15% capacity expansion in New Mexico to be completed in 2027.

France’s Orano, meanwhile, is considering building a facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, that would be the state’s largest investment ever.

Small reactor startups like Kairos Power and TerraPower are projecting they will launch their inaugural commercial power plants around 2030. And those reactors might not be able to wait out an enrichment setback.

General Matter expects to begin production at Paducah before 2030. But industry insiders question General Matter’s ability to move as quickly as it’s promising. While the company’s Paducah site is cleared and ready for initial building, according to construction head Chris Williams, it has not yet entered the historically yearslong process of applying for a federal license that would allow for the start of safety-related construction.

The company plans to submit its application to the NRC by the end of September, and the agency has dramatically sped up reviews in recent months, but General Matter is also advocating for a Congressional workaround that cleared both House and Senate committees on bipartisan votes.

General Matter’s focus on speed is an issue for competitors who are quietly critical of the company. They worry that the company’s lack of experience in the high-stakes technology, coupled with a dash for quick deployment, will lead to cutting corners on long-term efficiencies or safety.

“There’s a cultural issue here that we can’t gloss over,” said an official with a competing company. “The nuclear industry has spent decades building our safety-focused culture, and we can’t sacrifice that. In a small industry, like ours, one issue from someone anywhere is everybody’s issue.”

But General Matter says it understands its safety obligations, and its technology is just refining engineering on well-established enrichment science.

“Safety is fundamental to our business model. Without it, we can’t win on speed, cost and efficiency,” Robinson said. “Our mission to fix what has stagnated for decades has attracted the best personnel in the industry, and whose centuries of combined nuclear experience will help us meet America’s energy needs faster and more reliably than any legacy incumbent.”

Besides, the company wears its outsider status with pride — and many love them for it.

“They offer a new approach to a broken industry. We need a new approach to uranium, and they bring it,” said a former DOE official, granted anonymity to speak freely.

text:
True Grok ?
Wayne did support troops in documented ways: he toured Vietnam in 1966 while researching The Green Berets, visited wounded service members, and in 1975 offered land in Arizona to help South Vietnamese refugees after the fall of Saigon. Those actions were reported at the time. 
Secretly gifting 1,200 homes was not. Similar feel-good John Wayne folklore (such as a 1958 Texas farm-auction story) has also been identified as invented.
No. The story is a fabricated viral meme. There is no evidence John Wayne secretly bought 1,200 houses for homeless Vietnam veterans. The claim (cash purchases of 1,200 foreclosed houses from 1950–1979, $43 million spent, keys left at VA hospitals with “Welcome home” notes, family unaware until bank records after his 1979 death) appears only in recent social-media posts and YouTube videos using nearly identical wording. 
It does not appear in contemporary news, biographies, obituaries, probate records, or accounts from his family.
@LibertyMatter77Wayne died on June 11, 1979. His estate was valued at about $6.8 million ($1 million in real property and $5.75 million in personal property) according to the will filed in Orange County Superior Court and contemporaneous reporting. Spending $43 million on houses would have far exceeded his documented wealth and would have shown up in probate. 
He also had earlier financial setbacks from poor investments. Other problems:
Large-scale U.S. involvement in Vietnam and returning veterans were not a 1950s phenomenon.
Quietly buying and transferring 1,200 properties in cash over nearly 30 years, without a paper trail, public notice, or family knowledge, is not how property records or estates work.
The specific “one vet” anecdote and exact numbers only circulate with the meme itself.

text:
I Spent Months Talking to Technical Co-Founder Candidates. Here Are 15 Things I Wish Someone Had Told Me First.

1/ "My team built" vs. "I built" is the whole conversation.
 At pre-seed, both founders are in the work. I needed a technical partner who still builds hands-on, not someone who only oversees it.

2/ Relevant 0→1 shipping beats years of experience.
 Someone who shipped solo beats someone who has only maintained existing codebases. And an enterprise SaaS builder is not the same as a consumer app builder.

3/ Naming tools is not the same as knowing tools.
 One candidate listed "Pinecone, LangChain, Bedrock, Claude," then couldn't explain how they'd build the product.

4/ If they push back on staying hands-on, that's your answer.
 If they're negotiating their way out of the work before it starts, imagine month three.

5/ Impressive resumes are often the least hands-on.
 A senior technical leader can be a great fit at another stage. At pre-seed, I needed someone who still builds.

6/ People apply for the title they want, not the role you posted.
 I posted a founding engineer role. One candidate opened with "I saw you're looking for a CTO."

7/ How they respond to your PRD tells you everything.
 One candidate's questions were all about financials and funding. There wasn't one about the product or the architecture.

8/ Some respond to your search, then pitch their own thing.
 They didn't come to build with me. They came to recruit me.

9/ Some inbound isn't candidates. It's sales.
 Agencies and consulting firms pose as co-founder interest.

10/ Watch how they respond to competition.
 One listed why big companies would crush us. Another found the wedge and started problem-solving.

11/ The best co-founder conversations feel normal.
 No ego, no lectures, no hidden agendas. It's just two people exploring whether to build together.

12/ AI infrastructure ≠ AI applications. 
Building GPU data centers and building an LLM-powered product are different skills.

13/ Cross-reference their YC profile, LinkedIn, and calendar invite.
 One candidate's YC profile said Texas, their LinkedIn said Ohio, and the calendar invite said Brazil. If location matters, verify before you spend time on a call.

14/ Technical depth without communication is a dealbreaker.
 If I relay customer feedback and you understand half of it, the product pays for it.

15/ Be clear about cash, equity, vesting, and expectations from the beginning. 
One candidate asked for a $700 monthly stipend before we'd started. Another was deep into cap-table math before we'd built anything together. Say what you can and can't offer on the first call, use standard vesting, and have startup counsel put it in writing.

Bonus/

The real test isn't "can you build?" It's "can we build together?" 
Can we communicate, challenge each other, and share the same urgency long-term? Some conversations came close. Sometimes the timing just didn't align.

Where things stand now with @ExecuteIQ: V1 is in active build, design-partner conversations are underway, and there's an audience built around the problem. If you're a hands-on technical builder, my DMs are open.

Day one is not zero.

text:
Five animals that can hurt a human badly. One thing decides which of them actually will. It is not size, not teeth, not temper.

Watch the video first. Then come back and read this, because by the end you will rewatch it and see a completely different clip.

I spent years around people who work with large animals for a living. Keepers, sanctuary handlers, wildlife vets, rescue crews. They all say the same sentence sooner or later, usually after someone on the internet asks a dumb question:

"The animal is not the risk. The mistake is the risk."

That sentence is the whole story. Everything below is the long version of it.

Buckle up. This is going to be long, and every part of it is built to change how you look at animals for the rest of your life.

PART 1. THE BITE IS A LANGUAGE

Most people think a bite means one thing: attack.

Biologists think of a bite as a full vocabulary. There is the warning bite that leaves no mark. There is the correction bite a mother delivers to a cub. There is the exploratory bite, where an animal tests what you are with the most sensitive tool it owns, its mouth. There is the play bite. There is the food bite, the panic bite, the dominance bite, the "get off me" bite.

Same jaws. Same muscles. Wildly different intent.

Here is the part that breaks people's brains. Animals are not born knowing how hard to bite. They learn it, the same way a toddler learns not to squeeze a hamster.

It is called bite inhibition, and it is built through play. Puppies do it. Bear cubs do it. Big cats do it. Two cubs wrestle, one clamps down too hard, the other squeals and stops playing. The biter learns something permanent: pressure has a cost. Play ends when the other one hurts.

Cubs that get that lesson grow into adults with an internal dimmer switch. Cubs that miss it, because they were orphaned, isolated, or raised without siblings, often grow into adults with only two settings.

Think about that. A creature with jaw muscles that could crush bone, and the only thing standing between your hand and a disaster is a habit it picked up rolling around in the grass at eight weeks old.

That is not a metaphor. That is the actual safety system.

And it is fragile.

PART 2. THE NUMBER EVERYONE QUOTES AND NOBODY UNDERSTANDS

You have seen the bite force charts. Grizzly bear, roughly 1,200 PSI in the commonly quoted estimates. Black bear, somewhere in the high hundreds. A human, around 160 to 200.

Those numbers are real enough to be useful and shaky enough that researchers argue about them constantly. Measuring the maximum bite of a wild animal is not exactly a controlled lab setting. Nobody hands a grizzly a sensor and asks it to try its hardest.

But here is what matters more than the number.

A bear does not need to bite at full force to change your life. It needs about a tenth of it.

The full-force number is a ceiling. What decides whether you walk away is how far below the ceiling the animal chooses to stay. And that choice is made in a brain, not in a jaw.

This is why two identical animals, same species, same weight, same enclosure, can be one of them safe to stand near and the other absolutely not. The hardware is the same. The software is different.

PART 3. WHY YOUR INSTINCT IS WRONG ABOUT WHO IS DANGEROUS

Ask a hundred people to rank which of five animals is most dangerous and you will get the same order almost every time. Big teeth first. Big claws second. Big size third.

Reality does not follow that list.

At Yellowstone, one of the most visited wildlife parks on Earth, bison injure more visitors than bears do. Not because they are hunters. They are grazers. They are the animal people walk up to for a selfie, because it looks like a cow with a beard.

A bull bison can weigh well over a ton, run around 35 miles per hour, and spin faster than you can process. It gives warning signals almost nobody knows how to read: a raised tail, a head bob, a snort, pawing the ground. By the time the average tourist notices any of that, the animal has already made a decision.

Meanwhile a black bear, the one that shows up in every horror story, is on average one of the most conflict-averse large predators alive. Most black bear encounters end with the bear leaving. Most.

Most is not all. And "most" is exactly the word that gets people killed.

The pattern is brutal and consistent. The animals that look harmless get approached. The animals that look terrifying get respect. And the respect is what keeps people alive.

PART 4. THE BIRD THAT SHOULD NOT BE ALLOWED TO EXIST

Let us talk about the ostrich, because nobody gives this animal the credit it deserves.

It is the largest bird on the planet. It can stand around nine feet tall. It can run about 43 miles per hour and hold a fast pace for a long time, which is why almost nothing on the savanna can catch a healthy adult.

It has two toes per foot. Two. Most birds have four. Evolution deleted the extras because a two-toed foot is a better running machine and a better weapon. The larger toe carries a claw that can reach several inches.

An adult ostrich kicks forward, not backward like a horse. That direction matters. A forward kick with that claw is a disemboweling motion, and there are documented cases of ostriches killing lions in defense.

Now look at its face. The eye of an ostrich is about two inches across, the biggest of any land animal. It is famously larger than its own brain, which is a fact people use as a joke and biologists use as a lesson: this animal invests in vision over thought, because on open ground the winner is whoever sees the threat first.

Here is the twist. That eye also makes ostriches extremely reactive to anything approaching fast, anything that moves suddenly, anything it does not understand. You are not being read as a person. You are being read as a moving shape.

A shape that moves slowly and predictably becomes background. A shape that lunges becomes a threat.

Remember that. It will matter again.

PART 5. THE SMALLEST ANIMAL HERE HAS THE MOST SOPHISTICATED LANGUAGE

Forget the big ones for a minute. The most impressive mind in this whole conversation belongs to a rodent the size of a loaf of bread.

Prairie dogs are talking. Not in a cute, anthropomorphic, internet way. In a peer-reviewed, decades-of-fieldwork way.

The linguist and biologist Con Slobodchikoff spent years recording their alarm calls and running them through analysis. What he reported is genuinely strange. Prairie dogs use different calls for different predators, and within those calls they appear to encode details: how big the threat is, its shape, its color, even how fast it is moving. In experiments, they gave distinct calls for people wearing different colored shirts.

Read that again. An animal that lives underground in a dirt town is broadcasting the description of a suspect, in real time, to hundreds of neighbors.

And those towns are enormous. At the turn of the twentieth century, a single prairie dog colony in Texas was estimated to cover tens of thousands of square miles and hold hundreds of millions of animals. It may have been the largest concentration of mammals on the planet outside of humans.

Then we spent a hundred years poisoning them.

Today the black-tailed prairie dog occupies a tiny fraction of its old range. And here is the part ecologists lose sleep over: prairie dogs are a keystone species. Their burrows shelter owls, snakes, and the endangered black-footed ferret. Their grazing changes the grassland itself. Remove them, and an entire ecosystem quietly unravels.

The small animal in the corner of the frame is holding up a continent.

They also greet each other with what looks exactly like a kiss, teeth touching, and researchers use it to identify who belongs to which family group. Even their affection is a security protocol.

PART 6. THE ANIMAL WE ALMOST DELETED

Now the bison.

In the early 1800s there were an estimated thirty million or more bison on the plains, possibly far more by some estimates. By the late 1800s, counts had collapsed to a few hundred wild animals. Fewer than a thousand. The largest land mammal in North America was pushed to the edge of extinction in roughly one human lifetime.

That was not an accident. Destroying the herds was a deliberate strategy, tied to hunting for hides, to railroads, and to the goal of removing the food supply of the Indigenous nations who lived on the plains. It is one of the fastest, most intentional collapses of a wild population in recorded history.

What saved the species was a handful of stubborn people. Ranchers who kept small herds. A few conservationists who refused to let the last animals go. Small groups at Yellowstone and on private land. Today, the population is back into the hundreds of thousands, though most live in managed herds, and only a small number are true wild, genetically unmixed animals.

Every bison you see today is a survivor of a bottleneck. Every one of them descends from an animal a few people decided was worth saving.

And what does that ancient, nearly erased animal do when a person walks up to it?

Depends entirely on the person.

PART 7. THE NOSE

Here is a number that changes how you think about bears: their sense of smell is often estimated at around seven times better than a bloodhound's. Some researchers put it even higher. Under the right wind conditions, a bear may detect food from several miles away.

Their nose is not a sense. It is a map.

A bear does not experience your yard the way you do. It experiences a layered chemical history: who walked here, what they ate, what is in the trash three houses over, what was cooked last Tuesday. It lives inside a landscape you cannot perceive at all.

This is why food is the heart of almost every serious human bear conflict. It is almost never about hatred. It is about calories. A bear that finds food near people learns something permanent: people equal food. And a bear that learns that loses its fear.

Wildlife agencies have a grim phrase for what happens next: a fed bear is a dead bear. Once a bear starts associating humans with meals, it gets bolder, it comes closer, and eventually it does something that gets it killed. The animal pays for the mistake, not the person who made it.

Every "cute bear near the cabin" video has a quiet second half that never gets posted.

PART 8. THE EXPERIMENT THAT SHOULD BE FAMOUS

In 1959, a Soviet geneticist named Dmitri Belyaev started an experiment in Siberia that would run for more than half a century.

He took wild silver foxes and applied one single selection rule. Not size, not color, not health. Just one thing: breed the ones that are least afraid of humans.

That was it. No training. No treats as a plan. Just pick the calmest in every generation and breed them together.

Within a few generations, the foxes started wagging their tails. Within about ten, some were seeking out human contact. Their coats changed. Some grew patches of white fur. Some developed floppy ears and curly tails. Their skulls and faces subtly shifted. Their hormones changed.

Selecting for tameness alone rewired the whole animal.

Scientists call this the domestication syndrome, and it is one of the most fascinating ideas in modern biology. It suggests that the difference between a wolf and a dog, or a boar and a pig, may come down to one dial: fear. Turn it down for enough generations and the entire body reorganizes around the new setting.

It also proves something crucial for everything above. Fear and aggression are not just moods. They are traits, written into the animal, adjustable over time.

And that leads to the question that the entire post has been circling.

PART 9. TAME IS NOT THE WORD YOU THINK IT IS

There are three words people use interchangeably, and they are three completely different things.

Domesticated means genetic. Thousands of years of selection changed the species itself. A dog, a cow, a horse.

Tame means individual. One animal, raised by humans, comfortable around them. The species is still wild. The animal is the exception.

Habituated means learned. An animal has stopped reacting to a stimulus because nothing bad has happened enough times. It has not become friendly. It has become unbothered.

Almost every viral wildlife video lives in the gap between these three words, and almost every viewer misreads it.

A bear that is tame is not a domesticated bear. It has no genetic safety net. It has a relationship, and relationships in the wild animal world are made of trust, routine, context, and years of small consistent signals.

Break the routine, and the relationship changes. Change the context, and it can vanish. Introduce a stranger and the whole structure can fail.

That is why the people who do this for real do not treat it like a magic trick. They treat it like a job with a checklist, and they never relax.

PART 10. WHAT THE PROFESSIONALS ACTUALLY WATCH

Ask someone who has spent twenty years around big animals what they are looking at when they approach one, and they will not say "the teeth." They will describe something much quieter.

The ears. Ears tell you attention and mood before anything else does. Pinned back means trouble. Swiveling means the animal is tracking something. Relaxed and soft means the animal is at ease.

The eyes. A soft, half-lidded look is one thing. A hard, fixed stare with wide whites is another.

The mouth. Panting, licking, yawning, lip smacking. Those are stress signals in many mammals, not signs of relaxation. A yawning animal is often a nervous animal.

The weight. Where the animal is leaning. Toward you, away from you, planted, coiled.

The distance. Every animal has a bubble, and the bubble changes with mood, hunger, season, and who else is nearby.

The timing. Feeding time, breeding season, a mother with young, an injury, a hot afternoon after a long stretch of no water. Same animal, completely different day.

Nobody reads all of this by instinct. It takes years, and it takes being wrong in small ways, safely, long before you are wrong in big ways.

The uncomfortable truth is that a person who looks calm around a dangerous animal is usually not calm at all. They are running a constant scan, a checklist, a set of exits. What looks like ease is actually discipline.

PART 11. THE MYTHS THAT HURT PEOPLE

Let us clear a few things off the table.

Myth: If an animal seems friendly, it is safe.

Friendly is a human word. To an animal, curiosity, hunger, play, and testing can all look identical from the outside. A bison that walks toward you is not necessarily greeting you. A bear that sniffs you is gathering data. A bird that steps closer is calculating distance, not affection.

Myth: Smaller animals are less risky.

Some of the most reliably damaging encounters in the world involve small or medium animals. Prairie dogs and other rodents carry fleas that can carry plague. Raccoons and bats carry rabies. The rule is not size. The rule is what the animal is carrying and how it feels about you.

Myth: Animals that were raised by humans are safe forever.

Raised by humans means they may lack fear of humans. That is not the same as lacking danger. In many cases it is the opposite, because an animal without fear does not retreat when it should. It does not warn you. It just acts.

Myth: If one person can do it, anyone can.

The person on the screen has thousands of hours you cannot see. You are watching the final second of a very long process, and the internet has a special talent for cutting off everything that came before.

PART 12. WHY THE ALGORITHM LOVES THIS AND WHY THAT SHOULD WORRY YOU

There is a reason clips like this travel.

Human brains are wired to pay attention to two things above almost everything else: threat and proximity. Put them together and you get the most reliable attention machine ever created.

A large animal plus a human body plus no barrier equals a stomach drop. That drop is a chemical event. Your amygdala fires, your heart rate shifts, and you stay glued to the screen until the tension resolves.

That is the entire business model of danger content. And it works so well that people begin to imitate it.

Every year, visitors at national parks approach wildlife for a photo and get hurt. Some seriously. It is one of the most predictable categories of preventable injury in the outdoors. Rangers put up signs, hand out warnings, and still watch the same story repeat, because a video makes something look easy that took someone a decade to earn.

If you take one thing from this whole post, take this: the safest way to love a wild animal is at a distance that lets it ignore you completely.

PART 13. THE STRANGE ECONOMICS OF RESPECT

Something surprising happens when you look at how long-term keepers describe their work.

They do not talk about courage. They talk about boredom.

Repetition. Routine. The same walk at the same time, the same tone of voice, the same hand position, the same order of steps. Consistency is the currency of trust with an animal that cannot understand words. The animal learns you the way you learn a piece of music: through pattern.

And they talk about humility. Every one of them can tell you about a moment when they were sure they understood an animal, and the animal proved otherwise.

The best in the field share a strange, quiet trait. They are not fearless. They are precisely as afraid as the situation deserves, no more and no less. They are calibrated.

That calibration is the entire skill. It is the difference between a professional and a tourist, between an expert and a person who has watched a lot of videos.

PART 14. THE THING NO ONE TELLS YOU ABOUT WILD ANIMALS AND TRUST

Here is where the story turns.

Trust between a human and a large wild animal is not a feeling. It is a negotiation that never ends.

Every day, the animal is deciding again. Not consciously in words, but through thousands of tiny calculations: is this person predictable, is this person safe, is this the same person as yesterday, does the tone match, does the smell match, does the body language match.

You do not earn trust once. You re-earn it every single time.

This is also why the same animal can behave differently with two different people standing in the same place. Animals do not respond to a species. They respond to an individual. They know who you are by your walk, your voice, your smell, the rhythm of your breathing.

There is something quietly beautiful in that. The bond is real. It is just not what most viewers think it is. It is not a friendship the way two humans have. It is something older and more precise: a shared understanding of rules.

And the moment the rules change, the bond is only as strong as the animal's mood that day.

PART 15. THE NUMBERS THAT PUT EVERYTHING IN PERSPECTIVE

Let us zoom out, because the real ranking of dangerous animals is humiliating for our instincts.

The deadliest animal on Earth is not a bear, not a shark, not a lion. It is the mosquito, responsible for hundreds of thousands of deaths a year through the diseases it carries. Snakes come next in most estimates, with tens of thousands. Dogs, mostly through rabies, follow.

Among large mammals, the hippopotamus is routinely named as one of the deadliest in Africa, with estimates around several hundred deaths per year. It looks like a giant, sleepy, smiling pool toy. It is territorial, fast on land, and its bite is devastating.

In North America, the animal that kills the most people is the deer, and almost entirely through car collisions. Cows injure and kill more people than most predators do, because far more people are near cows.

The pattern is the same everywhere. Risk is not about how scary the animal looks. It is about how much contact there is, how little we understand the signals, and how many mistakes stack up.

Fear is a terrible risk calculator. Knowledge is a good one.

PART 16. WHY THE WEIRDEST ANIMALS ARE THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE

Every animal in this story teaches a different lesson about the same idea.

The bear teaches you that strength is a choice. The jaw can do anything. The mind decides what it will do.

The ostrich teaches you that perception is a weapon. It sees more than it thinks, and it reacts to shapes, not people.

The prairie dog teaches you that intelligence does not need size. A language can live inside a creature small enough to fit in your hands.

The bison teaches you that calm and danger can share a body. A gentle grazer and a two thousand pound wall of muscle are the same animal.

And the second bear teaches you the most important lesson of all, the one no algorithm will ever reward: sometimes the smartest thing a human can do around a powerful animal is nothing.

Just stay out of its space. Let it be an animal.

PART 17. THE QUIET REVOLUTION IN HOW WE TREAT ANIMALS

For most of human history, we understood animals through two lenses: food and threat. Something to eat, or something to fear.

A third lens has been growing for the past few decades, and it may be the most important shift in how our species relates to the rest of life on Earth. The lens of mind.

Research on animal cognition keeps overturning what we thought we knew. Crows plan tools. Octopuses solve puzzles and escape tanks. Elephants mourn. Rats appear to laugh when tickled. Prairie dogs describe their enemies. Bears remember locations and people for years.

The old line between human thought and animal instinct has become a smudge.

That does not mean animals are people. It means they are something we are only beginning to understand, and something that deserves much more humility than we have historically shown.

And the animals that can be studied up close, in sanctuaries, in long-term care, in careful relationships with experienced humans, are giving us data we could never get from a distance. That research, the slow patient kind, is where the real progress is coming from.

PART 18. WHAT TO DO WITH ALL THIS

Here is the practical version, in case you ever stand near a large animal in real life.

Keep your distance. In national parks, the common guidance is at least 25 yards from most large animals and 100 yards from bears and wolves. That is not a suggestion. That is a number written after people got hurt.

Never feed wildlife. Not once. Not a little. Not for a photo.

Never turn your back and run. Many animals trigger a chase response when something flees. Back away slowly, keep your eyes on the animal, and give it a route to leave.

Learn the warning signals of the species you are in front of. Different animals warn in different ways, and the difference can decide the outcome.

Respect the season. Mating season, calving season, and protective mothers make ordinary animals unpredictable.

And when you watch a video of a person doing something extraordinary with a dangerous animal, remember the label most of those clips carry, in small red letters, for a reason.

PART 19. NOW GO BACK AND WATCH IT AGAIN

You have read about bite inhibition, about the domestication experiment, about the animal that talks, the animal that was nearly erased, the bird with the biggest eye on land, and the nose that smells the world in layers.

Scroll up. Press play again.

Watch the pauses. Watch the timing. Watch how still everyone is. Watch what the animals do with their ears, their eyes, their weight, and their mouths in the seconds before anything happens.

The first time, you saw something scary and something cute.

This time, you will see a conversation.

If this changed how you see animals, share it with someone who needs to read it before they walk up to the next big animal at the park.

Every animal here is a reminder that the wild does not owe us a happy ending. It offers us one chance to learn and that chance is worth protecting. Stay curious. Stay humble.

And follow for more. There is a lot more where this came from, and none of it is what the internet told you.

text:
Diplomacy Becomes an Algorithmic Signal:

President Trump began the day having rejected Iran’s latest proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Oil rose as markets removed some of Friday’s diplomatic optimism.

Reports later suggested that Washington might offer sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian assets in return for progress on the nuclear issue. Oil surrendered part of its advance and stocks recovered from their lows.
Trump then denied that he had offered sanctions relief. Iran insisted that its position on uranium enrichment had not changed.

Deal on. Deal off. Markets were not pricing a diplomatic settlement. They were reacting to fragments of information about a negotiation whose participants could not even agree that the negotiation existed. The result was a form of geopolitical headline roulette.

West Texas Intermediate finished at $93.23, up 0.68%, while Brent rose 0.64% to $98.46. Those closing moves look modest, but they conceal a much larger intraday struggle over whether oil flows through the Gulf will improve or deteriorate.

Saudi Arabia’s restarted East-West pipeline offers some relief by moving crude to the Red Sea and bypassing Hormuz. But it does not replace the strait’s enormous capacity, and the system remains exposed to damaged infrastructure, limited throughput and security risks around the Red Sea.

A bypass is useful.
It is not peace.
