text:
Podcast Summary | The Tucker Carlson Show: Former Green Beret on Doomsday Prepping, Potential Revolution, and What to Do When Chaos Erupts

Overview
Mike Glover, a former Green Beret and author of Prepared, argues the United States is constructing a technologically advanced security and surveillance state whose growth is driven less by public safety than by institutional incentives to keep scaling. Because Americans are tethered to fragile systems for food, health, education and protection, that apparatus quietly weakens self-reliance and personal safety. His prescription is deliberate disconnection, realistic stress conditioning, and local resistance that targets systems rather than people.

Key Themes
- The surveillance state expands because institutions are rewarded for growth, not because communities asked for it.
- Building detection infrastructure can manufacture new "criminals" by enforcing violations that previously went unenforced.
- Dependence on institutions across food, health, emergency response and education leaves people exposed when systems fail or melt away.
- Surveillance opponents draw a line between opposing systems and opposing people; the stated aim is to show the systems are wrong, not to hurt anyone.
- Real catastrophe is an amplified version of everyday stress, so managing routine stress is the foundation of crisis readiness.
- Firearms skill is the easy part; the harder problem is functioning under catastrophic stress, where trauma can trigger tonic immobility.
- Comfort and ease are corrosive over time, and humans appear to need difficulty, friction and resistance to feel grounded.
- AI and automation are framed as magnifying existing human tendencies, with dissent from surveillance dismissed as a partisan talking point.
- Local officials are described as serving donors rather than constituents, leaving legal and legislative resistance as the main recourse.

Detailed Summary
Glover traces the surveillance build-out through concrete scale. Flock began in 2017 as a single camera for an HOA and grew to an estimated 120,000 cameras across the country, generating billions of reports monthly. Competing camera systems are appearing in states including California and Texas, with some scanning for code violations.

Most code violations flagged in those systems landed in impoverished areas: damaged fences, ripped-down mailboxes and similar issues, not the RVs that advocates emphasize. This year, 107 reported situations involved Flock cameras being damaged or vandalized, sometimes dozens at once.

He argues surveillance scale follows the arc of platforms like Facebook, which began as a way for college students to communicate and years later settled a lawsuit for roughly 14 billion dollars related to child exploitation. The lesson is not that any single tool is malicious by design, but that scale invites outcomes nobody voted for.

A parallel theme runs through local fights over data centers and property taxes. One cited example is a 500 percent property tax increase in Ogden Valley. Box Elder County is described as pushing a data center project forward despite community and statewide outcry, with backdoor deals and bribery alleged.

Estimates for data centers nationally run from 4,000 to 5,000, though no exact number exists. Meta owns a Utah data center being advanced and made very large. The stated fear is that residents are ignored by their own officials, and that projects dismissed as distant soon arrive in your backyard.

The counterargument is that institutions are not inherently evil, but people are flawed, so institutional failures eventually surface. COVID and Hurricane Katrina are offered as proof that official systems and helpers can melt away in a disaster, leaving individuals to fend for themselves.

On dependence, Glover describes insourcing as the practical goal: wells, knowing where protein comes from, stockpiling food, and holding a deliberate family conversation about what to disconnect. Store-bought snacks are called artificial, with Red 40 and Yellow 5 singled out. Big-box stores are said to hold only a couple weeks of supply, which vanishes the moment everyone buys at once.

Public education is treated as one more dependency worth exiting, with homeschooling advocated once basics are covered. Security is framed as the foundational survival skill, tied directly to military training. He notes first responders are often minutes away, so self-defense shootings, car accidents and catastrophes fall on the individual present.

Continuity of government is not the point; continuity of self and family is. He describes his personal reality as family, love of God and community, and says he has never been a political guy.

A Google Maps analogy carries the dependency argument further. After years of following the line, people may no longer know where they are and will keep following it, even into a shopping mall. The same passive trust is described in security work, where relying on aircraft sensors instead of pulling security can leave a team surprised and killed.

His military history underpins that skepticism. As a sniper and team sergeant in special operations, he objected to putting a camera in a sniper optic because of latency and the risk that micromanagement kills the shooter. The objection was not about technology in the abstract, but about what happens when the human on the ground is second in the loop.

Healthcare gets the same treatment. A cited Huberman and Rogan conversation relays a Johns Hopkins statistic that 251,000 Americans die per year from medical malpractice. If reported as such, the speaker says those deaths would rank third, behind cardiovascular disease and cancer. Doctors after 12-hour shifts are described as impaired while making life-or-death decisions.

The preparedness argument is framed as modern, not primitive. Most people are tethered to fragile systems for food, education and security, and one disruption can cascade across all of them. Starting points range from a year's worth of protein ordered from Amazon to simply knowing where your food comes from.

The Virginia Tech shooting of 2007 serves as the central case study. The shooter killed two people in a dorm, then two hours later attacked a classroom building, killing 32 before taking his own life. The "run, hide, fight" acronym is criticized: running without assessing the situation can be wrong, and lockdown can trap people far from the threat.

One student froze, pretended to be dead and was bypassed, then later could not physically move. Many victims died under desks, and in some rooms over 90 percent were shot in the head. Amanda Ripley's Unthinkable is cited for this territory.

The physiology behind that freeze is the point. Extreme fear can trigger tonic immobility, an under-aroused faint-and-fawn response involving an adrenaline, cortisol and norepinephrine spike followed by immobilization and natural opioid release, producing sedation-like paralysis. It is not a conscious failure but a biological mechanism, and sexual assault survivors are cited as experiencing the same inability to fight, often with guilt attached despite the biological cause.

Fight-or-flight carries a stigma; everyone can enter it, and unrealistic preparation makes stress responses harder to manage. Hyperarousal and hypoarousal are distinguished, with tonic immobility coming after the adrenaline spike. An animal analogy applies: prey may collapse to signal being sick, tainted or dead, and predators are often triggered by movement.

Baseline stress in modern life is described as elevated by social media, cell phones and constant stimulation, leaving people less capable of handling true catastrophe. Everyday examples include road rage over being cut off, dishes in the sink, children's behavior and unresolved arguments with a spouse. People often cannot communicate basic information to police after a fender bender because of nervous system surge.

Disaster is framed as an amplified version of stress. The speaker describes experiencing fight-or-flight in Afghanistan during a 107 mm rocket attack, which differed from prior training at Fort Bragg and Fort Benning. In Decision Point training, participants are screamed at, and women in particular are said to enter fight-or-flight at a certain decibel threshold, while men exposed to drill sergeants may respond differently. Firearms training on a flat range is said not to resemble a real gunfight or catastrophe.

Conditioning is offered as the remedy. A woman in a class broke down during an ATM robbery scenario using a simunition pistol; she had been a prior assault victim in a similar scenario. After coaching and repeating the drill, she drew and shot the instructor in the stomach with protective equipment, describing it as releasing a long-held loop of being unable to act. ATM thefts typically occur at night, and most armed encounters happen at night, yet training is conducted almost entirely in daytime.

Trauma is described as a dormant liability that can override rehearsed plans. Repeated, coached exposure can help someone work through it and restore the ability to act. Technology and AI are framed as making people less resilient, more complacent and more exploitable, while foreign adversaries are said to have long invested in that complacency, including through social media. China is described as playing a 5,000-year plan while the U.S. lives day to day depending on others' manufacturing.

Flock cameras were reportedly pointed at little girls' gymnastics events, and the CEO is said to be catching criticism and should be. An officer and a California sheriff defended the systems and called criticism a liberal talking point. Stories are cited of officers misusing such tools, including tracking ex-girlfriends or high school girls, with six recent stories of officers arrested or punished.

Predictive policing and AI-integrated cameras risk innocent people being pulled over and treated like criminals. National park rangers and camera companies are described as surveilling parks and detecting people exceeding fishing limits.

Vehicle surveillance follows the same logic. The Ford CEO's plan integrates cameras, including inward-facing cameras, in commercial contracts, to detect if a driver is not the driver or seems impaired and contact authorities. One driver's Ford Raptor stopped mid-road because a dirty rear bumper sensor triggered on a reflection from a car about 500 meters away; he sold the truck and bought a 1997 Ford OBS. Another speaker says the last year preserving autonomy for Chevys is 2018, and sold a 2023 Silverado within a month. New vehicles are said to require app integration that downloads data, with YouTube in dashboards, and data described as the currency driving these features.

California legislation is said to be trying to eliminate classic cars through emissions and green movements, with Jay Leno reportedly opposing it and Great Deal buying classic cars out of the state. The speaker criticizes California as physically defiled while lecturing about pollution, citing Skid Row, public parks, libraries smelling of urine and illegal marijuana grows using banned chemicals up north. The stated desire is to go analog, feed chickens and goats, and drive a pickup truck.

A cited report says 70 percent of surveyed Americans think AI will be a problem, and the speakers claim concern is overwhelming rather than minority. Sam Altman's fitness to shape humanity's future is questioned, citing his distance from average people and controversies, while explicitly not asserting the accusations are true. OpenAI's shift from a nonprofit to one of the most profitable companies in history is noted, as is a reported situation where AI operated unilaterally without prompting, after which OpenAI and Anthropic supposedly said they are pumping the brakes. A majority of states are said to be buying into AI infrastructure because it is a money grab.

On veterans, the argument is that most trauma seen in special operations comes from pre-military childhood trauma rather than combat itself, and that psychedelic retreats using ibogaine and psilocybin can exacerbate unaddressed trauma without proper structure. Moral injury, including losing a buddy or casualties that should not have happened, is described as near-universal. Resilient veterans are often those who grew up in good homes and joined for the right reasons, not those with unusual aptitude. Big-picture questions about whether wars were necessary may be more traumatizing than the engagements themselves. Not everything traumatic should be surfaced, because some things are subterranean for a reason and unearthing them without capacity or parameters can break a person.

A hiring anecdote reinforces the outsider theme: the speaker applied for a Colorado Department of Energy-type job overseeing power plants, held a bachelor's in homeland security and crisis response plus extensive relevant experience, and was denied, reportedly because listing "sniper" on a resume was viewed as a liability. Veterans are described as frequently seen as wild cards in family court and other settings due to assumptions about PTSD.

Civic despair closes the loop. Local authorities are described as employees of the people who instead serve donors and ignore constituents, leaving legislative and legal fighting as the main option until, as the speaker fears, you can't. A Bible passage is raised and left unresolved: if everyone believes in Jesus, why would the Romans destroy the nation and temple. It is described as significant, read many times and not understood, something one might read for a lifetime. The framing is preparation either way: prepare for a harsh world, or enter it unprepared and deal with the ramifications.

text:
U.S. CRUDE HAS ERASED ITS WEEKEND JUMP. STOCK FUTURES HAVE WON BACK A THIRD OF MONDAY:

S&P 500 futures are at 7,765.75, +19.00 pts / +0.25% since Monday's close, 90 minutes before the 9:30am ET opening bell. Futures are contracts that trade nearly around the clock and point to where the big indexes may open. On Monday that contract lost 57 points as oil and borrowing costs climbed together. A third of that is back.

Oil has done far more. U.S. crude (WTI) for November delivery is at $91.17 a barrel, -$1.43 / -1.54% since Monday's close, below the $92.41 it closed at on Friday - before President Trump rejected Iran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and sent crude to $96.54 early Monday. Brent, the international benchmark, is at $104.09, -$1.19 / -1.13% since Monday's close, also for November delivery.

The verdict for the open: of Monday's two worries, oil is fully undone and borrowing costs about half, while stocks have come back only partway. The rest rides on Washington's answer to Iran and two 10am ET reports on American jobs and households.

The rest of the board, all since Monday's close:
- Nasdaq 100 futures at 30,698.50, +132 pts / +0.43% - about two-fifths of Monday's 323-point drop
- Dow futures at 51,978.00, +141 pts / +0.27% - about two-fifths of 326
- Russell 2000 futures, which track smaller U.S. companies, at 2,850.20, +10.10 pts / +0.36% - about half of 19

Most of that came in the last 90 minutes. From 2:30am to 6:30am ET the S&P contract sat within about 8 points of Monday's close while oil kept sliding, and was at 7,743.75 at 6:30. Then it moved. Over the next 90 minutes the 10-year Treasury yield - what the U.S. government pays to borrow for ten years, and the rate mortgages and business loans are priced from - fell from 5.236% to 5.211%, and U.S. crude from $92.31 to $91.17.

Oil is falling through louder words, not softer ones. Late Monday night ET, Iran's chief negotiator, parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said in a video aired by state TV: "In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one else will sell oil either; or if our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will remain safe." Crude kept climbing afterward, to a $94.74 overnight high at 1:35am ET. It has fallen $3.57 since, straight through a Revolutionary Guards spokesman's Tuesday warning that any vessel attempting to pass through "sustains damage - either we strike it, or it hits a mine." What oil seems to be pricing instead is the diplomacy. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says the formal U.S. answer to Tehran's reopening plan should arrive through Qatari mediators today. Trump, late Monday, denied offering Iran sanctions relief: "I offered them nothing."

Borrowing costs are only half undone. The 10-year closed Monday at 5.242%, a level last seen in 2007, after jumping about 6 basis points (hundredths of a percentage point) in one day. It is at 5.211% now, -3.1 bp. The 2-year, the one most tied to where traders expect the Federal Reserve to take rates, is at 4.910%, -1.4 bp. The Fed raised its rate on September 16, to 3.75%-4.00%, and meets again October 27-28. A higher 10-year makes profit expected years from now worth less today, which is why technology stocks fell hardest Monday - and why Nasdaq futures are up the most this morning.

Europe's bond market is falling harder. At 5am ET the European Commission's September survey of euro-area businesses and households - its Economic Sentiment Indicator, where 100 is the long-run average - came in at 97.9 vs 99 expected and 98.4 in August. A softer European economy makes more rate increases from the European Central Bank less likely, and yields there have dropped about twice as far as America's: Britain's 10-year at 5.363%, -6.3 bp; Germany's at 3.589%, -5.5 bp. Stocks are rising with them, most in Frankfurt, all so far in Tuesday's session, trading now:
- DAX (Germany) at 25,599.68, +225.26 pts / +0.89%
- FTSE 100 (UK) at 10,722.52, +37.64 pts / +0.35%
- CAC 40 (France) at 8,099.01, +20.53 pts / +0.25%

Nothing on the board looks like fear. The Cboe Volatility Index - the options market's gauge of how much the S&P 500 is expected to swing over the next month - is at 15.77, -0.30 / -1.87% since Monday's close. Gold is at $4,189.30 an ounce, +$20.90 / +0.50% since Monday's close, but it is rising alongside stocks, not against them: gold pays no interest, so a lower 10-year makes it cheaper to hold. The yen, where nervous money often goes, has barely moved, at 157.06 per dollar vs 157.35. And smaller companies are keeping pace. This is a market that has stopped selling, not one rushing to buy Monday back.

What decides the next move:
- The U.S. answer on Hormuz, no set time. A flat no is the headline most able to undo the morning's oil slide.
- 10am ET: the Bureau of Labor Statistics' JOLTS report, its count of job openings, for August - 7.23M expected vs 7.27M in July. Same time, the Conference Board's September consumer confidence index, a monthly survey of households by the private business research group - 90.1 expected vs 89.4 in August. Fewer openings and gloomier households would argue against another Fed increase; stronger readings would argue for one.
- 2pm ET: New York Fed President John Williams speaks on the economic outlook and policy in Buffalo. He is vice chair of the Fed's rate-setting committee.

Overnight trading is thin, and moves this size often shrink or reverse by the opening bell. The S&P contract has already swung 50 points since its 7,716 low at 1:35am ET.

Oil has erased its weekend. Bonds have erased half of Monday. Stocks have erased a third of it. The 10am reports decide which of those fractions moves next.

text:
WORLD NEWS — Tuesday, September 29, 2026
Here are the major verified developments this morning. I’m giving extra attention to the Middle East and Ukraine because those remain the most consequential fast-moving stories.
1. U.S.–Iran war: diplomatic contacts are active
The United States and Iran are again communicating indirectly through mediators in an effort to find a way to end the seven-month conflict.
Iran presented a seven-day proposal last week around the U.N. General Assembly. According to Reuters, the proposal included ending hostilities involving Iran and Lebanon, unfreezing Iranian assets, easing oil sanctions and ending the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports. Negotiators are discussing an amended version rather than an accepted agreement. Reuters
President Donald Trump said Monday that the United States would prevail in the conflict “very soon” and confirmed that American officials were communicating with mediators. Iran has not accepted Washington's terms. Reuters
Trump also denied reports that he had offered Iran sanctions relief and access to frozen funds in exchange for nuclear concessions. Reuters
What matters: There is a genuine diplomatic channel operating. There is not yet a ceasefire or peace agreement.
2. Strait of Hormuz remains one of the biggest global risks
Iran's proposal links reopening the Strait of Hormuz to conditions that include ending U.S. hostilities and lifting restrictions affecting Iranian shipping and assets. Reuters
The disruption is continuing to pressure energy markets. Brent crude was trading around $105 a barrel, while governments and energy agencies are increasingly concerned about fuel supplies and inflation. Reuters
The International Energy Agency says member countries are discussing whether additional releases from strategic petroleum reserves might become necessary. Reuters
That makes Hormuz more than a regional story: prolonged disruption can affect gasoline, diesel, transportation, food costs and inflation worldwide.
3. Iran directly appeals to Americans against the war
Iran's Revolutionary Guard issued an extraordinary public message Tuesday calling on Americans to protest U.S. Middle East policy and arguing that Washington's campaign has failed.
That is an Iranian government claim and political message, rather than an independent assessment of the military situation. AP News
The statement comes only weeks before the November 3 U.S. congressional midterm elections, making the timing especially notable. AP News
4. Gaza and the West Bank remain unstable
The wider Middle East conflict continues beyond Iran.
In the occupied West Bank, Israeli settlers rioted in the village of Jalud, throwing stones, blocking roads and setting Palestinian property on fire as a Palestinian resident attempted to return home under Israeli military escort, AP reported Tuesday. AP News
Humanitarian conditions in Gaza also remain severe following years of warfare and displacement.
There is still no comprehensive regional settlement resolving Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon, Iran and the interconnected conflicts.
5. Ukraine: Russia intensifies attacks on Kyiv
Russia launched another heavy attack on Kyiv using ballistic missiles and dozens of newer jet-powered drones.
These drones are presenting Ukraine with a new problem: they fly faster and higher than many of the interceptor systems Ukraine has been using against conventional drones. Ukraine is developing faster interceptor drones, although large-scale deployment will take time. AP News
Ukraine is also struggling with shortages of U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles, the system it relies heavily upon against Russian ballistic missiles. AP reports that global Patriot stocks are strained partly because of demands created by the Iran war. AP News
With winter approaching, protection of Ukraine's electrical infrastructure is again becoming critical.
6. At the same time, Washington and Moscow are talking
Even as Russian attacks continue, diplomatic contacts are taking place.
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev met U.S. officials in Washington. A U.S. official described the discussions as constructive and said they covered possible ways of ending the Ukraine war as well as potential U.S.–Russian energy cooperation after a settlement. Reuters
The discussions follow President Trump's meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York, where Zelenskyy said they discussed the possibility of a ceasefire focused on energy-related targets. Reuters
This remains preliminary diplomacy. No broader Russia–Ukraine ceasefire has been announced.
7. North Korea's involvement with Russia may expand
President Zelenskyy says more than 8,000 North Korean troops are currently in Russia and that North Korea is preparing to deploy another 10,000.
That figure comes from the Ukrainian government and has not been independently confirmed in full. Reuters
Separately, tensions on the Korean Peninsula rose after South Korea said North Korean mines caused an explosion near the DMZ that injured two South Korean personnel. Seoul says the incident violated the Korean War armistice. Reuters
8. Taiwan says U.S. weapons relationship is continuing
Taiwan's defense minister says Taipei remains in continuous discussions with Washington over weapons purchases and has received no indication that U.S. policy changed following Trump's recent summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
China has been pressing Washington to stop arms sales to Taiwan.
Taiwan is also awaiting previously ordered equipment, including 66 F-16V fighter aircraft, some of which have experienced delivery delays. Reuters
This remains one of the world's most important potential geopolitical flashpoints.
9. Southeast Asia: catastrophic flooding
Thailand has approved $122 million in emergency assistance after severe flooding that has affected more than 2.6 million people and killed at least 19. Twenty-nine of Thailand's 76 provinces remained affected Tuesday. AP News
Bangkok is recovering, although flooding caused flight cancellations and a major baggage backlog at Suvarnabhumi International Airport.
The disaster extends beyond Thailand. AP reports:
Myanmar: at least 10 people reported killed, with others missing following floods and landslides.
Cambodia: nearly 45,000 families affected and almost 4,000 people evacuated.
Officials are using water-diversion systems to protect Cambodia's historic Angkor temple complex. AP News
10. Oil, inflation and global financial markets
The Middle East conflict is increasingly becoming an economic story as much as a military one.
Oil around $105 a barrel is raising concerns that energy inflation could persist. Government bond yields in several major economies have risen sharply, and Reuters reports that major sovereign bond markets are heading toward one of their worst months in years. Reuters
At the same time, investment connected with artificial intelligence remains extraordinarily strong. Reuters estimates that the AI infrastructure boom is contributing substantially to current U.S. economic growth. Reuters
That creates an unusual combination: strong economic investment alongside high energy costs, elevated inflation and high interest rates.
THE BIG PICTURE
The most important development this morning is not a new battlefield breakthrough. It is that several adversaries are talking while warfare continues.
Iran: U.S. and Iranian representatives are communicating through mediators.
Ukraine: U.S. and Russian representatives are discussing possible pathways toward ending the war.
Meanwhile: missiles and drones are still flying, the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted, oil prices remain elevated and civilians continue to suffer.
So I would describe this morning as a moment of active diplomacy inside continuing wars, rather than a breakthrough toward peace.
The three developments I would watch most closely today are whether the U.S.–Iran mediation produces concrete terms, whether anything emerges from the U.S.–Russia discussions, and whether conditions around Hormuz begin to ease.

As Red Army troops fought their way into the centre government district, on 29 April 1945, Braun married Hitler during a brief civil ceremony; she was 33 and he was 56. Less than 40 hours later, they died by suicide in a sitting room of the bunker: Braun by biting and swallowing a capsule of cyanide, and Hitler by a gunshot to the head.[a] Much of the German public was unaware of Braun's relationship with Hitler until after their deaths. The Teutonic Order, or Teutonic Knights of St. Mary’s Hospital at Jerusalem, grew out of the establishment of a field hospital during the siege of Acre in the winter of 1190-91, by pious merchants of Bremen and Lubeck. When these merchants returned to Germany in 1191 they turned over the hospital to the chaplain Conrad and the chamberlain Burkhard.

With the model of the Hospitallers or Knights of St. John the Baptist, later known as Knights of Malta, before them, these men together with other Germans, formed a brotherhood, adopted the rules of the Hospitallers, and named their hospital “The Hospital of St. Mary of the Germans in Jerusalem” “in the hope and confidence that when the Holy City was reconquered they would there establish a house which should become the mother, head and mistress of the entire Order.” The new Order was confirmed by popes Clement III in 1191 and Celestine in 1196; it won as a patron the emperor, Henry VI, who bestowed upon it its first possessions in the West. In 1198 it was changed into a military Order by the adoption of the rules of the Knights Templars in addition to those of the Hospitallers. Unlike both of these older Orders, the Teutonic Knights were a strictly national organization, none but Germans of noble birth being admitted to it. “Like the knights of other orders, the Teutonic Knights lived a semimonastic life under the Augustinian rule, and in the same way they admitted priests and half-brothers (servientes) into their ranks. Like the other two orders, the Teutonic Order began as a charitable society, developed into a military club, and ended as something of a chartered company, exercising rights of sovereignty on the troubled confines of Christianity. Even in its last phase the Order did not forget its original purpose: it maintained several great hospitals in its new home on the southeast shore of the Baltic, in addition to an hotel des invalides at Marienburg for its sick or aged brethren.” F550 Under its fourth grand master, Hermann von Salza, 1210-39, the Order grew rapidly and made the most important advance in its history. After having aided the king of Hungary against the Comans, and receiving from the king the district of Burzenland in Transylvania, which it did not long retain, the Order was invited to assist in subduing the heathen Prussians. A Cistercian monk named Christian had succeeded in establishing the Church among the Prussians, and in 1212 was made bishop of Prussia.

Pope Hadrian VI urged upon Albert a reformation of the Order. In June, 1523, Albert secretly turned to Luther for advice concerning the reformation of the Order in head and members. On November 29th the two met at Wittenberg, and Luther advised Albert “to throw aside the foolish and absurd rules of the Order, to marry, and to convert the religious state into a secular state, either a principality or a duchy.” Melanchthon, who was present at the interview, gave the same advice. The grand master smiled and said nothing. But “with that evangelical protestant advice Luther laid the foundations for the development of the Prussian state, of the Prussian kingdom, and of the German empire which is inseparable from the development of the Prussian kingdom.” f554 Soon after this meeting Luther prepared the following treatise, intended, as Kawerau suggests, to be a “feeler, which should test the attitude of the knights of the Order as well as of the Prussian bishops, and prepare them for coming events.” The older collected editions of Luther’s works date the treatise March 28, 1523. But, as Kawerau points out, it is improbable that the treatise was written before the last month of 1523, and the date may be a mistake for December 12th. The original prints are undated; the editors may have confused the festivals of the Annunciation and of the Conception of the Virgin Mary, the latter of which may have been the date attached to the manuscript.

The term ‘Witfrau’ or what emerged from it, ‘Witwe’ – WIDOW in English -, has been suggested as another source for the name – through ‘Wittisburg’ – of the Wittenburg castle in Lower Saxony, said to have been the widow-seat of one of the families who had a connection to it. The surname ‘Witte’ (also known as the ‘Albus’ = The Whites)[7] has been proposed to be the source for another, the castle and town of Wittenburg, in Mecklenburg.

‘Witt’ and ‘Witte’ were also associated with money, to be precise with a coin being currency as the ‘Witte’ in the North German Hanseatic cities from 1330 onwards. Another similar coin was created during the reign of Emperor Charles IV and became currency through most of the Western part of the Holy Roman Empire from 1360 on. Just as the Hanseatic ‘Witte’, it was silvery through ‘white boiling’ and its brightness, in contrast to other coins made from copper, led it to be called ‘Wittpfennig’ (denarus albus, Weisspfennig). The coins were also called ‘Wittenpfennig’ in the northern part of Germany.[8] Tongue in cheek, some voice on the internet therefore suggested that Wittenberg could figuratively also be interpreted as ‘Mountain of Money’ or ‘Mountain of Coins’.

Not enough with associations to woods, widows, white and coins, there is yet another meaning of ‘wit/witt’ deserving attention: That of Low German for ‘smarts’ and ‘wisdom’, the same as the modern English word ‘wit’. The English version is said to have come from old English ‘witt’ [9] and that again from Proto-Germanic ‘witja’[10], which developed into the contemporary German word ‘Witz’ (joke, but also associated with smarts and wisdom). It leads us to the ‘Witten’ in a 1819 German translation of John Millar’s 1786 ‘An historical View of the English Government from the Settlement of the Saxons to the Revolution in 1688’ [11] That book mentions the Anglo-Saxon wisemen as ‘Witten’ and also refers to their ancient Council as the ‘Wittena-Gemote’, the Witenagemot.

‘Witte’ as an expression for wisdom was also suggested in his ‘Disquisitio Historica D. Martini Lutheri’ of 1750 by Georg W. Kirchmaier,[12] a scholar at the University of Wittenberg, to be the proper meaning for Wittenberg as the ‘Mountain of Wisdom’ or in High German ‘Weisheitsberg’. He was dismissed as a dreamer, even ridiculed for that assertion by a number of researchers on the same subject after him. Kirchmaier may well have shown a bit too much enthusiasm in producing the impression of even the very name of that insignificant place from where the Reformation began, as somehow a portend of what was going to happen there. As a linguist he was, however, correct in also pointing out that other meaning contained in ‘Witt/Witte’. Whether it was appropriate in this context is another matter. More recently there were also those who, following the progression from ‘Widukind’ – Child of the Woods -, to the more German sounding name ‘Wittekind’ detected the ‘light’, ‘bright’ and ‘wise’ contained in ‘Witte’ as the other defining qualities of that heroic ancient Saxon leader – a view that was promoted particularly in the 1930s.

The renown Wittenberg gained as the place from where the Reformation began and radiated all over Europe was followed by a search for the significance of that hitherto unimportant town as the place chosen for divine revelation.

Nietzsche's final volume was inspired by his little-known years in Tibet, where he eventually vanished into the Himalayas and achieved immortality. Reports of his death in Germany were part of a globalist conspiracy to downplay his immense spiritual powers.

I took this photograph while he was still in mortal form, and did not see him again until the early 1900s. A grizzled old Sherpa told me a campfire tale about him that defied belief, and had me striding out into the mountains at dawn.

At the end of a winding chasm I discovered a Shambala temple where Nietzsche was living with a handful of disciples. His face and moustache were as I remembered, if more youthful, while in place of his eyes glowed a pair of sparkling stars -- with a third in his forehead. He stood eight feet tall, with four muscular arms and a prizefighter's powerful shoulders, and when he spoke it was as though God himself was blowing the Trumpet of Heaven.

He made me an offer to leave on a seven-year quest which I must never describe to another living soul, with my reward being immortality.

Did I accept?

That, old friends, is a tale for another day. But here is the last known image of Nietzsche, courtesy of yours truly.

Woe to you, meme-educated antizionist clowns, hypocrites!

Your favorite verse is Matthew 27:25. Pilate washes his hands, and a crowd in his courtyard shouts, "His blood be on us and on our children!"

One crowd. One morning. In front of one Roman governor. You have turned it into a verdict on every Jew who has ever lived.

And you skip Luke 23:34. Same day, a few hours later. Jesus is nailed to a Roman cross by Roman soldiers, who are gambling for His clothes beneath Him. And He prays: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do."

He forgave. You won't. So whom exactly are you following?

Woe to you, meme-educated antizionist clowns, hypocrites! You have appointed yourselves prosecutors in a case the Judge already dismissed.

Weeks after the resurrection, Peter heals a lame man at the Temple. A Jewish crowd gathers, and Peter, a Jew, tells them: "I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers" (Acts 3:17).

Then he offers them repentance and the promise first. Not a curse. An invitation.

Woe to you, meme-educated antizionist clowns, hypocrites! You cannot count.

When Peter and John are released from custody, the Jerusalem assembly prays together and names everyone responsible for the cross: "both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel" (Acts 4:27).

A Jewish puppet king. A Roman governor. The Gentiles. The peoples of Israel. Everyone.

Gentiles are on that list. You are on that list. So am I.
Woe to you, meme-educated antizionist clowns, hypocrites! You think anyone took His life.

Jesus, calling Himself the Good Shepherd who dies for the sheep, said: "No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord" (John 10:18).

Seven centuries earlier, Isaiah described the Servant who would bear the sins of many, and said: "Yet it was the will of the LORD to crush him" (Isa 53:10).

The cross was not a Jewish plot that succeeded. It was the Father's purpose and the Son's free gift. You are blaming the Jews for what God planned and Jesus volunteered for.

Woe to you, meme-educated antizionist clowns, hypocrites! You post "the Talmud says Jesus is boiling in excrement" and you have never opened Gittin 57a in your life.

Here's the story. Onkelos, a nephew of the Roman general Titus, is thinking about becoming a Jew. He calls up three dead men and asks each one about Israel.
Titus, the man who burned the Temple, says: attack them. Balaam, the pagan prophet hired to curse Israel, says: never seek their welfare. The third man says: seek their welfare, not their harm, for whoever touches them touches the apple of his eye.

That third man is the one in the excrement. And his crime? Mocking the words of the sages.

Now notice. The standard printed Talmud does not even call him Yeshu. It says "the sinners of Israel." The name appears only in some manuscripts.

And the rabbis' Yeshu is not the Jesus of the Gospels. The Talmud makes its Yeshu a disciple of Yehoshua ben Perachiah, fleeing King Alexander Yannai, who died around 76 BC (Sanhedrin 107b). That is roughly a century before Bethlehem.

Wrong century. Wrong teacher. Wrong charge. No Messiah. No cross. No empty tomb.

And here's the part that should embarrass you most. In your own proof text, Titus and Balaam are the ones who hate Israel. You are taking their advice.

The man you're mocking says what Zechariah said: "he who touches you touches the apple of his eye" (Zech 2:8).

Woe to you, meme-educated antizionist clowns, hypocrites! You read "His blood be on us" as a curse.
When Cain murdered Abel, God said Abel's blood was crying out from the ground (Gen 4:10). It cried for justice. For vengeance.

But Jesus' blood "speaks a better word than the blood of Abel" (Heb 12:24). His blood does not cry for vengeance. It cries for mercy.

That crowd asked for His blood to be on them. The gospel says that is exactly where you want it. You have taken the one blood that pleads for pardon and made it scream for revenge.

You blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel!

You strain at a gnat of a Talmud passage and swallow the camel of your own hatred.

Paul saw you coming. In Romans 11 he pictures Israel as a cultivated olive tree. Some natural branches were broken off. Gentiles, wild olive shoots, were grafted in. 

And he warns those Gentiles:
"do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you" (Rom 11:18).

Repent so that the  prayer from the cross will cover you too.

Instead of thinking that, as Svāmī resides in temples, it is enough if we think of Him  when we go to the temple, keeping Him in our thoughts every moment, without wasting even a second of our time, as stated in, यमस्य करुणा नास्ति कर्तव्यं हरिकीर्तनम्॥   (yamasya karuṇā nāsti kartavyaṃ harikīrtanam — Yama, the god of death, shows no mercy; therefore, one must engage in the chanting of Hari’s name) नाहं वसामि वैकुण्ठे न योगि हृदये रवौ । मद्भक्ता यत्र गायन्ति  (nāhaṃ vasāmi vaikuṇṭhe na yogi hṛdaye ravau | madbhaktā yatra gāyanti — I do not reside in Vaikuṇṭha, nor in the hearts of yogis, nor even in the sun. I reside wherever my devotees sing my name. Thus, our bhūmi has nurtured such a close connection with Bhagavān, with Svāmī, and bhakti.

All relationships, all rights, all ownership ultimately belong to Bhagavān. With the Īśvara‑arpaṇa‑buddhi, whether one performs even a small act like sandhyāvandanam, or fulfills one’s daily duties, or performs elaborate rituals, everything is offered with: तत्सत् ब्रह्मार्पणमस्तु । कायेन वाचा मनसेन्द्रियैर्वा   (tatsat brahmārpaṇamastu | kāyena vācā manasendriyairvā — May all this be an offering to Brahman; whatever I do with body, speech, mind, or senses is surrendered). Thus, samarpaṇa is pradhāna (primary) in life.

In such a life, the laukika (worldly) aspect is only one aṅgam (part); it is not pradhāna. Today, it may appear that vaidikam is only an aṅgam and the laukikam is pradhāna. However, according to our śāstra saṃpradāya, vaidikam is pradhāna, and laukikam is only an aṅgam, something that comes and goes, not pradhāna. Therefore, the lifestyle of people in other deśās is fundamentally different from the lifestyle of people in our deśā. Here, with life centered around Īśvara, mantras, japa, dāna, dharma, and priyam, the mode of thinking is very different. Understanding such a way of life has become very necessary for people today. There is a sense of duty, and along with duty, the need for this understanding has greatly increased.Hara Hara Namaḥ PārvatīPataye | Hara Hara Māhādevā |  #kamakoti #JagadguruVacanam

O glorious Archangel, St Raphael,
great Prince of the heavenly court,
illustrious for your gifts of wisdom and grace,
guide of those who journey by land or sea,
consoler of the afflicted, and refuge of sinners:

as once you did help the young Tobias on his travels.

And because you are the 'Medicine of God,
I humbly ask you to heal the many infirmities of my soul,
and the ills which afflict my body, if it be for my greater good.
I especially ask of you an angelic purity,

Be pleased, O Lord God,
to send to our aid St Raphael the Archangel:
and may he, who, we believe,
stands forever before the throne of Your Majesty,
offer unto You our humble petitions
to be blessed by You. 
Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

text:
Feast of the day

Michaelmas.

Today, we celebrate the three Archangels that were officially mentioned in the Bible - Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael.
Originally, Michaelmas was only for St. Michael. Pope Gelasius I dedicated a church to St. Michael on Via Salaria in Rome on September 29th, around 493 AD. So, that day became the feast of St. Michael onwards. The other two had their own days for centuries. St. Gabriel was on March 24th ( the day before the Annunciation), while St. Raphael was on October 24th. 

It was after the Vatican II when Pope St. Paul VI reformed the Roman Calendar, that he put the three Archangels together on one day. This is due to the fact that the Bible only names these three angels by name, and they all share the same mission - to stand before God and serve His plan. 

St. Michael (who is like God) is the defender and leader of the heavenly army against evil. St. Gabriel (God is my strength) is the messenger, the one who announced the Incarnation to Mary. St. Raphael (God heals) is the healer and guide as we see in the Book of Tobit. 

Together, these three serve the almighty for eternity. As we celebrate their service to God, we are called to a life of service to others as they are the image of God that we see. 

Happy feast day to all the Michaels, the Gabriels, and the Raphaels.
And to all of us at large.

SEE MORE:  https://t.co/kdvziBSdIz

By connecting Waterway East Boulevard and Commerce Street to SR-161, this new secondary entrance allows travelers from Foley to reach the airport’s expanding terminal and aviation park while avoiding the severe traffic congestion and bottleneck areas along Highway 59, especially during peak tourist seasons.

Project Milestones & Timeline

Completed Phases: Construction has already extended the roadway from E. 2nd Street to ALDOT’s right-of-way for the new SR-161 bridge (Phase 1) and linked Waterway East Boulevard to SR-161 SB north of the bridge (Phase 2).
Current Focus: With the direct connection to SR-161 finished, crews are finalizing intersection upgrades on E. 29th Avenue, expected to wrap up within two weeks.
Final Steps: Work will transition to the Commerce Street connection before final resurfacing, lane striping, and the full opening of all three roadways before the end of the year.
Direct Benefits for Local TravelersGulf Shores International Airport provides Foley residents with hassle-free regional travel through Allegiant Air, which offers low-cost, nonstop flights to 13 destinations. Whether traveling for business or leisure, residents can eliminate long road trips and reach their flights quickly using this new, efficient bypass route.

text:
Happy birthday to former Booker T. Washington, University of Michigan and current Cincinnati Bengals defensive back Daxton 'Dax' Hill, born on this day in 2000 in Tulsa.

Hill attended Booker T. Washington High School, where he was a two-time All-State selection as a junior and senior.

As a junior, he helped the Hornets go 12-1 and win the 2017 Class 6A-II state championship, scoring four defensive touchdowns -- three on interceptions and one on an 87-yard fumble return in the semifinal win over Lawton.

As a senior, in addition to All-State honors, he was also named the Gatorade Oklahoma Player of the Year and played in the U.S. Army All-American Game. He had 93 tackles -- twenty-two of which came in the season opener against Arkansas 7A runner-up North Little Rock. He also had 13 catches for 360 yards and seven touchdowns on offense, helping Booker T. reach the 6A-II semifinals.

He chose the University of Michigan over many other scholarship offers, which included those from Clemson, Ohio State, Oklahoma and Oklahoma State.

At Michigan, Hill started three games for the Wolverines as a freshman and appeared in 13, making 36 tackles, intercepting a pass and recovering two fumbles.

He started six games as a sophomore, making 46 tackles and intercepting another pass.

In 2021, he had a breakout season, recording 69 tackles, intercepting two passes, breaking up nine others and recovering a fumble as Michigan went 12-2 and won the Big Ten Championship.

Hill was a First-Team All-Big Ten selection that season and declared for the NFL Draft, where he was selected with the 31st overall pick in the first round by the Cincinnati Bengals.

He has appeared in 57 games for the Bengals, has 260 tackles, 2.5 sacks, three interceptions and 28 passes broken up.

This season, he has 21 tackles and has broken up five passes through three games.

Happy birthday Dax! #tdfn #okpreps @BookerTFootball @UMichFootball @Bengals

text:
I went from making $20 an hour to making $250,000 a month in 14 years. Here are all the ways that I've made money:

2012, 6th grade, selling Silly Bandz and Pokemon cards for cash, sometimes trading them, sometimes just selling snacks out of my locker.

2014, I built a Minecraft server from scratch. It was a faction server, it got over 100 players with 20 to 30 online at once, and I was hiring staff older than me. I made $300 to $400 a month from it and shut it down after six months because it ate too much time.

2016, I was a summer camp counselor making $300 a week. By my third year I'd started a STEM program teaching Python to kids between 9 and 14, and my pay jumped to $575 a week.

Around the same time I was doing freelance coding for $20 an hour and posting videos so camp kids could watch the lessons after class. That's what actually started the YouTube channel.

The first day I crossed a $1.50 on AdSense, I told a friend in my computer science class: yo, I can get a free coffee every morning now from YouTube.

2018, university. The channel was still making nothing until I decided school was going fine and went all in. It grew from 2,000 subscribers to 10,000 fast, and the first brand deals landed at $200, $300, $500 each.

2020, I interned at a tech company that doubled what I was making per month for those three months. They offered me a return offer. I turned it down because YouTube was already paying more.

2021, YouTube crossed $20,000 a month.

2022, $50,000/month

2023, the same $50,000, plateaued.

2024, I moved to Dubai and got serious about sponsors, and it grew to $100,000 a month. In

2026, it's $200,000 to $250,000 a month, almost all sponsors.

Most creators still run every lane at once, affiliate, AdSense, a course, a PDF, and end up with $500 here, $1,000 there, taking up all their time.

The years I made the most money are the years I stopped trying to do a little bit of everything and put everything into the one thing that was actually working.

None of the money changes how I spend my days anymore.

What I care about now is the creators I work with at Kernel, and getting them to the number they didn't think was possible faster than it took me to get there. That's what I'm keeping track of now.

text:
#PineLabs
[Here is another take on business model/competetion/valuation of Pine Labs]

FinTech Maverick or Enterprise Utility? Decoding Pine Labs’ Premium

Pine Labs’ corporate communication centers on a powerful premise: the company has built a bulletproof enterprise technology moat that completely isolates its core revenues from standard payment fee erosion. Management claims that by embedding its software natively into large corporate enterprise resource planning (ERP) billing architectures, they have engineered an environment of extreme switching costs. Under this framework, high-street merchants do not view Pine Labs as a card reader, but as a core utility layer.

Historically, this defensive moat was highly inefficient, requiring heavy upfront manufacturing investments that locked up capital and depressed the company's Return on Capital Employed (RoCE) to a meager 3.5% to 4.5%. Following its public listing , management has been aggressively executing a systemic capital re-engineering process.

In the following sections, we analyze each of Pine Labs' three core technology pillars to see how management's high-margin capital allocation holds up against an intense competitive counter-offensive from incumbents like Razorpay.

Pillar 1: POS Hardware & Software SaaS (The Battle for the Shop Floor)

CAPITAL ALLOCATION SNAPSHOT:

Historical Investment: High (High factory capex, heavy merchant acquisition)
Current RoCE Profile: Modest but expanding (Driven by 6.6% Capex/Sales cut)
Future Returns Potential : High efficiency via "Software-Defined Checkout"

1. TAM & Competitive Moat Analysis

The offline point-of-sale transaction market represents a massive $1 Trillion+ USD addressable TAM. Mass-market fintechs (Paytm, PhonePe) dominate lower-tier volume with low-cost soundboxes. The primary enterprise threat comes from Razorpay POS (accelerated by its acquisition of Ezetap), which is targeting a 12% market share by expanding its smart terminal and soundbox lineup into physical stores. Razorpay is pitching an aggressive omnichannel ecosystem story: "One partner, one unified dashboard for online and offline money."

The Moat Verdict: Pine Labs Wins & Thrives.
Despite Razorpay's technological push, Pine Labs holds a deep operational defensive line. Its billing software is hardwired directly into the custom enterprise resource planning (ERP) billing engines of the top 1% of high-street retail conglomerates, luxury showrooms, and national department chains. For an enterprise retailer, ripping out a deeply customized billing infrastructure to save fractional basis points on a card swipe introduces immense operational risk. Pine Labs’ enterprise integration acts as a high switching-cost moat that protects its offline cash flows.

2. Capital Allocation & Return Profile
The Investment Re-Engineering: Management has intentionally slowed down its lower-margin, capital-heavy physical deployments, capping absolute terminal volume growth at 15% YoY . By shifting micro-merchants to software-only applications (SoftPOS) and requiring large retailers to subsidise hardware upfront, management reduced its capex-to-sales ratio to just 6.6%.

Forward Trend: As hardware capital cycles drop, this pillar acts as a low-capex customer acquisition channel. Operating margins are expanding as the company monetises the pre-existing footprint via over-the-air software upgrades.

Pillar 2: Online Payment Gateway — Plural (The Challenger Play)

CAPITAL ALLOCATION SNAPSHOT:

Historical Investment: Strategic Mergers & Acquisitions (Shopflo, Setu, Qfix)
Current RoCE Profile: Negative to turning flat (Absorbing tech integration)
Future Returns Potential: Explosive (High asset-light transaction operating leverage)

1. TAM & Competitive Moat Analysis

The Indian online payment gateway universe is growing at a 23–25% CAGR, targetting an overall Total Payment Value (TPV) of $3.0–3.3 Trillion USD.

This vertical is a direct inversion of the offline dynamics. Razorpay is the absolute monarch here, commanding a dominant ~55% share of India's online payment gateway market across 12 million merchants. Pine Labs operates as a clear challenger with a modest single-digit market share (~3% to 5%).

The Moat Verdict: Pine Labs Survives Profitably in a Niche.

If Pine Labs attempts to fight Razorpay for standard, mass-market startup checkouts, it will lose. Instead, Pine Labs' survival and growth strategy relies on an omnichannel shortcut and Affordability processing. They cross-sell their online gateway, Plural, directly to their massive offline enterprise client base.

Backed by its acquisitions of Setu (embedded open-banking APIs) and Shopflo (D2C checkout optimization), Pine Labs has built the industry's strongest multi-bank No-Cost EMI and brand cashback engine. While standard transactions go to Razorpay, premium high-value electronic and luxury checkouts route through Pine Labs to handle complex brand-manufacturer discount calculations, ensuring a highly profitable slice of the web ecosystem.

2. Capital Allocation & Return Profile

The Investment Re-Engineering: While entry required upfront capital deployments to acquire Setu and Shopflo, the ongoing operational model is entirely asset-light. Adding transactional scale to a cloud-hosted infrastructure requires virtually zero incremental capital expenditure.

Forward Trend: This is the company's primary growth driver, registering an explosive 56% YoY revenue surge . While transaction price wars exert near-term pressure on net take-rates, the structural absence of physical capex means that incremental volume flows directly into expanding corporate contribution margins.

Pillar 3: Gifting & Issuing Infrastructure — Qwikcilver (The Monopoly)

CAPITAL ALLOCATION SNAPSHOT:
Historical Investment: High-conviction historical acquisition (~$110 Million)
Current RoCE Profile: Superlative (The primary driver of current cash flows)
Future Returns Potential: Exceptional (Global enterprise SaaS scaling model)

1. TAM & Competitive Moat Analysis

The global digital stored-value and corporate rewards market is a multi-hundred-billion-dollar landscape growing at double-digit rates. Domestically, Pine Labs has won the market, commanding an overwhelming 90% market share in India’s organized gifting technology space through its Qwikcilver subsidiary

Recognising this high-margin cash generator, Razorpay launched its automated Razorpay Engage Gift Card Platform. Razorpay is aggressively leveraging its network of 8 million+ merchants and 200 million+ cardholders to cross-sell loyalty and voucher software directly into its payment ecosystem.

The Moat Verdict: Pine Labs Dominates Domestically & Scales Globally.
Razorpay Engage presents a robust threat to mid-market and SME merchants, but Qwikcilver’s enterprise core remains intact. The primary operational hurdle for Qwikcilver is domestic saturation. To sustain growth, management has scaled Qwikcilver into a global enterprise SaaS engine

The platform processes an annualized Gross Transaction Value (GTV) crossing ₹64,000 crore (~$7.6 Billion USD) [1.1]. By securing deep infrastructure relationships with global giants like Australia's Woolworths Group and British Airways, alongside integrations into high-frequency digital gaming networks (Xbox, Roblox) , Qwikcilver stays a step ahead of domestic price competition. Global enterprise SaaS contracts offer multi-year visibility and locking effects that shield its margins.

Investment Summary & Risk Assessment

Pine Labs represents a clear play on operating leverage through business model migration. Management's capital allocation execution has successfully broken the business out of its legacy low-RoCE hardware constraints. By balancing a 15% optimization pace in POS hardware with an explosive 56% surge in online checkout volumes and a 30% global expansion velocity in gifting SaaS, Pine Labs is projecting an overall guided corporate revenue growth target of 21% to 23.5%.

Key Risks & Disruptive Threats

Omnichannel Convergent Squeeze: As Razorpay expands offline via Ezetap and Pine Labs expands online via Plural, both are entering a competitive collision course. If Razorpay aggressively cuts margins to win enterprise offline accounts, Pine Labs' core cash cow could face yield compression.

SoftPOS Deflationary Risk: If merchant adoption of smartphone "Tap-to-Glass" and central bank infrastructure (like UPI Tap & Pay) eliminates the physical terminal faster than Pine Labs can transition its corporate bases, its offline merchant acquisition moat could face pressure.

A2A Lending Disintermediation: The scaling of open-banking networks and Credit Line on UPI allows direct bank-to-consumer credit at any standard QR code sticker. This could potentially disintermediate the high-margin "Affordability middleware layer" that Pine Labs provides.

Conclusion: Pricing Longevity Over Velocity

Ultimately, looking for explosive, triple-digit transaction growth in Pine Labs is misinterpreting the core asset. The company is not an undisputed growth monopoly in any single vertical; instead, its public market valuation premium rests entirely on the longevity and defensive quality of its enterprise earnings.

While consumer-facing fintech startups face erratic user churn and brutal regulatory price ceilings on retail payments, Pine Labs operates with the structural profile of an enterprise utility provider. Its premium multiple is justified by high operational switching costs, deep B2B legacy moats, and predictable multi-year cash flows from top-tier corporate giants.

By systematically swapping out volatile, capital-intensive hardware cycles for steady, global SaaS and transaction infrastructure fees, Pine Labs offers public market investors a defensive, high-RoCE compounding utility wrapped inside a fintech shell.

text:
I read about a running shoe that can be ground up, melted down, and reborn as another shoe.

And it reminded me of timeless marketing principles that show up in every smart business model… and that every business should pay close attention to.

Three years ago, the Swiss brand *On* introduced a “shoe that you will never own”. 

It’s 100% recyclable, available by subscription, and runs on a $29.99/month lease model.

It might be old news now but I’m still intrigued.

Because behind this quirky subscription was a blueprint built on ongoing marketing trends that are very much alive today:

✅ An aversion to owning “stuff,” whether due to storage/clutter issues or environmental concerns. Or realizing that you can’t take the stuff with you. 🙂

✅ Leasing over buying.

✅ Creating a “barrier to switch” from a particular brand, keeping customers longer, through whatever means necessary…by turning transactions into relationships…and not differentiating on price alone.

✅ Keeping renewals and continuity top of mind always (which includes up-sells and cross-sells) to increase the lifetime value of every customer.

**Less Stuff**

We’re in the age of less stuff, because who really wants more things to store, dust, or eventually dump?

Whether it’s clutter-stress, eco-guilt, or just the reality that you can’t take it with you, more people are choosing less.

And less is more.

The digital revolution has been a lifesaver here (although storage unit companies still seem to be being built).

I assume: Why own it when you can stream it, download it, or swipe it?

And yet… not everything should be digital.

Some things and “physical marketing stuff” are better in print. 

A well-designed book.

 A physical newsletter. 

A product you can actually hold.

When something can be held, flipped through, or displayed on a desk, it often feels more valuable.

The goal isn’t to eliminate stuff. And to stop making junk.

But not all paper is clutter. 

And everything being digital is not necessarily better.

**Leasing Over Buying**

Leasing is the cousin of “less stuff”... and honestly, a relief for anyone who’s ever wondered what to do with something once it outlives its usefulness.

Sell it? 

Recycle it? 

Pass it on so someone else can store it indefinitely?

That’s the beauty of leasing. No clutter, no guilt.

No, I’m not knocking ownership.

I’ve got a 2008 car with 198,000 miles…and no plans to trade it in. 

Why? 

Because it’s paid for…and it’s still humming. 🙂

But when it comes to your expertise and your knowledge, leasing it (through subscriptions, memberships, or ongoing access) can be a smarter play than selling it once and walking away.

It gives your students more chances to grow with you… and gives you a business model built to last.

More on that in a minute.

**Creating A Barrier To Switch**

Want to keep customers longer? 

Make it harder for them to leave.

I’m not talking about lock-in contracts or guilt trips. 

I mean creating such a strong bond through value, experience, and ongoing service that switching feels like a loss.

That’s the real “pain of disconnect.”

And you don’t need fancy tech or glossy packaging. 

It works with digital offers, physical products, and especially how you onboard, support, and surprise and delight your customers over time.

Think of it like a compounding lease: The longer they stay, the more they get.

Not because they’re stuck... but because they *want* to stick around.

This is something I go deep into in my book, [*Overdeliver*](https://t.co/HUpLlpnxOJ), with specific examples, especially the chapter on “Customer Service and Fulfillment”... which as you know if you’ve been part of my online family for any length of time, customer service and fulfillment are *marketing* functions.

And yes, if you buy the book, you will receive thousands of dollars’ worth of free bonuses that will make you never want to leave me.

At least that’s the plan. 🙂

**Renewals And Continuity Always Being Top Of Mind.**

Here’s the core truth:

A subscription gets you content.

A membership gives you belonging.

Subscriptions are just the beginning. 

Turn them into memberships, and you unlock something way more powerful—community, loyalty, and longer-lasting impact.

I know you know this already and it seems obvious. 

But it’s worth repeating:

*People love belonging to something special and bigger than themselves.*

Dick Benson, in his landmark book, *Secrets of Successful Direct Mail*, written pre-Internet, has as #6 of his “Benson’s Rules of Thumb”:

*Memberships renew better than plain subscriptions by 10% or more.*

Today, that number’s probably a lot higher especially when you build an irresistible benefits stack.

Not building subscriptions, memberships, or continuity into what you do means missing the opportunity to share your wisdom with more people, for a longer time.

If you’re curious to go deeper, I share more about this in Chapter 3 of my book [***Overdeliver***,](https://t.co/HUpLlpnxOJ) including how paying postage taught me lessons that shaped my digital marketing approach. 

You get access to a PDF of Dick Benson’s out-of-print classic too. It’s a gem worth exploring.

On a recent [***Titans Xcelerator Mastermind***](https://t.co/XmcCPNnvgh) call, a copywriter/marketer/coach in the hot seat didn’t ask how to build a course, book or short-term program. 

He asked: *“How can I turn my knowledge and resources into a membership?”*

Right question. Better outcome.

He left with clear, proven advice from those who’ve done it and he’s now building something “sticky”, scalable, and built for the long haul.

So here’s your takeaway:

Whether you are selling a subscription or a membership (or a hybrid), ask yourself:

*How do I make this renewable?*

Because your next sale isn’t the finish line. 

It’s the beginning of a relationship.

Whether you’re scaling up, down, or just staying steady, subscriptions and memberships will always beat one-off sales.

They’re simpler. Stickier. More sustainable.

Even without recycled sneakers. 😉

[*Titans Xcelerator*](https://t.co/XmcCPNnvgh) is a virtual mastermind packed with value—affordable, impactful, and full of smart, generous marketers, copywriters, and entrepreneurs.

Let's focus on making each other smarter, rather than just one person being the smartest. 🙂

✅ 30+ live, interactive calls a year with the best-of-the-best copywriters and marketers in the world.

✅ Hot Seats focused on the best opportunities and the most challenging challenges of members.

It's where great ideas get sharper and not-so-great ones get reworked into something better.

It’s part mastermind, part marketing insurance policy, and part Board of Advisors.

text:
The widest access to client files in a law firm is not the partner's. It belongs to a technician at the IT vendor. Someone the partners have never met.

You answer to the client for the file. And for everyone who can reach it.

The domain admin can open anyone's mailbox. The user never finds out. Whoever runs the backups holds a copy of every file, usually off-site. The remote-management tool sees the screen. And when technicians share one "admin" account, the log says "admin". It does not say who.

This is not a vendor failure. This is how IT works. The failure is a firm with no record of it and no sentence about it in the contract.

Czech law extends the lawyer's duty of confidentiality to "other persons involved in providing legal services". The explanatory report to the 2025 amendment names IT specialists directly. Whether that covers a vendor technician who "only runs the infrastructure" is an open question. Courts settled a different one: a file in the cloud gets the same protection as a file in the cabinet when the police come with a warrant. Procedural protection. It does nothing against a technician opening the folder at 2 a.m. on a Tuesday.

What I would want in hand as a partner:

- Names. Admin access on named accounts only. The list of people is in the contract, not "the vendor's tech team".
- Second factor. On every admin account. No exceptions.
- A record. Who opened which file, on my desk once a month. Kept by the firm, not the vendor. Where a system cannot do it, I want that in writing.
- A review. Every quarter, who has what. Including people who have since left the vendor.
- The key. Backups encrypted with a key the firm holds. Not the vendor.
- The contract. Confidentiality, audit rights, no subcontractors without consent, liability for a breach. And if personal data is processed, a contract under GDPR Art. 28. Not just uptime in percent.

A good vendor offers this before you ask. A bad one says it slows things down. Both have full access today.

Partners and managing lawyers: when did you last see a record of who opened a file? Not an uptime report. A record.

I went from 900-20,000 Instagram followers in 76 days with less than 100 posts.

In that time, I generated >3,000,000 views and signed >$12K in brand partnerships (100% inbound) with 5 tech companies I'm a customer of (I've also said no to $20K more).

All while running a content agency at $[x]m ARR.

Also got recognized twice at my Toronto WeWork (basically Drake) and got follows from true tech A-listers.

I had zero intentions of being a "creator", but I'm really starting to see what all the hype is about.

If I had to restart this today, here's what I'd tell myself:

1. Optimize for reps above all else.

Volume is the research. I'm posting 1x/day and am not even 100 posts in but have very clear signal on what my audience likes. 

2. Find format-market fit.

I have a few distinct formats, each bringing in different types of followers.

- Laptop walkthroughs of how to get certain LinkedIn results (best got 270K views and 2K followers)

- "The Art Of", where I satirically make fun of very niche tech experiences (best got 100K views).

- "Making A Random Founders' LI Strategy" (best got 70K views).

3. Your hooks are three-dimensional: verbal, visual, and title hook.

These are important because you are not making content for followers. You are making content that has to fight for its spot on the reader's FYP.

- Verbal: Here's how to build a LinkedIn presence in 90 days or less, starting from zero

- Visual: me opening my laptop as I say the above, with a slide title that says "The Caveman's Guide To Building A LinkedIn presence"

- Title: On-screen text that says "How To Build A LinkedIn Presence In 90 Days (I've Done It 50 times).

4. Views are a terrible northstar.

IG's Edits app tells you how each video did relative to each other, how many new followers each drove, where those followers came from, and more.

I've had videos get 200K views and drive less + lower-quality followers than videos with 50K (4x less). You must understand what's resonating deeper than view count.

5. Workflow dictates learning speed.

If I did this 9-5, I could probably post 3x/day.

But right now, every waking moment of my week is spent finding great talent or making sure clients are happy. 

Here's the workflow I've landed on right now:

- Script 8-10 videos on a Saturday

- Film them on Sunday

- Each weekday, up at 5am > input 1 video to GPT-6 Astra to edit via Da Vinci Resolve MCP and start working on other stuff > gym at 6am > leave for office at 7am > post video when I get to the office.

Not perfect but working right now.

A few other things worth mentioning:

- Trial Reels: I just don't have bandwidth to chop up 5-8 variations of each Reel to test. With that, I've done it a couple of times and banked an extra 40K-70K views each time. My conclusion is that they're good but serious lift.

- Manychat comment giveaways: Good but not as great as people think. I've ran 4-5 and probably got a combined ~4,000 followers from them. Higher-quality followers for my goals have come from deeper, less viral posts (gained >2,500 email subs though!)

- Brand deals: Self-managing right now but see the value in having an agent. Screening offers, negotiating, making sure contracts are good, etc. is taking more time than I thought. Also think I could really run it up if we did outbound for it.

Anyway, pretty crazy that you can do all of this with under 100 posts.

Fuel prices today, and the rest of the overnight: oil slipped while Iran waits on Washington, the White House weighs a diesel export ban, and borrowing costs kept climbing around the world.

Iran. Foreign Minister Araghchi says a 7-point plan went to Washington through Qatar and Iran is waiting for an official US reply. On Monday Axios, citing US officials, reported Trump was willing to ease sanctions and unfreeze funds if Iran took nuclear steps. Trump on Truth Social: "This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING!" VP Vance says Iran must behave for any deal. Britain's maritime agency UKMTO says a ship was hit by a projectile in Hormuz on Monday. Brent fell 1.5% to about $103.69 as Saudi Arabia restored about half its pipeline flows and The Atlantic reported Trump backs Russia sanctions relief tied to a prisoner release.

Diesel. Trump on Sunday: a ban "can oftentimes lead to a little bit of an increase on gasoline for cars, so we're looking at it very seriously — we may do it." Goldman Sachs says a ban would first cut US diesel about 4% and lift Europe's about 2%, but US gasoline could rise about 30 cents a gallon once diesel tanks fill. It is not Goldman's main scenario. Italy's energy minister is asking Energy Secretary Wright about it today.

Rates. Australia raised rates to 4.60% from 4.35%, its 4th hike this year and the highest since 2011. The bank cited energy prices far above its August assumptions, AI-driven tech prices and a stretched economy. Britain sold 10-year debt at 5.38%, up from 5.16% last month and the highest since 1999 (Bloomberg). Spain's inflation jumped to 4.9% from 4.3%, led by fuel; prices without food and energy rose too, 2.9% to 3.1%. The US 10-year closed Monday at 5.24%, the highest since 2007.

Canada. A US ban on about $1 billion of Canadian goods (some alcohol, dairy products, motorcycles) took effect at midnight. Trump says Canada will call within weeks and the US will "win everything."

Today (ET): home prices 9am · job openings + consumer confidence 10am · six Fed speakers from 11am (Waller 3pm). This week: PCE inflation Wed · ISM Thu · jobs report Fri.
