text:
📰 DAILY Top 10 NEWS BRIEFING
Tuesday, September 29, 2026

1. 📉 Wall Street Falls as Oil and Treasury Yields Rise
2. 🇮🇷 Iran Sends New Ideas Through Qatar as U.S.–Iran Talks Continue
3. 🇮🇶 U.S. Forces Prepare to Leave Their Last Bases in Iraq
4. 🇰🇷 South Korea Says North Korean Mines Caused DMZ Blast
5. 🤖 Trump Hosts Major AI CEOs in Washington Today
6. ⚖️ Supreme Court Weighs Immigration, Prediction-Market and Religion Cases
7. 🔎 Google Challenges EU Orders Requiring Greater Access for AI Rivals
8. 🚀 Starship Engine Failure Raises Questions for NASA’s Moon Timeline
9. 🌧️ Bangkok Flooding Disrupts Flights as Thailand Begins Recovery
10. 🩺 Iowa’s Rising Cancer Rates Become a Midterm-Election Issue

1. 📉 Wall Street Falls as Oil and Treasury Yields Rise
FACT
At the latest completed U.S. session — Monday, September 28 — the S&P 500 closed at 7,683.69, down 0.77%, the Nasdaq Composite at 26,820.38, down 0.92%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average at 51,481.51, down 0.67%. The S&P suffered its largest one-day percentage decline since August 20. 

BACKGROUND
Higher crude prices revived inflation concerns and pushed Treasury yields higher. Markets are now pricing roughly a 70% probability of another Fed rate increase in October, compared with about 18% a month earlier. Tuesday morning U.S. stock futures were roughly flat. 

WHY IT MATTERS
The market’s problem is increasingly the interaction of oil → inflation → interest rates → equity valuations. That makes upcoming labor and inflation data particularly important for determining whether Monday’s decline becomes a broader correction or remains a rates-driven pullback.

2. 🇮🇷 Iran Sends New Ideas Through Qatar as U.S.–Iran Talks Continue
FACT
Iran said it discussed new proposals with Qatar that could be relayed to Washington in an effort to end the war, while President Donald Trump denied reports that he had offered sanctions relief and access to frozen Iranian funds in exchange for nuclear concessions. Reuters

BACKGROUND
Trump rejected an earlier Iranian proposal over the weekend, but Qatar has continued mediating. Meanwhile, oil prices rose for a second consecutive session Tuesday as traders remained concerned about Middle East supply disruptions.

WHY IT MATTERS
The negotiations now matter well beyond the battlefield. Any credible agreement affecting Gulf shipping could quickly move Brent crude, inflation expectations, Treasury yields and global equities.

3. 🇮🇶 U.S. Forces Prepare to Leave Their Last Bases in Iraq
FACT
U.S. forces are scheduled to withdraw from their remaining bases in Iraq by Wednesday, completing a pullout agreed in 2024. Roughly 4,500 U.S. personnel died in Iraq over more than two decades of American military involvement. 

BACKGROUND
U.S. troops invaded Iraq in 2003, withdrew in 2011 and returned in 2014 as part of the campaign against Islamic State. Iran-aligned groups are portraying the latest withdrawal as a strategic victory, while some Iraqi security officials warn that Islamic State sleeper cells could exploit reduced U.S. intelligence and logistical support. 

WHY IT MATTERS
The withdrawal closes a major chapter in U.S. Middle East policy but could alter the regional balance of power. It may simultaneously increase the influence of Iran-backed groups and test whether Iraqi forces can contain remaining Islamic State networks without direct U.S. support.

4. 🇰🇷 South Korea Says North Korean Mines Caused DMZ Blast
FACT
South Korea’s defense minister said North Korean mines caused the September 21 explosion that injured two South Korean personnel in the DMZ and called the incident a violation of the Korean War armistice. A joint investigation with the United Nations Command found another North Korean anti-personnel mine south of the Military Demarcation Line. 

BACKGROUND
South Korean officials believe the mines were placed during North Korea’s recent border-fortification work. Seoul says it has response options but also intends to seek direct talks with Pyongyang to establish the facts. North Korea has not publicly commented. 

WHY IT MATTERS
The incident tests President Lee Jae Myung’s attempt to stabilize relations with North Korea. A similar mine incident in 2015 triggered loudspeaker broadcasts and a serious military confrontation along the border. 

5. 🤖 Trump Hosts Major AI CEOs in Washington Today
FACT
President Trump is scheduled to meet today with House Speaker Mike Johnson and major AI executives, including Mark Zuckerberg and Dario Amodei. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and OpenAI President Greg Brockman are also expected to participate. 

BACKGROUND
The meeting comes as policymakers debate how aggressively the United States should regulate rapidly advancing AI systems while preserving American leadership in the technology. 

WHY IT MATTERS
Washington is increasingly treating AI simultaneously as an economic-growth technology, national-security asset and regulatory problem. Direct discussions between political leaders and the industry’s largest companies could shape the next phase of U.S. AI policy.

6. ⚖️ Supreme Court Weighs Immigration, Prediction-Market and Religion Cases
FACT
The Supreme Court of the United States is considering whether to add several major disputes to its new term, including the Trump administration’s immigrant-detention policy, regulation of prediction markets such as Kalshi, and Texas’ requirement that public schools display the Ten Commandments. Reuters

BACKGROUND
The administration argues that certain noncitizens already living in the United States can be treated as “applicants for admission” subject to mandatory detention without bond. Separately, states argue that sports-related prediction contracts amount to gambling, while platforms say they are federally regulated financial derivatives. 

WHY IT MATTERS
These disputes could produce important rulings on immigration detention, federal-versus-state regulatory authority and the First Amendment’s religion clauses. The Court’s new term begins next Monday. 

7. 🔎 Google Challenges EU Orders Requiring Greater Access for AI Rivals
FACT
Google has challenged two European Union orders requiring it to provide greater access to services for AI developers such as OpenAI and to make search data available to competing search engines. Google argues the requirements could undermine privacy safeguards. 

BACKGROUND
EU regulators imposed the requirements under the Digital Markets Act, which is designed to limit the ability of dominant technology platforms to use their market position to disadvantage competitors. 

WHY IT MATTERS
Search data and access to established digital ecosystems can be major competitive advantages in AI. The case therefore goes beyond traditional antitrust enforcement and could help determine how much infrastructure dominant technology companies must share with emerging AI competitors.

8. 🚀 Starship Engine Failure Raises Questions for NASA’s Moon Timeline
FACT
A Raptor-engine malfunction during SpaceX’s 14th uncrewed Starship test flight Monday shortened the mission, although Starship reached orbit and completed its first commercial satellite deployment. Investigators now need to determine whether the failure was isolated or reflects a broader propulsion-system problem. 

BACKGROUND
NASA plans to use a Starship-derived lunar lander in its Artemis program, while Blue Origin is developing a competing lander. NASA officially aims to return astronauts to the lunar surface by 2028, ahead of China’s planned crewed lunar landing by 2030. 

WHY IT MATTERS
Starship’s reliability is now tied directly to the U.S. lunar timetable. A design-wide engine problem could delay not only SpaceX’s commercial plans but also NASA’s effort to return astronauts to the Moon for the first time since Apollo. 

9. 🌧️ Bangkok Flooding Disrupts Flights as Thailand Begins Recovery
FACT
Bangkok is beginning to recover from severe flooding, but Thai Airways plans to cancel roughly 30 flights Tuesday — about 30% of its scheduled Bangkok departures. About 5,600 bags remained stranded at Suvarnabhumi Airport. 

BACKGROUND
Bangkok received about 320 mm — 12.6 inches — of rain in two to three days, nearly its normal rainfall for the entire month of September. Heavy rain and flooding across Thailand since September 16 have killed at least 23 people. 

WHY IT MATTERS
The disruption illustrates how extreme rainfall can rapidly overwhelm transportation systems in major global cities. Thailand’s government has approved emergency funding and a much larger long-term drainage project as it confronts the infrastructure challenge. 

10. 🩺 Iowa’s Rising Cancer Rates Become a Midterm-Election Issue
FACT
Cancer rates have emerged as a significant issue in competitive congressional races in Iowa ahead of the 2026 midterms, as candidates face voter concern over the state’s unusually high cancer burden.

BACKGROUND
The debate is increasingly connecting public health with questions about agricultural practices, environmental exposure, healthcare access and research funding. Candidates differ over the causes and the appropriate government response.

WHY IT MATTERS
The issue shows how health and environmental concerns can become electoral questions rather than remaining primarily scientific or regulatory debates. Iowa’s competitive races also mean the political consequences could extend to control of Congress.

The comparison with 1945 is Medvedev’s political assessment. The reported remarks provide no quantitative basis for that historical ranking.

For markets, the critical question is whether tensions translate into new sanctions, disruption to energy infrastructure or a wider military confrontation. Those developments could increase supply costs, weaken confidence and pressure European corporate margins.

The diplomatic channel also matters: substantive progress toward protecting infrastructure or reducing hostilities could ease some of those risks. Discussions alone offer no guarantee of an agreement.

WATCH NEXT

• Concrete outcomes from U.S.–Russia diplomatic contacts.
• Changes in military deployments and NATO responses.
• New sanctions or disruptions affecting energy and trade.

text:
Blocking Immune Cells Protects Memory and Brain Tissue in Alzheimer’s | Neuroscience News

Summary:

Researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis have discovered that blocking immune cells from entering the brain preserves memory and brain tissue in mice with Alzheimer’s-like tau pathology. The therapy cut brain-infiltrating T cells in half and preserved 40% more tissue in memory centers, without having to cross the blood-brain barrier or reduce tau levels.

Key Facts:

- Memory and Tissue Preserved: Mice treated with a CXCR3-blocking antibody preserved approximately 40% more tissue in memory centers and performed significantly better on memory tests than untreated counterparts, despite brain tau tangle levels remaining unchanged.

- Targeting the Infiltration Pathway: The treatment blocks CXCR3, a receptor on activated T cells that follows the chemical trail of CXCL10 into the brain, reducing brain-infiltrating T cells by roughly 50%.

- No Blood-Brain Barrier Penetration Needed: The therapeutic antibody acted exclusively at the brain’s border without entering brain tissue itself, demonstrating that neurodegeneration can be halted by targeting peripheral immune signaling.

In neurodegenerative disorders known as tauopathies, most notably Alzheimer’s disease, twisted tangles of tau protein accumulate inside neurons, followed by widespread cell death in critical cognitive hubs. Yet a growing body of evidence indicates that tau aggregates may not be the direct executioners of brain cells; rather, the immune system’s destructive inflammatory reaction to tau drives much of the devastation.

Existing treatments like lecanemab and donanemab target amyloid plaques, which emerge early in Alzheimer’s and promote subsequent tau pathology. While these drugs can modestly slow cognitive decline, they do not halt ongoing cell loss and offer no clinical benefit for primary tauopathies, where tau accumulates in the total absence of amyloid.

Now, a study led by researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis offers a new therapeutic strategy. Published in Neuron, the team demonstrated that blocking a specific chemokine gateway keeps destructive immune cells out of the central nervous system, substantially reducing neurodegeneration.

“In tauopathies, including Alzheimer’s disease, there’s no treatment right now that actually decreases neurodegeneration,” said senior author David M. Holtzman, MD, the Barbara Burton and Reuben M. Morriss III Distinguished Professor in WashU Medicine’s Department of Neurology. “If we can show that we’re really decreasing brain cell death, it’s certainly worth trying to pursue that pathway to prevent the most devastating consequences of these diseases.”

Cutting Off the T-Cell Trail

Previous work from the Holtzman laboratory revealed that when tau accumulates in the brain, T cells primed in external lymph nodes flood into the affected regions and trigger cell death. However, the precise homing mechanism guiding them across the brain border remained unresolved.

T cells navigate along chemical gradients called chemokines. The researchers observed that a specific chemokine, CXCL10, spikes significantly in both tau-model mice and human Alzheimer’s patients. Activated T cells carry a surface receptor called CXCR3, which directly tracks this CXCL10 trail into neural tissue.

In experimental mice lacking either CXCL10 or the CXCR3 receptor, the researchers found that T cells failed to breach the brain, even when acute inflammation was artificially triggered.

Building on this insight, the team administered an antibody targeting CXCR3 every five days for three and a half months to young mice exhibiting tau buildup. The results were dramatic:

- Infiltrating T cells inside the brain were reduced by roughly 50%.

- Treated animals preserved roughly 40% more brain tissue in vital memory circuits.

- Cognitive performance on memory assays was significantly better than in untreated controls.

- The protective effects occurred even though overall tau tangle burden remained completely identical between groups.

Treating Brain Disease from the Outside

One of the largest hurdles in neuropharmacology is designing drugs capable of crossing the tightly sealed blood-brain barrier. The researchers discovered that the CXCR3 antibody accumulated only at the structural borders of the brain rather than entering deep parenchyma.

“For this therapeutic approach, if it is safe, you wouldn’t have to design the drug to get into the brain, which is a big deal since most molecules don’t cross the blood-brain barrier well, and you don’t have to get rid of the tau to get this therapeutic effect,” Holtzman explained.

Because T-cell-directed therapies already exist for autoimmune conditions like multiple sclerosis, the findings provide a compelling rationale for evaluating existing clinical immunology pipelines against Alzheimer’s and related tauopathies.

The playbook of the populist state is incredibly simple, and it never changes:

Socialism shuts down industries.
Socialism shuts down farms.
Socialism shuts down enterprises.

They panel-beat this destruction to make it look like a revolution, calling it "expropriation" and "wealth redistribution."

But when you strip away the cosmetic optics and the toxic PR, the underlying reality is chilling.

This is not a mistake; it is a feature of the system. You cannot control a self-sufficient population.

A citizen who owns a business, a farmer who grows his own maize, and an industrialist who employs workers has zero reason to bow to a political party. They have independent leverage.

The politicians dismantle the means of production. They replace the productive farmer and the private enterprise with state monopolies and bureaucratic red tape.

And once the local economy is completely broken and the shelves are empty, the politicians arrive in their luxury German SUVs to perform the ultimate act of "generosity."

They bring you government food aid.

They turn your basic survival into a monthly subscription model managed by the ruling party.

It is a calculated strategy designed to keep you permanently dependent, submissive, and perfectly in line.

If you wear the right party t-shirt and vote for the "messiah," you get a bag of grain. If you speak up and demand structural competence, your family starves.

Never celebrate a political ideology that destroys the factories and the fields just to hand you a cardboard box of government relief.

When a state takes away your ability to produce wealth, they haven't liberated you, they have house-trained you.

True freedom is not a food hamper delivered by a politician who sips champagne in a wealthy estate while you sit in the dust.

True freedom is the independent capacity to create, produce, and build your own future on your own terms.

Stop cheering for the very people who broke your legs just because they offered you a government-branded crutch. Economic independence will always beat state dependency. Wake up.

The receptionist directs them to a room just across from the desk, where they find 7 other people already seated, waiting.   

They take a seat, resignedly.

She soon sweeps into the lift and travels up to the 4th floor, leaving a cloud of Chanel Madmoiselle in her wake.

What’s just happened here? 

Why did the Receptionist refuse to check in Sarah, John, and the other 7 people?

The answer?

Premier Inn’s upsell. 

Check in time is 3pm.

text:
Wake Up Foley Its National Coffee Day

September 29th marks National Coffee Day, an annual occasion dedicated to celebrating the rich, energizing beverage that powers mornings and fuels connection across the country. Whether enjoyed as a straightforward drip, a smooth cold brew, or a carefully crafted specialty espresso, coffee remains an indispensable part of daily life for millions of Americans.

A Brief History of Coffee in the United StatesCoffee’s history in the United States is deeply tied to the nation’s independence and cultural evolution. First introduced to North America in the 17th century, coffee became America’s dominant morning beverage following the Boston Tea Party of 1773. When American colonists protested British tea taxes, drinking tea was widely discarded as unpatriotic, prompting a dramatic shift toward coffee as the patriotic drink of choice. Its role only grew in subsequent centuries: coffee served as essential military rations during the Civil War, World War I, and World War II to maintain troop morale. By the mid-20th century, the official workplace “coffee break” became embedded in American corporate and industrial culture, eventually leading to the artisanal roasters and specialty coffeehouses that thrive across the country today.

How Much Coffee Does America Drink Every Day?Today, America’s love affair with coffee is stronger than ever. According to statistics from the National Coffee Association, roughly 66% of American adults—approximately 170 million people—drink coffee every single day. Nationwide, the country consumes an estimated 500 million cups of coffee per day, averaging around 2.8 cups per coffee drinker.

Celebrate National Coffee Day in Foley by stopping by Drowsy Poet at the Foley Station. Housed in a charmingly converted old auto shop, Drowsy Poet offers locally roasted coffee, signature drinks like the Salted Blondie, and cozy indoor and outdoor seating. Alternatively, head over to Gypsy Queen Java on West Laurel Avenue to enjoy artisanal lattes, fresh panini sandwiches, and a vibrant, free-spirited community atmosphere complete with a relaxing lounge area. Both local favorites provide the perfect welcoming space to slow down, connect with neighbors, and enjoy an exceptional cup of coffee.

text:
Below is a list of some national, international, global and local observances for September 29, 2026:

World Heart Day, established by the World Heart Federation with WHO support, raises global awareness that cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death; it was first observed on the last Sunday of September in 2000 before shifting to a fixed September 29 date in 2011. The idea originated with cardiologist Antoni Bayés de Luna, who sought a single coordinated day after realizing millions of preventable deaths occurred without a dedicated international reminder.⁠ Www-britannica-com.translate

National Coffee Day marks the unofficial U.S. celebration of the world’s famous agricultural commodity, with 2.25 billion cups consumed daily; many chains offer free or discounted drinks. Coffee’s legendary origin involves an Ethiopian goatherd named Kaldi whose flock became unusually energetic after eating red cherries, a discovery that later led Pope Clement VIII to taste the “devil’s drink” and declare it should be baptized rather than banned.⁠ Drentio

National Silent Movie Day, launched in 2021 by film archivists, honors the roughly 40-year era (circa 1889–1930) when cinema relied on intertitles, expressive acting, and live musical accompaniment rather than recorded sound. An estimated 80 percent of American silent features are now lost because nitrate stock was flammable, studios reclaimed silver from prints, and vault fires destroyed negatives.⁠ Silentmovieday

VFW Day commemorates the September 29, 1899, founding of the Veterans of Foreign Wars in a Columbus, Ohio, tailor shop by 13 Spanish-American War veterans seeking mutual aid. The organization later merged with similar groups from Colorado and Pennsylvania and has advocated for benefits including the GI Bill and the national cemetery system.⁠ Info.mysticstamp

Michaelmas (Feast of Saints Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael; also called Goose Day or National Poisoned Blackberries Day) is the traditional Western Christian quarter day marking the end of harvest, the start of autumn terms, and rent payments. Folklore holds that Lucifer, cast from heaven by St. Michael, landed in a blackberry bush and cursed the fruit by spitting, stamping, or worse, so blackberries picked after this date were considered spoiled.⁠ Wikipedia

National Goose Day revives the Michaelmas custom of eating a “stubble goose” fattened on leftover harvest grain; an old rhyme promised that eating goose on the day would prevent poverty for the year. Queen Elizabeth I is sometimes credited with popularizing the dish after receiving news of the Spanish Armada’s defeat while dining on goose.⁠ Nationalgeographic

National Biscotti Day celebrates the twice-baked Italian almond cookie (cantucci) whose name comes from the Latin biscoctus. Roman soldiers carried an earlier dry version because the double baking removed moisture and gave it a long shelf life on campaigns.⁠ Daysoftheyear

National Starbucks Day and related brand observances such as National Dunkin’ Day and National Mocha Day coincide with Coffee Day and encourage people to enjoy specialty coffee drinks. Starbucks and similar chains often run promotions that amplify the day’s visibility in the United States.

International Day of Awareness of Food Loss and Waste, proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2019, highlights that roughly one-third of all food produced—about 1.3 billion metric tons—is lost or wasted each year. The date was chosen to focus attention on both farm-to-market losses and household waste.

Confucius Day observes the traditional birthday of the Chinese philosopher Kongzi (551 BCE), whose teachings on ethics, family, and social harmony shaped East Asian culture; some calendars place the commemoration one day after the exact traditional date. Taiwan marks Confucius’ birthday as a public holiday on September 28.

Urban National Wildlife Refuge Day encourages city dwellers to visit and support wildlife refuges located in metropolitan areas, reminding people that conservation habitats exist even in densely populated regions.

National Attend Your Grandchild’s Birthday Day is an informal observance urging grandparents to participate in or remember a grandchild’s birthday, emphasizing intergenerational connection.

Broadway Musicals Day (National Broadway Musicals Day) celebrates the American musical-theater tradition with performances, sing-alongs, or simply listening to show tunes.

World Interaction Design Day, observed on the last Tuesday of September, brings together designers worldwide to demonstrate how interaction design can improve daily life through workshops, talks, and local events. It was launched in 2018 by the Interaction Design Association in partnership with Adobe.⁠Eventguide

National Assessor’s Day, also on the last Tuesday of September, honors property-assessment professionals whose valuations fund schools, roads, and public safety; it was initiated in 2018 by EagleView and the International Association of Assessing Officers to increase public understanding of the role.⁠Eagleview

Victory of Boquerón Day is a national public holiday in Paraguay commemorating the September 29, 1932, recapture of Fort Boquerón from Bolivian forces during the Chaco War. The 20-day siege became a turning point that boosted Paraguayan morale despite inferior numbers and equipment.⁠Publicholidays

National Police Remembrance Day in Australia honors officers killed in the line of duty, with ceremonies held across the country on this date.

National Corn Day (Día Nacional del Maíz) in Mexico celebrates maize as a cultural and dietary staple central to Indigenous and national identity.

Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles), a seven-day Jewish festival that began at sundown on September 25, 2026, continues through this date; families eat in temporary outdoor booths (sukkot) recalling the Israelites’ wilderness dwellings.

Additional lesser-known or niche observances recorded for the date include National Energy Drink Day, Swedish Fish Day, International Adhesive & Sealant Day, World Day of Primary Immune Thrombocytopenia, 929 Day, Mutation Day (Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles), MAGS Day, National Day of Belongingness, National Day of Accountability, National Carson Day, National Bot Restock Day, Free Web Search Day, Coffee Lovers Day, Shakira Day, and International Day of Bids and Proposals.

text:
The reply by @LxxLatin treats “Tuskegee” as an event rather than a data source and asserts that it consisted of a shootout started by a Black mob that subsequently lost. That claim does not correspond to any single, well-documented incident that matches the description.

The parent post by @Chris_1791 presented Tuskegee Institute tabulations showing 215 recorded lynchings from 1926 through 1968 (plus two later cases widely accepted as meeting the historical definition). Those figures were offered to counter statements that treat lynching as a mass phenomenon of recent memory. Tuskegee Institute, under Monroe Work and later directors, compiled what remains one of the more conservative and systematically defined series: an extra-legal killing carried out by private persons acting in open defiance of law. The Institute deliberately excluded many police shootings, secret murders, and some riot deaths that other compilers included.[](<https://t.co/YGosffVTdX>)

Two historical episodes associated with the name Tuskegee are sometimes invoked in these discussions, neither of which is a classic lynching or a clear “Black-mob-initiated shootout.” In 1923 the Ku Klux Klan marched on the newly opened Tuskegee Veterans Hospital to protest the planned replacement of white staff with Black physicians and administrators. Armed students and residents from the Institute formed a defensive perimeter; the Klansmen passed through town and dispersed without exchanging fire. The hospital ultimately received a Black staff. In 1966 the shooting of civil-rights activist Sammy Younge Jr. by a white service-station attendant produced large student protests in Tuskegee, some of which turned violent, but the original killing was an individual act, not a mob lynching.[](<https://t.co/fIT9upAZpS>)

Online commentary frequently conflates Tuskegee with the 1921 Tulsa events, where an armed group of Black residents appeared at the courthouse to prevent a rumored lynching and a shot (accounts differ on who fired first) precipitated a larger massacre. Greenwood itself had been named after a district Booker T. Washington established in Tuskegee. Such conflations illustrate how place names and statistical series become shorthand in contemporary arguments about the scale, definition, and initiation of historical racial violence.

The exchange therefore belongs to a longer debate over classification: which deaths count as lynchings, how many occurred after the peak decade of the 1890s, and whether some recorded cases were mutual combat or responses to crime rather than one-sided terror. Tuskegee’s own records and definitional debates with the NAACP in the 1930s already reflected those tensions. The reply’s specific factual assertion, however, lacks a matching primary incident.

guidance for FY27 around 25,000.

Chandrasekaran said it out loud:
if TCS has half a million people,
the day is not far it has half a million AI agents.

7,500–8,000, down from a 10,000 plan.

NASSCOM: India tech workforce grew only 2.3% in FY26.
that is not a boom. that is a crawl.

Unstop Talent Report 2026:
most engineering students on that survey were still unplaced
even while companies said they were “hiring.”
jobs exist. the old campus lottery does not.

and this is the split nobody explains well.

Ninja-type seats are thinner.
Digital / Prime / Specialist Programmer seats still pay.
₹3.3–3.6 LPA generalist track vs ₹7–12 LPA if you can actually do AI work.
Infosys specialist tracks go higher than that.

LinkedIn: India AI engineering hiring jumped about 60% YoY.

fastest among big markets.

so the market did not close.
it stopped paying for “I know Java and I did a todo app.”

why would a services firm pay you ₹6 LPA
to write the boilerplate Cursor drafts in four minutes?

that is the question.
most campus resumes do not answer it.

what actually works now. India version.

1. stop treating “I can write code” as the offer.

the hireable version is:
take a messy ticket
write a spec
let Claude Code or Cursor generate
then catch the broken auth before it ships.

if you cannot recognize bad auth,
you cannot review 400 lines of agent output.
you are just clicking approve.

code enough to see the lie.
then use the agent to go faster.

2. DSA still matters. for thinking, not for coaching-centre flex.

NQT / InfyTQ / product screens still filter this way.
you do not need 500 problems.
arrays, strings, hashmaps, trees, graphs.
100 problems you understand.

that same habit is how you notice the agent looping.

3. one real thing. not five tutorial corpses.

weather app.
calculator.
movie db.
college “management system” that never left localhost.

that GitHub is a graveyard.

build one thing your batch actually used.
deploy it.
let people break it.
fix it.

50 users on a notes tool
beats five dead repos when a GCC interviewer opens GitHub.

if you used AI to ship it, say which parts you rejected.

4. pick a lane that India is actually buying.

“full stack fresher” means nothing in 2026.

pick one and prove it:
LLM feature on a real API
backend + basic infra you can stand up
a small data pipeline
android/iOS app that is on a store
not “I watched a LangChain video.”

mass generalist is the slot AI already ate inside TCS/Infosys delivery.

5. talk like a person who has been on a project.

“it was broken so I fixed it” dies in the first HR screen.

“401 because the token died before refresh, so I added a buffer”

is how you survive a senior who is tired of freshers.

explain the project out loud in Hindi or English.
if your roommate gets it, you get it.

the honest bit.

the easy path is gone.
NQT, wait, join, bench, get trained on a live project.
that pipeline shrank.

what is left:
own something end to end
debug systems you did not write
reject bad agent code
show one vertical

2029–31 the same firms will cry about a senior shortage
because they refused to train juniors now.
the people who force an offer anyway become that bench.

if you are a 2025 or 2026 CS fresher, do this:

> DSA. 100 real problems.
> one shipped project with users.
> one vertical, deep.
> one LLM API inside that project.
> GitHub that looks like a person.
> ability to explain it without a script.

most of your batch will do none of that
and keep asking if BTech CSE is dead.

it is not.
the version that only types what the model says is.

text:
Jamie Dimon: A Plan for the Western World’s Revival

A U.S. trade pact with Europe could encompass friendly democracies and revive the old alliance.

I never want to read a book with the title “2050: How the West Was Lost.” The story might begin around the millennium, amid the West’s deteriorating military capabilities and economic fragmentation due to our inability to execute strategic policy. But we still have time to write a different story.

A renewed commitment to American values and alliances coupled with bold reforms by Europe would be a geopolitical and economic home run, guaranteeing the Western world’s strength for the next 250 years.

America still remains a global beacon of freedom and hope. Billions of people would move here if they could because of our opportunities. And if global investors could invest in only one country, it would be the U.S.

America’s global leadership rests on three pillars. If any one of them fails, it could doom the whole enterprise. The first pillar is maintaining the world’s pre-eminent military. The second is remaining the world’s pre-eminent economy, which is foundational to having the pre-eminent military. (The U.S. dollar’s role as the global reserve currency depends on both pillars.) The third pillar is reinvigorating the American dream and American values, which are weakening for too many of our fellow citizens. We must rededicate ourselves to the values and principles that made this nation great, including free enterprise.

To remain the pre-eminent global economy, the U.S. must improve its domestic economic policy. We should strive to grow 3% a year. If we had done this over the past 20 years or so, our gross domestic product per person would be $20,000 higher. Scores of federal, state and local rules and policies impede growth. Many of them can be reformed at no cost. But I will focus my attention on strategic foreign economic policy.

Since World War II, America has fostered economic and military relations, trading with more than 100 nations and forming more than 50 military alliances. The levers to accomplish our foreign-policy goals include trade policy, through tariffs, quotas, investment policies, regulatory barriers and other instruments. Another lever is industrial policy, which encompasses subsidized loans, tax rules, export credits, immigration policies, government investment and development finance.

We need to exercise all these tools to protect national security and resiliency. Foreign economic policy should maximize growth and competitiveness, both in the U.S. and for American companies doing business internationally. This would strengthen our allies economically and bind them closer to the U.S. and like-minded Western democracies. If the economic and military bonds among the world’s democracies weaken, there could be negative consequences for America. Our adversaries want to see our allies far less dependent on the U.S. and far more dependent on them.

Institutions that helped undergird the peace and prosperity of the past 75 years, such as the United Nations, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, need reform. Some are reforming but any changes should bring the U.S. and its partners closer together, not drive them apart.

Many countries talk about a coalition of “middle powers” for military and economic purposes. In many ways, such a coalition already exists: Europe. Unfortunately, the Continent has been declining militarily and economically for decades. Europe and the U.S. share deeply held values and the Continent is still America’s largest trading and investment partner. But Europe relies on exports for nearly 60% of its energy, has a disjointed defense industrial base, faces a manufacturing threat from China, and has a tangle of rules that hamstring capital formation and technology innovation. If this continues, Europe will be in the dire position of failing to meet its military and social needs.

It is in America’s interest that Europe succeed. But as recent years have shown, the old trans-Atlantic bargain is breaking. That doesn’t mean the trans-Atlantic relationship has to. For decades, the bargain was straightforward: The U.S. provided the backbone of European security, Europe largely accepted American leadership, and both sides believed the arrangement served their national interests. The status quo is being renegotiated. Europe’s weakness has led many in the U.S., often for good reason, to be hostile toward the Continent. And many in Europe react to tariffs and other policies with hostility toward Washington. We are in a vicious circle.

Europe is being asked to shoulder more of its own defense (and that of the Arctic) while simultaneously facing a competitiveness challenge from China. A Europe that can mobilize capital, scale innovative companies, consolidate defense production, reduce strategic dependencies and generate stronger growth would be a more capable security partner, a more resilient economic partner and a stronger counterweight to Beijing’s economic power.

To succeed, the Europeans must reform how their economy functions. They know what to do, which is to adopt the more than 300 recommendations in two 2024 reports, one by Enrico Letta and the other by Mario Draghi, both academics and former Italian prime ministers. Yet so far, fewer than 16% of the reforms have been implemented, tipping Europe into the “slow agony” of decline Mr. Draghi warned about.

If the European Union strengthened its internal market structure by completing the Capital Markets Union and Banking Union, it would transform the Continent’s ability to scale and compete. A more integrated financial system would unlock investment for strategic industries, enhance stability and reduce fragmentation costs. It would enable more European banks to compete globally and make the Continent a more attractive environment for foreign firms.

This is the moment for bold ideas, and I believe the U.S. should offer Europe a major inducement: If it executes meaningful economic and military reforms, including everything that we consider crucial for security and resiliency, the U.S. will negotiate one big, beautiful economic and free-trade agreement with Europe. Many of the current disputes between Europe and the U.S. are minor compared with this agreement’s size and benefits. This pact could be extended to friendly democracies including Canada, Mexico, Japan, South Korea, Australia and the Philippines.

It would be an economic and geopolitical game changer for the U.S., Europe and our other allies. It would allow us to set the global rules on trade and would bind Western allies together in the face of autocratic pressure.

This is a long shot, and it has been tried before. In the 2010s, the U.S. and its allies almost accomplished this with the nearly finalized Trans-Pacific Partnership—a trade pact with 12 Pacific Rim economies including Japan, Canada and Australia. We should resurrect that agreement as well as the Transatlantic Trade and Investment Partnership between the EU and the U.S. This would create economic growth among all member nations and protect them from mercantilist behavior by China or others.

Those pacts were derailed because politics moved against free trade, amid fears of lost jobs, lower wages and business displacement. Such concerns are valid. Too many efforts to help those most affected by trade deals fell short. Therefore, we must match this big idea with equally bold steps to help affected workers or businesses. The American dream should work for everyone, and Washington and the private sector must step up to meet the moment.

The world is very different from 10 or 20 years ago. The risks today are enormous and the stakes couldn’t be higher. A strong America with robust military and economic alliances is the foundation for a prosperous and peaceful world. 

Let’s write a new book, “2050: How the West Regained Its Mojo.”

Mr. Dimon is chairman and CEO of JPMorganChase.

text:
The Relationship Was the Biggest Deal

Xi Jinping left Washington without a grand bargain. The more consequential development may have been what Trump and Xi made possible between them.

I had planned to cut a short video to accompany this essay. Then the White House published its own 90-second edit of the visit. It makes the argument better than anything I could have made.

Xi Jinping left Washington without a grand bargain. That made the verdict easy: extraordinary ceremony, modest agreements.

That may be exactly backwards.

The most consequential outcome was not any single agreement. It was the relationship Donald Trump and Xi Jinping chose to build — and what that relationship may now be capable of.

Trump personally received Xi at Joint Base Andrews. At the other end, the two presidents and their wives sat down for tea before a final visit to the National Archives. Between those moments came the military honours, formal talks and state dinner. The White House described the visit in unusually personal terms: “Friendship, Strength, and Success.”

Xi did not merely receive the gesture. At the state dinner, he publicly thanked Trump and Melania for the “special arrangements” and the care put into them. By the end of the visit, both governments were using the same formulation: a “constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity.”

This was mutual political investment. Its importance is not sentimental.

Bureaucracies negotiate issues. Leaders can change the relationship among the issues.

A trade official sees tariffs. A defence official sees deterrence. A technology regulator sees chips. Governments already have institutions designed to coordinate among them.

But coordination is not the same as political repricing.

At the highest level, leaders can decide how much weight one dispute should carry against the value of the relationship as a whole.

---

THE TOTAL ACCOUNT

Personal diplomacy cannot erase structural rivalry.

Trump cannot make Congress, the Pentagon or America’s alliances disappear. Nor can a warmer relationship remove the commercial, technological and security calculations already embedded in policy on either side.

But leaders can alter the political range within which that machinery operates.

When the relationship itself is assumed to be adversarial, almost every dispute acquires strategic meaning. A tariff becomes evidence of containment. A technology restriction becomes part of a broader security struggle. A maritime incident spills into economic relations.

A different signal from the top does not remove those disputes. It can change how much of the relationship they are allowed to consume.

Trump and Xi arrive at this point through different political traditions. Trump habitually personalises great-power diplomacy. Beijing speaks instead of the “strategic guidance” of head-of-state diplomacy. The vocabulary differs, but the operating logic can converge: at the top sits the authority capable of rebalancing the whole account.

That matters because the pattern did not begin in Washington.

Since Busan, reciprocity has appeared mainly as a sequence of transactions: tariffs, agricultural purchases, rare earths, technology restrictions. None of this demonstrates a hidden master bargain. It does show that movement in one part of the relationship can create political room elsewhere.

The sequence from Beijing to Washington adds another layer. One state visit was followed by another. Political investment itself began to acquire an element of reciprocity.

That raises the harder question:

What happens when reciprocity begins to travel between issues?

At the simplest level, reciprocity is visible. A tariff concession meets a purchase commitment. One restriction is adjusted after movement on another.

Cross-domain reciprocity would work differently.

An economically valuable relationship could affect how much political risk a government is willing to create elsewhere. Greater predictability around sensitive security interests could influence how much commercial openness the other side is prepared to preserve.

There is no public evidence of soybeans being traded for Taiwan, chips for military restraint, or any other crude quid pro quo.

But ruling out a one-for-one trade is not the same as ruling out cross-domain accommodation.

The visit offered one small, concrete example of how far a political signal can travel. Both governments formally recalled that China and the United States had been allies in the Second World War and fought side by side to win it. The White House placed that language alongside an equally explicit reaffirmation of America’s post-war forward military presence in the Indo-Pacific; the Chinese outcomes document carried the wartime-allies formulation as well.

On paper, it was a historical statement. Politically, it carried meaning beyond the bilateral relationship without requiring either side to abandon its existing security position.

That is a small example of how a signal agreed in one part of the relationship can acquire weight somewhere else.

If this logic ever reaches core interests, the stakes rise sharply.

For Beijing, the hardest test would lie in issues it regards as central to sovereignty and security, above all Taiwan and the regional security environment surrounding it. For Washington, politically valuable returns may lie in very different domains: agricultural access, supply chains, consumer-facing economic pressures and other priorities with immediate domestic consequences.

The point is not that these interests have already been linked in a bargain.

It is whether a relationship able to see the whole account eventually changes how each side prices restraint, flexibility or cooperation in decisions once treated as separate.

Reciprocity has not demonstrably reached that level. Washington matters because the relationship may now have more capacity to carry it there.

---

THE HARDER PROPOSITION

This is where Xi’s repeated use of Trump’s own political language matters.

Beijing has increasingly described its preferred relationship as one in which cooperation remains the mainstay, competition is kept within limits and differences are managed. In Washington, Xi again said the two countries could contribute to each other’s success through healthy competition.

That leads to a harder proposition than another tariff deal:

Does the other side’s success always have to be recorded as your loss?

Much of the strategic debate in both countries assumes that it does.

Chinese technological progress can erode America’s relative advantage. American controls on advanced chips and AI can constrain capabilities Beijing regards as central to its future. Military gains by one side can deepen insecurity on the other.

Taken far enough, that logic makes denying the other side gains an objective in itself.

The language of mutual accomplishment points elsewhere. It does not require either country to stop competing. It asks whether competition must always be organised around preventing the other side from succeeding.

If either side stops treating the other’s success as an automatic strategic loss, the competition does not disappear. Its purpose changes.

Neither government has reached that point. But the proposition can now be stated openly at the highest political level. That itself is a change.

---

THE G2 BEIJING NO LONGER DISMISSES OUTRIGHT

Trump’s use of G2 language adds another dimension.

China still rejects the idea of a world jointly managed by two powers. Asked directly in March whether Beijing would accept a G2 framework, Foreign Minister Wang Yi stressed that more than 190 countries shape the international system and rejected the proposition that the world should be “run by major countries.”

That position has not changed. Beijing’s handling of the label has.

After Trump called the 2025 Busan summit a “G2 meeting”, China’s Foreign Ministry was asked directly whether a G2 grouping was emerging. It did not simply reject the premise. Instead, the spokesman said China and the United States could jointly shoulder major-power responsibilities and accomplish more for both countries and the world, before reaffirming multilateralism and a multipolar order.

Beijing continues to reject G2 as a system in which Washington and Beijing run the world.

It has become less inclined to deny the exceptional weight of the US-China relationship itself.

Trump’s G2 conception and China’s multipolar vision still point toward different international orders. But they increasingly overlap on one practical requirement: Washington and Beijing need an unusually stable, direct and politically consequential relationship at the top.

That is why the spectacle in Washington matters.

The relationship was not merely conducted.

It was deliberately displayed.

The ceremony was not policy, and it did not substitute for policy. It showed how much political capital both sides were prepared to invest in the channel through which policy would subsequently be managed.

The agreements beneath it offer a smaller-scale version of the same logic. AI dialogue, trade mechanisms and military crisis communication are functional interfaces. Each can manage problems inside its own domain. None can decide how damage in one domain should affect another.

That requires a political interface above them.

The difficult disputes do not have to disappear. What matters is whether they can remain bounded enough to be managed while still connected to a wider relationship in which choices in one domain alter incentives in another.

Washington did not establish a new international order. It did not settle the central disputes between the United States and China.

What it displayed was less formal: two leaders assigning unusual political value to a relationship capable of connecting interests that no single negotiation can contain.

The test is whether reciprocity can keep moving upward — from individual transactions, to the relationship among issues, and eventually to the value both sides assign to the relationship as a whole.

The more structurally distinct the two systems become, the more the relationship at the top becomes the interface between them.

text:
Morning Coffee Macro | Tuesday, September 29, 2026

Hormuz reopen hopes are fading into the week after President Trump rejected Iran's seven-day truce offer over the weekend. Mediators are still shuttling messages, but Washington and Tehran remain stuck on sequencing: Iran wants sanctions relief and an end to the port blockade before any strait reopen, while the US wants the nuclear file addressed in any deal. That stalemate keeps a geopolitical premium in crude, with Brent holding above $107 and WTI near $94 after another overnight bid.

That oil hangover is still the main macro story, even as US oil proxies cool in the premarket after Monday's spike. USO is near $146 (about 2.5% under Monday's close near $150), and XLE is soft near $61.50, while the 10-year Treasury yield remains elevated after printing above 5.27% on Monday, its highest in about 19 years. Australia's RBA just hiked another 25 bp to 4.6%, a 15-year high, explicitly citing fuel-driven inflation, a clear echo of the same oil shock hitting global central banks.

Equity futures are trying a modest bounce after Monday's Wall Street slide (S&P 500 closed roughly 0.8% lower). Premarket, SPY is near $767.50 (prior close $765.61), QQQ near $739.80 (prior close $736.53), DIA near $515.60, and IWM near $281. Asia stayed heavy overnight, with the Nikkei off about 1.3% and the Hang Seng about 0.6%. Traders are marking the calendar for this week's US data stack, including PCE and Friday's jobs report, with markets still pricing a solid chance of another Fed hike in October.

Crypto is steadier than the overnight oil tape but still trading the same higher-for-longer rate backdrop. Bitcoin is marked near $84,300 (prior day open near $83,200), and Ether near $2,730, holding the low-$83k support zone after last week's fade from the mid-$86ks. Risk appetite is fragile: yields near multi-year highs raise the hurdle rate for non-yielding assets, so crypto stays pinned to the bond and oil narrative until PCE lands.

On the dollar side, DXY is firm near 101.2 as hike odds stay bid. EUR/USD is soft around 1.136, and USD/JPY sits near 157.4 to 157.5, still short of the 160 intervention watch zone. Gold is attempting a bounce (GLD near $381 after Monday's selloff) even as real yields stay high, a reminder that geopolitics and rate fears are pulling safe havens in opposite directions.

Simply Macro Explanation
Oil and Hormuz diplomacy still set the tone. As long as the strait stays constrained and crude holds three digits, inflation fears keep yields elevated, the Fed hike path alive, and risk assets on a short leash. Today's modest equity and crypto bounce is a pause, not a regime change. Watch PCE and payrolls this week for the next real swing.

Representatives Don Beyer (D-VA), Lori Trahan (D-MA), and James Gallagher (R-CA) joined in sponsoring this legislation. By investing in the scientists, researchers, and companies developing the next generation of energy technology here in the United States, we can advance our clean energy goals, create good-paying jobs, and strengthen our energy independence. America has always been at its best when we lead the world in innovation, and fusion is our opportunity to lead once again.”

Daily Commentary
Markets are opening the week on softer footing, with early selling pressure developing as elevated oil prices remain front and center. Higher energy prices can quickly revive inflation concerns, so traders will be watching whether crude continues to push higher—and whether that starts to pressure rate-sensitive growth stocks and broader risk appetite.  This week’s macro narrative will likely be driven by any fresh U.S.–China headlines, particularly around trade policy, technology restrictions, tariffs, and supply-chain developments. These headlines can create fast rotations across semiconductors, industrials, energy, China-exposed names, and the broader tech complex.  The other major catalyst is Micron (MU) earnings later this week. MU has become an important read-through for the AI infrastructure trade, especially demand for high-bandwidth memory, data-center spending, and the broader semiconductor cycle. A strong report and constructive outlook could reinforce momentum in chips and AI-related leaders; disappointment could spark a more meaningful shakeout after a strong run.  My focus remains on the market’s current leadership. AI names have controlled the tape for much of the past month, and until that relative strength breaks down, that is still where I want to concentrate my watchlist. Rather than forcing trades during early weakness, I’ll be watching for:  AI leaders holding key support and showing relative strength versus the indexes  Semiconductors reacting constructively into and after MU earnings  Whether oil strength broadens into energy-sector leadership or becomes a drag on the overall market  U.S.–China headlines that could trigger quick sector rotations  Pullbacks that offer controlled-risk entries rather than chasing extended momentum  The key question is whether this is simply a routine pullback within an AI-led uptrend—or the beginning of a broader shift in market leadership.

Overall Bias

My bullish bias remains intact heading into Micron’s earnings report this week. MU has the potential to be a major catalyst for an already red-hot memory and semiconductor trade, especially as investors continue to focus on AI-driven demand for high-bandwidth memory, DRAM, NAND, and data-center infrastructure. Micron’s commentary on AI memory demand, supply discipline, pricing trends, and hyperscaler spending will likely matter just as much as the headline earnings numbers.  I’ll be watching MU closely for a constructive reaction after the report, along with relative strength across the broader semiconductor complex. text:
The problem with pay of state employees is that there seems to be a concensus in the government that more pay is good. That it makes people wealthier. But it's not a view that is driven by looking at both sides of the equation, ie. where does the money come from. 

It used to be, going back many decades, that it was a priviledge to be a WA State employee. People wanted a state job because it offered a reliable but low paycheck, good benefits, and they could contibute their talents to a good cause, running the state in a sensible manner that benefitted fellow Washingtonians. They didn't need to live high on the hog, they had societal respect and security.

Over time state workers salaries exceeded what someone of the same talent could find in the private sector, it became increasingly difficult to fire lazy, unreliable or incompetent public employees, and it started attracting people whose primary consideration was not what they could do to help their state, but what the state could do for them. The higher the pay, the less desirable the worker that is attracted. That seems counter-intuitive but it's what I've seen play out. It comes down to WHY people want to work for the state, to be an important part of the function of government, or to latch onto a job that pays above the private sector and that it's almost impossible to get fired from, no matter how terrible their job performance. 

Now WA has a dysfunctional government with about five times as many employees as is actually required to run the core functions, and a bunch of additional state employees in non-essential parts of government who are even less productive than those running the essential functions. It's completely out of hand and that's just one reason why the state budget has ballooned out of control and run off businesses. 

The other reason is fraud and abuse. Using taxpayer money to lube the political wheels that keep elected officials in power. It's done through grants to "good causes" which is the primary driver of why government, collectively, loves to not solve homelessness, drug addiction, theft and assault, and violent crime. Because they need these problems to continually get voters to give them more money to spend on themselves via their friends and donors. It's almost impossible to fix because state legislators become part of the machine.

1937 | Peel Commission (Britain). Zionists accepted partition in principle. Arab leadership rejected it.
• 1947 | UN Partition Plan. Jewish Agency accepted. Arab states + Palestinian leadership rejected it. War followed.
• 1967 | Israel offered land-for-peace to Arab states after the war. Arab League at Khartoum rejected it: no peace, no recognition, no talks.

• 2002 | Arab Peace Initiative (Saudi/Arab League). Offered 1967-line Palestinian state for Arab recognition of Israel. Israeli governments did not accept it as written (refugees + full withdrawal terms).
• 2003 | Quartet Roadmap. Both sides signed on in principle, then missed conditions. It collapsed; not a single signed “no.”
• 2007–08 | Annapolis + Olmert–Abbas. Olmert offered a detailed two-state map. Abbas did not accept/sign it. Abbas later said he wasn’t given the map; Olmert said Abbas wouldn’t commit.
• 2013–14 | Kerry talks (Netanyahu–Abbas–US). Talks collapsed. Each side blamed the other. No single signed rejection.
• 2020 | Trump plan. Israeli government treated it as a basis. Palestinian Authority rejected it.

text:
Whitmer has not given Michigan drivers anything close to what Kemp just did. Georgia paused its 33-cent-per-gallon state gas tax for 30 days. Michigan still collects one of the highest state fuel taxes in the country—about 52 cents a gallon after the 2025 road-funding deal Whitmer signed that swapped the old sales tax for a bigger flat excise tax.

She has refused to suspend that tax even as prices climbed. In 2022 she vetoed a six-month gas-tax holiday the Legislature sent her. This year she has backed a federal holiday while declining to pause Michigan’s own levy, arguing the money is needed for roads. Other states (Georgia, Indiana, Utah) cut or paused theirs anyway.

The main thing she actually did was an April 2026 executive order that let eight metro Detroit counties keep selling cheaper, higher-vapor-pressure summer fuel instead of switching to the more expensive blend. That was worth an estimated 10–20 cents a gallon in those counties and was later extended by the Legislature. It is a modest, temporary blend waiver—not a tax cut—and it does not apply statewide the way a tax holiday would.

Michigan prices have still run well above many neighbors. The state tax structure she helped lock in, plus her earlier veto of a holiday, is why drivers keep asking why Kemp-style relief never showed up in Lansing

How many Michigan Voters remember that Whitmer spent years pushing an EV-first agenda while gas drivers kept paying one of the highest state fuel taxes in the country.

Her MI Healthy Climate Plan set a target of infrastructure for 2 million EVs on Michigan roads by 2030. Registrations have been in the ballpark of 80,000–100,000 — a few percent of that goal. The same plan called for a huge charger buildout that also lagged.

In 2020 she created the Office of Future Mobility and Electrification. In 2023 she ordered the state fleet converted to zero-emission vehicles (light-duty by 2033, heavier vehicles by 2040). Years later the fleet still had only about 41 EVs out of roughly 14,000 vehicles. She also repeatedly asked for EV rebates, sales-tax breaks, and charger money; lawmakers often funded far less than she requested.

The pitch was that electrification would cut emissions, help Michigan automakers, and eventually lower costs. In practice it meant subsidies and mandates for a technology most drivers were not buying, while she vetoed a gas-tax holiday and left the high per-gallon tax in place. When the EV market cooled and politics shifted, the message softened to “we don’t care what you drive” — after years of treating the gas-powered majority as the problem to be phased out.

So the contrast with Kemp is straightforward: he cut the gas tax. Whitmer spent political capital on EVs and climate targets and offered drivers a limited fuel-blend waiver instead.

Benson supports a federal gas-tax pause and blames Trump/James/the Iran war. She has rejected pausing Michigan’s own ~52-cent tax. Her line is almost word-for-word Whitmer’s: it would “blow a hole in our budget,” kill road work, and Michigan shouldn’t have to because “we didn’t start this war.” That’s the same refusal Kemp just ignored in Georgia.

She’s also in the same energy lane. She backs the clean-energy transition law Whitmer signed, talks more renewables, weatherization, transit and EVs as the answer when gas spikes, and treats the high state fuel tax as untouchable road money. Different office, same coalition, same tradeoff: keep the tax, point at Washington, sell climate/clean-energy as the long-term fix.

She’s not Whitmer on the ballot. She’s the continuity candidate on the policy that matters at $4.80–$5 gas: no state tax holiday. If voters wanted a Michigan Kemp, Benson is not that.
Michigan under Whitmer already ran the experiment. Highest-tier state fuel tax, no holiday when prices blew up, a veto of a tax pause when it was offered, an EV/climate target that never came close to 2 million cars, and a “we can’t touch the road tax” line while neighbors and Georgia cut theirs. Benson’s answer this month is the sequel: freeze the state tax, demand Washington do the 18-cent piece, blame the war, talk weatherization and clean energy. Same hole in the wallet, same explanation.

Putting the democrat team back in charge does not reset the price of a gallon. It protects the revenue stream they built and the energy agenda they already passed. The problems people are living with — $4.80–$5 gas, a tax structure that stayed high on purpose, relief that never matched Kemp — are not accidents. They are the policy. Voting for continuity is voting to run it again.
