text:
No, Senator Sanders.

Before we even start, I want you to sit with something for a second.

You typed this on a phone. It bounced off a cell tower, ran through a fiber line, and landed on X's servers. Which live in... a data center. Every one of your 55 likes, every repost, every one of those 7,000 views got processed inside the exact kind of building you're calling a threat to humanity. Your fundraising emails? Data center. Your Senate website? Data center. The little donate button for the Fighting Oligarchy tour? Oh, you already know.

What's next, a senator using a data center to tell seven thousand people that data centers are threatening humanity... wait. I'm being told that's this post.

Bernie, you're a fax machine at a Tesla dealership. You're running dial-up in a fiber-optic world. Your breaker tripped somewhere around 1987 and nobody ever went down to the basement to flip it back on.

Okay. Deep breath. Here's the thing. I teach physics. Electricity is literally my unit. I've got a whole chapter on it in the textbook I wrote. So you just wandered into my classroom, Senator, and I'm going to need you to take a seat in the front row where I can keep an eye on you.

Let's start with your 75 percent.

That number isn't a law of physics, Bernie. It's a poll. I spend all year teaching sixteen-year-olds the difference between a measurement and a sermon, and you just handed the whole country a sermon with a percent sign on it.

That poll asked people if they'd oppose a data center NEAR WHERE THEY LIVE. Of course they would! You know what else people don't want next to their house? A landfill. A prison. A highway on-ramp. A power plant. A Walmart. A middle school marching band that practices at seven in the morning. I promise you I could get 75 percent "no" on half the stuff that makes modern life work, as long as I put it in their backyard. That's not a verdict on data centers. That's called NIMBY. "Not in my backyard." It's the oldest reflex in American local politics, and every town council in the country has watched it happen a thousand times.

And here's the part you conveniently skipped. When a Fox poll this season asked people about building data centers in REMOTE areas instead, a majority said yes, go ahead. So Americans aren't saying "data centers are threatening humanity." They're saying "please don't put it next to my kid's school." Those are two totally different sentences, Bernie. You mashed them together like a toddler with two colors of Play-Doh and called it art.

That number also moved fast. About a year ago the same kind of question was basically a coin flip. So what happened in twelve months? Did data centers start eating puppies? No. What changed is what people were being fed on their screens, day after day after day. Polls tell you what people have been told. They don't grade the homework.

And majorities have been wrong before. Prohibition was so popular they put it in the Constitution. Fourteen years later they had to take it back out. That's an appeal to popularity, and it's exactly why the Founders built a constitutional republic instead of a show of hands.

Quinn's Law Number Six: facts are the enemy of liberalism. Put a denominator under the scary number, and the scary number stops scaring anybody. So the denominator always gets left off.

Now your electric bills. And I'm going to do something here that you never, ever do, Bernie. I'm going to admit the part where you've got a point.

Bills in a lot of this country ARE going up, and data centers are a real piece of it. The PJM grid covers Virginia, Maryland, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and my own state of Ohio. Its capacity price went from about 29 dollars per megawatt-day for 2024-25 to about 329 dollars for 2026-27. The grid's own independent market watchdog pinned a big chunk of that jump on data center demand. I live in Ohio. I open that bill. I've got four kids and a teacher's paycheck. I am not going to insult the working families reading this by pretending it's fake.

But then you go completely off the rails.

Your answer to "this new customer is making the grid more expensive" is "ban the customer." Bernie, that's like a restaurant getting a giant catering order and deciding to close the restaurant because the kitchen's too small. Normal people build a bigger kitchen and make the catering customer pay for it.

And that's exactly what's been happening while you were busy yelling. States have been writing what they call large-load tariffs. They make the giant data centers pay for their own new power lines and generation, and put real money down, so if a project gets canceled, grandma isn't stuck paying for a transmission line to nowhere. When AEP here in Ohio made data centers put up real collateral, the pile of power requests shrank way down, because a whole lot of the fake requests evaporated the second somebody had to pay a deposit. Funny how that works. That's called accountability, Bernie. A moratorium doesn't make the tenant pay for a single thing. It just ships the whole building overseas.

And the "AI billionaires" you keep yelling about? They're the ones writing the checks for new power. Microsoft signed a 20-year deal to bring Three Mile Island Unit 1 back to life. Google signed with Kairos for small nuclear reactors. Amazon's buying nuclear power in Pennsylvania. Meta's signing nuclear deals in Ohio and Pennsylvania. Those are new, clean, carbon-free power plants, getting built because of the exact buildings you want to ban.

And you, Senator, have spent decades fighting nuclear power.

So let me get this straight. You want lower bills. AND less carbon. AND no new nuclear. AND no new gas. AND no data centers. Bernie, that's a circuit with no ground. All it's going to do is shock somebody.

You know what static electricity is? I show it to my freshmen with a balloon. It makes a lot of noise, gives you a little spark, and produces absolutely no current. It can't power a single thing. That's your entire energy policy, right there, stuck to the classroom ceiling.

Now the environment. Somebody at every one of these rallies holds up a jar of water, so let's talk water.

The Congressional Research Service put direct on-site data center water use at around two percent of U.S. water consumption. Two. Percent. And the biggest chunk of what gets blamed on data centers is really the water used at the power plants that make the electricity. That's an electricity problem wearing a water costume.

Now put that next to some other numbers. Golf courses in this country use hundreds of billions of gallons a year. And American cities lose TRILLIONS of gallons a year to leaky pipes. Old, cracked, busted water mains that nobody ever fixed. The water we lose to leaks makes every data center in the country look like a kid with a squirt gun.

Bernie, have you ever held one rally about leaky water mains? Ever once called a golf course a threat to humanity? No. Because a cracked pipe doesn't come with a billionaire you can slap on a poster.

And the industry's already moving to closed-loop cooling, recycled wastewater, and cooling right on the chip that sips a fraction of the water. So the grown-up answer is easy. In a dry area, require closed-loop or recycled water. Write the rule. Done. Don't freeze the entire country because of a jar.

You're about as bright as a brownout, Senator. The lights are flickering, and everybody in the house can tell something's wrong except the guy standing next to the fuse box.

And "threatening humanity." Oh, Bernie.

Your bank lives in a data center. Your pharmacy lives in a data center. Hospital records live in data centers. When I was a medic, we used to fight to get a patient's history in time to matter. Now it pops up in seconds, because of a building you want to ban. The weather model that tells Florida a hurricane's coming lives in a data center. The 911 dispatch systems in a whole lot of counties run through one. Your Social Security check gets processed in one.

"Threatening humanity" isn't a measurement, Senator. It's a sermon. And a sermon with no data is just a guy yelling in a parking lot.

Oh, and last week you were pushing a bill to ban superintelligence. Then you drew little red boxes around the net worths of the people who build AI chips. Now it's data centers. You're a weather vane in a windstorm, Bernie. You point wherever the loudest gust is blowing that day and call it a principle.

Now. The "Chinese psyop" part. This is where you really stepped in it.

Is every parent in Virginia who doesn't want a humming building next to the elementary school a Chinese agent? Of course not. Most of the anger is local, and it's real. I'll say that out loud. But that's not what you said. You said Americans have NOT fallen for a Chinese influence operation. Period. Like the whole idea is ridiculous. Like it's a punchline.

It's not a punchline, Bernie. It's a paper trail.

Earlier this year OpenAI reported banning a cluster of accounts it tied to a Chinese company doing contract work for provincial government clients. They were using AI tools, in Chinese, over VPNs, to pump out English posts and comics about American families paying for AI's electricity. OpenAI said the operation didn't CREATE the American debate. It tried to jump into a debate that already existed and pour gasoline on it. X later flagged a big network of suspected fake Chinese accounts, and some of them were posting about U.S. AI, energy, and power bills. Researchers who looked said it didn't get much reach. Okay. Fine. A burglar who can't get the window open is still a burglar.

And this isn't even new. Back in 2022, the security firm Mandiant caught a pro-China network it called Dragon Bridge. They used fake accounts pretending to be worried Texans to stir up local opposition to a rare earth plant the Pentagon was backing. Pretend to be the neighbors. Rile up the neighbors. Kill the project. Beijing wins. Same playbook.

Meanwhile, what's China doing with its OWN data centers? Building them as fast as the concrete can set. They've got a whole national program called "East Data, West Computing" to build massive computing hubs across the country, with reported investment plans in the hundreds of billions.

Think about that, Bernie. China is sprinting to build data centers at home, while networks and state media tied to Beijing push stories to Americans about how scary and expensive data centers are. If these buildings were really "threatening humanity," why is the Chinese Communist Party building them like it's trying to win a race?

Because it IS trying to win a race. The one you want America to sit out.

Quinn's First Law: liberalism always produces the exact opposite of what it promises. Ban the data center in Virginia, and the computing doesn't vanish. The demand doesn't vanish. The building just goes somewhere that doesn't hold hearings, doesn't care about water, doesn't care about carbon, and isn't going to share the technology with anybody. You don't save the planet. You hand the future to Beijing with a bow on it and call it environmentalism.

You're running a 9-volt battery in a 240-volt world, Senator. There isn't enough juice in there to light up the problem, much less fix it.

And now I'm going to get personal. Because I wore this country's uniform for 23 years, and this next part isn't a debate to me.

Grand Forks, North Dakota. A Chinese company called Fufeng, tied to a big corporation in Shandong, bought about 370 acres to build a corn mill. About 12 miles from Grand Forks Air Force Base, which runs sensitive drone and surveillance missions. The federal review board said at first it didn't even have jurisdiction, because of a loophole. The Air Force put it in writing and called the project a significant threat to national security. The city council finally killed it in 2023.

Cheyenne, Wyoming. A company majority-owned by Chinese nationals, called MineOne, bought land within about a mile of F.E. Warren Air Force Base. That's a nuclear missile base, Bernie. Minuteman III. They set up crypto mining there. They never reported the deal. The government reportedly found out from a tip, and the neighbor who reportedly sounded the alarm was Microsoft, which runs a data center right next door. In May 2024, President Biden ordered them to sell and get out.

Read that one again, Senator. Slowly. A Chinese-linked operation set up shop next to a nuclear missile base, and the warning reportedly came from the data center next door. The data center was the watchdog. And you want to put the watchdog down.

Val Verde County, Texas. A Chinese billionaire with deep ties to the Communist Party bought well over 100,000 acres near the border and near Laughlin Air Force Base, where the Air Force trains its pilots. Texas has been fighting over it for years.

Washington finally woke up. In late 2024 Treasury added dozens of military bases to the list where foreign land deals get reviewed. That happened because of Grand Forks and Cheyenne. Not because somebody was paranoid. Because the loophole was real, and the Air Force said so out loud.

When I was deployed, we didn't let anybody we didn't trust set up a folding chair outside the wire, let alone buy the field. So when you laugh off "Chinese psyop" like it's a late-night joke, Bernie, you're punching the wrong guy. China probes every single gap it can find. A fake-account farm. A corn mill next to a drone base. A crypto pad next to a missile field. An English-language cartoon about your power bill. And every time, it's counting on Americans to be too busy fighting each other to notice. You just proved them right.

Your antenna isn't picking up all the channels, Senator. Honestly, I'm not sure it's even plugged into the wall.

And then there are the stories you'll never tell at a rally.

Quincy, Washington, was a small farm town. Microsoft built on a bean field back in 2006. Today the data centers pay the majority of the town's property taxes. The town got new schools and a water reuse plant, and residents' tax rates dropped.

Loudoun County, Virginia, is the data center capital of the world. Data center tax money is over a billion dollars a year and pays for a massive share of the county budget. The real property tax rate dropped a lot over the past decade, and the Tax Foundation estimated the average homeowner there would be paying thousands more a year without the industry. Schools. Roads. Fire trucks. Paid for, in large part, by the buildings you want to ban.

Is it perfect? No. Some states handed out way too many sweetheart tax breaks, and once a data center's built, it doesn't employ a ton of people. So fix the DEAL, Bernie. Make the tax breaks shorter. Make them pay for their own power lines. Make them use recycled water. That's what grown-ups do. A ban is what you do when you can't do the math.

And speaking of billionaires, let's talk about the man with the microphone.

Three houses, Bernie. One of them's a lake house. $221,000 on chartered private jets in ONE quarter of 2025, on your "Fighting Oligarchy" tour, and reportedly over half a million for the whole year. Flying around at up to 15 grand an hour to tell everybody that OTHER people's energy use is threatening humanity.

Do you know how much fuel a private jet burns, Senator? I teach energy. A private jet can burn more fuel per passenger on one trip than a lot of working families burn driving to work for weeks. And you want to lecture America about whose energy use is wrecking the planet?

I keep watching Democrats cry about the rich while they ARE the rich. So here's my standing offer, one more time. Before you say "billionaire" again, file your taxes with the standard deduction. No itemizing. Pay DOUBLE what the IRS says you owe. Post it. And while you're at it, fly commercial. Middle seat. Back row. Right next to the bathroom. Unplug the jet, Bernie, before you unplug my kids' future.

Quinn's Law Number Twenty-Five: liberals are great at spending other people's money. And apparently other people's electricity too.

Since you never bring a plan, here's one. Free of charge, from a physics teacher.

Get the power plan approved BEFORE anybody breaks ground. Make big data centers pay for their own new power lines and generation, with real money down so a canceled project doesn't land on a working family's bill. Require closed-loop or recycled water in dry places. No eminent domain. Short tax breaks, not 30-year gifts. Money set aside for cleanup if they ever close. Train local kids in the trades to run and maintain these buildings, because those are good jobs. Publish the power and water numbers so the neighbors can see them.

And on China? Close the loopholes around military bases. Make foreign farmland filings actually mean something. Keep adversary money out of our data centers, our fiber lines, and our power grid.

That's how you protect the guy paying the electric bill AND the country, at the same time. You don't ban the building. You make it pay its own way, and you keep Beijing off the property.

So let's grade it, Senator.

You posted an anti-data-center message through a data center. You treated a backyard poll like a law of nature. You blamed rising bills on the one customer actually writing checks for new nuclear power. You called two percent of the nation's water "destroying the environment" while trillions of gallons leak out of old pipes. You laughed off Chinese influence operations that security firms and AI companies have actually documented, while China sprints to build the very thing you want to ban. And you did every bit of it as a millionaire who flies private.

Final grade: F. And I'm grading on a curve.

You're a blown transformer, Bernie. Lots of smoke. One loud pop. And then the whole neighborhood goes dark.

But what do I know? I'm only a combat medic who wore the uniform for 23 years, a physics teacher who makes teenagers show the denominator, and a father of four in Ohio who'd like to keep both his electric bill AND his country, and doesn't think he should have to choose.

text:
Anyone can make an assertion without evidence but then why didn't Leo Frank and his attorney's put that  alleged event in their appeals to the defense-friendly trial judge or higher courts? It would have been grounds to get their client a new trial. 

If the Jury Was Threatened, Why Didn't Leo Frank's Lawyers Use It?

If a mob really shouted “Hang the Jew,” in the trial as Arthur Burton Rascoe asserted 16 months after the trial, or threatened Leo Frank’s jurors with death unless they convicted the defendant, one question is hard to avoid: 

Why did Frank and his lawyers fail to use such an event while trying to stop the trial, throw out the guilty verdict, and win another trial?

Frank’s lawyers did complain about crowd behavior.

The defense complained about an applause by someone inside the courtroom, cheering outside the courthouse, and cries of “Hurrah for Dorsey.” 

The defense put these complaints into the official legal record, called witnesses about them, gathered sworn affidavits, used the issue in Frank’s request for another trial, and they carried his case to the Supreme Court of Georgia. Yet the later story about a mob threatening the jurors with “Hang the Jew,” or “Hang the Jew or we’ll hang you,” does not appear in these 1913 complaints. It doesn't appear in the three competing Atlanta newspapers. It doesn't appear in anything Rosser, or Arnold stated or wrote. It was a hoax fabricated in Chicago, the birth place of the ADL, the place where Albert Lasker was one of the primary "angel" investors of the Frank defense campaign, which I and others write about extensively. 

What Was a Motion for a Mistrial?

A motion is a formal request asking a judge to do something. A motion for a mistrial asks the judge to stop a trial while it is still going on because a serious problem has supposedly made a fair trial impossible going further.

On Monday, August 25, 1913, after Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey finished his closing argument, Frank’s attorney Reuben Arnold asked Judge Leonard S. Roan to declare a mistrial. The jury was removed from the courtroom while Arnold made his request. The Atlanta Journal described Arnold’s request as a formal motion for a mistrial and listed the crowd incidents he relied upon (Atlanta Journal, 1).

Arnold complained about applause inside the courtroom and cheering outside the courthouse. He referred to Friday, August 22, 1913, when a crowd reportedly cheered Dorsey after court recessed, and Saturday, August 23, 1913, when another demonstration occurred as Dorsey left the courthouse. Arnold said people cried “Hurrah for Dorsey” while the jury was nearby. He also complained about applause for Dorsey on Monday, August 25, 1913, while jurors were in a nearby room.

Judge Roan acknowledged hearing some cheering, although he said he did not hear the words “Hurrah for Dorsey.” Bailiffs were questioned. Some admitted hearing noise or cheering, while others said they did not hear the words Arnold reported. Arnold himself testified about what he heard. 

Yet, the surviving reports do not give us a reliable headcount or identify every person who joined the cheering, so we shouldn't pretend to know who every person in the crowd was. We don't know how many, where they were, or if they were working subrosa for the defense. There's always the possibly they were a plant that was staged to generate the incident. The defense had allegedly planted much evidence against Newt Lee, the death notes, the time card alteration, the blood soaked shirt. It's not beyond the realm of possibilities that the cheering was generated by the defense, but like everything there needs to be evidence for or against to sustain, or argue or debate something. 

Arnold argued these public demonstrations could intimidate or influence the jury. Judge Roan denied the mistrial request, gave the jury its legal instructions, and sent the jurors out to decide the case. The jury returned a guilty verdict later on August 25, 1913.

What Does “Preserved in the Record” Mean?

When I say Frank’s lawyers “preserved” the “Hurrah for Dorsey” complaint, I mean they placed it into the official court record. A court record is the collection of testimony, motions, rulings, affidavits, and other papers used in a court case.

This defense action is important because a higher court normally reviews what happened in the lower court by reading this record. If a lawyer wants a higher court to review an alleged error, the lawyer usually needs to raise the issue and make sure a written record exists showing what supposedly happened. The Georgia Supreme Court's tribunal reviewed this record and other defense motions from November 1913 all through 1914 at various stages and episodes. 

Frank’s lawyers did exactly this with the crowd complaints. Arnold raised the issue in court on August 25, 1913. Witnesses were questioned about the cheering. After Frank was convicted, his lawyers gathered affidavits about crowd behavior and again used public demonstrations as part of their effort to get another trial after the adverse verdict.

So when we ask why the defense preserved the comparatively mild cry of “Hurrah for Dorsey,” this is where it was preserved: in Frank’s own court proceedings and in the legal papers used to challenge his conviction.

What Was a Motion for a New Trial?

A motion for a new trial is different from a motion for a mistrial. A mistrial request asks a judge to completely stop a trial while it is still underway, not pause it, but end it. A motion for a new trial is made after the jury has returned a verdict. It asks the judge to throw out the old verdict and hold another trial.

Frank’s lawyers filed a motion for a new trial after his conviction. They later expanded it with more than one hundred claimed errors or reasons for another trial. Lawyers often call each separate legal reason a ground. In plain English, a ground is simply one reason offered to the judge for granting a new trial. Judge Roan rejected all 100+ grounds. The judge refused a new trial for Leo Frank after giving the defense an opportunity to present a long document of alleged errors on paper and orally argue their perspective.

The crowd complaint did not disappear. Frank’s lawyers again raised applause, cheering, public demonstrations, and possible influence on the jury. They supplied affidavits from people who claimed to have seen or heard some of these events and argued the public atmosphere around the courthouse had hurt Frank’s right to a fair trial.

Judge Roan heard the arguments and reviewed the large amount of material presented by the defense. On Friday, October 31, 1913, he denied Frank’s motion for a new trial. Frank’s lawyers then took the case to the Supreme Court of Georgia (Atlanta Georgian, 3).

So Where Is the Alleged Death Threat?

This is where the later “Hang the Jew” confabulation becomes difficult to fit into the 1913 legal record. Frank’s lawyers preserved complaints about applause, cheers for Dorsey, the location of jurors, the distance between jurors and crowds, and arguments over what the jurors might have heard.

If people openly threatened to kill or lynch jurors unless they convicted Frank, such an incident would have been far more serious than people shouting “Hurrah for Dorsey.” It would have supported the exact argument Arnold was already making. Frank’s defense was claiming outside public pressure could intimidate the jury and damage Frank’s right to a fair trial.

Yet the 1913 legal material discussed here does not show Arnold telling Judge Roan about a mob shouting “Hang the Jew” at the jury. The defense material concerning crowd demonstrations discussed here does not supply such a threat either. Frank’s lawyers documented far smaller demonstrations, but this much more serious alleged death threat is missing.

Its absence does not prove nobody in Atlanta ever made an antisemitic remark. It does not prove every spectator behaved properly. The narrower historical question is much easier to state: Where is the contemporary evidence for a mob threatening Frank’s jurors with death unless they convicted him? 

Where are the affidavits? Where are the courtroom eyewitnesses who said they heard these alleged antisemitic death threats? Where is the police report? Where is any complaint from Frank’s lawyers to Judge Leonard Roan saying jurors had been threatened with violence?

Where are the reports from the police officers and bailiffs who guarded the jurors and escorted them between the courthouse and their rooms at the Kimball House? Where are the Atlanta newspaper reports describing a mob shouting “Hang the Jew” at the jury? Where, in Frank’s motion for a mistrial, his motion for a new trial, the supporting affidavits, or his appeals, do his lawyers describe such a threat?

Frank’s defense complained about applause. They complained about cheering for Solicitor General Hugh Dorsey. They preserved cries of “Hurrah for Dorsey.” They gathered affidavits about crowd noise and argued jurors might have heard it.

Yet they did not raise a supposed “Hang the Jew” death threat. That's doubtful if it actually happened.

No comparable 1913 legal record has been produced showing Frank’s lawyers complained to the judge or any judge (state or federal Supreme Court tribunal) about such a threat, reported it to police, obtained affidavits from eyewitnesses, or used it as a reason for another trial.

Instead, the dramatic story appears later, far away from Atlanta, in a newspaper published hundreds of miles away in Chicago, Illinois, on the shore of Lake Michigan, one of the Great Lakes shared by the United States and Canada. And it was invented a year and four months after the trial ended by a young journalist two years out of college and building a career.

If such a serious threat really occurred within hearing of the jury, the obvious historical question remains: 

Why is it missing from the contemporary legal record created by the very lawyers searching for evidence of jury intimidation?

The Georgia Supreme Court Reviewed the Evidence

Frank’s appeal went to the Supreme Court of Georgia, the highest state court in Georgia. On February 17, 1914, the court affirmed Frank’s conviction by a vote of 4 to 2 in Frank v. State, 141 Ga. 243, 80 S.E. 1016 (Georgia Supreme Court, 4).

To say the court affirmed the conviction means the higher court allowed the conviction and judgment to remain in place. The court did not hold another murder trial. Its job was to review the legal record, examine Frank’s claims of error, and decide whether the law required another trial.

Another important legal phrase is sufficiency of the evidence. It simply means whether enough legal evidence existed for a jury to reach the verdict it reached. It does not mean every justice had to believe every witness, nor does it mean the Supreme Court held a second trial and decided all of the facts again.

The four-justice majority expressly said it had carefully considered the evidence and found the evidence sufficient to uphold the verdict. The majority also found no substantial error requiring another trial. In other words, four justices directly rejected the argument claiming the trial evidence was legally too weak to support Frank’s conviction.

Two justices dissented, Chief Justice William H. Fish and Justice Hiram Warner Beck. A dissent is an opinion written by judges who disagree with the majority on one or more legal questions. Fish and Beck disagreed with the majority mainly over evidence concerning Frank’s alleged prior sexual conduct, including testimony from Jim Conley and C. B. Dalton. They believed some of this evidence should not have been admitted for the jury to hear.

But Fish and Beck did not say the evidence in the murder case was legally insufficient to support the conviction. Their dissent attacked certain evidence admitted during the trial. They did not write an opinion saying the State had failed to present enough evidence for a guilty verdict. No justice on the Georgia Supreme Court wrote an opinion declaring the trial evidence legally insufficient.

Frank’s lawyers then asked the Supreme Court of Georgia for a rehearing. A rehearing is a request asking the same court to look at its decision again. The disagreement between the justices over the evidence issue remained, but all six justices agreed to deny Frank’s request for a rehearing.

This does not mean every justice agreed on every legal question. They plainly did not. But it is important when discussing later claims of an unfair trial. The majority found the evidence sufficient to support the verdict, and the two dissenters based their disagreement on the admission of certain evidence rather than a finding of legally insufficient evidence.

Why “Hurrah for Dorsey” Is Important

“Hurrah for Dorsey” is important in the spectrum of complaints, precisely, because it was not a death threat. Frank’s lawyers considered ordinary cheering important enough to document because they hoped to show improper public influence on the jury. Read that again, a solicitor being cheered as he walks out of court was considered significant enough for the defense to raise it as evidence why Leo Frank deserved a new trial. 

They identified dates, locations, noise, distances, applause, and witnesses. They argued about whether jurors could hear the demonstrations. They raised these complaints in the August 25, 1913 mistrial fight and again during their effort to win another trial.

If a direct death threat against the jurors had occurred within their hearing, it would have been much stronger evidence for the same defense argument. Yet the dramatic antisemitic lynching ultimatum found in later accounts is absent from the contemporary crowd complaints examined here.

The Later Story Becomes Much More Dramatic

A much stronger version appeared later during the public campaign to save Frank from execution. 

On Sunday, December 27, 1914, about sixteen months after the verdict, Burton Rascoe published a long article in the Chicago Sunday Tribune. Rascoe claimed men in the courtroom distracted jurors by shouting a warning telling them they had better hang Frank or face violence themselves (Chicago Sunday Tribune, 5). The article by Rascoe reads as if it were written by a crazed fanatic with no pretense of objectivity. In one sentence he's raving about Jew hatred, in another, he's dehumanizing a Negro witness, without any self awareness for the irony of complaining about bigotry or prejudice. Read the article, it's in the references. There's an audiobook on the same page if anyone is too lazy to read the text.

This later account raises basic source questions. Who shouted the threat? On what day did it happen? Where was the speaker standing? Which juror heard it? Which Atlanta newspaper reported it in 1913? Which defense lawyer raised it? Which affidavit recorded it? Where does it appear in Frank’s mistrial request or new-trial papers? Who? What? When? Where? How? and, Why? That's how we trace evidence. We look at when it emerged, and who brought it forward. Was it a radical pro-Frank activist? Does their writing reflect objectivity? Parts of Burton Rascoe's article could just as easily been published in a KKK Ku Klux Klan newsletter the way he wrote it with such extreme partisanship. The defense lawyers used the same language and worse, it was a tirade of racial invective, meant to fool the jury, but the saw right through the BS.  Skin color could not be used as a race card or a White privilege card to trump testimony, physical and circumstantial evidence. The jury voted on the evidence, not on Klan rhetoric, not on false accusations of antisemitism, Jew-hatred or religious prejudice. Most thinking people can not be manipulated with such tribal extremism over evidence.  Justice was more important than race is how the jury decided. Truth was more important than tribe. 

These questions become more important because the 1913 defense record is not silent about crowd conduct. 

Frank’s lawyers preserved lesser demonstrations in detail. The problem is not an absence of crowd complaints. The problem is the absence of this particular death-threat story from legal proceedings built, in part, around claims of outside pressure on the jury.

Blog: The Origin and Growth of the “Hang the Jew” Story

The Mary Phagan Kean Legacy Project has a much longer source study devoted to this claim: 

“Notorious or Infamous? The Antisemitic Death Threat Hoax: ‘Hang the Jew, or We’ll Hang You!’” 

The research study traces changing versions of the story from the original period through later newspaper, magazine, book, and internet accounts and compares later claims with the earlier legal record (Mary Phagan Kean Legacy Project, 6).

The article also explains citogenesis and citation laundering. 

Citogenesis happens when repeated copying makes a claim look well established even when later writers may all be repeating the same earlier source. 

Citation laundering happens when a weak or poorly supported claim passes through later books and articles until readers have difficulty seeing how little support existed at the beginning.

The dates are especially important for the chronology and timing reference. In August 1913, Frank’s lawyers documented applause, cheering, and alleged cries of “Hurrah for Dorsey.” In October 1913, they used claims of unfair influence while asking Judge Roan for another trial. On February 17, 1914, the Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the conviction, with the majority expressly finding sufficient evidence to uphold the verdict. The much more dramatic published story of jurors being openly threatened with violence appears later.

Dinnerstein in 1968 vs Dinerstein in 2014

The evidence is insufficient according to Leonard Dinnerstein in 2014, see image and read it thrice:

This leaves one plain question at the center of the issue: If Frank’s jury truly heard an antisemitic death threat warning them to convict him or face violence themselves, why did Frank’s own lawyers fail to use it while they were already documenting far less serious crowd behavior as evidence of an unfair trial?

Roan.” Contemporary report describing Arnold’s formal mistrial motion, the August 22 and August 23 demonstrations, witness questioning, and Judge Roan’s ruling.

https://t.co/SxWL6prrMo

text:
Happy birthday to former Putnam City, Southern Methodist and NFL defensive back Bryan McCann, born on this day in 1987 in Lawton.

McCann was a three-sport athlete at Putnam City High School, lettering in football, basketball and track and field.

As a senior, McCann was one of the state's top players entering the season and performed like it.

He had two touchdown catches in the season opener against Putnam West, then returned a kickoff 80 yards for a touchdown in a win over Yukon.

A week later, he had a 31-yard touchdown catch, an interception and returned a punt 70 yards for a touchdown in a win over Choctaw.

But the following week, he suffered a broken leg against Lawton and missed the rest of the season.

McCann had several scholarship offers, including those from Northwestern, Oklahoma State, Rice, Stanford, Texas Tech, Tulsa and UAB, but selected Southern Methodist.

At SMU, McCann had 38 tackles, broke up four passes and intercepted a pass in earning All-Freshman Conference USA honors.

In 2007, he started all 12 games, making 59 tackles and intercepting four passes. As a junior, he intercepted three more passes and added 35 tackles and a sack.

In his final season with the Mustangs, McCann had 54 tackles, intercepted three passes and had 824 yards on 34 kickoff returns.

In 2010, McCann signed with the Dallas Cowboys as an undrafted free agent. He was promoted to the active roster in November and in his second game, he returned an interception against the New York Giants 101 yards for a touchdown, breaking the then-Cowboys-record for longest interception return.

The play earned him NFC Defensive Player of the Week honors.

A week later, he scooped up a punt that had been batted back into play by the Detroit Lions' John Wendling and returned it 97 yards for a touchdown, earning him NFC Special Teams Player of the Week and NFL Rookie of the Week.

In 2011, the Cowboys released McCann to make room for a receiver due to injuries to starting wideouts Miles Austin and Dez Bryant.

He later played with the Baltimore Ravens, Oakland Raiders, Miami Dolphins and Arizona Cardinals. He completed his career with 31 tackles, three for losses, one interception, recovered two fumbles, and had more than 1,000 yards in combined kickoff and punt returns.

After his playing career, McCann returned to SMU and earned a Master's Degree in Computer Science and Computer Software Engineering and is now an AI Engineer for SIDEARM Sports, a leading digital provider for college athletics.

In 2023, McCann was inducted into the Putnam City Athletics Hall of Fame.

Happy birthday Bryan! #tdfn #okpreps @PCHighFootball @SMUFB @Cowboys

This month marks 15 years since everything changed for then Arizona Congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords. That was when a gunman opened fire at a constituent event she was holding in her district. Nineteen people were shot, including Giffords. Six people were killed. The gunman shot Giffords in the head at point-blank range. The St. Charles Church (Karlskirche) is considered architect Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach's greatest work. It is also a Viennese icon and an expression of the Austrian joie de vivre.

Johann Bernhard Fischer von ErlachIn 1713, one year after the last great plague epidemic, Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor, pledged to build a church for his namesake patron saint, Charles Borromeo, who was revered as a healer for plague sufferers. An architectural competition was announced, in which Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach prevailed over, among others, Ferdinando Galli-Bibiena and Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt. Construction began in 1716. After J.B. Fischer‘s death in 1723, his son, Joseph Emanuel Fischer von Erlach, completed the construction in 1737 using partially altered plans. The church originally possessed a direct line of sight to the Hofburg.

Architecture
As a creator of historic architecture, J.B. Fischer united the most diverse of elements. The façade in the center, which leads to the porch, corresponds to a Greek temple portico. The neighboring two columns, crafted by Lorenzo Mattielli, found a model in Trajan‘s Column in Rome. Next to those, two tower pavilions extend out and show the influence of the Roman baroque (Bernini and Borromini). Above the entrance, a dome rises up above a high drum, which the younger J.E. Fischer shortened and partly altered.

The iconographical program of the church originated from the imperial official Carl Gustav Heraeus and connects St. Charles Borromeo with his imperial benefactor. The relief on the pediment above the entrance with the cardinal virtues and the figure of the patron on its apex point to the motivation of the donation. This sculpture group continues onto the attic story as well. The attic is also one of the elements which the younger Fischer introduced. The columns display scenes from the life of Charles Borromeo in a spiral relief, however they also recall the Pillars of Hercules and act as symbols of imperial power. The entrance is flanked by angles from the Old and New Testaments. This continues in the interior as well, above all, the dome fresco by Johann Michael Rottmayr of Salzburg and Gaetano Fanti which displays an intercession of Charles Borromeo, supported by the Virgin Mary. The cardinal virtues surround the scene. The frescos in a number of side chapels are attributed to Daniel Gran. The high altar painting portraying the ascension of the saint was conceptualized by the elder Fischer and executed by Ferdinand Maximilian Brokoff. The altar paintings in the side chapels are by various artists, including Daniel Gran, Sebastiano Ricci, Martino Altomonte, and Jakob van Schuppen. As strong effect emanates from the directing of light and architectural grouping, in particular the arch openings of the main axis. The color scheme is characterized by marble with sparring and conscious use of gold leaf.

Meta's Muse agent is attacking one of the economy's most profitable weak spots | Barbara Booth, CNBC

For years, subscription businesses have benefited from a simple fact of consumer behavior: people are much better at signing up than canceling.

They forget what they joined. They stop using services but keep paying. A $9 or $15 monthly charge can disappear into a credit card statement for months or even years.

With the rollout of Meta Muse this month, an AI personal agent that can handle tasks across many areas of personal life, it quickly became clear that subscription bloat was an easy target.

Muse can help consumers identify and cancel recurring subscriptions. While subscription-management services have existed for years, Muse brings that capability into a much broader personal assistant, potentially making forgotten recurring charges much easier to surface and cancel.

And the timing matters. Close to half (44%) of U.S. consumers increased their subscription spending in 2025, with average annual spending rising to $1,887, or about $157 a month, according to a report published by Mastercard and FT Strategies in April. Subscription spend rose 7.7% year-over-year in July, faster than overall card spending, according to Bank of America payments data, with entertainment and retail subscriptions accounting for about 43% of the total.

Neale Mahoney, an economics professor at Stanford University and director of the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, has studied how much subscription businesses benefit when consumers fail to cancel.

"We found that when people are forced to decide, they are about four times more likely to cancel," Mahoney said, citing data from his 2025 American Economic Review paper "Selling Subscriptions," co-authored with Stanford economists Liran Einav and Ben Klopack.

That distinction matters in an AI agent world.

The Stanford researchers estimated that sellers can roughly double revenue because of consumer inertia, when people forget or put off canceling, and cancellation friction, when ending a subscription takes too much time or effort. AI personal agents could weaken both, Mahoney said. But not every subscription is equally vulnerable. A physical subscription, such as pet food, is hard to forget when the product keeps arriving at your door, he said, while a digital service, such as credit monitoring, can quietly keep billing long after a consumer stops thinking about it.

Ultimately, the AI personal agent's intervention with this consumer psychology could have implications far beyond the subscription and influence decision-making deep within the core financial services that banks take for granted today.

"Muse and similar agentic AI assistants could soon sweep household cash automatically into accounts paying 3.3% to 5.0%, instead of the 0.1% national average on checking accounts. If every household used AI agents to optimize the return on their cash balances, banks could lose a large share of the cheap deposits they rely on to make loans, which would be a problem for the entire financial system," Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok wrote in an analysis last week.

'More of life is becoming a recurring bill'

Consumers already were becoming more aggressive about cutting subscriptions.

ScribeUp, which builds subscription-management technology into banking apps for banks, credit unions, and fintech companies, says its members are now 1.8 times more likely to initiate a cancellation than they were a year ago.

"More of life is becoming a recurring bill. Those bills cost more every year, and it becomes increasingly difficult for consumers to keep track of everything they are paying for," said Jordan Mackler, the company's co-founder and CEO. He said that increase predates ScribeUp's newer AI capabilities and reflects a broader change in consumer behavior.

According to the company, the median ScribeUp user now has more than 12 recurring subscription payments, while 1 in 4 has 20 or more. In addition, the share of users with at least eight rose from 62% to 71% over the past year.

Price hikes can accelerate the exit. Mackler said cancellations at an individual merchant can jump as much as 50% when prices rise. Health and fitness subscriptions have seen the sharpest increase in cancellation activity, up 3.8 times year-over-year, followed by video streaming at 2.2 times, news and media at 2.1 times, and music streaming at 1.9 times, said Mackler.

Mackler said AI is increasing the number of subscriptions ScribeUp can help consumers manage. The company currently tracks roughly 200,000 unique recurring billers. Before adding its newer agentic capabilities this year, it could automate cancellations for only a few hundred major subscription companies.

The average canceled subscription costs $17.39 a month, and Mackler said ScribeUp saves users more than $300 a year on average on recurring bills they didn't realize they were paying for or no longer needed.

An end to the costly economics of forgetting?

Subscription companies are already dealing with significant customer turnover. The Mastercard report found average monthly churn — the percentage of subscribers who cancel or fail to renew in a given month — is 20%. But more than half of U.S. subscription businesses surveyed said at least 10% of their subscriber base was inactive, meaning those customers were still subscribed but were not actively using the service.

As consumers gain more control over recurring charges, subscription companies may need to compete harder to keep them.

Hitee Chandra Jha, principal product manager at Zendesk who specializes in product-led growth and customer retention, said companies may need to make value more visible before a customer reaches the cancellation screen.

For some companies, that could mean treating cancellation less as an all-or-nothing event. Jha said a streaming service whose customer has finished watching a series might be better off offering a pause rather than a desperate discount. A fitness-app user who has reached a goal could be moved to a maintenance tier or offered another path to stay engaged, she said.

Data from subscription-management company Recurly suggests that kind of flexibility can work. In its 2026 State of Subscriptions report, based on 76 million unique subscribers across more than 2,200 businesses, it found that the use of "pause before cancel" options jumped 337%, and three out of four customers who paused eventually returned.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg envisions Muse as the "centerpiece" of an AI strategy that will be surrounded by still unproven consumer hardware, from augmented reality glasses to the Muse Charm keychain fob-like device, but it is a bet that the market has recently rewarded the company for making.

The AI has encountered pushback from Amazon, which blocked Muse from shopping on its site, saying the agent's access violated its terms of service. There are also significant concerns about privacy when giving an AI access to financial information. But 43% of consumers said they are comfortable with AI managing their subscriptions, according to the Recurly data.

"Treating cancellation as a transition, not just a loss, is what differentiates a mature retention strategy from a defensive one," Jha said. "The best defense against AI-assisted cancellation is not friction," she added.

Mastercard's research points in the same direction. Of the consumers surveyed, 74% said they are more likely to subscribe when cancellation is easy, while 70% said they are more likely to resubscribe. Another 34% said they would remain subscribed if they were given the option to pause rather than cancel.

Instead of spelling the end of subscription growth, AI could instead put more pressure on companies to find new ways to convince customers of value.

ScribeUp has seen that once users trust that the recurring charges on their accounts are the ones they actually chose, they become more comfortable with subscriptions overall and increase their total subscription spending.

"If consumers trust that they can easily see, manage, and cancel recurring charges, our data shows they are likely to expand their overall recurring spend and are more willing to try new services in the first place," Mackler said.

According to Mahoney, a healthier market should produce businesses that don't rely on ways to slow consumers down but give them more ways to stay on their own terms. "When people are trapped in subscriptions they don't want or can't get out of, market forces are limited, and companies don't have the incentives to have a high-quality product at a low price. They can just rely on a locked-in install base," he said.

Whether it is AI or the consumer taking action, when people stop paying for something they no longer want and spend that money elsewhere, "that's good for consumers, it's good for markets, and it's good for firms that are making products that people want," Mahoney said. "That's economics working the way it's supposed to work."

Raymond LOUIS Heenan (November 1, 1944 – September 17, 2017) was an American professional wrestling manager, color commentator, and wrestler. He performed with the American Wrestling Association (AWA), the World Wrestling Federation (WWF, now WWE) and World Championship Wrestling (WCW) under the ring name Bobby "The Brain" Heenan.

Heenan was known for his skill in elevating villainous on-screen talent by drawing negative reactions for himself and his wrestlers from the crowd. He was paired with numerous wrestlers, including Nick Bockwinkel, whom he led to win the AWA World Heavyweight Championship, and he became an integral figure in the 1980s professional wrestling boom by managing King Kong Bundy and André the Giant in WWF main event matches with Hulk Hogan at WrestleMania 2 and WrestleMania III respectively. The wrestlers under his tutelage were collectively known as "The Heenan Family" at various times throughout his career.

Known for his quick wit and comedic ability, Heenan also served as a color commentator and is remembered for his on-screen repartee with Gorilla Monsoon. Outside of wrestling, Heenan authored two books, appeared on numerous television shows, and briefly hosted a parody talk show titled The Bobby Heenan Show on WWF Prime Time Wrestling. Heenan retired in 2001 at WrestleMania X-Seven after a seventeen-year stint as a commentator in professional wrestling but he continued to make sporadic appearances in several promotions. In 2002, he was diagnosed with throat cancer, which limited his appearances in later years, and died from complications of the disease in 2017. Among other honors, he has been inducted into the Professional Wrestling, WWE, and Wrestling Observer halls of fame. Multiple wrestling commentators have described him as the greatest professional wrestling manager of all time.

Early life
Heenan was born in Chicago, Illinois, on November 1, 1944.[5][6][1] His father Robert Heenan was a railroad worker, and his mother Mildred Bernadette Kambrz was a hotel manager. Heenan dropped out of school in the eighth grade to support his mother and grandmother.[7] He grew up a fan of pro wrestling and baseball. As a fan of wrestling growing up in Chicago and Indianapolis, he started in the wrestling profession early on, carrying bags and jackets for the wrestlers, and selling refreshments at events.[7][4]

These three names share a deep linguistic and historical connection, primarily originating in Ancient Mesopotamia, the Middle East, and the Caucasus.
Sargon
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Greek and biblical translation of the Akkadian regnal name Šarru-kīn. It combines šarru (Akkadian for "king") and kīnu (meaning "true," "established," or "legitimate").
Historical Significance: It is most famously associated with Sargon of Akkad (24th century BCE), the legendary founder of the Akkadian Empire. Later, the Neo-Assyrian ruler Sargon II (8th century BCE) adopted the throne name to establish the legitimacy of his rule.
Sargis
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Classical Syriac and Armenian form of the Latin name Sergius. It originates from the ancient Roman gens (clan) Sergia, which etymologists suspect may connect to the Latin verb servare ("to guard" or "to preserve").
Sako
Origin & Etymology: Sako operates on a few different historical tracks depending on the region:
In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
In the Balkans: In Albania, it functions as a standalone occupational surname for a "church servant" or as a nickname for the Muslim name Isak (Isaac).
In Asia: It is also an unrelated Japanese surname (written as 佐古) meaning "help" and "ancient".

text:
Bullfrog brains can make their own backup fuel | University of Missouri

For decades, scientists believed most animals relied on a steady supply of glucose, the body's primary fuel source, to power their brains. When glucose runs out, neural activity begins to fail, potentially leading to lasting brain damage.

Now, researchers at the University of Missouri's College of Arts and Science have discovered that bullfrogs don't follow that rule. Instead, when glucose becomes scarce, their brains can produce an alternative energy source known as ketone bodies, allowing critical neural functions to continue.

A backup made inside the brain

In most animals, ketone bodies are produced in the liver when glucose levels drop during conditions such as fasting, starvation or prolonged exercise. The liver breaks down fatty acids into these energy molecules, which then travel through the bloodstream to organs, including the brain, where they are used as fuel.

But Mizzou's team discovered that bullfrogs can bypass that process. Instead of relying entirely on the liver, their brains can generate ketones locally, creating an emergency energy reserve where it's needed most. The findings are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

"Scientists generally believe ketones are delivered to the brain from elsewhere in the body," said Joseph Santin, an associate professor of biological sciences and lead author of the study. "That's what makes this discovery so exciting. It's like finding a backup generator inside a building that everyone assumed had only one power source."

Surviving winter's energy shortfall

The finding helps explain how bullfrogs survive one of the most challenging periods of their year. Each winter, they enter a hibernation-like state that slows their metabolism and depletes energy reserves.

By spring, when oxygen and energy stores are running low, the animals must immediately reactivate essential brain circuits that control bodily functions. The newly discovered metabolic backup system may be one reason they can make that transition so quickly and successfully.

The research builds on years of work in Santin's lab exploring how frogs endure conditions that would severely damage or even kill most animals. Previous studies revealed that this hibernation-like state helps protect neural circuits during extreme oxygen deprivation. The new findings uncover another layer of that survival strategy: the ability to maintain brain activity when glucose metabolism is compromised.

The discovery also raises questions about what triggers the switch to ketone production and how long bullfrogs can sustain it. Researchers do not believe the metabolic shift is permanent, but it appears to provide a robust backup system when the brain's usual energy supply falls short.

Possible clues for human brain disorders

While the findings offer new insight into amphibian biology, Santin believes they may also help scientists better understand the human brain because bullfrogs and humans share many of the same fundamental biological processes.

By revealing how brains adapt when energy supplies become limited, the research could open new avenues for studying neurological disorders linked to impaired energy metabolism, including Alzheimer's disease, ALS and schizophrenia.

text:
When you look at this 1902 photograph, you aren’t just looking at a house made of dirt and grass. You are looking at the architecture of hope. Building a sod house was the ultimate act of defiance on the Nebraska prairie. It was a declaration that this family intended to stay, to thrive, and to carve a future out of the very ground beneath their feet. The treeless horizon behind them offers no shade and no shelter, yet they stand together with a dignity that transcends their humble circumstances.

The raw, unedited quality of this vintage image—the scratches, the grain, the light leaks—brings us closer to their reality than any history book ever could. Life here was measured in buckets of water and rows of tilled earth. Wealth wasn't found in bank accounts but in the strength of a shared bond. As they gather for a meal outside, you can see that their pride is their greatest armor.

They were pioneers in every sense of the word, turning 'nowhere' into 'somewhere.' It’s a humbling reminder that our ancestors faced the unknown with nothing but their hands and each other. Their story is written in the soil of the plains, a legacy of resilience that still echoes in the wind today.

California taxpayers spent AT LEAST $11 BILLION last fiscal year SUBSIDIZING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS and their households, according to a new City Journal investigation. 

Democrat Xavier Becerra wants their taxpayer-funded healthcare PROTECTED (of course he does). 

Becerra, who is running to replace Gavin Newsom, has criticized California’s decision to freeze new comprehensive Medi-Cal enrollment for undocumented adults.

He argues that excluding poor immigrants from routine healthcare is “foolish” because they will eventually seek more expensive treatment in emergency rooms.

“I’d be smart and not limit care,” Becerra said while defending continued Medi-Cal coverage. “That means keeping them on Medi-Cal.”

Republican Steve Hilton has taken the opposite position.

“Stop taking money from California taxpayers who can barely afford their healthcare to give free healthcare to citizens of other countries who shouldn’t even be here,” Hilton said.

That choice will be on California’s ballot Nov. 3.

The $11 billion estimate comes from an investigation by Christopher Rufo, Kenneth Schrupp and Austen Hufford.

The reporters visited four Southern California public-services offices. Workers reportedly explained how illegal immigrants can access certain programs directly or receive benefits through eligible U.S.-born children.

California operates what City Journal describes as the country’s largest welfare system, spending more than $180 billion annually on healthcare, food assistance and other programs.

Medi-Cal accounts for most of the estimated cost.

California’s Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that approximately 1.7 million undocumented residents have comprehensive Medi-Cal coverage funded by the state.

That coverage costs California’s General Fund approximately $10 billion annually, which is more than DOUBLE the original projection.

The reporters also investigated California’s Cash Assistance Program for Immigrants, or CAPI, which provides monthly payments to qualifying elderly or disabled noncitizens.

“If you are a citizen, you cannot get CAPI,” a Glendale welfare officer told them. “I don’t care about legal or not. Not being a citizen is the key.”

At a Los Angeles office, another worker explained how illegal-immigrant parents can receive CalWORKs benefits on behalf of their U.S.-born children.

“Because she is not and the child is, she only gets money for the child, and not for her,” the employee said.

A June HHS report found that California accounted for nearly 60,000 of approximately 85,000 “child-only” cash-welfare households nationwide in fiscal 2024.

Those California households received approximately $617.5 million. That's more than 81 percent of the nationwide spending identified in that category.

City Journal modeled a California household containing two illegal-immigrant parents, two U.S.-born children and one illegal-immigrant grandparent.

When healthcare, housing assistance, cash payments and other public services were combined, the estimated value exceeded $100,000 annually.

California also promotes tax credits that do not require Social Security numbers, offers subsidized automobile insurance regardless of immigration status and no longer allows its LifeLine phone program to require a Social Security number.

A Los Angeles phone vendor told the reporters that applicants could qualify using a Mexican consular identification card.

California finally froze new comprehensive Medi-Cal enrollment for undocumented adults in January 2026. Existing enrollees were permitted to keep their coverage.

Meanwhile, CMS says it is recouping more than $1.6 billion in federal Medicaid funds from California through voluntary recoveries and deferred payments involving cases with unsatisfactory immigration status.

This election is a referendum on whether California will finally put its own citizens and taxpayers first. Or give Gavin Newsom’s agenda another four years under Xavier Becerra.

Becerra must be defeated.

If you bought a politician's coin, or you're waiting for the next one, this law is about you, and it doesn't do what the headline says.

Here's what happened, in order.

Sunday, Governor Newsom signed Assembly Bill 2409. A meme coin is a token whose price comes from hype, a joke or a famous face, not from a business. The law does two things. California officials can't issue one. And from 2027, crypto platforms can't offer California residents a meme coin launched by a federal, state or local official.

It passed 77 to 0 in the Assembly and 40 to 0 in the Senate. Not one vote against.

Newsom's office pointed at the TRUMP coin: by the reporting it cited, close to a million buyers lost over $3 billion while Trump took roughly $636 million. The White House rejects that its business interests create conflicts.

The reflex: "Politician coins are dead."

Three numbers nobody attached to that sentence.

1. January 1, 2027. The listing ban only covers coins issued on or after that date. Anything launched before stays tradeable. The coin named in the governor's own statement is untouched by the law it inspired.

2. Zero criminal penalty. It's a civil law. The worst outcome for an official who breaks it: a court order to stop, and giving back the profit. No fine on top, no prison.

3. One state's reach. California can't stop a federal official from launching a coin. What it can do is stop platforms from selling that coin to Californians. The lever is the exchange, not the politician.

So this was not the end of politician coins. It was a line drawn at the exchange, starting in 15 months.

Where it actually changes: the federal Clarity Act had its own rules for officials and crypto, including blind trusts. It failed a key Senate vote, so for now this state law is the stronger rule on the books.

What this gives you for the next politician-linked token:

Check the launch date before the headline. Before 2027, no California listing restriction applies.

Check where you buy, not who issued. The restriction hits the platform serving California residents.

Read "banned" as "civil". Profits can be clawed back. Buyers' losses aren't covered by this law.

Reply with a politician-linked coin you've seen, and I'll tell you whether AB 2409 would touch it, for every reply before midnight CET.

text:
Hello Mike,I’m Terry Gross, host of Fresh Air, and I’m reaching out because I was particularly interested in the remarkable range of your work, from the groundbreaking science fiction world of Nexus to your darker novels and the hard-edged crime and motorcycle stories of the Biker series.Your novel, Road Runner: A Noir Mystery, caught my attention because of the unusual combination of a missing teenager, a dangerous cult, organized crime, technology, and a rescue mission that takes Josh Pratt deep into the Colorado Rockies. The story places a reformed motorcycle hoodlum and private investigator in a world where violence, faith, loyalty, technology, and survival collide in complicated ways.I’m especially intrigued by Josh Pratt himself. His history as a motorcycle hoodlum who found God in prison and eventually became a private investigator creates a character whose past is never entirely separate from the person he has become. I’d love to explore what draws you to characters who live in morally complicated worlds, and how you think about redemption, violence, faith, and the possibility of transformation when creating them.Your career also offers a fascinating story of transformation. You broke into comics with Nexus, co-created with Steve Rude, and went on to create or write for a remarkably diverse range of characters and worlds, while also writing journalism, short stories, novels, and graphic fiction. I’d be interested in the experiences and turning points that shaped your movement between these different forms of storytelling and what each medium has taught you about character and narrative.The contrast between the dark subject matter of your work and the humor you bring into many of your stories also interests me. Road Runner contains cult violence, organized crime, kidnapping, and survival, yet your broader work is known for finding humor in bleak and brutal situations. I’d love to explore what humor allows you to do with difficult material that straightforward darkness cannot.I’d also be interested in the way your background in journalism and magazine writing has influenced your fiction. Writing for publications ranging from The Boston Globe and AARP Magazine to Creem and Argosy must have exposed you to very different audiences and subjects. I’m curious about what those experiences taught you about observing people, finding stories, and capturing the details that make fictional worlds feel authentic.Most of all, I’d like to explore the experiences and moments in your life that have had the greatest influence on the way you think about storytelling, redemption, violence, faith, humor, human nature, and the kinds of complicated characters who continue moving forward even when their past refuses to stay behind them.The conversation would be a prerecorded virtual interview. Please let me know if you would be open to participating, and we can discuss a convenient date and time.Warm regards,Terry Gross
Host, Fresh Air

text:
Mary Slusser believed she was saving Nepal's heritage.

She saw a country in the midst of rapid modernisation, and feared that its temples, monuments and sacred objects would be neglected or lost. To take artefacts abroad, under her wing, was to ensure they would be preserved in museums and "cherished for future generations."

But the objects Slusser collected were not the remains of a vanished civilisation. Nepal's gods were still being worshipped. Deities were consecrated and offered food and flowers in rituals performed by particular families or members of a guthi.

The consequences of removing an object extended well beyond the loss of a physical artefact. For ritual objects made from human bone, their disappearance was linked to the loss of the knowledge and practices surrounding their use.

Slusser believed these objects needed to be rescued from Nepal. Our investigation, published earlier this month, asks a harder question: who was rescuing whom, and from what?

Photos:  Slusser’s photographs of ritual regalia carved from human and buffalo bone that she purchased for her collection. In at least one case, the rituals associated with such regalia ceased after it was taken from its original context and custodians. Courtesy of the Mary Slusser Collection, National Museum of Asian Art Archives, Smithsonian Institution

text:
OIL KEPT FALLING AFTER 8AM. STOCK FUTURES GAVE BACK HALF THEIR GAIN ANYWAY:

S&P 500 futures are at 7,755.75, +9.00 pts / +0.12% since Monday's close, with the 9:30am ET opening bell half an hour away. Futures are contracts that trade nearly around the clock and point to where the big indexes may open. Shortly before 8am this one touched 7,770.75, +24.00. U.S. crude has kept sliding since then. The 10-year Treasury yield turned back up, and stock futures have moved with the yield, not with oil.

The verdict for the bell: the oil relief is already in the price and stopped lifting stocks about an hour ago. The number stocks are following into the open is the 10-year yield, and it has spent that hour creeping back toward Monday's close. The first American data able to move it lands at 10am.

The rest of the board, all since Monday's close:
- Nasdaq 100 futures at 30,643.50, +77.25 pts / +0.25%, off a 30,717.75 high after 8:15am
- Dow futures at 51,906.00, +69.00 pts / +0.13%, off a 52,002 high around 8am
- Russell 2000 futures, which track smaller U.S. companies, at 2,844.70, +4.60 pts / +0.16%

Moves made before the opening bell often shrink or reverse by the time regular trading starts. This morning is doing it in real time: roughly half of the gain at this morning's highs is gone, with no new headline and no new data.

The 10-year yield - what the U.S. government pays to borrow for ten years, and the rate mortgages and business loans are priced from - is 5.232%, down 1.0 basis point (hundredths of a percentage point) from Monday's 5.242% close. From about 7:30 to 8:05am it sat at 5.209%, its low of the morning, and stock futures topped within minutes of that low. It has climbed 2.3 basis points since, most of that after 8:35am. The 2-year, the maturity most tied to where traders expect the Federal Reserve to take rates, made the same round trip: near 4.91% at 7:30am, back to 4.924% now, unchanged on the day.

A higher 10-year makes profit a company expects years from now worth less today. That is what hit stocks on Monday, and it is why a move of about two hundredths of a percentage point is worth watching this close to the bell.

Oil went the other way the whole time. U.S. crude (WTI) is at $90.49 a barrel, -$2.11 / -2.28% since Monday's close, down from $91.16 at 8am. Brent, the international benchmark, is at $103.11, -$2.17 / -2.06%. Crude is falling on talk, not on a deal. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said late Monday he expects Washington's formal answer today, through Qatari mediators, to Tehran's plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. President Trump called that plan "unacceptable" on Saturday, and he has denied a report that he offered Iran sanctions relief: "I offered them NOTHING." A flat no today is the headline most able to push oil back up.

The places money runs to when it is scared are quiet. The Cboe Volatility Index - the options market's gauge of how much traders expect stocks to swing over the next month - is at 15.89, -0.18 / -1.12% since Monday's close. Gold is at $4,186.80 an ounce, +$18.40 / +0.44% since Monday's close. The Japanese yen is unchanged at 157.35 per dollar. This is a market pricing what it costs to borrow, not one bracing for a shock.

One stock will open far from all of this, for reasons that have nothing to do with oil or yields. Fair Isaac (FICO) at $840.89, -$22.20 / -2.57% on Monday, and $671.66 premarket, -$169.23 / -20.13% from that close. It sells the FICO score lenders use to decide who gets a loan and at what rate. Monday night, Bill Pulte, director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, said on X that the mortgage pricing his agency controls will move to a single grid that puts VantageScore, a rival credit score, on equal footing with FICO's classic score. He gave no start date and published no new grid. It follows the agency's September 9 decision letting approved lenders use VantageScore 4.0 without asking permission first. Monday's $832 low was already Fair Isaac's lowest price in a year, and the premarket price sits about 66% under its October 2, 2025 high of $1,998.01. Fair Isaac is on none of the six Len5 watchlists, and it fails the Quality Len5 as well: owners' equity - what it owns minus what it owes - was minus $4.1B on June 30, so its debt exceeds it.

What lands after the bell today:
- 10am ET: the Bureau of Labor Statistics' JOLTS report, its count of job openings, for August - 7.23M expected vs 7.27M in July
- 10am ET: the Conference Board's September consumer confidence index, a monthly survey of households by the private business research group - 90.1 expected vs 89.4 in August
- 2pm ET: New York Fed President John Williams on the economic outlook and policy, at the University at Buffalo
- No set time: Washington's answer on Hormuz

The Fed raised its rate on September 16, to 3.75%-4.00%, and meets again October 27-28. Fewer openings and gloomier households would argue against a second increase; stronger readings would argue for one.

Oil fell through the whole last hour and still could not keep the stock bounce alive. The bell rings at 9:30 on a market taking its cue from a 5.23% 10-year, and the first two American numbers able to move that rate arrive half an hour later. If the yield slips back under this morning's 5.209% low, the lost half of the bounce has room to return. If it climbs through Monday's 5.242%, the half that is left is at risk.

Not investment advice.

text:
Here we are, with AI at the nexus of freedom and innovation vs safety and order. In an attempt to rationionalize the fear of AI, I’ve compared AI to other industries such as nuclear weapons, nuclear power, the Aerospace industry but they’re all imperfect comparisons. Maybe autonomous transportation is a better comparison of the risks and benefits of Super Intelligence?

Autonomous transport offers a similar technology based business model, has a similar appeal to mass adoption, similar economic characteristics and shares the risk of killing it’s customers though probably not at an extinction level. The Autonomous Transport products are regulated by existing transportation authority and regulations that are shared between the Federal, State and Local Governments.

Then, risk is indirectly regulated by a robust federal and state product liability framework of statutes and case law. That has worked reasonably well for rolling out robotaxis, so why can’ that work for AI?

Consider the economic impact 'guard rails' on innovation: Slowing down and even stopping new discoveries and new technologies. Not for the world, just for the US. AI is an existential threat to humanity alright, just not the threat the politicians are promoting. It’s the uninformed backlash threat that could ensure the extinction of America’s competitive advantage.

Then there is the ‘Tragedy of the Commons’ dilemma: where individual economic actors (such as Big AI), acting rationally in their own self-interest, release ever more powerful AI models despite the risk of unintended effects that undermine the sustainability of the AI ecosystem.

But maybe Big AI’s call for increased AI regulation is really a push for a Product liability shield (the ‘it wasn’t me’ defense) to fend off perhaps the biggest threat to their massive IPOs? Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996 did just that for Big Tech and is often described as "the 26 words that created the internet", in Section 230(c)(1) which states: "No provider or user of an interactive computer service shall be treated as the publisher or speaker of any information provided by another information content provider." Is Big AI seeking a similar provision for AI models and agents?

The obvious question that follows has to be, if product liability is a key ingredient in protecting society from unsafe products and Big AI leaders such as Dario Amodei (CEO, Anthropic) are saying their products are not safe ("I think there's a 10% to 20% chance that AI goes really wrong, in the sense of human extinction“...) and they need protection, then how can Anthropic and OpenAI raise money to fund a fundamentally unsafe product? It’s oxymoronic and recapitulates the Ludites of the 19th century. It looks to me like Big AI is spiking their own IPOs. Once again, investors should think long and hard about investing in the Anthropic and OpenAI IPOs. https://t.co/ohVLi0gJRB

text:
A lot of commentators don't know the difference between Buran and the Shuttle, and so miss what Energia actually was.

The Shuttle was one integrated system: its main engines sat on the orbiter. Energia carried its own engines and could fly with or without Buran, which made it the most powerful rocket of its time, with up to 100 t to LEO. It was designed with the Moon and Mars in mind.

Its first launch didn't carry Buran at all. The payload was Polyus, an 80 t spacecraft, arguably the largest ever launched. The second and final launch deployed Buran successfully.

Energia was also built with some reusability in mind, with plans to recover its boosters. Despite 1980s tech, a launch cost roughly $2.5B in today's dollars, against about $4B for SLS.

After the USSR collapsed, Energia's chief designer Boris Gubanov flew to the US to offer the rocket for American and international missions. It went nowhere. One of the most powerful rockets of the 20th century was retired and never flew again.
