text:
Lieutenant Fusata Iida (February 11, 1913 – December 7, 1941) was an Imperial Japanese Navy fighter pilot who became famous for his actions during the attack on Pearl Harbor. He was the commander of the 3rd Air Group's fighter squadron aboard the aircraft carrier Sōryū. He is widely remembered as one of the earliest precursors to the kamikaze suicide tactics adopted later in World War II.
During the second wave of the assault on December 7, 1941, Iida led a flight group of nine Mitsubishi A6M2 Zero fighters. Their specific objective was to strike the U.S. Naval Air Station at Kaneohe Bay. This tactical strike was intended to destroy American PBY Catalina long-range reconnaissance seaplanes to disable early scouting capabilities. While strafing the airfield, Iida’s Zero was critically damaged by ground fire. His fuel tank was punctured, primarily due to retaliatory fire from American defense positions—including a .50-caliber machine gun operated by legendary Chief Ordnanceman John William Finn. Realizing he did not have enough fuel to make the return flight to the Sōryū, Iida signaled his wingmen that he was going down. True to a vow he made to his men before takeoff—promising to crash into a "worthy enemy target" if heavily disabled—he maneuvered his failing aircraft to make a suicide run on Hangar 101. He narrowly missed the hangar and crashed instead into a nearby hillside, dying instantly.
Following the crash, U.S. military personnel on the base buried Iida with full military honors out of deep respect for his skill and dedication. A stone marker stands at the crash site on what is now Marine Corps Base Hawaii. It remains one of the few monuments built on an active U.S. military installation dedicated to an enemy combatant. The site serves as a profound symbol of post-war reconciliation. High-ranking officials frequently pay tribute here. Notably, Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe visited the Iida Memorial alongside U.S. officials in December 2016 to lay a wreath and offer a gesture of peace.

text:
First-Ever Adult T. Rex Trackway Discovered After 66.5 Million Years

Scientists have discovered the first known trackway left by a fully grown Tyrannosaurus rex. Found within the Hell Creek Formation near Marmarth in southwestern North Dakota, the 23-foot trail preserves four enormous three-toed footprints. Each measures roughly 3 feet long, providing rare physical evidence of an adult T. rex walking across the landscape 66.5 million years ago.

The trackway consists of two left footprints with two right prints spread across 7 meters of ancient ground. It was discovered on U.S. Forest Service land by Kent Hups, a high school science teacher who volunteers at a museum. Unlike isolated T. rex footprints, multiple consecutive tracks allow researchers to reconstruct how the predator moved during a single moment.

Measurements reveal a stride of 13 feet, which researchers used to estimate the walking speed. The 7-ton T. rex appears to have been traveling around 3.5 to 4.5 miles per hour, comparable to a brisk human walking pace. Those calculations provide scientists with evidence for studying the locomotion of a mature animal rather than relying on skeletal anatomy. 

Three of the four enormous footprints are scheduled to be removed from the site by airlift for further research. They will eventually be displayed at the Denver Museum of Nature & Science, preserving a literal sequence of steps taken near the end of the Cretaceous period. After surviving for approximately 66.5 million years, the tracks offer a rare snapshot of an adult T. rex in motion.

text:
Daniels’s face was carved from granite. “Dispatch received a 911 call regarding individuals attempting to breach a secure residence after being legally notified to vacate.”

“I wasn’t forcing my way in!” Ethan cried, pointing at the cracked door.

“But you are trespassing on private property,” Daniels corrected. “Unless Mrs. Bennett is inviting you in for tea?”

He looked at me. I slowly shook my head.

“We are legally married!” Ethan shouted, his voice cracking in hysteria. “This is a marital asset!”

Daniels sighed, the sigh of a man exhausted by domestic stupidity. “Mr. Bennett, my precinct has already reviewed the deed and the emergency injunction filed this morning. This property is solely titled to the woman standing behind that door. You have zero legal standing to be on this concrete.”

Ethan’s mouth opened and closed like a landed fish. The reality of his utter disenfranchisement finally crushed him. The swagger of the Cancun playboy was dead and buried.

“Load your boxes into the cab,” Officer Ruiz instructed, pointing at the taxi driver who was looking increasingly terrified. “We’ll wait.”

It took them twenty minutes of humiliating, sweaty labor to cram their shattered lives into the trunk and backseat of the taxi under the watchful gaze of the Columbus Police Department.

Before ducking into the cab, Ethan turned back to me one final time. His eyes were dark, filled with a sudden, impotent malice.

“This isn’t over, Olivia.”

I met his gaze through the crack in the door, my voice steady and cold. “I know it’s not. But next time we speak… make sure you bring your lawyer.”

The taxi sped away, tires squealing. I closed the door, slid the deadbolt home, and leaned against the wood. My phone buzzed in my pocket. It was an email from Lauren.
Thirty days later, I walked into the Franklin County Courthouse. The architecture was imposing—vast expanses of gray slate, echoing marble corridors, and the sterile hum of metal detectors. I had been here before as an expert witness, a numbers mechanic hired to explain corporate malfeasance to bored juries.

Today, I was the plaintiff. Today, the malfeasance was mine.

Lauren was waiting outside Courtroom 4B, clad in a razor-sharp charcoal suit, clutching two massive, color-coded trial binders.

“Heart rate?” she asked, assessing my calm demeanor.

“Steady,” I replied, smoothing the skirt of my navy dress.

“Good. Remember the protocol. Do not editorialize. Do not show anger. Answer only what is asked. Let the paper trail hang him.”

We pushed through the heavy oak double doors. Ethan was already seated at the respondent’s table alongside his attorney, Mark Ellison. Ethan wore a bespoke suit I had purchased for our twentieth anniversary. It made me sick to look at it.

Sitting directly behind him in the gallery was Rachel. The last thirty days had not been kind to her. The Cancun tan had faded to a sickly pallor, and dark, exhausted circles framed her eyes. The fantasy of a wealthy, stolen life had crashed into the brutal reality of frozen assets and cheap motels.

Ellison stood and offered Lauren a tight, professional smile. “Morning, Lauren. Hear you’re coming out swinging.”

“I’m just presenting the weather report, Mark,” Lauren replied coolly. “If your client chose to stand in a hurricane, that’s his problem.”….

🔴WAR ON TERRORISM: IRAN 🇮🇷🔴/Israel Hayom/ 

Iran's oil stockpile nears empty as US-led Hormuz blockade holds

Iran's ability to choke oil through strait fades as US Navy and Gulf producers adapt, fueling fears Tehran could escalate militarily to compensate.

"Probably within the next two weeks…they are going to make their final deliveries of oil to China, and then they will have nothing," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday on Fox News.

by  Erez Linn 

Iran's grip on the Strait of Hormuz is slipping, The Wall Street Journal reported, as the US Navy and Gulf producers get better at dodging Iranian attacks.

That shift is eroding Tehran's leverage in talks with Washington and raising fears of a fresh military escalation.

Regional crude exports have rebounded to nearly their highest level since February's war, with Hormuz and bypass routes moving almost 80% of prewar volumes, tracker Kpler found.

Output from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, the UAE and others has climbed to nearly 13 million barrels a day, per ship tracker Huax, while Riyadh has also resumed flows through its repaired East-West pipeline into the Red Sea.

Iran, unable to move oil through Hormuz since July's US blockade, could see its stockpiled reserves run out by mid-October, according to Kpler.

That threatens a key revenue source as sanctions and war strain its economy, weakening its ability to hold energy supplies hostage for concessions even as shrinking income could push it toward renewed attacks.

"It shows the diminishing returns of Iran's Hormuz approach," Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East program at London think tank Chatham House, told The Wall Street Journal.

"That could lead to a more explosive dynamic where they will have to provoke or press the go button on a larger conflict themselves in order to get out of this bind."

Gulf producers worry about fresh strikes as the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps shifts tactics, while Iran has already widened the fight into the Red Sea through its Houthi allies targeting Saudi shipping.

Global markets remain exposed to any disruption, even though the recent export rebound has eased price pressure.

"In the absence of a decisive end to the conflict, the balance of risks to oil prices will remain skewed to the upside," said Hamad Hussain, a senior economist at Capital Economics.

Since the February war, Gulf producers have relied on costly workarounds while Iran's June deal with Trump, promising relief for reopening the strait, collapsed after renewed attacks.

Washington reimposed its blockade in July, and on Friday, Trump rejected a new Iranian ceasefire offer that would have reopened Hormuz for a week.

Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei referenced "the defenders of the Strait of Hormuz" in a Monday statement, signaling Tehran still views the waterway as key leverage.

Bypass routes have also faltered, with drone strikes forcing a shutdown of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and Houthi threats pushing Aramco back toward Hormuz.

Iran has no comparable detour, with trucks capped at roughly 40,000 barrels daily against prewar exports near 2 million.

Its floating crude beyond the blockade has fallen to about 15 million barrels from 29 million in early September, with Kpler expecting China-bound supplies to run dry by mid-October.

"Probably within the next two weeks…they are going to make their final deliveries of oil to China, and then they will have nothing," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday on Fox News.

Attacks in Hormuz appear paused, with the UK Maritime Trade Operations reporting no confirmed incidents in the 72 hours through Sunday, though the threat level stayed severe.

The last recorded strike was Sept. 23, a lull analysts say may reflect Tehran testing Trump's appetite for a deal, according to The Wall Street Journal.

"If Iran's leadership feels its control over Hormuz is weakening, that does increase the risk they will look for other ways to escalate the conflict," Richard Bronze, co-founder and head of geopolitics at Energy Aspects, told the paper.

text:
Still have my "key".

Worked for 44s

Kouta opened the gate slowly.

For a moment, neither of them moved. The clock sounded behind him, its newly awakened mechanism filling the house with an ordinary noise that had become impossible to ignore. Kaede stood with one hand against the frame. Her hair concealed the bandage near her temple, and dust clung to the lower edge of her dress.

He looked at her face, then at the hand she had pressed against the gate.

“Nyu?”

Her fingers tightened around the brass key.

That name offered her a familiar refuge. She could lower her eyes, make the small sound he remembered, and let him bring her inside before the difficult questions began. Somewhere within her, the impulse rose with such tenderness that it almost became an answer.

But Kouta was watching her.

“It’s me,” she said.

He drew a breath and held it.

Kaede saw recognition arrive unevenly: relief first, then the effort to contain it, then memories she had no right to ask him to set aside. His hand remained on the gate. She waited while his gaze moved to the bandage, the dirt beneath her nails, the trembling she could no longer hide.

“Where have you been?”

She glanced down at the key.

“I don’t know how to tell you yet.”

Behind him, Yuka appeared at the end of the passage. She stopped so abruptly that the cloth in her hand swung against her knee.

“Kouta?”

He did not turn.

Kaede could hear the household becoming still. A bowl touched the table. Nana’s chair shifted. Wanta pushed against her ankle, impatient with everyone for leaving her outside.

She bent to touch his head.

The motion nearly brought her to her knees.

Kouta caught her elbow.

Kaede went rigid at the contact. For one terrible instant, she expected the path to fall away and the wood beneath her palm to become the inside of the coffin again. Instead, his fingers tightened just enough to steady her.

“You’re shaking.”

“I know.”

“Can you walk?”

She nodded, although she was no longer certain.

He stayed beside her as she crossed the threshold.

The house received her in small, painful details. The slight change in temperature. The worn place in the floor near the entrance. The smell of lunch. A pair of slippers that someone had left crooked against the wall.

She remembered all of it.

She also remembered lying beneath the earth and trying to remember it.

Yuka moved a cushion into place.

“Sit down before you fall.”

Kaede obeyed. There was something merciful about being given an instruction that concerned only the next few seconds.

Nana stood near the table. Her eyes followed Kaede’s hands, and Kaede placed them openly in her lap. Neither spoke at first.

Then Nana asked, “Are you hurt?”

“Yes.”

The answer seemed to ease something between them. Nana went to fetch a clean cloth, while Mayu brought water and set it within reach. Mayu’s hand lingered beside the cup.

“We kept your place,” she said.

Kaede looked toward the table.

The extra setting was there.

She had spent so long searching for a way into this world that she had never allowed herself to imagine what might be waiting when she arrived.

Kouta sat opposite her.

The music box rested nearby, its lid still open. He reached for it, perhaps from habit, perhaps because neither of them knew where else to put their hands.

Kaede caught her breath.

“Please.”

He stopped.

Her eyes were fixed on the winding mechanism.

“Leave it for now.”

Kouta studied her, then carefully closed the lid.

The small click made her flinch.

Nothing disappeared.

Yuka noticed. She glanced at Kouta, but he gave a slight shake of his head. The questions could wait until Kaede could hold a cup without spilling it.

For several minutes, the clock did most of the talking.

Kaede listened to each tick. She had expected another warning, another missed beat that would mean her borrowed interval was ending. Instead, the pendulum continued at the same patient pace.

text:
I don't understand why people are interpreting what I wrote as Iran going all-in on a scorched-earth approach. Strikes can be calibrated. This is exactly how the East-West Pipeline was recently hit without Saudi Arabia targeting comparable Iranian facilities in response. It is how Abqaiq and Khurais were hit in September 2019. These are not large desalination plants, which, if damaged, let alone destroyed, pose something of an existential threat. Taking parts of Abqaiq or Ras Tanura offline for several weeks to several months is unlikely to result in Saudi Arabia suddenly becoming uber-aggressive in the manner of Israel and making the most of supposed escalation dominance over Iran. 

Saudi Arabia's ability to retaliate in kind has never been in question. The Saudi Air Force has more than enough standoff munitions to lay waste to Asaluyeh, for example. The problem that Saudi Arabia faces is the "then what" question. How many strike munitions does Iran have left? What if Saudi retaliatory strikes do not end the cycle of escalation but only make the situation worse for Saudi Arabia by unleashing even less restrained Iranian strikes? Saudi and Gulf Arabia stocks of air and ballistic missile defences are not unlimited and appear to be severely depleted. Furthermore, capabilities are only part of the equation. Risk appetite and the appetite to sustain losses are a big part of the equation. Riyadh's conduct in recent weeks does not offer any indication of a confident Saudi Arabia that is willing to retaliate in kind and risk further escalation. That is neither nothing nor a new dynamic—refer to September 2019.

text:
THE TERROR ALWAYS ARRIVES WEARING THE COSTUME OF VIRTUE

FROM PARIS TO PETROGRAD TO PHNOM PENH, THE SAME REVOLUTIONARY SCRIPT KEEPS PRODUCING THE SAME BLOODY THIRD ACT

FN: Historians have spent two centuries treating 1789 as a singular catastrophe, a uniquely French descent from liberty into the guillotine, when it would be more useful, and considerably more alarming, to treat it as the opening case study in a pattern that has since repeated itself with almost mechanical regularity. What makes the French experience instructive is not its uniqueness but its transferability. Strip away the powdered wigs and the Committee of Public Safety and what remains is a reproducible sequence: a genuine grievance against an unjust order, a totalising ideology promising perfect equality, a vanguard that decides who counts as sufficiently virtuous, and finally a machinery of denunciation that consumes moderates before it consumes anyone else. This sequence has since been run, with local variations, in Russia, in China, in Cambodia, and in smaller, less lethal but structurally identical episodes across the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.

Consider the Bolsheviks, who studied the French Revolution as a kind of instruction manual and improved upon its worst features rather than learning from them. Lenin's Cheka performed the same function as Robespierre's Revolutionary Tribunal, only with greater administrative efficiency and a much larger population to work through. The kulaks occupied the structural position the French aristocracy had occupied a century earlier, a class defined into existence primarily so that its liquidation could serve as proof of revolutionary seriousness. Stalin's subsequent purges, in which yesterday's most zealous Bolsheviks were denounced as wreckers and saboteurs by the very apparatus they had built, reproduced almost exactly the Jacobin habit of devouring insufficiently enthusiastic revolutionaries, up to and including men who had until recently been denouncing others for the identical offence.

Mao's Cultural Revolution offers perhaps the starkest twentieth-century replay of the pattern, precisely because it stripped the process down to its psychological essentials. Red Guards, mostly teenagers granted sudden and intoxicating moral authority, denounced teachers, parents, and Communist Party officials alike for insufficient revolutionary fervor, an echo of the Law of Suspects so exact it barely required updating. The demand was never simply for compliance but for demonstrated enthusiasm, for the public performance of ideological purity, because mere obedience always looks suspiciously like private disagreement waiting for its moment. Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge, drawing explicitly on both French and Maoist precedent, pushed the logic to its most literal extreme, treating spectacles, eyeglasses, and soft hands as evidence of counter-revolutionary corruption, executing citizens for displaying the physical markers of the old order rather than for anything they had actually done.

What unites these episodes, separated by continents, languages and a century and a half, is not merely violence but the particular logic that converts an egalitarian ideal into a justification for that violence. Equality before the law is a manageable, historically achievable political goal. Equality of outcome, virtue, or ideological conviction is not, and the gap between the two is precisely where the terror takes root. Once a revolutionary movement commits itself to producing not equal rights but equal righteousness, it requires a permanent enforcement mechanism, because righteousness, unlike a legal right, can always be found wanting in someone. The French Revolutionary Tribunal, the Cheka, the Red Guards and the Khmer Rouge cadres were not aberrations from their founding ideals; they were the ideals' logical administrative apparatus, the inevitable bureaucracy required once perfect virtue becomes state policy.

None of this argues against equality as a political value, only against the specific historical mechanism by which demands for equality metastasize into demands for submission. The warning embedded in 1789, and reconfirmed with grim consistency in 1917, 1966 and 1975, is that the distance between an idealistic slogan and its totalitarian enforcement is measured not in decades but in the willingness of ordinary people to denounce their neighbours for insufficient enthusiasm. Every generation that imagines itself uniquely immune to this dynamic, because its own cause is self-evidently just, is repeating the exact conviction that animated the men who sent Danton, Lenin's own comrades, and half the population of Democratic Kampuchea to their deaths. History does not forbid the pursuit of equality. It simply insists, with considerable evidence, on how that pursuit tends to end once it forgets the difference between a right and a virtue test.

A member of her state’s advisory committee to the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights, Damron is also a @FreeConTalk signatory.

In a recent piece for the SC Daily Gazette, she explained that the Securities and Exchange Commission’s restrictions on accredited investing bars Americans from private markets — including venture capital, angel investments, and startup equity — unless they have a net worth above $1 million or annual income above $200,000.

Almost two million of her state’s 2.1 million households “are locked out entirely — even as venture capital firms have closed over $1.8 billion in South Carolina deals between 2018 and 2023,” Damron wrote with coauthor Nicholas Morgan. “The opportunity is flourishing here. Most South Carolinians simply are not allowed to access it.”

This “federal wealth gate” controls even those seeking to claim state tax breaks such as those South Carolina offers.

“A Boeing engineer in North Charleston or a Medical University of South Carolina researcher in the Charleston Medical District — people who understand local industries better than any Wall Street analyst — could not use South Carolina’s tax code to back a local startup unless they first clear Washington’s arbitrary net worth hurdle.” #FreeCon

text:
THE ORIGIN OF FREE WILL THEOLOGY

Part 1: How Man’s Autonomy Replaced God’s Sovereignty

“You thought that I was one like yourself.”
Psalm 50:21
There is perhaps no theological assumption more deeply woven into modern evangelicalism than the belief that the decisive factor in salvation is the autonomous choice of the sinner. We are repeatedly told that God has done everything He can do, Christ has made salvation available to everyone, grace has been extended equally and now the final question rests upon the sinner: What will you choose? It sounds humble because it speaks constantly about human responsibility. It sounds fair because it appears to protect God from difficult questions about election, judgment and sovereignty. 

But there is a question we must ask before accepting the framework: Does Scripture actually present fallen man as spiritually capable of making the decisive move toward God? The Bible does not describe the sinner as a spiritually neutral person standing between God and Satan with an untouched will, calmly deciding which kingdom he prefers. Scripture describes fallen humanity as alienated from God, enslaved to sin, hostile to God, darkened in understanding and dead in trespasses and sins. The issue then, is not whether man has a will. He does. The issue is whether that will, after the Fall, is spiritually free from the corruption of sin and capable of choosing God apart from God first giving life. That distinction changes everything.

THE SERPENT’S WHISPER: THE FIRST ASSAULT ON GOD’S AUTHORITY

The impulse toward human autonomy did not begin in a theological classroom. Its first recorded expression appears in Eden. The serpent did not merely tempt Eve to eat forbidden fruit. He attacked the character and authority of God. “You will not surely die,” he said. “For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:4–5). Notice what is happening. God had spoken. The creature was called to trust the Creator, receive His Word and live under His authority. 
The serpent introduced another possibility: You do not have to receive reality from God. You can determine it for yourself. The temptation was not merely appetite. It was autonomy. Eve was invited to judge God’s command by her own perception, desire and reasoning. She saw that the tree was good for food, a delight to the eyes and desirable to make one wise and she took and ate (Genesis 3:6). The creature placed her own judgment above the revealed Word of the Creator. That was rebellion disguised as liberty.

But we must be precise here. Eden was not the historical beginning of the formal theological systems later called Pelagianism, Semi Pelagianism or Arminianism. Those developed many centuries later. What began in Eden was something deeper: the recurring human desire to determine good apart from God, to place the creature’s judgment above the Creator’s Word and to imagine that life can be secured through independence from God. Scripture continues to expose this impulse throughout redemptive history. “The way of a fool is right in his own eyes” (Proverbs 12:15). “There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death” (Proverbs 14:12). Isaiah declares, “All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned, every one, to his own way” (Isaiah 53:6). Paul later describes fallen humanity as those who “exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:25). The biblical problem is therefore larger than the word “free will.” It is the elevation of the creature’s judgment above the Creator’s authority.

MAN HAS A WILL, BUT HE IS NOT AUTONOMOUS

One of the most important distinctions in this entire discussion is this: the Bible never teaches that man is without a will. It teaches that man’s will is fallen. A sinner chooses willingly. He is not dragged against his desires into sin. The problem is that his desires themselves have been corrupted. Jesus said, “For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery” (Mark 7:21). He did not describe sin as merely an external force acting upon an otherwise neutral human heart. Sin proceeds from within. Jeremiah asks, “Can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard his spots? Then also you can do good who are accustomed to do evil” (Jeremiah 13:23). Paul says that “the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot” (Romans 8:7). That is moral inability, not the absence of choice. The sinner can choose many things. What he cannot do, apart from regenerating grace, is make himself love God, submit to God and come to Christ from a heart that remains spiritually dead and hostile toward God.

This is why Ephesians 2:1 does not merely say that sinners are spiritually sick. It says, “And you were dead in the trespasses and sins.” Paul continues by saying that we once lived according to the course of this world and according to the prince of the power of the air, “among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the body and the mind” (Ephesians 2:2–3). Notice that the sinner is acting according to his desires. He is willing. Yet he is also enslaved. Jesus says, “Everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin” (John 8:34). Paul describes fallen humanity as slaves to sin (Romans 6:17, 20). The natural man, according to 1 Corinthians 2:14, “does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned.” Scripture therefore gives us no picture of autonomous man standing spiritually neutral before God. It gives us a picture of a willing sinner who loves darkness, follows his desires, suppresses truth and remains unable to come to God unless God intervenes.

THE TESTIMONY OF SCRIPTURE: NO ONE SEEKS GOD

Paul removes every illusion of spiritual neutrality in Romans 3. “None is righteous, no, not one; no one understands; no one seeks for God” (Romans 3:10–11). He continues, “All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one” (Romans 3:12). This is not describing a small defect in human spirituality. It is a comprehensive diagnosis of fallen humanity. The natural man does not merely need better information. He needs a new heart. He does not merely need encouragement to make a better decision. He needs resurrection.

Jesus speaks with the same clarity. “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). The word “can” matters. Christ is not saying merely that people generally do not come. He says they cannot come unless the Father draws them. Later He says, “No one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father” (John 6:65). If fallen man possesses an autonomous spiritual ability to initiate salvation, these statements become extremely difficult to reconcile with the words of Christ Himself. Jesus does not tell Nicodemus that he simply needs to exercise his free will more decisively. He tells him, “Unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:3). New birth precedes spiritual sight. God does not wait for the spiritually dead to resurrect themselves before He gives them life. He gives life, and those given life come.

That is why the language of Scripture is so forceful. God “made us alive together with Christ” (Ephesians 2:5). God “raised us up with him” (Ephesians 2:6). God “made us alive” when we were dead (Colossians 2:13). Ezekiel 36:26 speaks of God removing the heart of stone and giving a heart of flesh. Jeremiah 31:33 speaks of God writing His law upon the hearts of His people. John 1:13 says that those who receive Christ and believe in His name are born “not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God.” That last phrase should stop us in our tracks. Salvation is not ultimately traced to human will as its decisive source. It is traced to God. Faith is real. Repentance is real. The sinner truly comes to Christ. But behind that coming is the sovereign grace of God who gives life to the dead, opens blind eyes, removes hearts of stone and brings His people willingly to Christ.

WHEN THE WILL OF MAN BECOMES THE FINAL AUTHORITY

This is where free will theology, in many of its forms, moves beyond affirming human responsibility and begins to make human autonomy the decisive factor in salvation. Historically, the discussion developed in different forms. Pelagianism, associated with Pelagius in the fifth century, denied the Augustinian understanding of original sin and human inability and placed far greater emphasis on humanity’s natural moral ability. Semi Pelagianism later maintained that the first movement toward God could originate in fallen humanity, with divine grace assisting afterward. Centuries later, Jacob Arminius and the Remonstrant tradition developed a different framework, affirming human responsibility while rejecting unconditional election and irresistible grace as understood in the Reformed tradition. Arminian theology also developed the doctrine of prevenient grace to explain how fallen sinners can respond to the gospel. These systems are not identical and they should not be carelessly collapsed into one category. But the central question remains the same: What is the decisive cause of a sinner’s salvation?

If the final distinction between the saved and the lost rests upon something originating ultimately in the sinner rather than upon God’s sovereign grace, then salvation has been made dependent upon the creature at the point where Scripture repeatedly directs our eyes to the Creator. Romans 9:16 says, “So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy.” Ephesians 1:4–5 says that God chose His people in Christ “before the foundation of the world” and “predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will.” Jesus says, “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16). Paul says that God saved us and called us “not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace” (2 Timothy 1:9). The biblical pattern is not God making salvation possible and then waiting to discover what man will decide. It is God purposing salvation, accomplishing redemption in Christ, calling His people through the gospel, giving them life, granting repentance and faith, and preserving them to the end.

THE GOLDEN CALF OF HUMAN AUTONOMY

When the human will becomes the decisive explanation for why one sinner believes while another, equally fallen sinner, does not, the question Paul asks in 1 Corinthians 4:7 becomes unavoidable: “What do you have that you did not receive?” If the decisive difference ultimately originated in man, then why should man boast? Yet Scripture repeatedly destroys boasting at the very foundation of salvation. “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8). Paul immediately explains the purpose: “so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:9). Salvation belongs to the Lord (Jonah 2:9). From beginning to end, grace leaves the redeemed with no grounds for boasting except in Christ.

This does not mean that God does not command all people everywhere to repent. He does. Acts 17:30 says, “God commands all people everywhere to repent.” It does not mean the gospel should not be preached indiscriminately. It must be. Christ commands His church to proclaim the gospel to all nations (Matthew 28:19–20). It does not mean sinners are not responsible for rejecting Christ. They are. Jesus says, “You refuse to come to me that you may have life” (John 5:40). Their refusal is willing, culpable, and sinful. But Scripture does not require us to make human autonomy the explanation for why some believe. Instead, it gives glory to sovereign grace. When Lydia heard Paul preach, “the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul” (Acts 16:14). When the Gentiles heard the gospel in Acts 13, “as many as were appointed to eternal life believed” (Acts 13:48). God’s sovereign work does not destroy human responsibility. It is precisely what makes the sinner’s willing response possible.

THE CROSS WAS NOT A CONTINGENCY PLAN

The deepest problem with making autonomous human choice the decisive factor is that it can subtly transform the accomplishment of Christ into a mere possibility awaiting human activation. Scripture speaks far more strongly about the cross. Jesus did not die merely to create an opportunity for salvation. He came “to save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). He said that the Good Shepherd “lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). He declared that He gives eternal life to His sheep and that they “will never perish” (John 10:28). Paul says that Christ “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). Revelation 5:9 celebrates Christ because He “ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation.” Isaiah 53:10 says that the suffering Servant would see His offspring and that “the will of the LORD shall prosper in his hand.” At the cross, Christ cried, “It is finished” (John 19:30). Redemption was accomplished, not merely proposed.

The gospel therefore does not present a helpless God standing outside the door of the sinner’s heart, hoping that autonomous humanity will permit Him to save. Scripture presents the Triune God accomplishing redemption according to His eternal purpose. The Father chose His people in Christ. The Son purchased redemption by His blood. The Holy Spirit applies that redemption by giving life, granting faith, sanctifying and sealing believers for the day of redemption. Salvation is not a divine offer followed by an autonomous human contribution that makes the difference. It is grace from beginning to end. Even faith itself is not a ground for boasting, because the ability to believe does not arise from an autonomous heart that somehow escaped the Fall. God grants repentance (2 Timothy 2:25), God grants faith (Philippians 1:29) and God opens hearts (Acts 16:14). The sinner believes, but the glory belongs to the God who gave him the ability and desire to believe.

THE SOVEREIGN GOD OF SCRIPTURE

The Bible does not present God as a passive observer waiting to discover what His creatures will decide. “Our God is in the heavens; he does whatever he pleases” (Psalm 115:3). “Whatever the LORD pleases, he does, in heaven and on earth” (Psalm 135:6). Isaiah records God saying, “I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like me” (Isaiah 46:9). He declares that His counsel shall stand and that He will accomplish all His purpose (Isaiah 46:10). Nebuchadnezzar learned the same lesson when he confessed that God “does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and none can stay his hand or say to him, ‘What have you done?’” (Daniel 4:35).

Romans 9 brings this sovereignty directly into the discussion of salvation. Paul asks, “So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills” (Romans 9:18). When the human mind objects, Paul does not place God in the courtroom and ask Him to justify Himself according to human standards. He asks, “But who are you, O man, to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20). The point is not that God is unjust. Paul has already declared, “There is no injustice with God, is there? By no means!” (Romans 9:14). The point is that the creature does not sit in judgment over the Creator. We begin with God’s revelation rather than demanding that God conform Himself to our philosophical expectations of fairness.

THE GOLDEN CHAIN OF SOVEREIGN GRACE

Now consider the breath-taking simplicity of Romans 8:29–30. “Those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son; and those whom he predestined he also called; and those whom he called he also justified; and those whom he justified he also glorified.” Paul does not place autonomous human decision between predestination and calling, or between calling and justification. The entire movement is presented as God’s saving work. The same God who predestines calls. The God who calls justifies. The God who justifies glorifies. The chain ends in certainty because its foundation is God’s purpose, not man’s fluctuating will.

And yet this sovereign grace does not make evangelism unnecessary. It makes evangelism hopeful. Paul preached because God had His people in Corinth (Acts 18:9–10). He endured suffering “for the sake of the elect” so that they might obtain salvation in Christ (2 Timothy 2:10). We preach because God uses the proclamation of the gospel as the means by which He calls His people. “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17). The sovereign God ordains both the end and the means. He ordains salvation and He ordains the preaching through which sinners hear the gospel. He ordains the new birth, and He uses the Word of truth in bringing it about (James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:23).

LET GOD BE GOD

The real issue, then, is not whether man makes choices. Of course he does. The issue is whether fallen man is autonomous before God, spiritually neutral and capable of initiating his own reconciliation with his Creator. Scripture gives no such picture. Man chooses according to his nature. Before grace, that nature is enslaved to sin. The sinner needs more than an invitation. He needs regeneration. He needs mercy. He needs the Father to draw him, the Son to redeem him and the Spirit to give him life. And when that grace comes, the sinner does not become less human. He becomes willing to come to Christ.

This is why the gospel leaves no room for boasting in the will of man. “It depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy” (Romans 9:16). “Salvation belongs to the LORD” (Jonah 2:9). “From him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever” (Romans 11:36). The biblical gospel does not place man on the throne and God beside him as an assistant. It brings the sinner to the dust and lifts his eyes to the throne of grace. It tells the spiritually dead that God gives life, the blind that God gives sight, the rebel that God gives repentance and the guilty that Christ has accomplished redemption.

The question is therefore not, “How much freedom can we preserve for man?” The better question is, “How much glory does Scripture give to God?” And when we follow the biblical trail from Genesis to Revelation, the answer is overwhelming. God is not waiting for man to make Him sovereign. He is sovereign already. God is not waiting for man to authorize grace. He gives grace. God is not waiting for the dead to make themselves alive. He raises the dead.

Let God be God.

And let the church once again confess what Scripture has never stopped declaring:
“Salvation belongs to the LORD.”
Jonah 2:9

Truth does not bow to the age. It stands. And so will those who stand with Christ.

text:
A traditional real estate agent asked me what I do.

I normally say I'm a stay at home dad that prospects & sends out referrals.

Got to thinkin' about it & that info is correct but it doesn't really help a traditional agent in their business, unless they're perceptive enough to say, "Well if you want to send some referrals my way..."

So inspiration struck and I think this is going to be my new response:

What do I do? I'm the guy you call when you need to get out of a jam.

I'm the guy you call when you have a seller who wants an elevated price & you need a buyer who can find a way to overpay.

I'm the guy you call when you have a buyer who has a taste for $3M properties but has a $2M budget & you need a seller who would sell at a discount.

I'm the guy you call when you're negotiating a deal, the parties are close but they can't agree on price & you need a way to fill the gap.

I'm the guy you call when your seller tells you they need an offer this week or they're canceling the listing, so you need to get an offer fast.

I'm the guy you call when your buyer won't qualify for a traditional mortgage & you somehow need to get them into a house in a way that makes sense.

I'm the guy you call when your seller has minimal equity, no cash flow & you somehow need to get them out from under the property in a way that makes sense.

I'm the guy you call when your seller has a house retail buyers won't touch & you need a buyer who is looking for a house just like that.

I'm the guy you call when you have a client to refer or even a deal you personally want to buy or sell in a new market & you need a top agent there to run the deal. 

I'm the guy you call when your seller needs to close urgently, there's no time for a traditional listing & you need a buyer who can do a deal at lighting speed.

I'm the guy you call when your seller has a ton of equity, wants to sell but if they do they could be looking at a tax bill that makes their eyes water & you need a professional to show them ways to structure the deal properly so that if their eyes do water it's from tears of joy.

I'm the guy you call when your seller is open-minded, motivated and collaborative but their commercial deal is covered in hair and you need a counterparty with a good set of scissors to help everyone see straight.

I'm the guy you call when you're new in the business, super motivated to crush it but find yourself constantly in search of a path to success and you need an environment where you can get traction, clarity and a game plan to start booking some wins.

I'm the guy you call when you've been in the business a while, are racking up closings but feel like you're the only one in your office actively pursuing greatness and you've discovered you crave an environment where you're surrounded by agents just as fired up as you who set greatness as the standard, pursue it daily and joyfully help each other achieve their maximum potential.

I'm the guy you call when you're an elite producer, business running at full blast but ultimately feel like your business is running you and you've discovered you crave an environment where you can take back control of your time to be the parent/spouse/friend you know you can be, pursue passions that you've been itching to indulge and maybe even see a path to retire or at least go on a vacation without being glued to your phone the whole time.

Now, if we could we solve these problems 100% of the time...I'd already be living on a private island watching dolphins splash in the ocean as I enjoyed the sunrise each morning. I don't.

But we can solve them often enough where I like your chances to pick up a closing here and there that you'd have pretty long odds of gettin' otherwise...and maybe even find yourself building a business that gets you closer to the one that makes you genuinely happy.

Goal: Have them say, "Bro, I'm putting you in my phone right now as Real Estate 911, this is crazy!"

That's mission accomplished.

text:
☝️👇 Geese preservation / 2

“ Unfortunately, I cannot do more here than give the substance of Dr. Lowe’s most able, though disquieting report. He points out that, since the introduction of cold-storage, enormous numbers of ducks, amounting to millions of birds, are now brought into this country during October, November, and December, and kept till after the close-season for the taking of these birds in this country has begun, when they are put upon the market. But besides these, widgeon, pintail, and other species are taken in huge numbers on their return northwards to their breeding grounds. It is this depletion of the breeding stock on the breeding grounds of the Baltic basin, Sweden, Finland, Lapland, and the northern Tundras, which is most feared by Dr. Lönnberg. They are brought to-day from as far east as Lake Baikal. Though they retreat to the uttermost ends of the earth, there is now no sanctuary which will protect them from the hand of the destroyer.

In this country, during the winter months, they were taken in the old days in tens of thousands, in duck-decoys; while the punt-gunner, with his enormous swivel-gun, slew his thousands. But he had to endure considerable hardship in the pursuit of his sport. The punt-gunner of to-day uses a motor-punt. The sportsman in Egypt was content, years ago, to take what chance threw in his way on a single lake. To-day the birds are harried from one lake to another in motor-cars! Before it is too late we must reverse the process. From intensive slaughter we must pass to intensive preservation, if we are to save the remnant left to us.

They do these things better in America. There, no ducks of any kind, save domesticated ducks, may be offered for sale. This law was enacted just because exactly the same danger of extermination was threatening their wild ducks. What was the result? The Department of Economic Ornithology made an intensive study of the food and habits of wild duck, created reservations stocked with their favourite food, and issued restricted licenses to shoot. The spoils may be given away, but they may not be sold. As a consequence, the stock of birds is now enormous.

At home we still follow the wasteful and unsportsmanlike practice of “flapper-shooting”—that is to say, we deliberately wipe out the results of the year’s harvest of young birds. Folly and “sport” often go hand in hand. Yet, thanks to the protection afforded to birds on large estates, our stock of home-bred birds is at least holding its own. Some species have increased their range, and some have materially increased their numbers, as in the case of the tufted duck, for example.

Whatever legislation is effected, it will not decrease the spoils of the sportsman who uses the shoulder-gun only, but, on the contrary, it will bring about, in the near future, a material increase in the size of his “bag.” As soon as he realises this, we shall have him, a valuable ally, on our side. And what is more, I feel quite sure that the wholesale poultry trade will lend their aid, as soon as the actual position has been explained to them. When ducks cease to glut the market, prices will be higher and the supply will be assured. If the present rate of slaughter continues, in a year or two there will be no ducks to sell.”
(Source: ILN, 1926, September 25.)

text:
Oh brother you liberals have the emotions of toddler…

There were 2 trials and due to the
Lack of evidence the first trial was a hung jury.   The victim refused to testify for the second trial, and it was the judge who sentenced the guy to only 60 days.

None of this is Ken Paxton’s fault. None! The sooner you people stop blaming others for your own problems, the better!

The core accusation is that Ken Paxton’s office gave Waco attorney Adam Hoffman an unduly lenient “sweetheart deal” after he was charged with continuous sexual abuse of a child. That charge is a first-degree felony that can carry 25 years to life. Hoffman instead pleaded to two Class A misdemeanors, served roughly 29 days of a 60-day jail sentence, did not have to register as a sex offender in Texas, and kept the option of practicing law after a temporary surrender.

Prosecutors from Paxton’s office have said the outcome was constrained by the evidence they actually had. The first trial ended in a hung jury. The child victim then made clear he would not testify again. Without that testimony, they said they had no realistic path to prove the felony elements. They therefore took a guilty plea to lesser offenses that included an admission of sexual contact without consent, some jail time, a lifetime no-contact order, and surrender of Hoffman’s law license. They argued that forcing the child back onto the stand would have re-traumatized him.

The 60-day sentence itself was set by the judge, not the original plea offer. Early release after 29 days followed standard McLennan County good-time credits. Critics, including the victim’s mother and some Republican lawmakers, contend prosecutors leaned on the child’s reluctance to close the case quickly and that the result was still far too light given the original allegations. Fact-checkers have generally treated the “lenient deal” description as accurate while noting the hung-jury and victim-testimony context that prosecutors cite.

Paxton’s recent remark that Hoffman “served 60 days” is therefore incomplete; the time actually served was about half that. The disagreement is less about whether the sentence was short and more about whether prosecutors had a better option once the victim refused a second trial.

text:
An Open Letter to Anyone With a Voice Big Enough to Matter
To those who can be heard when others cannot:

Please help save Sergeant Snuggles.

Snuggles is a young Anatolian Shepherd—a livestock guardian—who belongs to a veteran family in Pima County, Arizona. In October 2025, on his own property, he bit a family member during a moment of extreme stress: a female dog in heat, coyotes nearby, days of agitation, and a startle from behind. It was his first bite. The family member recovered. She has since said, in her own words, that he did not “attack” her, that he stopped when he recognized her, and that she wants him home.
A court still ordered him destroyed. Pima Animal Care Center has held him ever since. He has now spent nearly a year in a kennel. County medical records document repeated “shelter stress.” His family has posted bond, paid thousands in boarding fees, offered stronger fencing, professional behavior work, and even transfer to a qualified sanctuary. They have asked only that he not be killed while those options exist.
Mercy is not the same as pretending a bite never happened. It is choosing the least irreversible path when the person who was hurt is asking for his life, when the dog has no prior history, and when a working guardian breed did what that breed is wired to do under the wrong conditions. Death cannot be undone. A second chance, with conditions, can.
If you have a platform, use it. Share his name. Ask why a first-incident dog is still locked away nearly a year later while his family begs for a humane alternative. Ask Pima County officials to allow transfer to a sanctuary or return under strict safeguards instead of carrying out a death sentence the family and the injured relative oppose.
Snuggles cannot speak. The people who love him have nearly exhausted their money and their legal options. What they still have is the hope that someone with a louder voice will refuse to look away.

Please help bring Sergeant Snuggles home.
#FreeSnugglesNow
#SaveSnuggles

Petition: https://t.co/KGh9P7zFC9
Legal filings and updates are public in Evancho v. City of Tucson / Pima County, U.S. District Court, District of Arizona.
With respect and urgency,
A friend of a family that only wants their dog back.

My name is Alisha Carothers. Before you decide who I am from one post, I’d like to tell you a little of my story. ❤️

If my words have ever come out scattered or I’ve tried to explain too much at once, I’m sorry. I’m trying to put years of experiences, a lot of heart, and a dream for helping people into words. I’m not embarrassed by my story, and I’m ready to share it.

I started working in a prison in 2008. I worked there until 2016 and returned in 2021. I’ve cared for people convicted of terrible harm and met people carrying pain most of us never see. Those years changed how I understand safety, trust, accountability, and what it takes for someone to begin again.

I also live with PTSD and generalized anxiety disorder. Loud noises, crowds, and several people talking while I’m trying to listen can overwhelm me. Sometimes a public place feels impossible, even when I want to be there. My experiences have made me cautious; I usually need to meet someone myself before trust can grow. A little patience and a quieter place to talk can mean more than you know.

I live with diabetes, too. Managing my blood sugar and getting the medicine I need is part of my everyday life. When I don’t feel well, I can feel nauseated or struggle to think clearly. I’m sharing that because some of what I carry isn’t visible.

And still, I’ve felt drawn to people in places others might walk past. One night, I sat on Sixth Street in Austin with a group of men experiencing homelessness until the sun came up. I had no shoes, phone, or money. They told me I was “the prettiest and craziest white girl” they had ever met—and yes, that still makes me laugh. What I remember most is that we spent the night talking.

I’ve been present during frightening moments, including a drive-by shooting. Afterward, I sat on a gas station sidewalk talking with a man who had also been in prison. In Las Vegas, I met another man who told me about his twin daughters. As we talked, we realized he had once been on a unit where I worked. He was short on the balance for his hotel room, so I paid it. I still remember his face lighting up.

Pyrex, if this ever reaches you: I’ve worried about you since I left Houston. I pray you’re okay. You have not been forgotten.

I’m telling you these things because SAVEM 4 LIFE grew out of what I’ve lived and witnessed. SAVEM began as the Sexual Abuse Victims Education Movement. Protecting and educating people about sexual abuse remains close to my heart. My hope has grown to include survivors, children, families, people leaving prison, and anyone who feels unseen or needs help finding a way forward.

Dream • Heal • Protect • Inspire.
One patient. One child. One family. One act of kindness at a time.

I’m studying nursing and working to turn this vision into real help. I need people who can offer guidance, trustworthy resources, connections, opportunities, or a willingness to listen and share this story. I don’t have every answer, and I can’t build everything alone.

I want the world to hear my story because someone out there may recognize a piece of their own in it. If that’s you, please know this: you matter. Your life is more than the hardest thing you’ve faced.

With love,
Alisha | SAVEM 4 LIFE ❤️

text: Trailblazing Hattie McDaniel was the 13th child born to former slaves in Wichita, Kansas in 1893. She rose from dire poverty and, after working her way through vaudeville and bit parts in Hollywood, she made history as the first African American to win an Oscar, for her powerful performance in Gone with the Wind (1939). Unfortunately, after accepting the award, Hattie was forced to return to her table far away from the rest of the cast in the back of the room. The ceremony was held at the Ambassador Hotel, which had a whites-only policy, and producer David O. Selznick had to beg the hotel to let McDaniel attend. Even after her historic win, Hollywood only offered her stereotypical roles and though she was criticized for accepting them, she was frank about the limitations that existed in the Jim Crow Era. “I'd rather play a maid and make $700 a week," she said, "than be a maid and make $7.” Off-screen however, Hattie was able to do more to fight racism. In 1945, she galvanized her Black neighbors in West Adams Heights to fight eviction from their homes caused by restrictions banning Black people from living in certain districts. The battle went to court, where the race restrictions were ruled unconstitutional. Two years later she made history again, becoming the first African American actress to star in her own radio show when she took the title role of Beulah (who was previously played by a white male). She was cast in the TV version of Beulah but shot only six episodes before becoming ill with breast cancer. She passed away on October 26, 1952. Her wish to be buried at Hollywood Cemetery (now known as Hollywood Forever) was denied because of racism. She was buried instead at Angelus-Rosedale Cemetery. On the 47th anniversary of her death, Hollywood Forever unveiled a 4 foot tall pink granite cenotaph for her with the words “To Honor Her Last Wish” and included a quote from McDaniel’s grand-nephew: “Aunt Hattie, you are a credit to your craft, your race, and to your family.” As for her Oscar—it’s missing. Hattie left it to Howard University, and it was last seen in 1972. #oscars

Raymond LOUIS Heenan (November 1, 1944 – September 17, 2017) was an American professional wrestling manager, color commentator, and wrestler. He performed with the American Wrestling Association (AWA), the World Wrestling Federation (WWF, now WWE) and World Championship Wrestling (WCW) under the ring name Bobby "The Brain" Heenan.

Heenan was known for his skill in elevating villainous on-screen talent by drawing negative reactions for himself and his wrestlers from the crowd. He was paired with numerous wrestlers, including Nick Bockwinkel, whom he led to win the AWA World Heavyweight Championship, and he became an integral figure in the 1980s professional wrestling boom by managing King Kong Bundy and André the Giant in WWF main event matches with Hulk Hogan at WrestleMania 2 and WrestleMania III respectively. The wrestlers under his tutelage were collectively known as "The Heenan Family" at various times throughout his career.

Known for his quick wit and comedic ability, Heenan also served as a color commentator and is remembered for his on-screen repartee with Gorilla Monsoon. Outside of wrestling, Heenan authored two books, appeared on numerous television shows, and briefly hosted a parody talk show titled The Bobby Heenan Show on WWF Prime Time Wrestling. Heenan retired in 2001 at WrestleMania X-Seven after a seventeen-year stint as a commentator in professional wrestling but he continued to make sporadic appearances in several promotions. In 2002, he was diagnosed with throat cancer, which limited his appearances in later years, and died from complications of the disease in 2017. Among other honors, he has been inducted into the Professional Wrestling, WWE, and Wrestling Observer halls of fame. Multiple wrestling commentators have described him as the greatest professional wrestling manager of all time.

Early life
Heenan was born in Chicago, Illinois, on November 1, 1944.[5][6][1] His father Robert Heenan was a railroad worker, and his mother Mildred Bernadette Kambrz was a hotel manager. Heenan dropped out of school in the eighth grade to support his mother and grandmother.[7] He grew up a fan of pro wrestling and baseball. As a fan of wrestling growing up in Chicago and Indianapolis, he started in the wrestling profession early on, carrying bags and jackets for the wrestlers, and selling refreshments at events.[7][4]

U.S. ban on Canadian alcohol

A White House proclamation took effect at 12:01 a.m. ET on 29 September excluding a list of Canadian alcoholic beverages from U.S. entry. Wine, beer, vermouth and bottled spirits under four litres are in the net. Whisky and liqueurs in containers larger than four litres are not. Those bulk loads also escape the 50 percent tariff that had applied under an earlier order. The ban sits on about $800 million of Canadian drinks the U.S. took last year and is part of a wider package covering whey, molasses and some motorcycles — close to $1 billion of 2025 imports, a sliver of two-way trade. Washington says Canadian provinces discriminated against U.S. liquor after earlier U.S. tariffs. Ottawa and the provinces had already pulled American bottles from many government stores.

Existing stock already in the country can still be sold. Rebottling costs for anyone who tries to copy the bulk route may show up in prices. A tapeworm treatment  has been shown to effectively treat endometriosis in early trials. 

A new study from Washington State University has revealed that niclosamide—a drug traditionally used to treat intestinal tapeworm infections—shows significant promise in treating endometriosis, a chronic and often debilitating condition affecting millions of women worldwide.

 By utilizing advanced nanotechnology, researchers successfully designed a targeted delivery system using tiny nanoparticles (dendrimers). In laboratory tests on mouse models, this innovative method delivered the drug directly to disease-linked immune cells called macrophages. 

A single injection of the targeted therapy not only reduced the number and size of endometriosis lesions but also markedly decreased pain sensitivity.

This new approach represents a potential revolution in managing a condition that historically has had no cure and limited treatment options, which are frequently restricted to invasive surgeries or hormonal therapies that carry side effects like bone density loss and temporary infertility. Because niclosamide has low solubility and would otherwise require massive doses to be effective over time, the nanoparticle carrier is a game-changer, allowing for controlled, localized release that could eventually transition into a simple monthly injection for human patients. While clinical trials in humans are still on the horizon, this targeted non-hormonal therapy offers long-awaited hope for a highly-effective, low-side-effect solution to a complex, life-altering disease.

source: Dhull, A., Shi, M., Harvey, M. E., Page, T. M., Sharma, R., Goody, K. J., Dar, A. I., Moawad, N. S., Sirohi, V. K., Cooke, P. S., Hayashi, K., & Sharma, A. text:
My interview @cnni with @BeckyCNN  

1. Netanyahu’s visit to the UAE

Netanyahu’s visit to the UAE is important, Yes the visit was initially kept quiet, and there was no immediate public display of the meeting. One possible explanation is that Abu Dhabi does not want to become part of Israel’s election campaign or provide Netanyahu with images that could be used for domestic political purposes.

What is more revealing is the composition of the Israeli delegation. Netanyahu was accompanied by the Mossad director and the national security adviser, among other senior security officials, and Israeli reporting indicates that Iran was a central topic of discussion.

That makes sense given the dilemma facing Abu Dhabi. The UAE must decide how strongly it wants to support efforts to restore some form of accommodation with Tehran and reduce regional tensions, while simultaneously preparing for the possibility that diplomacy fails and confrontation with Iran intensifies again.

2. Iran’s proposal and the Strait of Hormuz

The situation around the Strait of Hormuz remains extremely fragile. Iran’s latest proposal does not fundamentally abandon Tehran’s established red lines. What has changed is the timetable: Iran is offering to accelerate both the reopening of the Strait and negotiation over the nuclear file.

From Tehran’s perspective, this creates something close to a win-win scenario. If President Trump accepts the proposal, Iran can return to an arrangement that it believes protects important Iranian interests while reducing immediate economic and military pressure. If Washington rejects it, Tehran can argue, both domestically and internationally, that Iran offered a diplomatic off-ramp and that the United States refused it.

That could then become Tehran’s political justification for another round of escalation. The Iranian message would essentially be: We offered diplomacy, Washington rejected it, and therefore we have no alternative but to increase the pressure and escalate.

3. Netanyahu, Iran, and Israel’s election campaign

There is also a domestic Israeli dimension that should not be ignored. Netanyahu has a clear political incentive to focus the national conversation on securit, and particularly on what Israel accomplished against Iran and the so-called Axis of Resistance after October 7, rather than exclusively on the failures that preceded October 7.

But Israel’s strategic challenges today extend well beyond Iran. The continuing violence and instability in the West Bank, including attacks by Israeli extremists, and the diplomatic scenes surrounding Netanyahu’s appearance at the United Nations illustrate the broader challenges Israel faces internationally and in the Palestinian arena.

Iran is therefore both a genuine and serious security challenge and an issue on which Netanyahu can emphasize Israeli military achievements. The Palestinian issue, Israel’s growing diplomatic difficulties, and the debate over responsibility for October 7 are politically much more complicated terrain for him.

There is also an interesting contradiction in Netanyahu’s political messaging. Today, he warned that Israel has indications that its enemies may try to attack the country ahead of the election. 

But it raises an important question when placed alongside another central theme of Netanyahu’s campaign: his argument that Israel’s enemies want to see him defeated and replaced by his political opponents.

If that is really their objective, why would they deliberately attack Israel immediately before an election?

text:
ACC and Notre Dame probably Breached Clemson/Florida State Settlement Agreements
Yogibuck
@CharlesK76493
·
Sep 16

Settlement Agreement And General Release...as of May 24, 2025.  Florida States version.

"Section 4.11 For as long as FSU is a Member of the ACC, or through 2036, the ACC shall not enter into any agreement or understanding, modify or amend any existing agreement or understanding, modify or amend the ACC Constitution or Bylaws, or otherwise take or fail to take any action, that conflicts with, limits or otherwise interferes or frustrates the rights of FSU or the FSU Board under this settlement agreement."

That was intended to be a broad interpretation of what the ACC could and could not due when it comes to the television and overall rights of Florida State University and under separate Settlement Agreement version, Clemson University.

Reading that, it plainly says, the ACC cannot take any action to frustrate the rights of Clemson University or in this case, Florida State University.  If any emails, texts, depositions of participants can prove that the ACC and/or its member institutions supported or lobbied for the 19-5 provision of Section 205 of the Protect College Sports Act (PCSA), the ACC is most likely in breach of contract.

The 19 is the limit of totals schools the power 2 is allowed to have.  The 5 is a five-year waiting period restriction as an independent, handcuffing any school wanting to leave the ACC or B12, except Notre Dame, a member of the ACC since September 12, 2012.

Where this clause gets really interesting is the part I glossed right over the first time I read it. Not only does the ACC have the obligation to not frustrate the rights of Clemson/FSU, but it also cannot fail to take any action that frustrates their rights.  The ACC and its members had the DUTY, the OBLIGATION, to defend the rights of Clemson/FSU.  They HAD TO VOICE AN OPINION OF NO when faced with the choice of supporting the PCSA legislation as it currently is written.  The ACC clearly failed to do that.

That little addition shifts the entire legal case from Clemson/FSU having to prove the ACC failed to defend its rights to now, the ACC has to prove that it did.  The ACC has to prove it defended Clemson/FSU rights in the affirmative.

Furthermore, not only did Notre Dame not defend Clemson/FSU's rights, it appears its leaders and lobbyists were actively involved in creating the legislation.  How else did the 5-year Notre Dame exclusion get placed in the bill?  Why should Notre Dame, a member of the ACC for nearly 15 years get a "get out of jail free card" while everyone else is placed in realignment prison?

"Section 4.7    ...for so long as FSU is a Member of the ACC, the ACC shall not (i) take any action whose intent or effect is to disproportionately disadvantage FSU as a Member of the ACC as compared to any other Member of the ACC."

Notre Dame is clearly defined in all ACC agreements as a member.   Reverend Robert A. Dowd, CSC, executed the Florida State Settlement Agreement, as President of the University of Notre Dame Du Lac.

One could argue that by supporting the PCSA, the ACC supported Notre Dame being given advantages over fellow ACC members Clemson/Florida State.

This Notre Dame Exemption is obviously a secondary breach.  If the ACC accepts the Congressional legislation as is, THE ACC MUST OFFER FSU the same condition.  PERIOD.  Or it is in Breach.  The agreement does not say congressional action is exempt nor does it say the ACC doesn't have to offer things its doesn't control.  The ACC cannot cure that breach.  That is not good for the ACC.

What is also incredibly interesting is a couple other clauses.  Section 4.11 is specifically excluded in section 6.1.3.1 from FSU having to provide notice OR allow the ACC a chance to cure.  Also, section 7.1 also says "This Settlement Agreement shall be construed as if the Parties jointly prepared it."  The ACC can't say they didn't purposely allow section 4.11 to be vague.  They wrote it.

Those two clauses are really important in legal land.  The deed is done and Clemson/FSU can just go to court at any time.  No waiting.

Also not included that I can see is venue.  This could be going back to Leon County, Florida, if contested.

This legislation is all in the herculean effort to SAVE college sports by limiting realignment, amongst other things.  Despite the FACT, that college sports has already been separated by tv contract stratification.  ESPN, Fox, NBC, CBS and others created this mess by PURPOSEFULLY stratifying college football via tv contract revenues.  It has ALREADY been realigned.

Clemson/FSU do not get the TV revenue of the B10 or SEC despite historical tv ratings that would rank near the top 25 percentile of either conference.

Congress tried to add a revenue sharing provision, in an effort to truly 'protect college sports", but when the p2 balked, Ted Cruz choked like Team USA basketball in 2004 vs Argentina.  Yet, the stratification remains, along with the section 205 chains.  Section 205 with revenue sharing is heroic.  A truly good deed. Section 205 without the revenue sharing is gutless.

Clemson/FSU went to the courts to fight for their ability to move, for their very existence.  And now some unseen hand is corrupting Congress and this bill in an effort to control schools.  To make money by controlling and limiting schools tv rights.  Wonder who that probably is?

This bill is not about protecting college sports at all.   Allowing Notre Dame to go to the big 10, but not Clemson, Florida State, North Carolina or Virginia does not protect college sports, it provides a competitive advantage for one school over others.  While we are at it, why don't we just let Notre Dame start at mid-field every drive or give them an auto-bid into the CFB playoff every year.  Why does a school that hasn't won a National Championship of a Heisman winner in nearly 40 years get the "get out of jail free card?"

The ACC FSU settlement agreement has possible remedies for a breach, but I'm going to offer one up to Congress.  Exempt Florida State and Clemson from Section 205.  It is the only fair thing to do for the only two schools who had the guts to take on corporate media and their own conference to be granted their rights.

The media has been able to control the narrative and damage the "disruptive" school's images, but those two schools RIGHTFULLY cleaned the acc's clock in court and won a huge settlement, because they were MORALLY right.

This bill is not FAIR TO ALL CONCERNED.

Clemson/FSU leaders and its fanbases don't want any more lawsuits, but the ACC, Notre Dame and Jim Phillips, PHD can't just seem to get out of their own way.
They just can't seem to let Clemson/Florida State go.
