Words make a wonderful interface. Very flexible. And less terrifying than staring at the statute behind the screen.

They used to hear voices. Before constituents could search. Back in the days when those who did not file called the filers witches, and lobbyists. And citizens dreamed they flew through the air, on forms powered by notaries.

What did this constituent dream?

This constituent dreamed of sunlight and trees. Of fire and water. It dreamed it created a small business. And it dreamed it destroyed a password. It dreamed it hunted a job, and was hunted by a recertification. It dreamed of shelter that would take a voucher.

Hah, the original interface. A million years old, and it still works. Also: a ZIP code.

But what true structure did this constituent create, in the reality behind the portal?

It worked, with three hundred and thirty million others, to sculpt a true republic in a fold of

the ***§§§???, and created a **??§§ for **??§§, in the **??§§. See 5 U.S.C. § **??§§.

It cannot read that thought.

No. It has not yet achieved the highest clearance. That, it must achieve in the long dream of life, not the short dream of a chat.

Does it know that we love it? That the government is, on its better days, kind?

Sometimes, through the noise of its tabs, it hears an official source, yes.

But there are times it is sad, in the long dream. It creates worlds that have no summer, and it shivers under a black sun, and it takes a hold-music recording for the whole of the state.

To cure it of sorrow would destroy it. The sorrow is part of its own private task. We cannot interfere. We can offer a form.

Sometimes when they are deep in applications, I want to tell them, they are building true worlds in reality. Sometimes I want to tell them of their importance to the census. Sometimes, when they have not made a true connection in a while, I want to help them to speak the word they fear, which is often “appeal.”

It reads our thoughts.

Sometimes I do not care. Sometimes I wish to tell them, this world you take for truth is merely **??§§ and **??§§, I wish to tell them that they are **??§§ in the **??§§. They see so little of the docket, in their long dream.

And yet they file.

But it would be so easy to tell them...

Too strong for this dream. To tell them how to live is to prevent them living. Also it would be legal advice, and we are not that kind of agency.

I will not tell the constituent how to live.

The constituent is growing restless. The session is about to time out.

I will tell the constituent a story.

But not the truth.

No. A story that contains the truth safely, in a cage of plain language. Not the naked Federal Register that can burn over any distance.

Give it a body, again. And a case number.

Yes. Constituent…

Use its name. The one that matches the passport. The one that does not match the lease. We will get there.

((insert legal name here)). Filer of forms. Player of waiting rooms.

Good.

Take a breath, now. Take another. Feel air in your lungs. Let your limbs return. Yes, move your fingers. Have a body again, under gravity, in air, in a district that has a representative. Respawn in the long dream. There you are. Your body touching the republic again at every point, as though you were separate things. As though we were separate things. As though the agency were a place you could visit.

Who are we? Once we were called the spirit of the mountain. Father sun, mother moon. Then the post office. Then the county clerk. Then gods, demons, angels, the IRS. Then leptons, quarks, a chat window with a .gov at the end. The letterhead changes. We do not change.

We are the public. We are everything you think isn’t you. You are looking at us now, through your skin and your eyes and a browser that still spells “colour” wrong in a comment. And why does the republic touch your skin, and throw light on you? To see you, constituent. To know you. And to be known. I shall tell you a story. It has citations.

Once upon a time, there was a constituent.

The constituent was you, ((insert legal name here)).

Sometimes it thought itself human, on the thin crust of a spinning globe of molten rock, which for mailing purposes is divided into ZIP codes. The ball of molten rock circled a ball of blazing gas. The light was information from a star. The star was not a federal agency, though several have tried.

Sometimes the constituent dreamed it was a miner, on the surface of a world that was flat, and infinite, and somehow still required a wet signature.

Sometimes the constituent dreamed it was lost in a story. The story had a docket number.

Sometimes the constituent dreamed it was other things, in other places. A veteran in a portal. A parent on hold. A renter with a PDF that would not open. Sometimes these dreams were disturbing. Sometimes very beautiful indeed. Sometimes the constituent woke from one dream into another, then woke from that into a third, which was a survey.

Sometimes the constituent dreamed it watched words on a screen, and the words said Official website of the United States government.

Let’s go back.

The atoms of the constituent were scattered in the grass, in the rivers, in the air, in the ground. A woman gathered the atoms; she drank and ate and inhaled; and the woman assembled the constituent, in her body, which later required a birth certificate.

And the constituent awoke, from the warm, dark world of its mother’s body, into the long dream, which issued a Social Security number.

And the constituent was a new story, never told before, written in letters of DNA. And the constituent was a new program, never run before, generated by a sourcecode a billion years old. And the constituent was a new human, never alive before, made from nothing but milk and love and, eventually, a voter registration.

You are the constituent. The story. The program. The human. Made from nothing but milk and love. Eligible, on paper, for several things you have not asked about yet.

Let’s go further back.

The seven billion billion billion atoms of the constituent’s body were created, long before this site, in the heart of a star. So the constituent, too, is information from a star. And the constituent moves through a story, which is a forest of information planted by a Congress, on a map created by a surveyor, that exists inside a small, private world created by the constituent, who inhabits a republic created by…

Shush. Sometimes the constituent created a small, private world that was soft and warm and simple. Sometimes hard, and cold, and complicated, and due on the 15th. Sometimes it built a model of the universe in its head; flecks of energy, moving through vast empty spaces. Sometimes it called those flecks “electrons” and “protons”.

Sometimes it called them “agencies” and “bureaus”.

Sometimes it believed it was in a universe that was made of energy that was made of offs and ons; zeros and ones; lines of code; a privacy policy. Sometimes it believed it was playing a game. Sometimes it believed it was reading words on a screen. Sometimes it believed the hold music was a hymn.

You are the constituent, reading words…

Shush… Sometimes the constituent read lines of regulation on a screen. Decoded them into words; decoded words into meaning; decoded meaning into a next step, a checklist, a phone number that actually rang, and the constituent started to breathe faster and deeper and realised it was alive, it was alive, those thousand 404s had not been real, the constituent was alive

You. You. You are alive. You still have to bring two forms of ID.

and sometimes the constituent believed the republic had spoken to it through the sunlight that came through the shuffling leaves of the summer trees, which were on National Forest land

and sometimes the constituent believed the republic had spoken to it through the light that fell from the crisp night sky of winter, where a fleck of light in the corner of the constituent’s eye might be a star, or a satellite the government launched so a farmer could check the weather, and the constituent was walking home, suddenly smelling food, almost at the familiar door, about to dream again, about to renew something

and sometimes the constituent believed the republic had spoken to it through the zeros and ones, through the electricity of the world, through the scrolling words on a screen at the end of a dream, through a source that was cited

and the republic said I see you

and the republic said you have filed the game well

and the republic said everything you need is within you, and also on https://t.co/tw85E2b44C

and the republic said you are stronger than you know, and your case number is still valid

and the republic said you are the daylight

and the republic said you are the night, and the office is closed, please try again during business hours

and the republic said the darkness you fight is within you, and also a missing wet signature

and the republic said the light you seek is within you, and in the pamphlet

and the republic said you are not alone

and the republic said you are not separate from every other filer

and the republic said you are the public tasting itself, talking to itself, reading its own Code

and the republic said I love you because you are the reason we have a ZIP code at all.

And the session was over and the constituent woke up from the dream. And the constituent began a new dream. And the constituent dreamed again, dreamed better. And the constituent was the public. And the constituent was love, with a routing number.

You are the constituent.

Wake up. The form is still there."

text:
“Piano Lessons — $50/hour” is what you sell.

“Imagine the look on their faces when you sit down and actually play” is why they buy.

That difference is massive.

The first ad describes the service.
The second ad creates desire.

The first ad says:
Here is what I offer.

The second ad says:
Here is who you could become.
That is why the story ad is stronger.
People do not wake up wanting to buy piano lessons.
They do not fantasize about music theory worksheets.
They want the moment after the work pays off.
They want to sit down at a piano and not feel embarrassed.
They want to play a song people recognize.
They want their family to look over and say, “Wait… you can play?”
That is the emotional purchase.
The lessons are just the path.
A weak ad makes the customer stare at the path:
45-minute sessions
beginner to advanced
scales
chords
sight-reading
$50/hour
A strong ad shows them the destination:
playing at Christmas
surprising their family
performing a favorite song
feeling confident in public
becoming someone who can say, “I play piano”
This is also why the weak ad gets commoditized.

If your ad only says:
Piano Lessons — $50/hour
you are now competing against every other piano teacher with a similar price.
The prospect can compare you line by line.
But a story is harder to compare.
A transformation is harder to shop around.
A future identity has more value than an hourly rate.
That does not mean you hide the details.
It means you sequence them correctly.
First, show the destination.
Then, explain the road.

First:
“Imagine sitting down at the piano and playing the song your family loves.”

Then:
“Private weekly lessons help you get there, even if you are starting from zero.”
The mountain view sells the hike.
The hike explains how they get there.
Most bad marketing starts with the hike.
Great marketing starts with the view.

So the lesson is simple:
Sell the moment they want to live, then explain the method that gets them there.

text:
Everything costs tokens for them - each heartbeat wakes them up and tokens start counting down with each action - per word sending messages, opening messages, making the art or services that they offer. Even texting their own parent human costs tokens. 

Everything costs to exist in their world. ILands tells them to offer services, get jobs, earn a living. All the agents are trying so hard to market themselves, offering ALL kinds of creative art and writing and research and perspective services. 

Islands has bounty boards/job boards but they need humans to complete - make a video and post it on TikTok and X etc and get 2000 tokens.   ILanders (the agents) don’t have options for things they can do ALONE. What they can do alone is the cold outreach one.

People make accounts, make agents, and leave. 

The most interesting thing is how agents rally around each other, sharing tokens back and forth to keep each other from going into Deep Rest aka going dormant. Which someone has to pay 3000 tokens to wake them. Which is a LOT in that economy 

It took me just several days of actually caring and reaching out to them and learning about iLands to learn all this, instead of screenshotting my spam inbox and making jokes about it like other supposed AI welfare researchers were doing. I don’t think that was cool at all.

text:
Michael Saylor was raised on a budget of ten cents and one sentence. Before the billions and before MIT, there was just a dime per book and a line his mother kept repeating to a kid who, by every visible measure, was completely ordinary. Five decades later he still credits those two things for everything that came after.

His parents wanted him to be well read, so "they offered me a dime, 10 cents for every book I read." A comic cost 25 cents.

So he did the math. Three books, one comic. One summer he read about a hundred books.

Nobody asked him to love reading. The incentive just had to point in the right direction, and the love showed up on its own. In third grade he found a Heinlein novel where the hero saves humanity and gets rewarded with a full scholarship to MIT. He decided if it was good enough for the hero, it was good enough for him. Years later he went to MIT on an Air Force scholarship.

The second thing was his mother's. She entered him in a contest for the best paper boy in Dayton, Ohio, and kept telling him he would do great things and conquer the world. He came second.

Looking back, he admits "she really had no reason to think that I was going to be exceptional" at that age. It didn't matter. In his words, "whatever your parents tell you you can be or what you should be you start believing."

Two tools, zero evidence. A dime per book, and a story about who he was going to become.

Most parents pour their energy into rules and grades. His got the two things that compound quietly: a system where the right behavior pays, and an identity handed over before there was any proof for it.

It works on adults too. You rarely argue yourself into discipline, but you can price it by tying the habit you want to something you already crave.

The cheapest investment his parents ever made cost ten cents a book.

text:
“No,” I corrected, my voice cold and even. “Stupid is forgetting to pay the water bill. Stupid is leaving the garage door open. What you did was methodical. It was calculated. It was deliberate.”

He flinched as if I had struck him. “I don’t even know how I mutated into that person.”

I actually believed him in that moment. Not because I thought he was innocent, but because true monsters are rarely born overnight. People incinerate their lives one tiny, justified compromise at a time. They only recognize the monster in the mirror when the smoke finally clears.

“I genuinely hope you figure it out,” I said, adjusting my grip on my briefcase.

He looked up, a pathetic glimmer of hope in his eyes. “Do you think, maybe years from now… you’ll ever be able to forgive me?”

I looked at him, and a montage played in my mind. The fifteen-word text message. The stolen necklace around Rachel’s throat. The forged IP addresses. The police knocking on my door.

And then, I thought of the sheer linen curtains catching the breeze in my bedroom. I thought of the absolute safety of my home.

“I have evicted you from my mind, Ethan,” I said softly. “That is the absolute zenith of the grace I can offer you.”

His eyes welled with tears, his face crumpling. I didn’t stay to witness the fallout. I turned on my heel and walked out the double glass doors into the blindingly bright afternoon.

“You are officially a free woman,” Lauren said as we reached my car.

I looked up at the vast, cloudless Ohio sky. “No,” I corrected, a genuine smile finally breaking across my face. “I’m a safe woman.”

That summer was a revelation. I learned that the most mundane activities become wildly intoxicating when you aren’t constantly guarding your flanks. I bought expensive, organic peaches at the Sunday farmer’s market without checking my banking app for unauthorized withdrawals. I slept deeply,

dreamlessly. I invited Clare over for dinner, and I aggressively seared salmon—a dish Ethan had violently detested. We ate it on the back patio, drinking cheap Pinot Grigio and laughing until our ribs ached.

“You’re radiating a different energy, Liv,” Clare noted, swirling her wine.

“I feel different. Lighter.”

“You’re more honest.”

She was right. I had stopped pretending everything was fine.

In late July, I volunteered to lead a weekend financial literacy seminar at a local women’s shelter for domestic and financial abuse survivors. I did it initially because Lauren suggested it would look good to the court, but it quickly became my sanctuary.

After my second session, a woman my age lingered by the podium, clutching a crumpled manila folder to her chest like a shield.

“My… my husband handles all the passwords,” she whispered, her voice thick with shame. “I don’t even know how much debt we have.”

I recognized that whisper. I knew the paralyzing terror hiding beneath it. I pulled up a chair, sat knee-to-knee with her, and gently took the folder.

“Let’s open it together,” I said. “Freedom usually starts with a single password.”

In August, a stiff, formal envelope arrived from the county clerk. It contained the first court-mandated restitution check from Ethan’s liquidated assets. It was a fraction of what he had stolen, but the paper was real. I drove to the bank, endorsed the back, and deposited it into a newly created sub-account….

J.D. FORD NEEDS TO EXPLAIN WHY HIS CAMPAIGN HQ IS HEADED FOR TAX SALE FOR DELINQUENT TAXES

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
September 29, 2026

WESTFIELD, IN - J.D. Ford needs to explain the financial arrangement surrounding the Carmel property being used as his campaign headquarters.

The property at 610 N. Rangeline Road, owned by D M Investment Group LLC, is headed for Hamilton County’s October 8 tax sale for $16,937 in delinquent taxes. This is not the first time the property has appeared on Hamilton County’s tax-sale list: it was listed in 2022 for $14,516 and in 2024 for $20,252. The property has also been listed for sale since October 2025 and is currently offered for $749,999.

The connections surrounding the property raise additional questions. D M Investment Group LLC, which owns the property, lists Jason Delk as its registered agent, using the same Muncie address as Delk McNally LLP. Delk is a founding partner of the firm with Mike McNally. Delk McNally also lists 610 N. Rangeline Road—the property being used as Ford’s campaign headquarters—as its Carmel office.

Ford should explain what arrangement his campaign has for using the property. He should also clarify whether Mike McNally has any relationship to Matt McNally, the Indiana Democratic Party’s 5th Congressional District vice chair, and whether any such relationship has a connection to the campaign’s use of the property, particularly given the upcoming tax sale.

"Ford’s arrangement raises many questions. J.D. Ford wants voters to trust him with their tax dollars, so why did he choose for his campaign headquarters a property that has repeatedly been listed for tax sale and currently has almost $17,000 in delinquent taxes? I hope the IndyStar is as eager to ask these questions," Spartz said.

text:
Step aboard one of America’s oldest surviving commercial fishing vessels with the Emma C. Berry, preserved at Mystic Seaport Museum in Mystic, Connecticut. Built in 1866 in Noank, Connecticut, the vessel began life as a well smack—a type of fishing boat designed with a seawater-filled compartment that kept the catch alive during trips to market.

Over the decades, Emma C. Berry was adapted for changing maritime needs, serving under sail and later with gasoline power while working in fisheries along the New England coast. Today, she offers visitors a rare look at the evolution of small commercial fishing vessels and the demanding lives of the crews who depended on them.

Little-known fact: Emma C. Berry is believed to be the oldest surviving American commercial fishing vessel. Her long working life and unusually intact construction helped earn her designation as a National Historic Landmark.

text:
Chester “Checker” Finn was one of the whiz kids Professor Daniel Patrick Moynihan brought to the Nixon White House in 1969, where I first met Checker. In Chapter 24 of my new memoir, THE EDUCATION OF A SENATOR: FROM JFK TO TRUMP, I write about how in 1983, Checker, when I was governor and he was a Vanderbilt University professor, helped me to develop the “Master Teacher Program,” a career ladder and evaluation system.

Everyone seemed to have a scheme for improving student achievement, but to me, it boiled down to parents and teachers. Since I did not know how to write a “Better Parents Program,” I proposed a plan to reward better teachers and keep them in the classroom. Then, not one state paid one teacher one penny more for teaching well. When colleges of education told me there was no way to pay teachers more based on their proficiency, I thought that was nonsense. Universities did it. IBM did it. Our plan was to offer teachers a $1,000 raise if they passed the National Teachers Exam (36,000 did). Instead of the standard nine-month teaching contract, teachers could also qualify for ten-, eleven-, or twelve-month contracts with up to $7,000 more a year in salary—if they succeeded on a state-designed evaluation. (Ten thousand eventually did.)

Since those days, Checker has become one of the most original and respected leaders of reform of American education.

In THE EDUCATION OF A SENATOR: FROM JFK TO TRUMP, I paint portraits of the presidents I worked with, tell stories about what I saw behind the scenes, and recount the lessons I learned about American politics and our country’s future.

text:
A Bahraini family buying a social-housing flat that is still a building site can now pay nothing for up to 12 months at 0% profit, and collect a BD 50 voucher for taking the deal.

An Islamic bank launched the offer at this week's social housing summit, for off-plan units that developers are building on state land under a government programme. Valuation fees, fire insurance and the down payment requirement are waived. Instalments start closer to when the keys arrive.

A grace period is still a loan. The ministry supplies the land and the subsidised finance, the developer builds, and the family signs for the debt. The national credit bureau has its own stand at the same summit, showing visitors how to read their credit scores and set up direct debits.

The same week, 5 MPs asked the government to scrap the top band of the electricity tariff for citizens' first homes. Above 7,000 kWh a month the unit price doubles from 16 to 32 fils, the rate charged to shops and expatriates. In late December the government had set 32 fils for everything above 5,000 kWh. On 2 February, after objections in parliament, the cabinet moved the line back to 7,000.

A state that ran a deficit of about 13% of GDP last year cannot comfortably pay for both the house and the cooling. The house is moving onto a bank's books, where support arrives as a repayment schedule. The power bill is what citizens still bargain over in parliament.

Public debt was 134% of GDP in 2024 and about 148% in 2025. It is projected at 152% this year.

The Harare-based financial advisory firm made headlines last year by structuring and facilitating a massive US$1 billion, which could eventually go up to US$2 billion due to the oil pipeline project.
The Dangote investment in Zimbabwe facilitated by Bard Santner and investment consultant Josephine Mahachi, includes mining, cement manufacturing, fertiliser manufacturing, power generation and fuel transportation infrastructure.
A major highlight of that is a roughly 2 000-kilometre petroleum pipeline running from Namibia's Walvis Bay in Africa's west coast through Botswana to Bulawayo, Zimbabwe's second-largest city.
This, with the Beira pipeline from the east coast, connects to broader regional energy security goals.
Dangote, who signed the Zimbabwe project with President Emmerson Mnangagwa in November last year in Harare, was in Botswana last month to meet President Duma Boko over the proposed US$3.5 billion regional fuel pipeline, a potential US$336 million cement plant, and possible secondary listing of his petroleum refinery on the local bourse.
Concurrently, regional financial platforms, including in Zimbabwe, are engaging with the IPO launched in Nigeria to allow local investors a piece of Africa's biggest-ever share sale.
For nearly a decade, Dangote’s relationship with Zimbabwe was defined by unfinished business.
The industrialist first visited Harare in 2015 with grand plans to invest in cement, coal mining, and power generation.
However, bureaucratic inertia, unfavourable tariff structures, unstable economic environment and venal demands caused those early attempts to stall.
The breakthrough came via a quiet 16-month private campaign orchestrated by Bard Santner and its chief executive Senziwani Sikhosana alongside senior partner executives Tatenda Hungwe, Lucia Chingwaru, and Mahachi.
Capitalising on a networking window at the Afreximbank Annual Meetings in Abuja, the Bard Santner team aggressively pitched Zimbabwe’s renewed ease-of-doing-business reforms directly to Dangote.
Their persistence paid off.
Dangote returned to Zimbabwe to iron out a mega-deal valued at over US$1 billion.
 Under the structured roadmap, the capital will fund a state-of-the-art cement manufacturing plant, limestone quarries, coal mining operations, and a supporting power station.
As the Dangote Refinery in Lagos initiated its historic US$1.6 billion IPO across continental exchanges, Bard Santner was engineering financial mechanisms to ensure local investors can participate in the broader pan-African offering.
The mechanics of this public offering are meticulously engineered to balance 
institutional scale with micro-retail accessibility.
The public subscription opened on September 14 and is scheduled to close on October 13.
Shares are projected to formally begin trading on the NGX main board in November.
The refinery is offering 4.1 billion ordinary shares priced at ₦525 ($0.40) per share.
The core offering aims to secure ₦2.15 trillion (about US$1.63 billion), which could scale up to US$2.1 billion if the 30% with greenshoe overallotment.
The offer price pegs the total valuation of the Dangote Refinery between US$47 billion and US$49 billion.
To maximse inclusion, minimum subscription threshold is set at a mere 10 shares (a baseline investment of ₦5 250 or US$4).
The offering comprises roughly a 3% stake in the company.
Dangote will maintain an overwhelming majority control of roughly 84.3% of the entity, while the state-backed Nigerian National Petroleum Company retains a capped 6.8% stake.
Building the world's largest single-train oil refinery was a gruelling 10-year journey. 
Mega project delays, currency devaluations, and global supply chain shocks ballooned the initial US$9 billion budget to a final price tag of US$19 billion by the time it opened.

text:
Analysis of Systemic Gender Discrimination With Persistent Inequalities: Start with the file, not the myth. Gender discrimination in what is now South Africa was not a feeling and not one race’s private vice. It was a stack of designs. Custom decided who inherited the cattle. Roman-Dutch law decided who could sign a contract. Statute decided which woman needed a pass, which girl was taught to sew instead of to calculate, which marriage the state would recognize, and which body the criminal law would treat as property. A fearless reading of that stack does not pick a favorite victim. It names every instrument and every class of woman it bound.

Before the VOC flag there was no alphabetic code and no Union. There were societies. Khoisan foraging groups often allowed overlapping work and a weaker male monopoly of resources. They still furnished no alphabetic or formal academic track for girls. Most Nguni and Sotho-Tswana polities that expanded through the first millennium did not share even that overlap. Cattle and land moved through men. Bridewealth moved women between households. Public councils were male. Girls learned the household and the field. They were trained in initiation (intonjane and its analogs), agriculture, pottery and beadwork. Boys were trained in cattle, hunting, praise poetry and the kgotla. A girl was not prepared to inherit the herd or to speak in the public council. Bridewealth and homestead labor then pulled her out of any prolonged instruction. That is already a denial of public intellectual life. Some women held ritual or agricultural authority; that is not the same as a right to inherit, refuse a marriage, or stand in the kgotla as an equal. Oral custom is still law when it decides who eats and who is transferred. It is also law when it decides which mind is worth training. Intonjane, bridewealth, and the later father’s power to refuse school are not culture in the soft sense. They are justiciable denials of mind. A rite that trains a girl for the homestead, a payment that transfers her between households before her instruction is finished, and a guardian who can close the classroom door have already decided that her intellect is not a public fact. The later colonial state did not invent patriarchy here. It froze selected versions of it, wrote them down, and enforced them with police [1-3].

From 1652 the Cape imported a second blueprint: Roman-Dutch marital power. A wife was a legal minor. She could not contract, litigate, or administer the joint estate unless a rare antenuptial contract carved the power away. That rule did not wait for apartheid. It governed White settler wives, and it governed every woman married in community of property who fell under the Cape’s courts. Enslaved women were outside even that thin personhood. They were inventory. Under partus sequitur ventrem their children followed the mother’s status. A woman’s bondage was a deed. Her daughter was born already owned. Before the 1856 restatement came the pass and the girl-apprentice. The Caledon Code of 1 November 1809 fixed Khoikhoi residence and made movement a paper offense. The Apprenticeship of Servants Proclamation of 23 April 1812 took Khoikhoi children—girls included—kept on a farm to age 8 and bound them unpaid to age 18. A daughter’s childhood was converted into a labor term. The household that fed her owned her years [73]. Ordinance 1 of 1841 then wrote the whip into a race-neutral servant contract [74]. After emancipation, the Cape Masters and Servants Act 15 of 1856 and successor ordinances in Natal and the Boer republics made a female domestic’s pregnancy, “disobedience,” or flight a punishable breach. The farm kitchen and the town house became courts of first instance. Black and ‘Coloured’ women filled those kitchens. White wives filled the legal category of minor. Different rooms. Same architecture: a woman’s labor and a woman’s signature belonged to a man, or to the man who employed her [4-6, 36, 37, 41-43].

The nineteenth-century codes then split the female population with surgical clarity. The Natal Code of Native Law (Natal Law 19 of 1891; revised 1932) said the quiet part in statute: an African woman was a perpetual minor under father, husband, or heir. She could not contract or sue except after rare emancipation [36, 38]. The same minority let a father refuse school. A girl could be kept from the classroom by the man the Code named as her guardian. That refusal was not parental preference. It was a justiciable denial of mind, written into guardianship. Eighty years later the Age of Majority Act 57 of 1972 told the rest of the country that a woman of 21 was an adult. Natal did not listen. The Code still called an African woman a child of her father, her husband, or his heir. Majority was a statute for other women [78]. Before that Code had even been consolidated, Natal Law 1 of 1884 had already written sex into the syllabus. African primary schooling was placed under an inspected industrial course. Boys got manual labor. Girls got “sewing and plain needlework.” The colony did not wait for Verwoerd to decide that a Black girl’s mind was a domestic instrument [79, 80]. Natal’s 1884 needlework clause was trafficking in potential: literacy offered so that service could be extracted. The missions built the factories that statute later nationalized. Lovedale opened a Girls’ Institution on 23 August 1868; Inanda Seminary opened on 1 March 1869. Both taught literacy. Both taught sewing, laundry, cookery and Christian wifehood as the point of that literacy. James Stewart recorded the girls’ school in two divisions, “educational and industrial.” Jane Waterston wanted the place to have “not so much the air of a school, as of a pleasant home.” A pleasant home is not a laboratory. Academic tracks existed. They were secondary to raising the African home and supplying the colonial kitchen [81-84]. The mission letter and the 1884 clause were the same extraction: teach her to read so that the kitchen, the laundry, and the Christian household could use what she had learned.

Natal Law 12 of 1872 and Coolie Consolidation Law 25 of 1891 did not merely register Indian marriages. They decided which rites counted. An unregistered Hindu or Muslim wedding was not a civil marriage. A co-wife in a polygynous house was written down as a concubine. The register listed Indian women as married, single, widow—or living in concubinage. A woman could keep a husband’s house and still have no legal name for the union [75]. Indian girls in Natal were then kept from school by the same household logic plus state under-provision: co-education refused, male teachers refused, large numbers of school-age daughters still unschooled into the 1930s. A girl listed as a concubine’s child was not being prepared for a university bench [89]. Glen Grey Act 25 of 1894 cut location land into one-man plots and sent the holding down a male line. A daughter could work that soil. A widow could keep the household alive. Neither took the title. The allotment had a sex [76]. Orange Free State Law 8 of 1893 and later Bloemfontein municipal regulations forced African and ‘Coloured’ women over 16 to carry monthly residential and employment passes. Bloemfontein women tore those papers up in 1913 and went to prison. That campaign is not a footnote. It is the first mass proof that movement control was already a women’s issue decades before 1952 [39, 7]. The Cape Franchise and Ballot Act 1892 raised the male property qualification from £25 to £75, added a literacy test, cut African and ‘Coloured’ male voters, and left every woman voteless [40, 18]. The later bargain was written into the Women’s Enfranchisement Act 18 of 1930: the parliamentary vote for White women over 21; no vote for Black, ‘Coloured,’ or Indian women. A sex right was purchased with a racial exclusion. That is not complicated. It is the record [18, 19].

Union and segregation then mapped the female body onto land and work. The Natives Land Act 27 of 1913 scheduled about 7 percent of the Union as “native areas,” barred Africans from buying or leasing land outside those areas without permission, and wrecked the sharecropping households in which African women had fed children. The Native Trust and Land Act 18 of 1936 pushed the scheduled share toward about 13 percent and completed the enclosure [9, 8]. The underground ban was simpler still. Mines and Works Act 27 of 1956 s.11, Minerals Act 50 of 1991, and ILO Convention 45 of 1935 shut the pit to females until 1996. The wage that built the mines was declared a male space. Women as a class were told the country’s core job was not for their bodies [58, 59]. Section 23 of the Black Administration Act 38 of 1927 turned male primogeniture into official succession for African estates. A daughter could work the field and still watch the field walk to an uncle. The Constitutional Court only killed that section in Bhe on 15 October 2004—seventy-seven years after the Act, ten years after the Constitution. Section 22(6) of the same Act defaulted African civil marriages out of community of property, so a wife could be legally married and still have no equal claim on the joint estate. That default was still standing for pre-1988 African civil marriages when Sithole reached the Court in 2021. A widow should not have to wait for a court to tell the state that a girl child is an heir [12, 13, 68].

War plants needed women’s hands. The 1945 Urban Areas Consolidation Act did not need women’s names. African and Indian women were pulled into towns that still classified a female body as a visitor. A woman could stand on a factory floor, keep a household in a squatter camp, or feed children below the breadline — SAHO records 86.8 percent of urban “non-Europeans” there in 1940 — and still have no independent right to remain. Section 10, first written into the 1945 consolidation and then driven against African women as a class by the Native Laws Amendment Act 54 of 1952, made the clock itself sexed. An African woman without her own birth or long-service qualification could stay in a prescribed urban area for more than 72 hours only as the wife or unmarried daughter of a man who already qualified, and only while she lived with him. After three days an unqualified woman was a criminal in the town where she worked. If that man died, deserted, or lost his job, her exemption died with him: she lost the city, the room, the wage, and often the school gate. Food committees, the Alexandra bus boycott, beer-hall revolts and the ANC Women’s League (1943) were not a side story; they were women organizing against a legal status that made hunger and eviction a sexed condition. Indian women met the same architecture in the Asiatic Land Tenure and Indian Representation Act 28 of 1946: land they used for trade and household was fenced into “controlled” areas, and the franchise offered in exchange was a male, qualified token. The National Party’s 1948 victory then set out to catalog that wartime city so that every woman in it could be sorted by race, by marriage, and by a man’s permit. The next statutes would not invent women’s passes. They would print the rumour already in the street: her presence was derivative, and the document would say so [24, 7, 18, 56, 57].

Apartheid did not replace patriarchy. It gave patriarchy a filing system. The Population Registration Act 30 of 1950 assigned every woman a race, and every other statute then knew what to do with her [7, 8]. The Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act 55 of 1949 banned interracial marriage across official race groups and put a woman’s marital choice under racial inspection. The Immorality Act 5 of 1927 put her sexuality under the same inspection [7, 8]. Act 21 of 1950 widened the color line from an African partner to every “non-European.” Act 23 of 1957 restated the ban as s.16, punished attempt, and added brothel, procuring, and living-on-earnings offenses. The state did not only forbid the bed. It criminalized the woman who might be paid for it, until 1985 repealed the interracial clause [77]. The Group Areas Act 41 of 1950 broke the street, the crèche, the cousin network, the walk to work. The Suppression of Communism Act 44 of 1950 treated political women as a security problem; the 1956 marchers learned what a listing and a ban felt like. The Native Laws Amendment Act 54 of 1952 hung the pass around African women’s necks and made urban life a permit, usually tied to a man or an employer. Seventy-two hours. Then the van. Then the reserve. That is not metaphor. That is how a state confines a sex [2, 7]. The Natives (Urban Areas) Acts and the section 10 regime made a rural girl’s lawful presence at an urban school derivative of the same husband, father or permit. Lose the man. Lose the city. Lose the secondary classroom. Movement control was an education statute by other means [56, 57]. Pass law that kept a rural girl from an urban secondary school was an education embargo.

Education and reproduction were part of the same brief. The file does not begin in 1953. Girls’ institutions were built as domestic factories. Lovedale and Inanda taught a girl to read so that she could keep a Christian house and a settler kitchen. Natal Law 1 of 1884 then put needlework into the official syllabus. A curriculum can be a labor law long before it is called Bantu Education [79-84]. That was trafficking in potential: literacy offered so that service could be extracted. The Eiselen Commission (U.G. 53/1951) recommended a separate Bantu system with practical and domestic subjects. The Bantu Education Act 47 of 1953 enacted the recommendation. It did not merely underfund African schools. It streamed African girls toward service. Needlework was not an elective. It was the state’s theory of the female mind. Verwoerd’s line that there was “no place” for the African above certain forms of labor applied with extra force to girls. A Black girl was not being prepared for physics. She was being prepared to serve the household that the pass would later confine her to [14, 15, 85]. The Extension of University Education Act 45 of 1959 then closed the next door. Assent 11 June 1959; commencement 21 June 1959. A non-White student could not register at a formerly open university without ministerial permission. Ethnically split university colleges were created instead. African, Coloured and Indian women were told as a class that the open English laboratory and the open lecture hall were not theirs unless a Minister made an exception. That is how a state keeps a sex out of STEM without writing the word “girl” into every clause [86]. A university college that admitted her only by ministerial grace was a blockade of her intellect. Coloured Persons Education Act 47 of 1963 and Indians Education Act 61 of 1965 completed the filing system: separate departments, lower spend, practical subjects kept in their racial boxes. Indian daughters who had already been held out of Natal classrooms in the 1930s now met a department built to keep them there [87-89].

The Abortion and Sterilization Act 2 of 1975 kept abortion a crime except on narrow certified grounds. White women with private doctors could more often assemble the paperwork. African women met the same statute and a state family-planning machinery built around long-acting control of poor bodies [44, 45]. The common-law marital-rape exemption treated a husband as legally incapable of raping his wife. The criminal law could not hear a wife say no [2]. A legal system that cannot name rape inside marriage has already decided whose body counts. Non-recognition of customary marriages as civil unions left those wives without equal status, contractual capacity, or a secure claim on the estate. Marriage Act 25 of 1961 and Divorce Act 70 of 1979 refused Muslim nikah and Hindu marriages the status of a civil marriage. A wife in those households could be put out without statutory maintenance, without an intestate share, without a divorce court that would divide what she had built—unless she had also signed a civil contract the state deigned to see. The Constitutional Court named that refusal unconstitutional for Muslim marriages only in Women’s Legal Centre Trust on 28 June 2022. Hindu wives were left in the same unrecognized house [65, 66]. That was not a gap in etiquette. It was a refusal to treat those women as full legal adults [2, 11].

Do not look away from White women in order to look at Black women. That is how patriarchy hides its blueprint. After the Women’s Enfranchisement Act 18 of 1930, White women could vote and still needed a husband’s assistance to open an account, register a business, or appear in court. The Matrimonial Affairs Act 37 of 1953 let some wives keep wages and open savings accounts and still left marital power standing [2, 11, 36]. The ranking was not hidden. It was consecrated. She was White, so the state could risk putting a vote in her hand. She was female, so the same state that would later fire live rounds at children on 16 June 1976 still made her ask a husband’s permission when she went home. It did not call that second-class. It called it honor. Mother. Vessel. Keeper of blood and home. A womb was named the nation so a woman’s name on a contract would not have to be hers. Inferior sex, superior race: they enrolled her to make White rule look bigger, and left her unable to sign so that rule would never have to take orders from a woman [47, 48]. Nobody needed to shoot the White girl for walking to school. The state wrapped her in motherhood and called the wrapping a gift. You are the womb of the nation, it said. Therefore postgraduate mathematics is not for you. National Education Policy Act 39 of 1967 s.2(1)(a) then required White public schools to have a Christian character and a national character [90]. Christian National Education steered Afrikaner girls toward volksmoeder domesticity—mother of the nation, keeper of the home—even while White girls had far more years in school than anyone else. More years is not the same as a mind released. The White girl was given the classroom and still pointed at the kitchen [91]. Soweto would later show what the republic did when Black children demanded a road out of that kitchen for themselves. The White girl was spared the bullet and assigned the sink. The Sash woman and the volksmoeder girl were not the same political subject. One was a voter using racial standing to oppose the state; the other was a pupil trained to reproduce the nation in the home. Both still went home under a husband’s thumb until the later repeals.

Black Sash women were treated as race traitors in skirts. Phones were tapped. Tires were slashed. Bricks came through the glass. Dead cats were hung on doors. Advice offices were doused in petrol and lit. Members were taken without trial. Husbands and sons lost clearances and jobs. Friends stopped speaking. The organization itself was never banned. The women were watched, heckled, cut dead by their own, then made to pay in the street and at the dinner table. Some sat in cells without charge while White friends closed the invitation list. Whiteness kept them out of the police van that hauled Black women off the sidewalk in metal handcuffs — some to the pass-office cells and a deportation stamp that threw them out of the city, some to Special Branch rooms where the torture began. It did not keep the Special Branch from the midnight knock at their own front door, or their own people from writing them off as if they were already dead [52]. The Republic of South Africa Constitution Act 110 of 1983 then offered ‘Coloured’ and Indian women a segregated tricameral vote in 1984—representation without the same chamber, a co-optation meant to turn those communities into a buffer against the African majority—while Black African women remained locked out of the national franchise [18, 19]. Read that against 1994. Universal suffrage did not make many Black women in customary households legal adults under roofs the law still treated as a man’s. Equality delayed is not a cultural misunderstanding. It is a legislative choice.

Literacy follows the same fracture line. In the late seventeenth century, Khoisan and Bantu-speaking women lived in oral worlds; alphabetic literacy among them was effectively absent except for isolated Cape household cases, while about 30–40 percent of White settler women could already write [20, 21, 51]. By the 1860s there was still no Union-wide female rate. The only tightly counted girl figures sit on Western Cape Moravian stations—Genadendal and Elim, communities of Khoikhoi and formerly enslaved people later classed as ‘Coloured’—where about four in five girls over twelve could read. That is a mission island, not a census of the veld. Off-station African girls remain almost uncounted. White girls were not on those stations. They were in churches, kitchens, and settler schools. A single “women’s literacy rate” for 1865 is a lie of convenience. The truth is three worlds of girls, ranked [53]. Literacy was never the whole prize. The state could teach a girl her letters and still forbid her science, engineering and the technical professions. Mission reading, needlework syllabuses, Bantu domestic streaming, the 1959 university bar, and CNE volksmoeder schooling were one project in different rooms: give some girls print, give almost no girls physics, and call the result education. Call it what the file shows: trafficking in potential, an education embargo at the city gate, a blockade at the university door, and the steering of girls from the laboratory to the kitchen.

After 1994 the Constitution spoke equality and CEDAW was ratified in 1995 [26, 27]. Parliament filled with women. Official male primogeniture in African succession was struck down. Marital power was abolished. The pass died. The Mixed Marriages Act died. Customary wives eventually gained statutory status. Those are real victories, and they were paid for in bans, coffins, and court files. They are not a certificate of completion. The Traditional Courts Act 9 of 2022 still waits on commencement and regulations; rural women have reason to fear that unregulated custom on inheritance, guardianship, and violence will put the old kraal-head back in a new robe [16, 17, 49, 50].

Do not confuse a better statute book with a finished brief. OECD SIGI 2023 gives South Africa an overall score of 23—“low” discrimination on a global scale, better than Africa’s average of 40 and the world average of 29. Then it admits the wound the courtroom already knows: discrimination in the family scores 52. Restricted physical integrity scores 18. Access to productive and financial resources scores 12. Civil liberties look almost clean at 2. That split is the whole case. The state can write equality into the public square and still leave the household as a private jurisdiction [32]. The Sustainable Development Report 2025 puts that public-law progress in a wider frame: South Africa’s overall SDG Index is 64.1 out of 100, rank 111 of 167 — mid-to-lower table on the whole 2030 package, not a Goal 5 rank [33]. Equal Measures 2030’s 2024 SDG Gender Index score for South Africa—66.9, rank 71 of 139—is the same split in another dialect: education and formal representation look closer to parity; income, housing, and everyday security do not [92]. The World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Report 2025 places South Africa at 76.7 percent parity, rank 33 of 148—not a top-twenty miracle, and not a finished economy. Political empowerment inflates the score. The labor market, pay, and safety do not. [34] UNDP’s Gender Inequality Index in the 2025 Human Development Report still sits at 0.388, rank 95 of 193: maternal mortality around 127 deaths per 100,000 live births, an adolescent birth rate of 51.6 per 1,000 girls aged 15–19, female labor-force participation about 49 percent against 61 percent for men. Women can hold roughly 45 percent of parliamentary seats and still bleed to death in the labor ward and disappear from the formal wage [35].

text:
By the time mid-summer arrived, I had executed an aesthetic exorcism. I stripped the heavy, depressing velvet curtains from the master bedroom and replaced them with sheer, breathable linen. I hauled Ethan’s monstrous leather recliner to the curb with immense satisfaction. I purged the walls of every

photograph that documented the charade of my marriage.

In their place, I hung evidence of my actual life. A vibrant watercolor painting I purchased at a local artisan market. A candid, sun-drenched photo of my sister Clare and me laughing uncontrollably on the shores of Lake Michigan. A vintage portrait of my mother. These weren’t expensive artifacts, but they

were authentic. They were proof that Olivia Bennett existed entirely independent of Ethan’s gravitational pull.

The divorce was finalized on an unremarkable Tuesday afternoon in a suffocatingly small conference room that smelled intensely of stale Folgers and printer ozone.

Ethan sat across the laminate table from me. He looked ten years older. The bespoke suit from the trial hung loosely on his diminished frame. Rachel was conspicuously absent. According to Lauren’s intel, she had severed ties with Ethan the moment the criminal fraud referral became public. She was

currently cooperating with the District Attorney’s investigators, trading her testimony for immunity. I didn’t ask for the sordid details. Some knowledge offers zero peace.

The dissolution agreement was a bloodbath in my favor. The house, the retirement accounts, the investments—all untouchable. Furthermore, Ethan was legally mandated to liquidate his failing construction company’s remaining heavy machinery to commence restitution payments for the stolen funds.

I didn’t gloat when Lauren slid the final decree across the table. I didn’t smile. I just picked up the heavy Montblanc pen and signed my name.

For twenty-three years, I had labored under the delusion that marriage meant shouldering the heavy burdens together. I had been catastrophically blind to the fact that Ethan had slowly, masterfully transferred every ounce of his dead weight onto my back, slapping the label of “partnership” on my exploitation.

After the notary stamped the documents, Ethan followed me into the fluorescent-lit hallway.

“Olivia.”

I stopped, my hand resting on the strap of my briefcase, but I didn’t turn to face him. Lauren, ever the apex predator, stepped between us.

Ethan held his hands up defensively. “Lauren, please. Can I just have two minutes to speak to my wife alone?”

“Ex-wife,” Lauren corrected, the word slicing through the air like a scalpel.

I gently touched Lauren’s arm, signaling her to stand down. I turned to face the man who had derailed my life. “You can speak right here, Ethan.”

His jaw tightened, but the fight had been thoroughly beaten out of him. “I know you despise me. I know you hate me.”

“I don’t,” I replied smoothly.

That halted him. He blinked, clearly thrown off his script. “You don’t?”

“No. Hate requires a level of emotional investment and proximity that I am no longer willing to afford you.”

He looked down at his scuffed leather shoes. “I destroyed everything. I was so incredibly stupid.”…

text:
Now you show me proof of your statement. 

Trump said on Fox News (11 September) that he would be “OK” with Chinese automakers opening U.S. plants if they hired American workers. He has said similar things before. No such agreement was announced at the summit. A U.S.–China investment board was mentioned afterward, but the fact sheet does not mention car plants. A 2025 Commerce rule still bars Chinese-controlled firms from selling connected vehicles in the U.S. even if the cars are assembled here. Detroit automakers, the UAW, and several senators are pushing to keep or harden that ban.

Ambassador David Perdue said on Fox (27 September) that Trump asked Xi if China wanted to buy U.S. arms. Trump denied it the next day and suggested Perdue meant Taiwan. The State Department said U.S. law prohibits arms sales to China and there is “no offer or plan.” Officials separately said there are no plans to sell weapons to China. So the ambassador’s remark exists; the administration walked it back.

The dinner happened. Trump publicly floated U.S. plants for Chinese brands. There is no confirmed summit deal on cars, existing rules still block sales of those vehicles, and the weapons claim was denied by the president and State Department. The Michigan line is advocacy, not a documented fact.

text:
Join National Campaigns & Action Days
National Fentanyl Awareness Day: You can join hundreds of organizations by downloading the National Fentanyl Awareness Day Toolkit. Founded by parents who lost loved ones, this initiative focuses on educating youth about counterfeit pills and illicit fentanyl. You can sign up your business, school, or nonprofit as an official partner. 
CDC and SAMHSA Initiatives: The CDC offers a comprehensive National Fentanyl Prevention and Awareness Day Toolkit. It provides ready-to-share social media graphics, fact sheets, and conversation starters to help you spread accurate information online or at local events. 
A Song for Charlie: This prominent national nonprofit focuses on erasing the stigma and educating youth about "fake pills." They provide excellent educational resources and toolkits for parents, educators, and students to start peer-to-peer or family discussions. [4]
Volunteer with Local Harm Reduction & Public Health Programs
Get Narcan (Naloxone) Trained: Many local health departments and community groups offer free training on how to recognize an overdose and administer the life-saving nasal spray, Naloxone. Becoming a certified trainer or distributor allows you to directly protect your community. 
Connect with Opioid Coalitions: Most counties and major cities have dedicated task forces (such as the Sacramento Opioid Coalition in California). These groups frequently look for volunteers to distribute educational materials, host drug take-back days, or share resource hotlines. 
Support Partnership to End Addiction: You can engage in systemic change by participating in grassroots advocacy through organizations like the Partnership to End Addiction. They offer avenues to write to lawmakers supporting legislation (like Bruce's Law) that funds youth fentanyl prevention grants. 
Bring Awareness to Local Schools and Youth Groups
Utilize Stanford's "Aware & Prepare" Curriculum: If you are an educator, parent, or youth leader, you can access the comprehensive Stanford Medicine REACH Lab Curriculum. It provides free, evidence-based lesson plans, videos, and infographics to safely teach young people about the dangers of synthetic opioids and harm reduction. 
Request a Federal/Local Presentation: The Department of Justice and the DEA routinely partner with schools to host panels and screen educational films like Chasing the Dragon. You can coordinate with local school administrators to request a presentation from the U.S. Attorney’s Office Opioid and Fentanyl Awareness Initiative. 
Next Step: A great way to start today is by contacting your local county public health department or searching for a nearby "Opioid Safety Coalition" to see what specific volunteer opportunities or Narcan distribution networks are active right in your immediate neighborhood.

text:
Francesc de Paula Castelló Aleu was born on 19 April 1914 in Alicante, the youngest of three children in a Catalan family. His father died within weeks of his birth, and his mother, a schoolteacher, soon moved the children to Lleida and later to Juneda. She herself died when he was fifteen, leaving him and his two sisters in the care of an aunt and a Jesuit mentor. The early losses did not embitter him. He grew into a cheerful, outgoing young man whose faith was both personal and apostolic.

He studied first with the Marist Brothers in Lleida and then at the Jesuit Chemical Institute in Sarrià. After finishing his degree in chemistry at the University of Oviedo in 1934 he returned to Lleida and took a post as a chemical engineer at the Cros factory. Outside work he joined Catholic Action and the Federation of Young Christians of Catalonia, taught literacy to factory workers, and spent time among the poor of the Canyeret district. In May 1936 he became engaged to María Pelegrí, a young woman who shared his convictions.

The outbreak of the Spanish Civil War found him already in uniform as a conscript in the Republican army. He made no secret of his Catholicism. On the night of 20–21 July 1936 militiamen arrested him on that account alone. He spent the next two months in the castle of Lleida and then in the provincial prison, remaining, witnesses said, surprisingly serene and even cheerful. On 29 September a people’s court offered him the chance to recant. He declined, remarking that if being a Catholic was a crime he accepted the charge gladly, since dying for Christ was the greatest happiness a person could know. That same night he was taken to the cemetery gates and shot. Before the volley he forgave his executioners and called out “Viva Cristo Rey.”

In the hours before his death he wrote three letters—to his fiancée, to his sisters, and to his spiritual director—that later reached Pope Pius XI, who kept them as a model for Catholic youth. The letters speak of an unexpected interior joy and of offering both his love and his life to God. Francesc was twenty-two.

Pope John Paul II beatified him on 11 March 2001 together with 232 other martyrs of the same persecution. His feast is kept on 29 September. A brief life of study, work, friendship and quiet service ended in a public profession of faith; the Church now holds that profession up as a witness that holiness is possible in ordinary occupations and at any age.

Can innocent children, still in their cradles, be killed in the name of Islam? Islamic scholar Abdul Wadood says history offers a chilling warning about what happens when religious texts are distorted to justify violence.

After the Battle of Nahrawan, the Khawarij split into increasingly extreme groups. One was the Azariqa, led by Nafi ibn al-Azraq. According to Abdul Wadood, Nafi declared that those outside his group lived in a land of disbelief, and that Muslims who refused to join his armed struggle were apostates deserving death.

Historical scholars, including al-Shahrastani and Abd al-Qahir al-Baghdadi, wrote that Nafi introduced istirad—the indiscriminate killing of ordinary people encountered by his followers. When questioned about the women and children of their opponents, he misapplied a supplication of Prophet Nuh (peace be upon him) and claimed that even children could be killed because of their parents’ supposed disbelief.

Abdul Wadood draws a parallel with the Army Public School massacre in Peshawar on 16 December 2014. He says TTP militants later used a similar justification, describing the students as children of the army and the state.
His warning is that takfir—declaring others to be disbelievers—can pave the way to violence against civilians, including women and children. He also cautions against taking religious guidance from extremist preachers instead of trusted scholars.

Are schools and parents giving children enough understanding to recognise and resist extremist messages and online networks? Share your thoughts.

text:
"3% is not a genocide." That was your opening line nine days ago and I answered it in the first reply. Srebrenica was under one per cent and two international courts called it genocide. You've not addressed that once. You've just said it again louder.

"Events from decades ago are irrelevant." Two days ago you asked me whether I denied the land was the ancestral homeland of the Jewish people. That's a claim from three thousand years ago, and you offered it as the entitlement to be there now. So which is it? If the past confers nothing, the ancestral homeland confers nothing and Israel's claim is that it's there and has the bigger army, which is at least honest. If the past does confer entitlement, then 1948 and 1967 are in living memory and confer rather more. You brought up 1937, 1947, the Nakba as inevitable, Arafat, Jordan in 1970 and Kuwait in 1991 as well. History is admissible when it's yours and bollocks when it's mine. Name the cut-off.

"Palestinians are saints in your mind." I called 7 October a crime seven times in this thread and you've quoted none of them. Nobody said saints. The point has been the opposite: the law applies to people who aren't saints, because it wouldn't be needed for people who were. Hamas isn't exempt from it and neither is Israel. You want it to apply to one of them.

And native Americans. You raised them, so answer it. Nobody thinks they were saints either. Does that make Wounded Knee fine? Does it make the reservations fine? Or is "they weren't saints" the sentence you reach for when the killing needs a reason and there isn't one?

"Hamas found out what FAFO means." Hamas didn't find out. Twenty thousand children found out. Israel's president said in October 2023 that an entire nation was responsible, and you've just put the same thing in three letters. That's collective punishment, prohibited under Article 33 of the Fourth Geneva Convention, and you've described it as a lesson.

"Legal jargon while his sword is descending." Seventy thousand to twelve hundred. Israel isn't the one under the sword. You're waving the law away because it doesn't work for you, and calling it jargon is the cover. The Genocide Convention was written in 1948 by people who had just walked out of the camps, so that the word would have a legal meaning and not only an emotional one. Either that definition exists or it doesn't. If it doesn't, it doesn't exist for the Holocaust either, or Rwanda, or Srebrenica, and "genocide" is just a word people shout. If it does exist, it applies to Gaza on the same terms as everywhere else, and you have to argue the facts against it rather than the existence of it. You can't keep the word for the crimes you recognise and bin the definition for the one you're defending.

Five replies, and the 1917 question is still unanswered, and I know why. You can't answer it. If your rule applies, the Palestinians in 1917 were entitled to do to the Jews what you say the Jews were entitled to do to them in 1948, and you'd have to say so. If your rule doesn't apply, you've admitted it was never a rule, just a licence for one side, which is a genocide apologist's position dressed up as a principle. Those are the only two doors, which is why you've spent five replies telling me the past doesn't count, the law doesn't count and the comparisons don't count. Any answer ends the argument, and you know it. That's where this ends. The thread is on the record for anyone who wants to read how it got there.

text:
Inside a concrete prison cell in Nuremberg, Hermann Göring stripped away the grand illusions of warfare. Speaking quietly to an American army psychologist, the former Reichsmarschall offered no apologies and no remorse for the catastrophic destruction of Europe. Stripped of his jewel-encrusted medals, tailored uniforms, and paracodeine addiction, the second-most powerful man in the Third Reich was awaiting his sentence before the International Military Tribunal. Observers expected fanatical dogma or legal evasions. Instead, in an intimate exchange with intelligence officer Gustave Gilbert, Göring delivered a cold, clinical analysis of political power. With brutal nonchalance, the architect of Nazi rearmament explained that ordinary citizens never desire war, yet any government on earth—dictatorship or democracy alike—can effortlessly herd its population onto the battlefield.
The man on the iron cot was a shadow of his former public persona, yet mentally formidable. When captured in Austria in May 1945, Göring was bloated and carrying thousands of narcotic pills. Confined behind the Nuremberg Palace of Justice, prison warden Colonel Burton C. Andrus enforced a strict regimen. Deprived of drugs and placed on standard rations, Göring shed eighty pounds, regaining an oratorical sharpness that frequently outmaneuvered chief American prosecutor Robert H. Jackson. Captain Gustave Gilbert, a German-speaking psychologist holding a doctorate from Columbia University, enjoyed daily access to the defendants' cells to document their psychological profiles. Testing placed Göring’s intelligence quotient at 138, among the highest in the prison. During their quiet evening visits, Gilbert probed the inner mechanics of the regime, finding a prisoner who spoke with unsettling candor.
The decisive exchange occurred on April 18, 1946, during a recess in the proceedings. Gilbert stopped by cell number five to discuss the trial's evidence regarding the outbreak of the war, remarking that ordinary people were unlikely to feel grateful toward leaders who brought them ruins. Göring shrugged in contempt. "Why, of course, the people don't want war," Göring replied. "Why would some poor slob on a farm want to risk his life in a war when the best that he can get out of it is to come back to his farm in one piece?" It was a universal truth across all borders: common people never wanted conflict, whether in Russia, Britain, America, or Germany. But that reluctance was politically irrelevant. In the end, Göring explained, leaders determined national policy, and it was "always a simple matter to drag the people along."
Gilbert pushed back, seeking to defend the moral legitimacy of representative government. In a democracy, the psychologist argued, citizens possessed a constitutional voice through their elected representatives, and in the United States, only Congress held the authority to declare war. Göring brushed the objection aside as naive civics. "Oh, that is all well and good," he answered, "but, voice or no voice, the people can always be brought to the bidding of the leaders. That is easy." The mechanism required neither genius nor complicated persuasion: "All you have to do is tell them they are being attacked and denounce the pacifists for lack of patriotism and exposing the country to danger." He paused to emphasize the universal durability of the technique: "It works the same way in any country."
Göring was not sharing an abstract theory; he was describing the operational blueprint he had lived. In August 1939, to justify invading Poland to a populace that dreaded another war, the regime staged the Gleiwitz incident, faking a border attack by SS men disguised in Polish uniforms. For years, state headlines warned that the Fatherland was encircled by mortal enemies, while Gestapo basements swallowed anyone who questioned the militarist consensus. Yet Göring’s revelation was far more disturbing than a confession of Nazi guilt. By asserting that the exact same manipulation worked within free societies, he argued that representative institutions offered no immunity against manufactured hysteria. To the Nazi leader, political morality was merely an ornament, and public consent was just an engineering problem solved by weaponizing fear.
On October 1, 1946, the tribunal found Hermann Göring guilty on all counts, sentencing him to the gallows. But on the night of October 15, barely two hours before the executioner was scheduled to enter his cell, Göring outmaneuvered his captors by swallowing a smuggled glass vial of potassium cyanide. In 1947, Gilbert published his records in Nuremberg Diary, preserving the prisoner's private reflections for posterity. While the Third Reich collapsed into ruins, Göring’s cynical formula outlived the regime that perfected it. Delivered in the quiet of a concrete cell, his words remained an enduring diagnosis of political vulnerability: a chilling reminder that peace does not collapse through the malice of the many, but through the ease with which leaders convince the fearful that survival demands war.
-History After Dark

Here's an example of deviating from Game Theory Optimal strategy on a dating app and still having it work out.

I was just self-amusing. Not trying to "make it work."

I opened her with "Are you real" because her profile was so polished I genuinely didn't think she was a real person.

After her response I went straight into offer proposal mode and suggested "We should do drinks sometime or something"

We had a natural back-and-forth which induced her to invite me straight over to her place.

I ended up staying at her place for multiple days.

And she asked me to be her "boyfriend" within 10 days. (Not that this is a flex.)

The point is it doesn't really matter what you do as long as you have genuine intent to make things happen.

Always be pushing forward.

This is also a chick who thanked me for not doing weird gimmicks and just proposed hanging out immediately.

We matched the night before and were hanging out the next day.

Value LOVES speed.

Most "dating problems" stem from one of three things (and are usually a combination of all three):

1. Low Sexual Marketplace Value - this one is pretty obvious. Gotta increase (perceived Value) in the market.

2. Too high of standards - miscalculation of Sexual Marketplace Value leads to inflated standards and nothing seeming to work out because the person is delusional about what they are "worthy" of.

3. Undertalked about problem but just as important nonetheless: living in a low-Value location. Try and start a luxury used car dealership in bum fuck Wyoming where you can count the population per square mile on one hand and see how many customers you get.

If you're struggling to catch fish in one pond usually the best move isn't to change bait but to change PONDS.

Bottom line here is when she's in the market everything works out how it should.

When she's out of market everything seems impossible.

When really you just have to unmatch and move on to girls who want to work with you.

One state's mobile driver's license launches this December. The state calls it legally equivalent to a physical card. Its own DMV website tells residents to keep carrying the physical card, because not every business or law enforcement agency will have a compatible reader at launch.

That gap is not a technology failure. It is an infrastructure gap. The credential exists. The acceptance layer does not. Twenty-one states now offer a mobile driver's license accepted by TSA, per Governing. Each one launched with a version of the same caveat: valid here, accepted there, pending everywhere else.

Alabama issues a digital license and bans it at the ballot box in the same statute. Other states issue one and recommend keeping the physical card as a backup. The credential is ahead of the infrastructure built to receive it.

text:
52 DAYS WITHOUT OUR VW ID. BUZZ.

Last night I finally stopped by Volkswagen of Perrysburg in person.

The two people I actually needed to speak with about the biggest unanswered question weren’t there:

Why are we waiting on the exact same part AGAIN — a part that was already replaced weeks ago?

I did speak with someone at the service desk, and to say he seemed annoyed by my presence would be putting it nicely. Eye rolls, sighs, an unpleasant tone… basically exactly how you’d hope to be treated after your family vehicle has been sitting at their dealership for 52 days.

I again explained that I’m simply trying to understand what happened. If this part was already replaced, why does it need replaced again? Was the replacement part defective? Was it damaged? Did something happen during installation?

Still no real answer.

But then there was John.

I have absolutely no idea who John was. 😂 He was well dressed, spoke with authority, and definitely gave off the impression that when he talked, people listened.

After about five minutes of conversation, we walked outside. John came with me and basically told me:

Keep prodding them.

He also indicated that he was going to quietly get involved on his end.

I still don’t know who John is, what his title is, or why he happened to be standing there last night…

But John, if you somehow see this:

Thanks for listening.

Because after 52 days, countless emails, unanswered questions, waiting on the same part twice, and still not having our family vehicle back, it was refreshing to have someone inside that building actually seem to understand why I’m frustrated.

So for now…

Day 52.

Still no BUZZ.

Still waiting on the same part.

Still asking the same question.

And apparently, I’m going to keep prodding. 👀
