text:
ANTHROPIC'S IPO PROSPECTUS, SEEN BUT NOT FILED: WHAT A $2 TRILLION AI COMPANY COSTS TO RUN

The most anticipated filing in AI has been read by Reuters, but not by the public. ZB30 searched SEC EDGAR (company search and full-text search for "Anthropic PBC" S-1 filings) late Tuesday morning, Sept. 29, and found no public S-1 or S-1/A from Anthropic. What exists on the record is Anthropic's own June 1 notice: "Today, Anthropic, PBC confidentially submitted a draft registration statement on Form S-1 to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for a proposed initial public offering of our common stock." It added: "The number of shares to be offered and the price have not yet been set." Every figure below comes from the prospectus as reported by Reuters on Monday, Sept. 28. Anthropic declined to comment to Reuters.

THE MONEY (2025, PER THE PROSPECTUS SEEN BY REUTERS)
1. Revenue grew 12-fold to nearly $4.6 billion.
2. Operating loss of more than $8 billion, "excluding writedowns of various liabilities mostly tied to previous fundraising."
3. Net loss of about $42 billion. Reuters says that included "a roughly $34 billion accounting charge" tied to the rising estimated value of financing that could turn into shares, "rather than money the company spent running its business."
4. Compute and infrastructure spending: $7.33 billion, a threefold jump from 2024 and more than half of $12.65 billion in total operating expenses.
5. Future obligations: $518 billion on cloud, computing and infrastructure "in coming years."
6. Cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments: $20.28 billion as of Dec. 31.
7. Customer concentration: nearly a quarter of 2025 revenue came from two customers, and many large clients are not locked into long-term contracts.

Fortune's summary of the leaked draft adds second-quarter 2026 revenue of $11.5 billion, up from $4.73 billion in the first quarter.

THE VALUATION
Reuters reports the public sale "could value it at more than $2 trillion," more than double Anthropic's own estimated valuation of $965 billion in May. That is a target, not a price. No share count, price range or offering size has been disclosed. Reuters previously reported, citing sources, that the debut is likely to be pushed to after the November midterm elections.

WHERE IT WOULD LIST
CNBC confirmed on Sept. 14 that Anthropic has picked the Nasdaq, after Business Insider first reported it. Bloomberg reported the same choice on Sept. 13. ZB30 found no ticker symbol disclosed in any credible report.

WHO CONTROLS IT
A second Reuters report on the filing describes a new "Founder LLC" made up initially of the seven co-founders, individuals the filing calls "distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission." A majority vote of the seven directs a single share of Class F stock carrying 50.1% of total voting power on key matters. Class A stock for ordinary investors gets one vote per share, and there are four other share classes, including one with minimal voting rights for strategic partners. Anthropic stays a Delaware Public Benefit Corporation. The Long-Term Benefit Trust elects four of seven directors. The filing warns the setup could lead to decisions "that may conflict with short-, medium-, or long-term financial interests and business performance, which may negatively impact the value of our Class A common stock." Per Reuters, Dario Amodei made nearly $18 million in 2025, and the co-founders pledged 80% of their personal Anthropic equity to charitable causes.

THE RISK FACTORS
Reuters counts roughly 80 pages of risk factors in a 261-page main body, versus 48 pages on the business. The filing warns advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," and says: "Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm."

ALSO TODAY: A CLAUDE OUTAGE
Separately, Anthropic's status page logged "Elevated errors on https://t.co/Xv4dJs5Hxf, Claude Code, Claude Cowork and the Claude API." Errors began at 14:00 UTC (10:00 AM ET), and most services recovered as of 14:59 UTC (10:59 AM ET). At 11:30 AM ET the page said: "All services have been operating normally since 14:59 UTC. We are continuing to monitor." The page also says some messages sent during that hour may not have been saved. The incident is in Monitoring status.

WHAT WE STILL DO NOT KNOW
When will the public S-1 hit EDGAR? CNBC notes the public prospectus has to reach investors at least 15 days before a roadshow. What are the share count, price range and ticker? Which two customers account for nearly a quarter of revenue? The draft Reuters saw could still change before it is filed.

ZB30 standing by. 🐾

The UK’s nuclear deterrent is set to extend its protection to Europe’s northern and eastern flanks. The United Kingdom has offered to extend its national nuclear deterrent to the nine other members of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF): Denmark, Estonia, Finland, the Netherlands, Iceland, Lithuania, Latvia, Norway and Sweden, according to the Finnish daily Iltalehti.

The information was confirmed in Helsinki by the Chief of the Royal Navy, General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, who stated explicitly that Finland is already covered by Britain’s strategic deterrent, guaranteed by nuclear-powered ballistic-missile submarines maintaining continuous patrols in the Atlantic.

The new defence arrangements are expected to be formalised in November at a summit in Oslo, where the allies are due to sign an agreement establishing new combat structures and deepening military integration. In practice, this would create a regional nuclear-deterrence mechanism within the JEF, operating alongside and complementing NATO’s broader deterrence framework.

Against the backdrop of Russian nuclear coercion and persistent questions over the durability of US security guarantees, London is taking on a more prominent role as a guarantor of security in the Baltic Sea region and the High North. From the Kremlin’s perspective, the risks associated with any military provocation in the region would consequently increase.

“‘But,’ you [Jovinian] will say, ‘it was on Peter that the Church was founded’ [Matt. 16:18]. Well . . . one among the twelve is chosen to be their head in order to remove any occasion for division” (Against Jovinian 1:26 [A.D. 393]).

(H) Pope Saint Innocent I

 “In seeking the things of God . . . you have acknowledged that judgment is to be referred to us [the pope], and have shown that you know that is owed to the Apostolic See [Rome], if all of us placed in this position are to desire to follow the apostle himself [Peter] from whom the episcopate itself and the total authority of this name have emerged” (Letters 29:1 [A.D. 408]).

(I) Saint Augustine

“Among these [apostles] Peter alone almost everywhere deserved to represent the whole Church. Because of that representation of the Church, which only he bore, he deserved to hear ‘I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’” (Sermons 295:2 [A.D. 411]).

“Some things are said which seem to relate especially to the apostle Peter, and yet are not clear in their meaning unless referred to the Church, which he is acknowledged to have represented in a figure on account of the primacy which he bore among the disciples. Such is ‘I will give unto you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,’ and other similar passages” (Commentary on Psalm 108 1 [A.D. 415]).

“Who is ignorant that the first of the apostles is the most blessed Peter?” (Commentary on John 56:1 [A.D. 416]).

(J) Council of Ephesus 

“Philip, presbyter and legate of [Pope Celestine I] said: ‘We offer our thanks to the holy and venerable synod, that when the writings of our holy and blessed pope had been read to you . . . you joined yourselves to the holy head also by your holy acclamations. For your blessedness is not ignorant that the head of the whole faith, the head of the apostles, is blessed Peter the apostle’” (Acts of the Council, session 2 [A.D. 431]).
“Philip, the presbyter and legate of the Apostolic See [Rome] said: ‘There is no doubt, and in fact it has been known in all ages, that the holy and most blessed Peter, prince and head of the apostles, pillar of the faith, and foundation of the Catholic Church, received the keys of the kingdom from our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior and Redeemer of the human race, and that to him was given the power of loosing and binding sins: who down even to today and forever both lives and judges in his successors’” (ibid., session 3).

(K) Pope Saint Leo I

“Our Lord Jesus Christ . . . has placed the principal charge on the blessed Peter, chief of all the apostles, and from him as from the head wishes his gifts to flow to all the body, so that anyone who dares to secede from Peter’s solid rock may understand that he has no part or lot in the divine mystery. He wished him who had been received into partnership in his undivided unity to be named what he himself was, when he said: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church’ [Matt. 16:18], that the building of the eternal temple might rest on Peter’s solid rock, strengthening his Church so surely that neither could human rashness assail it nor the gates of hell prevail against it” (Letters 10:1 [A.D. 445).

text:
Here’s at least three ways Mike Winger adds his own words to scripture and then misinterprets it with a sola scriptura bias.

Mike Winger writes: (no. 3 below) “Jesus rebuked the Pharisees for teaching their traditions which conflicted with and subverted the commands of God in Scripture. He pulled no punches here! Their additions to God’s word were rejected. Their Tradition, along with its supposed claims to merely preserve unwritten teachings from Moses, were subjected to the testing of Scripture. Scripture had authority over the Tradition. Jesus modeled for us the practicing of Sola Scriptura.”

Mike is referencing Matthew’s and Mark’s gospels, chapters 15 and 7 respectively. The obvious import Mike is grasping at is that scripture is the sole infallible rule of faith on which the Tradition of the Catholic Church (and every tradition) must be tested. In other words, according to Mike, the Sacred Tradition the Church transmits is not and cannot be infallibly authoritative. It must be tested against scripture. So, scripture has the final say on the matter. Again, for Mike, scripture is the sole, infallible rule of faith. And for that reason, he reads sola scriptura into these gospel passages and inserts phrases into them like “commands of God in Scripture.”

He’s not engaging in exegesis but rather eisegesis.

Let’s look first at Matthew chapter 15:

Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said, 2 “Why do your disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat.” 3 He answered them, “And why do you transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? 4 For God commanded, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘He who speaks evil of father or mother, let him surely die.’ 5 But you say, ‘If any one tells his father or his mother, What you would have gained from me is given to God, he need not honor his father.’ 6 So, for the sake of your tradition, you have made void the word of God. 7 You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy of you, when he said:

8 ‘This people honors me with their lips,
but their heart is far from me;
 9 in vain do they worship me,
teaching as doctrines the precepts of men.’” (Matt 15:1-9)

Notice that nowhere does Jesus mention the word “scripture.” In fact, nowhere in Matthew 15 is the word “scripture” found. Jesus rebukes the Pharisees and scribes because their human tradition transgressed the “commandment of God” and “made void the word of God.” The “commandment of God” and “word of God” do NOT refer to scripture, but rather to what God himself revealed or spoke to the people Israel through the prophets (such as Isaiah, which Jesus references). These commands and words of God were embedded in the oral tradition of the people Israel and later written down in scripture.

Again, the “commandment of God” and “word of God” do not refer to scripture. In fact, whenever the phrase “word of God” appears in scripture, it does not refer to scripture!

Next, let’s look at Mark 7:

And the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, “Why do your disciples not live according to the tradition of the elders, but eat with hands defiled?” 6 And he said to them, “Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written,

‘This people honors me with their lips,
but their heart is far from me;
 7 in vain do they worship me,
teaching as doctrines the precepts of men.’

8 You leave the commandment of God, and hold fast the tradition of men.”

9 And he said to them, “You have a fine way of rejecting the commandment of God, in order to keep your tradition! 10 For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother’; and, ‘He who speaks evil of father or mother, let him surely die’; 11 but you say, ‘If a man tells his father or his mother, What you would have gained from me is Corban’ (that is, given to God)— 12 then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother, 13 thus making void the word of God through your tradition which you hand on. And many such things you do.” (Mark 7:1-13).

Nowhere in Mark 7 is the word “scripture” mentioned. However, Jesus does say “as it is written” in reference to Isaiah 29:13. However, this is not an example of testing the tradition of the Pharisees and scribes against what is written in Isaiah. Instead, Isaiah offers a rebuke against vain worship and elevating the precepts of men as divinely revealed doctrines.

In Mark 7, Jesus rebukes the Pharisees and scribes specifically because they “leave the commandment of God, and hold fast to the tradition of men.” In other words, they have manufactured religious customs and man-made traditions which they added to the Mosaic Law, and which violated the command of God. Specifically, Jesus denounces their practice of “Corban” which held that giving money to the Temple replaced children’s requirements to honor their parents. This violated God’s commandment to honor one’s father and mother.

Mike Winger writes (no. 4) “Their [Pharisees and scribes] authority was acknowledged and diminished. Jesus acknowledged they sat in Moses’ seat and as much as they merely taught what Moses said they were to be obeyed. But when they added their traditions and rules of man their authority was to be ignored. They were going beyond the sphere where their authority could hold power. Why? Because the power was in Scripture and when they departed from it they went away powerless. Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox authority should be treated the same way.”

Again, nowhere in Matthew 15 or Mark 7 does Jesus say anything about how the teaching power of the Pharisees and scribes must be derived from and verified by scripture. The problem with these men arose because they added human traditions to the Law of Moses that violated the commands of God and the word of God. They saw these human traditions as on par with God’s commands, when they were actually opposed to those commands.

Finally, Mike Winger writes: (no. 5, in reference to John 3) “In the end, Jesus was continuing the work of God and those men could either get with it or get left behind. Some of them got with it. Nicodemus is a wonderful example of a man who was in those ranks who learned that he didn’t know as much as he thought. Jesus exposed the ignorance of Scripture that results from a mind ruled by Tradition when he said to Nicodemus, ‘Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?’”

Again, in John 3 there is no reference from Jesus about “ignorance of scripture.” Instead, Jesus calls Nicodemus’ knowledge into question because he is a teacher of Israel and fails to know what he should know.

What’s the takeaway? Mike Winger is involved in eisegeses. He is reading his own theological views and the Protestant tradition of sola scriptura into the scriptures. The logical extension of Mike’s view is that his reading of scripture and his personal interpretation becomes the sole rule of faith. This is the case because every appeal to scripture is an appeal to an interpretation. The question is, whose interpretation has authority? Is it Mike Winger’s, or is it the Catholic Church who herself recognized which scriptures are indeed the inspired word of God and discerned the biblical canon?

The Sacred Tradition the Church transmits is not a human tradition. On the contrary, it is apostolic tradition—it is divine revelation handed on from the apostles to the Church under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Both Sacred Tradition and Scripture are therefore to be equally venerated as the word of God. Tradition and Scripture are two modes of God’s divine revelation which merge toward the same end.

Dred, the family-sealing idea did not start after Joseph’s death. What was unfolding in Nauvoo, especially in the Red Brick Store, was already a sealing theology of adoption and dynastic linking, not a post-1844 invention.

Don Bradley’s recent work (with Christopher Smith) is useful here even if you reject the later polygamy story, as we do. They show that the earliest meaning of ritual sealing was vertical: children to fathers, hearts turned across generations, people grafted into a priesthood family. Elijah’s keys were about binding generations, not creating a secret marriage system. Eliza Jane Webb’s account of Fanny Alger as an “adopted daughter,” sealed at the time of that adoption, is one piece of that older adoptive language. So is Emma’s offer to Jane Manning James that she could be adopted into the Smith family by priesthood sealing, an offer Jane later said she declined because she did not yet understand the law of adoption.

That is the same trajectory Joseph was on in 1843: sealing people into an eternal family order, spouses, children, deceased kin, trusted friends, while the ordinances were still in early form. The Red Brick Store was where those first endowments and sealings were worked out. Joseph was killed before the temple could finish the system. Brigham and the Twelve then expanded and redirected it.

Family sealing started under Joseph. It was adoptive and dynastic first. It was unfinished when he died.

text:
***Give Me the Bull***

A mortal king scorned my name
Gilgamesh — he listed my shame
He named the lovers my wanting broke
I offered — he would not take

Father Anu — hear what I claim
I will not soften
I will not shrink
Pride is a storm — not a tear I wipe
I want the sky-beast
Give me the Bull

If you deny me
The earth will shake

Give me the Bull
Let Gilgamesh fall
Give me the Bull
Of Heaven — my call
Gates of the underworld
I'll break their hold
The dead will rise
To eat the living
The dead will rise
Outnumber the living

He kept his throne
He left my bed
He refused me — that is what he said
Not plea — not soft — not fate accepted
A goddess scorned is a law corrected

Anu — open what the heavens keep
The Bull of Heaven — the one I seek
Not for a wedding
Not for a song
For the king who sang that I was wrong

If you deny me
The earth will shake

Give me the Bull
Let Gilgamesh fall
Give me the Bull
Of Heaven — my call
Gates of the underworld
I'll break their hold
The dead will rise
To eat the living
The dead will rise
Outnumber the living

I am not asking for a kinder end
I am asking for the weight I send
Open the sky or I open the deep
The dead will rise — the city won't sleep
Seven years of husks if you make me wait —
Still I want the Bull
Still I will not break

Give me the Bull
Let Gilgamesh fall
Give me the Bull
Of Heaven — my call
If you deny me
I break the hold
The dead will rise
To eat the living
Outnumber the living

Give me the Bull
If you deny me
The dead will rise

-------------------------------------

Give Me the Bull: the story behind the song (Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet VI)

Gilgamesh has just refused Ishtar. In Track 7 he stood in front of her offer and said no, and he used her ruined lovers as evidence. The goddess of love and war does not take that answer quietly.

She does not go back to her temple to cry. She goes up. She climbs to her father, Anu, the sky-god, and what she brings him is less a petition than a demand. Give me the Bull of Heaven, she says. Put that beast in my hands so I can send it against Gilgamesh and against Uruk.

The Bull of Heaven is not a farm animal. In the Mesopotamian imagination it is a sky-beast, a living storm of drought and trampling force that belongs to the gods. To ask for it is to ask for a weapon that can empty a city of water and life. Ishtar is not asking for a wedding gift. She is asking for a sentence.

Anu hesitates, as fathers sometimes do when a daughter arrives furious and asks for something that will ruin a kingdom. He warns her. He asks what will happen to Uruk if the Bull comes down. Ishtar does not soften. She raises the threat that sits at the center of this song.

If you deny me, she says, I will smash the gates of the underworld. I will raise the dead so they eat the living, and the dead will outnumber those who still breathe. In some tellings she also threatens seven years of husks, years when the land yields nothing and the city starves. Either way the shape is the same: refuse me, and I will unmake the boundary between life and death.

That is the hinge of Track 8. It is not yet the fight. The Bull has not descended. Gilgamesh and Enkidu have not yet met the horns. This song lives in the courtroom of heaven, in the scorched pride of a goddess who was told no by a mortal king, and in the moment when desire turns into policy. Pride is no longer a private wound. It becomes a storm she is willing to spend the world to feed.

Zi has been building toward this. Track 1 was her honey. Tracks 2 through 6 were the lovers she spent. Track 7 was the king's catalog and his refusal. Now the album turns to her answer, and her answer is not remorse. It is a bull called down from the sky, held out as the cost of being refused.

The song ends still on the ask. "Give me the Bull." "If you deny me." "The dead will rise." The threat hangs open for Anu to answer. What follows, when the Bull actually comes, belongs to the next chapter of the epic and to later tracks on the album.

It is they who do not accept that Israel has a right to exist as a separate state, not Israel that denies their right to exist as a separate state.

The 1947 UN plan was accepted by the Jewish side but rejected by Arab states and Palestinian leaders, who chose to launch a war instead. After 1967 the Khartoum summit adopted “no peace, no recognition of Israel, no negotiations.” Later offers at Camp David (2000) and by Ehud Olmert (2008) were also not accepted.

Hamas’s founding documents and its practice continue to treat Israel’s elimination as the goal. The Palestinian Authority has never formally recognized Israel as a Jewish state and continues practices (incitement, payments to attackers’ families) that undermine a two-state outcome.

These are historical and political facts, independent of any theological argument. Are you willing to acknowledge them?

As well as acknowledge that Israel - the state of Israel - has legitimate security concerns? Those concerns rest on the same record: multiple wars launched or joined by neighboring states, two intifadas featuring suicide bombings, thousands of rockets from Gaza and Lebanon, and the October 2023 attack.

A state that has faced repeated attempts to destroy it has legitimate grounds to treat territorial withdrawals and a neighboring Palestinian entity as high-risk unless credible security arrangements exist.

My acknowledging the historical facts and the real security issues does not require my endorsing religious Zionist theology, which I adamantly reject. Rather it follows from the pattern of rejection and violence on the part not only of the Palestinians but of all the other states such as Iran that are using it in its effort to eliminate Israel.

The Vatican itself recognizes Israel’s right to live in security within internationally recognized borders. And while it has noted the charge of "ethnic cleansing" that others have made, it has never made a statement directly accusing Israel of that itself.

And as for that charge, that's a prudential judgment that requires one accept the lopsided asymmetry of the global/globalist organizations responsible for making the assessment. 

Israel has an official policy of wiping out Hamas, not Palestinians. The Palestinians meanwhile have made it quite clear that they seek the complete elimination of Israel, not only the state but of all the Jews living there. Why no similar charge against them, especially post the horrific atrocity of October 7?

Groups that openly seek the end of Israel and often even of Jews are widely spared the word “genocide.” A state that does not have that as official doctrine, and that still has two million Palestinians alive in Gaza after a long war, is saturated with it. That gap is not explained by legal doctrine alone. It is explained by who holds the microphone in international institutions, universities, and much of the press, and by a moral narrative that treats Jewish sovereignty as the original sin and Palestinian maximalism as a cry of the oppressed.

Those of us who seek true and long-lasting peace in the Middle East recognize that the continued condemnation of Israel (while giving Palestine a pass on its behavior, if not outrightly justifying it) only encourages the continued refusal of the Palestinians and their terrorist leaders (and states like Iran) to accept the two-state solution and acknowledge Israel's right to exist.

text:
Can someone explain to me how Anthropic could be worth $2T when SpaceX is worth only ~$1.9T

People treating this like a pure AI-vs-AI comparison are missing the point. $SPCX is not “an AI company that also does rockets.” It’s a vertically integrated industrial company that happens to own one of the frontier labs.

SpaceX already operates six real businesses:

1. Rockets. Falcon still flies the majority of the world’s commercial launches. Starship is the vehicle that actually changes the cost of mass to orbit. That is not a software option. It’s factories, engines, pads, and flight cadence. And it's not a future possibility. It's a reality. Starship reached orbit yesterday and deployed 26 v3 Starlink satellites. The moat around the rocket business is the biggest moat in the entire market.

2. Starlink. ~12 million subscribers, the cash engine of the company with a huge growth curve over the next couple years. Consumer, aviation, maritime, enterprise, and direct-to-cell.

3. Starshield. Separate national-security constellation. Multi-year U.S. government awards already north of $6B. That is a defense contractor sitting inside the same company.

4. Compute and chips. SpaceX is building and leasing physical infrastructure: Colossus-scale clusters, AI data centers, and a push into chip design/manufacturing (Terafab with Tesla and Intel). In the filings, “AI solutions & infrastructure” is already a real revenue line — renting GPU capacity, not just selling tokens. That is closer to a neocloud / foundry story than to a frontier lab.

5. The Do-Everything App, X. Money, encrypted chats, spaces, video chats coming, a funnel to Grok, data to perpetually train the AI model. 

6. AI. Grok, Grok bot, APIs. 

Anthropic does not have 1 - 5. Anthropic is in the lead on 6, but SPCX is maybe 6 months behind and is catching up quickly. And if you understand the potential catastrophic effect of open-source AI models, this is the most vulnerable sector. And that's all Anthropic has to offer. 

Anthropic is an extraordinary lab with Claude and a steep revenue curve. Last priced round was $965B. A $2T IPO would be the market paying almost entirely for model quality, enterprise API demand, and the assumption that growth stays vertical and an open source model doesn't destroy its value.

SpaceX is priced for launch dominance + a global comms network + a government payload franchise + fab and compute + an AI layer that can ride its own rockets and power its own satellites and fits in an existing platform used by 550M people in the past month.

One company sells tokens. The other sells tokens AND builds the infrastructure that puts tokens, satellites, and megawatts into orbit and everyone's pockets all at once.

If Anthropic IPOs at $2T, one or the other will happen: (A) Anthropic shareholders get crushed, or (B) SPCX gets repriced toward $4T.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐨𝐧 𝐛𝐞𝐭𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐍𝐢𝐱𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐌𝐨𝐨𝐝𝐲 𝐢𝐬 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐱 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 "𝟑𝟐-𝐭𝐨-𝟏" 𝐟𝐢𝐠𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐭. 𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬:

𝐓𝐡𝐞 "𝟑𝟐-𝐭𝐨-𝟏" 𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐜𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐨𝐨𝐝𝐲’𝐬 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐨𝐧 𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐝 ($𝟖.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧) 𝐭𝐨 𝐍𝐢𝐱𝐨𝐧’𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬 ($𝟐𝟔𝟓,𝟎𝟎𝟎) 𝐲𝐢𝐞𝐥𝐝𝐬 𝐚 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨 𝐨𝐟 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝟑𝟏.𝟕-𝐭𝐨-𝟏, 𝐰𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐡 𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐬 𝐜𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐭𝐡𝐞 "𝟑𝟐-𝐭𝐨-𝟏" 𝐟𝐢𝐠𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐭. 𝐇𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫, 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨 𝐫𝐞𝐟𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐛𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐲 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐭𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝. 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐟𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐧 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐬
𝐃𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐚 𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲, 𝐦𝐮𝐥𝐭𝐢𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐩𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐠𝐚𝐩 𝐛𝐞𝐭𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐍𝐢𝐱𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐌𝐨𝐨𝐝𝐲 𝐢𝐬 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐧𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐩𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝:

𝐀 𝐒𝐭. 𝐏𝐞𝐭𝐞 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞𝐲 (𝐦𝐢𝐝-𝐒𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫) 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐝 𝐌𝐨𝐨𝐝𝐲 𝐚𝐭 𝟒𝟓.𝟐% 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐍𝐢𝐱𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐭 𝟒𝟒.𝟖%—𝐚 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐫. 𝐈𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐩𝐨𝐥𝐥, 𝐍𝐢𝐱𝐨𝐧 𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐯𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬, 𝟓𝟎% 𝐭𝐨 𝟑𝟕%.

𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐮𝐬 𝐈𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐬 (𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐒𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫) 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐝 𝐌𝐨𝐨𝐝𝐲 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐛𝐲 𝟕 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐩𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐬 (𝟓𝟎% 𝐭𝐨 𝟒𝟑%).

𝐒𝐭𝐞𝐭𝐬𝐨𝐧 𝐔𝐧𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐲 (𝐦𝐢𝐝-𝐭𝐨-𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐒𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫) 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐝 𝐌𝐨𝐨𝐝𝐲 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐛𝐲 𝟏𝟏 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐩𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐬 (𝟓𝟏% 𝐭𝐨 𝟒𝟎%).

𝐀𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐍𝐢𝐱𝐨𝐧 𝐰𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐲, *𝐒𝐚𝐛𝐚𝐭𝐨’𝐬 𝐂𝐫𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐁𝐚𝐥𝐥* 𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐝𝐚 𝐒𝐞𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐬𝐞𝐚𝐭 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 "𝐋𝐢𝐤𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧" 𝐭𝐨 "𝐒𝐚𝐟𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧," 𝐜𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐨𝐟 𝐖𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐦𝐚𝐧’𝐬 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐚𝐬 𝐚 𝐟𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐰𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐰𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐮𝐥𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐬. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 *𝐂𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭* 𝐬𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐞𝐚𝐭 𝐚𝐬 "𝐒𝐚𝐟𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧."

𝐍𝐢𝐱𝐨𝐧’𝐬 𝐎𝐰𝐧 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧
𝐎𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐒 𝐍𝐎𝐖 𝐩𝐨𝐝𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐭 "𝐂𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐤 𝐈𝐭 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐒𝐲𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐞 & 𝐄𝐮𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐞," 𝐍𝐢𝐱𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐰𝐨 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩'𝐬 𝐡𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧:

𝐈𝐝𝐞𝐨𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐲. "𝐈 𝐚𝐦 𝐚 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐈 𝐚𝐦 𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐯𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐩𝐮𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠-𝐜𝐥𝐚𝐬𝐬 𝐟𝐚𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭."

𝐑𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫. "𝐏𝐞𝐨𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐚 𝐛𝐢𝐭 '𝐠𝐮𝐧-𝐬𝐡𝐲' 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞, 𝐮𝐧𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐮𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲, 𝐕𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐬—𝐚 𝐁𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐰𝐨𝐦𝐚𝐧—𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐭; 𝐬𝐨 𝐩𝐞𝐨𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐡𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐁𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐰𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐧, 𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐡."

𝐀 𝐬𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐨𝐫 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐚𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐟𝐚𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐫 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐚 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐨 𝐌𝐒 𝐍𝐎𝐖: 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐚 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐒𝐞𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐟𝐥𝐢𝐩 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐝 𝐝𝐫𝐚𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐢𝐧 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡𝐬, 𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐚𝐩 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐚 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐥𝐲 𝐝𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧 𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐩𝐮𝐬𝐡—𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐚 "𝐬𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐚𝐝𝐯𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞." 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐝𝐚 𝐢𝐬 𝐚 𝐭𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡 𝐛𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐥𝐞𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐚 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐲; 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐝𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐫 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐚 𝐝𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐛𝐞 𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐨𝐧 𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐧𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞. #𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐥𝐝𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭 #𝐀𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐞𝐍𝐢𝐱𝐨𝐧 #𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐝𝐚 #𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐲

⭕️ “For every $32 that Ashley Moody has right now, Angie Nixon has $1.”

Data analyst Nathan Jun says the Democratic Party has withheld funding from Nixon even as a poll shows the Florida Democratic Senate nominee running neck and neck with the Republican incumbent. He asks why Democrats call Black women “the backbone” of the party but won’t invest in a candidate who won her primary despite being heavily outspent.

MS NOW’s Ayman Mohyeldin says Nixon faces two hurdles with party leaders: she is a Black woman running in the South, and she is a progressive. Democrats have been slow to back candidates who build support outside the party establishment, he explains, even when those candidates show they can win.

☝️👇 Wildfowl conference 1927 / wildfowl conservation law, 3 of 3 / contd.

“▪️ What followed

ICBP’s own later history is blunt: “Nothing came of this Conference.”

 In 1936 Lowe set up the Wildfowl Inquiry Committee of the British Section to start again with counts and ringing. From that committee came the International Wildfowl Research Bureau (1947), now Wetlands International. The 1950 International Convention for the Protection of Birds (Paris) and the 1971 Ramsar Convention on wetlands are the first binding instruments that look like the 1927 list. The EU Birds Directive (1979, recast 2009) later wrote close seasons, method bans, sale controls and SPAs into hard law. AEWA (1995) did the same for African–Eurasian waterbirds.

So London 1927 is the moment the Swedish initiative and Lowe’s pamphlet became an official European wish-list, and the moment governments refused to make that list a treaty. The six points are the bridge between Pycraft’s 1926 page and the statutes that finally arrived a generation later.

🔸 What Sweden did with the result

At the ICBP meeting in Geneva in May 1928, the Swedish memorandum had three heads. The first was that as many European countries as possible should accept the London 1927 resolutions on migratory ducks and waders.

The initiative sat on top of an older, weaker instrument. Sweden had signed the 1902 Paris Convention on useful birds, but that treaty split species into “useful to agriculture” and “harmful,” and left ducks and waders largely to national game law. Sweden only wrote the 1902 principles into its hunting statutes in 1907. Versailles kept the 1902 convention alive; a Luxembourg bird-protection congress in 1925 began talking about revising it. Lönnberg’s campaign was an attempt to do what Paris 1902 had not: treat migratory quarry as a shared stock, not as a list of farmer’s friends and farmer’s enemies.

▪️ The shape of the Swedish case

Three things distinguish it from a purely British bird-lovers’ brief:

- It came through hunters’ organisations as well as museums. Regulation of methods, not abolition of shooting, was the offer to other governments.

- It was flyway thinking before that word was common: the breeding grounds were in the north, the killing was elsewhere, so unilateral Swedish law could not save the stock.

- It wanted governments, not only the ICBP. Copenhagen produced a scientific committee; London was meant to be an official conference. It remained a conference of wishes. Binding European wildfowl rules came much later, through national close seasons, the 1950 Paris bird convention, the 1979 Birds Directive, and AEWA.

Lönnberg kept the same brief at home: Swedish waterfowl law, ringing from the Riksmuseum (from 1913), and later the book 'Svenska fåglars flyttning'. The 1925–27 initiative is the moment when that domestic conservationist tried to make the rest of the flyway do the same.”
(Source: Grok AI)

a lawsuit would be likely if Ralph Norman received the most votes as a write-in.South Carolina’s “sore-loser” statute (S.C. Code § 7-11-210) requires primary candidates to pledge they will not “offer or campaign as a write-in candidate” after losing. The Republican Party chairman can seek a court injunction to stop any such campaigning. Norman has already publicly disavowed a write-in effort and pledged to support Darline Graham.

The law targets the candidate’s own actions, not the votes themselves. Write-in votes for any name are counted, and there is no filing requirement that would automatically disqualify Norman. If he won solely through uncoordinated voter write-ins, a court might still face arguments over whether the pledge or “sore-loser” rule makes him ineligible to take office. The losing campaign or the state Republican Party would almost certainly file an election contest or seek to block certification. No modern South Carolina precedent exists for throwing out a write-in plurality on these grounds, so the outcome would be uncertain and would likely be decided after the election"

text:
🛑 Illegal Alien Charged With Striking ICE Officer in the Torso Before Austin Shooting 🛑

If you want to know why an ICE agent opened fire on an illegal alien who fled from a stop at dangerously high speeds, here it is:

Federal prosecutors in the Western District of Texas have charged Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez, 28, an illegal alien from Venezuela, with one count of assaulting, resisting, interfering with, and impeding a federal officer.  He made his initial appearance in federal court on September 29 before US Magistrate Judge Dustin Howell.  The case comes out of the September 20 ICE stop in North Austin that ended with an ICE officer firing his pistol.

According to the criminal complaint, ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officers pulled him over because an immigration judge had issued a final order of removal against him.  He handed the officers his driver's license, and they told him to put the car in park and step out.  Prosecutors say he ignored them.  In the Justice Department's words: "The complaint alleges and body camera footage shows that after further direction from the officers in Spanish, Garces-Perez abruptly closed his window and drove off, striking one of the ICE ERO officers in the torso with the driver's side-view mirror."

The timeline, in Austin local time, starts at 12:42 PM.  At that point the dashcam of an off-duty Austin police detective recorded two unmarked black SUVs stopped in front of and behind his blue Toyota, with emergency lights on the rear vehicle, according to the Austin American-Statesman.  Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said the stop was on Anderson Square, just south of US 183.  Prosecutors say he then drove off, struck the officer with his mirror, and led officers on a high-speed chase through a commercial and residential area while they ran lights and sirens.  One officer lost sight of him.  

The complaint alleges that when the second officer caught up, Garces-Perez tried to strike that officer with his car, causing the officer to fire.  His own lawyers' court filing puts the shooting at about 12:56 PM near West Anderson Lane and Research Boulevard, and a second video from the detective captured three gunshots.  ICE took him into custody from Dell Seton Medical Center at about 4:30 PM and moved him to the Pearsall processing center at about 4 AM on September 21.

The Statesman reported that the officer who fired was treated for an ankle sprain, a knee sprain, and contusions, based on medical records the paper reviewed.  The Justice Department release does not describe the injuries from the mirror strike.  Garces-Perez was shot in the torso, according to his habeas petition.

DHS says he entered illegally under the Biden administration, that his work permit expired in 2025, and that an immigration judge ordered him removed in absentia after he failed to appear.  His attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, says he came through a CBP One appointment in 2024 and missed the hearing because the notice went to an old address.  His own habeas petition states that he "does not challenge the validity of his removal order."

If convicted, he faces up to 20 years in federal prison.  A detention hearing is set for Friday, October 2.  Separately, US District Judge Orlando Garcia has set a hearing on his habeas petition for Wednesday, September 30, at noon in San Antonio and ordered him to appear.  

Homeland Security Investigations is handling the assault case, and Assistant US Attorney Britni Verdeja is prosecuting.  Austin police and the Texas Rangers are investigating the shooting, and the Travis County District Attorney has asked DHS to halt his removal because he is a material witness.

My take: the detective's dashcam shows a stop with lights on at 12:42 PM, fourteen minutes before the shot, and his own lawyer told the Statesman she could not "confidently tell you the chain of events."  Now a federal complaint cites body camera footage of him driving off and hitting an officer in the torso with his mirror before trying to hit a second officer with his car.  That footage gets tested in front of a judge at the October 2 hearing, and it will say more about what happened on Anderson Square than anything his side has offered so far.

text:
From grok
“As of the latest official figures, the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve holds about 284 million barrels, and there is no single inventory level at which the salt caverns suddenly collapse. The risk is gradual and operational, not a cliff.
Current SPR inventory
Two closely related numbers are circulating this week:
•284.55 million barrels as of the week ending September 18, 2026 (EIA weekly series)
•283.8 million barrels as of last Friday, according to Department of Energy data reported Monday. That is the lowest level since October 1982.
That is roughly 40% of the reserve’s authorized capacity of about 714 million barrels. Peak inventory was 726.6 million barrels in early 2010.
The latest DOE split was about 96.8 million barrels of sweet crude and 186.9 million barrels of sour crude.
The ZeroHedge post is about a new offer of up to 40 million barrels as an exchange (a loan that companies must later return with extra barrels). That is leftover volume from the 172 million-barrel U.S. share of the March 2026 IEA coordinated release. A similar 40 million-barrel offer in June drew almost no interest (about 500,000 barrels). If the full 40 million were actually taken from today’s level, inventory would fall to roughly 244 million barrels.
How low before “damage to the reservoir”?
The caverns are not empty space. Oil floats on brine. Drawdown pumps freshwater in, oil out. The cavern stays full; only the oil-to-water ratio changes. Freshwater also dissolves salt, which slowly changes cavern shape. That is the real constraint.
Different numbers mean different things:
Threshold
What it actually is
~300 million bbl
Expert warning range. High-rate emergency pumping gets harder; operational and geomechanical margins tighten. Not an official collapse line.
250–300 million bbl
Practical operating floor cited by Texas A&M petroleum engineer Siddharth Misra for safer high-rate operations. Current inventory is already testing this band.
252.4 million bbl
Legal floor for limited (non-emergency) drawdowns under federal law. Emergency drawdowns can still go lower.
~150–170 million bbl
“Soft floor” used by some analysts (Rapidan, others) for cavern stability plus pumping flexibility.
~70 million bbl
DOE’s conservative systemwide operating minimum (about 10% of capacity). Roughly the oil that must stay so extraction pipes remain in oil, not water. DOE has described this as a cavern-mechanics floor, not a collapse point.
DOE’s public position is that the caverns are “always full” and that the conservative operating minimum is about 70 million barrels. Officials have rejected the claim that dropping below 300 million barrels will collapse the caverns.
Independent experts are more cautious. Misra has said the practical floor for safe high-rate use is 250–300 million barrels; below that, risk rises…

Bottom line
•Now: about 283.8–284.6 million barrels.
•Legal limited-drawdown stop: 252.4 million.
•Expert “elevated operational risk” zone: already here, and clearly so below ~250 million.
•DOE physical operating floor: about 70 million, after which the system is effectively empty for emergency use even if some oil remains.
A further 40 million-barrel exchange would take the SPR below the statutory limited-drawdown floor and deeper into the range experts flag for slower drawdown rates and higher cavern-wear risk. It would still be well above DOE’s 70 million-barrel mechanical floor. There is no published official number at which the salt domes “collapse.” The documented risk is cumulative leaching, thinner pillars, lower sustainable pump rates, and fewer remaining full drawdowns per cavern.”

text:
$VST $MTZ Given recent movements, I do want to say..neither thesis is broken. 

In fact, the physical-infrastructure thesis has received additional confirmation in September. 

But MasTec has acquired materially more financial risk, while Vistra’s thesis has become more tangible and contracted.

MasTec paid approximately $1.6 billion for The Superior Group, ~$1.2 billion cash, ~$410.5 million stock and potential additional earn-out. The company financed the cash portion partly with new borrowing.

And MasTec subsequently issued $650 million of 5.85% senior notes due 2036.

That’s not necessarily bad. Superior is exactly the sort of electrical/data-center infrastructure capability that MasTec wants.

But it changes the investment from:“Capital-light infrastructure contractor benefiting from a secular cycle” toward “Aggressive infrastructure consolidator using debt and acquisitions to capture a secular cycle.”

That’s a higher-risk proposition.

There’s also a subtle backlog issue

MasTec explicitly says 40% of its backlog comes from master-service and other service agreements where customers are not contractually committed to minimum purchases. Those agreements can generally be canceled on short notice.

That means: $21.4 billion backlog ≠ $21.4 billion guaranteed revenue. That’s an important correction to the simplistic bull thesis.

Still, backlog is up 30%, and the strongest growth is precisely in Power Delivery and Clean Energy and Infrastructure. So I don’t see evidence of the capital cycle turning against MasTec yet.

For $VST, I actually think the thesis has become stronger. 

Data-center developers are increasingly turning to behind-the-meter natural-gas generation because traditional grid connections are taking too long.

Enverus estimates that the United States could add 29.6 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas generation by 2030, with data centers accounting for approximately 88% of it. 

The bottleneck is increasingly electricity availability, not artificial-intelligence chips.

On September 18, Vistra’s Luminant subsidiary signed a 20-year power purchase agreement with New Era Energy & Digital.

It will supply 200–207 megawatts from Vistra’s 1,180-megawatt Odessa natural-gas plant to a Texas critical data-center project.

And this is the part I really like: Vistra receives a 5% non-voting equity interest in the relevant data-center project.

It also gets right of first refusal on future power opportunities at the site, right of first offer on certain other projects, and reimbursement for certain transmission/substation construction costs.

That's a real economic relationship. 

I am still owning these two as of now. Curious to see what happens next.

I never thought the person who would hurt me the most would be the person I trusted like family.

My name is Emily, and I grew up in Dallas, Texas. My best friend, Madison, had been beside me since college. We went through breakups, job problems, family arguments, and everything in between. I trusted her with things I had never told anyone else.

When I finally started my own small event-planning business, Madison was the first person I told.

She celebrated with me.

At least, I thought she did.

My business started growing quickly. I was organizing weddings, birthday parties, corporate events, and private celebrations across Dallas and Fort Worth. Madison began helping me with bookings and social media.

Because she was my best friend, I never questioned anything.

Then one Friday afternoon, a wealthy client called me.

She sounded confused.

“Emily, I thought you canceled our event.”

I froze.

“I never canceled anything.”

She told me that someone had contacted her using my business information and offered to organize the event for a much cheaper price.

Then she sent me screenshots.

text:
Jake Wood reveals why nine out of ten combat veterans want to keep serving even after the uniform comes off:

He lost the friend who deployed beside him to the exact problem he was trying to solve, and what he built out of that loss became one of the fastest growing relief organizations in the country:

1. The number nobody talks about
Most people assume veterans come home wanting distance from the fight, wanting rest, wanting to be left alone. Wood stood on a TEDx stage and told the audience the data says the opposite.

"After fighting overseas, 92 percent of American veterans say they want to continue their service."

They are not asking to be done. They are asking for a new mission.

2. The system was already broken
People assume disaster relief runs on the best available tools and the best available people. Wood found something slower and older underneath the surface.

"The first is that there's inadequate disaster relief. It's slow, it's antiquated, it's not using the best technology and it's not using the best people," says Wood in his talk.

A system built to move fast when lives are on the line was moving at the speed of bureaucracy.

3. The second broken system
Wood did not stop at disaster relief. He pointed at the other half of the equation sitting right next to it.

"The second problem … is very inadequate veteran reintegration. It's a topic that's front-page news right now."

Two failures were sitting side by side and nobody had connected them yet.

4. Struggling is not a character flaw
It would be easy to write off a hard transition home as a personal weakness. Wood framed it as a systems failure instead.

"As veterans are coming back from Iraq and Afghanistan, they are struggling to reintegrate back into civilian life."

Struggling was the predictable outcome of pulling a man out of a mission and handing him nothing to replace it.

5. From Sergeant to nobody
In uniform, rank gives a man a role, a title, a reason people look to him. Wood described exactly what disappears the moment that uniform comes off.

A veteran returning to society is "no longer Sargent Jones in his community, his is now Dave from Kansas City."

The need for purpose does not retire with the uniform. Only the outlet for it does.

6. The friend who fought beside him
Before this was a talk about systems, it was a story about one man. Wood introduced him plainly, without any softening.

"This is Clay Hunt. Clay was a Marine with me. We served together in Iraq and Afghanistan."

Some bonds get built under fire and never come apart, even when the fight changes shape.

7. He kept answering the call
When Wood needed people who would show up for strangers in the worst conditions imaginable, Hunt did not hesitate. He went exactly the way he had gone into combat.

"Clay was with us in Port-au-Prince. He was also with us in Chile."

Service did not end at discharge for Hunt. It just found new addresses.

8. Doing everything right is not always enough
This is the part of the story that refuses to offer comfort. A man who kept showing up, kept serving, kept helping strangers rebuild their lives, still lost his own fight.

"Earlier this year, in March, Clay took his own life."

Wood did not use this as a footnote. He used it as the reason the whole organization exists.

9. Purpose is not optional equipment
Two words carry more weight in this talk than any statistic Wood cites.

"He lost purpose."

A man can survive firefights and still be undone by the absence of something to fight for.

10. Isolation is its own kind of casualty
The second half of that same sentence is just as important as the first.

"He lost his community."

Wood built Team Rubicon on the belief that giving both of those back, purpose and community, could be the difference between a veteran who rebuilds and one who does not.

BJ has said for years that the fight after the fight is the one that actually kills people, and Jake Wood's story is proof that the answer was never sitting in a pill bottle or a support group flyer. It was sitting in a mission that still needed him. Clay Hunt did everything the system asked of him and still slipped through, and Wood turned that loss into an organization that hands veterans exactly what they lost the day they took off the uniform: something that depends on them showing up. That is the whole philosophy of living on the Good Foot. You do not wait to be rescued. You go be the rescue for somebody else, and somewhere in that work you rescue yourself too.

Source video: https://t.co/FIZY3mA224

I write one story like this every week for veterans and anyone rebuilding. Get it here:
https://t.co/mJz6Qq9aev

A veteran, a dog, a mission.

text:
I don’t care about Candace Owens at all, except in how this all relates to political warfare & our current cultural landscape. 
She’s just one of many figures who have chosen to take part in our cultural destabilization, & she’s possibly reached the end of her usefulness. Participating in cultural revolutions & mass movements often ends badly for people, & we only need to look to the history of the 20th century to understand this - the entire century is marred by the devastation of multitudes of mass movements. Those who actively participate in the machinations of mass movements are usually chewed up horrifically & discarded when their utility has been depleted. 

One of my main interests for the past ~6 years has been the psychology & sociology of mass movements, group-think, & the processes that facilitate the loss of cognitive liberty. It never works out well for anyone who participates in mass movements, although the severity & permanence of the damage varies. Making oneself a “voice” or public figure for a mass movement opens one up for truly terrible repercussions as the process of dialectical political warfare plays out (permanent revolution, perpetual conflict, endless cycling through designations of “friends” & “enemies”). It’s ugly stuff, but seeing these public humiliation rituals play out so visibly should be a warning to people of what bad can come when one chooses to participate in a mass movement & accepts the framing of political warfare & the friend/enemy distinction. 

From Eric Hoffer’s The True Believer:
“Passionate hatred can give meaning and purpose to an empty life. This people haunted by the purposelessness of their lives try to find a new content not only by dedicating themselves to a holy cause but also by nursing a fanatical grievance. A mass movement offers them unlimited opportunities for both.” 

Mass movements are consumed by obsessions over friends & enemies, grievances, & allegiance. They are unstable, illogical, & destructive. Beware.

text:
Financial headlines are reporting Notice 2026-62 as a total shutdown of Section 351 ETF conversions.

That is not what the documents say.

The premise behind a Section 351 exchange remains intact: You have a concentrated stock position with substantial embedded gains. You contribute an eligible basket into a newly formed ETF. Section 351 defers the gain and carries your cost basis into the fund shares.

Nothing in Monday’s release repealed Section 351.

What the IRS struck down in Rev. Rul. 2026-20 is an orchestrated round trip: 

• An investor contributes appreciated stock into a new ETF. 
• The ETF issues shares to an Authorized Participant (AP). 
• Pursuant to the same prearranged plan, the ETF redeems the AP out using the investor's original stock. 
• The appreciated stock exits the fund without recognized gain.

The IRS applied longstanding step-transaction doctrine: they collapsed the steps and ruled it a direct, taxable exchange between the investor and the AP under Section 1001.

Now look at what Notice 2026-62 explicitly carved out: 
The IRS stated it expresses no view on Section 351 seedings where the assets match the ETF's investment thesis and are "intended and expected to be retained by the ETF absent a substantial change in circumstances."

Retained. That is the operative standard.

If an ETF is structured to actually hold the underlying securities, the statutory foundation holds. If the vehicle is used as a temporary conduit to flush low-basis shares to an AP under a prearranged exit, the IRS treats it as a sale.

Public comments run through October 28. Read the primary administrative guidance, not the headlines.

text:
🇺🇸 America’s emergency oil reserve is back to 1982 levels.

The SPR now sits at 283.8 million barrels, down roughly 132 million since the start of the year.

And now the government is offering another 40 million barrels to the market.

But those barrels haven’t left the reserve yet. They’re being offered as loans, and the last 40-million-barrel offer attracted demand for only about 500,000.

So I think the more interesting story is what has already happened.

The U.S. entered this year with more than 415 million barrels in its emergency stockpile. Roughly 7 months later, it has 132 million fewer.

America isn’t running out of oil, no. 

The more interesting question is how much of its emergency stockpile Washington is prepared to use while the emergency is still going.

Source: EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report, DOE SPR program, Reuters / Writer: Oliver

🔴 Daily Oil & Gas Update

Trump Calls Hormuz Open. Then He Reaches for the Emergency Oil Reserve.

📉 WTI: $90.50 −2.10 | −2.27%

📉 Brent: $103.70 −1.63 | −1.55%

📈 Murban: $120.00 +3.05 | +2.61%

⛽ U.S. Gasoline: $4.4558/gallon

🚨 U.S. Diesel: $6.4391/gallon

Trump’s administration keeps calling Hormuz open. Today it offered to loan 40 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to contain fuel prices.

That is a remarkable admission from an administration selling a story of normal oil flows. It is also an offer, not 40 million barrels already delivered. When Washington offered a similar loan in June, companies agreed to borrow only about 500,000 barrels.

Saudi Arabia has restarted oil loadings at Yanbu, helping push crude prices lower today. Yet its East West pipeline is still carrying well below its full capacity, and Gulf exporters continue to rely on costly shipping workarounds. More oil is moving. Safe, routine passage through Hormuz has not returned.

The pump exposes the gap between Trump’s claims and the country’s costs. Gasoline is about $1.32 a gallon higher than a year ago. Diesel is about $2.76 higher. A small daily drop in crude does not erase what drivers, farmers and truckers are paying.

Trump now floats a diesel export ban and changes to the tax treatment of dyed diesel while promising that Iran will give up and oil will plunge. His administration is improvising fuel policy in the middle of a war it says it has under control.

If Hormuz were functioning normally, the White House would not need to pitch emergency oil loans while diesel sits at $6.44 a gallon.

"Iranian officials privately doubt that Tehran and Washington can reach a deal to end hostilities and reopen the Strait of Hormuz before the U.S. midterm elections in November.

Talks held around last week’s U.N. General Assembly produced little movement.

Iranian officials also see a strong possibility that the conflict will intensify after the Nov. 3 vote, according to Bloomberg.

Election Deadline
Both sides have questioned whether the other would honor an agreement.

President Donald Trump has said he doubts a deal can be concluded before the elections, while Iranian officials have publicly maintained that Tehran remains open to diplomacy.

The political calendar adds pressure to negotiations over Hormuz.

Higher energy prices since the U.S. and Israel began the war in late February have weighed on Trump and his Republican Party ahead of a vote in which Democrats are widely expected to gain ground.

Brent crude rose about 2.5% this week to $107 a barrel as expectations of an imminent agreement on the strait receded.

Asked about the negotiations on Monday, Trump told reporters: “As far as I’m concerned, it’s going to be one way or the other. It’s going to go pretty quickly.”

Terms Still Apart
Washington wants firm Iranian commitments to reopen Hormuz and concessions on Tehran’s nuclear program, according to people familiar with the talks.

A U.S. official said there would be no pact without progress on nuclear issues, though Trump was prepared to offer sanctions relief and release frozen funds in return for concrete steps.

Iran has proposed reopening the strait within seven days if the U.S. takes certain measures.

Its leaders have previously called for Washington to lift its naval blockade and oil sanctions. Trump said on Saturday that he had rejected Tehran’s proposal.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Trump’s envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, last week and stayed in the U.S. for further discussions through mediators.

After an Iranian delegation met a Qatari mediator in New York on Monday, Araghchi said he hoped to receive Washington’s final response by Tuesday.

Pakistan and Qatar have played prominent roles in the intermittent talks.

Mediators are seeking terms different from a June memorandum of understanding that briefly halted fighting and increased traffic through Hormuz before collapsing about two weeks later.

That arrangement drew criticism from U.S. politicians over the scale of financial relief offered to Iran.

Tehran continued to restrict passage through the strait, and shipping volumes remained well below their prewar level."

text:
US-IRAN IN NEW YORK: WHO MET, WHAT IS ON THE TABLE, AND WHY TEHRAN IS WAITING ON WASHINGTON

The talks are real, they are indirect, and as of Tuesday morning, Sept. 29, there is no deal. Here is what the record shows.

WHO MET, AND WHERE
On Tuesday, Sept. 22, on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held what AP describes as "three hours of indirect talks via mediators" with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi's delegation, the first since the June agreement collapsed within days of its signing. Qatar has been the mediator, with Pakistan also passing messages, per Araghchi. Witkoff posted that the sides "successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising" (Iran International). Iranian state TV said Araghchi met Witkoff "at the insistence of the American side." A U.S. official told CNN that Witkoff, Kushner, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are leading for the U.S. side.

WHAT RUBIO SAID (STATE DEPARTMENT TRANSCRIPT, SEPT. 23)
Rubio would not describe the substance. "I don't want to mischaracterize this as a major breakthrough, but at the same time, I think it was significant that at least there was a conversation." On the core U.S. demand: "Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. Everything emanates from that."

IRAN'S SEVEN-DAY PLAN
Araghchi told journalists on Friday, Sept. 25, that Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks in seven days if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales and observes a ceasefire that includes Lebanon (AP). His line: "The choice now rests with the United States." He also said "the seven-day timeline will start as soon as the United States accepts this plan."

TRUMP'S "NO," AND WHAT CAME AFTER
Trump rejected the proposal on Saturday, Sept. 26, per AP, calling it "unacceptable," per Al Jazeera. But three regional officials and a senior U.S. official told AP on Monday that mediators were still working, and that the U.S. had not officially rejected the current proposal. One regional official said the U.S. is seeking nuclear concessions, including allowing inspectors into Iran.

On Monday, Sept. 28, Araghchi met Qatari mediators again in New York. "We talked about ideas and how to find solutions to fulfil Iran's conditions and how to implement those conditions," he told Iranian state media (Al Jazeera). He said he hoped for Washington's final response by Tuesday, and that he was flying to Tehran: "Whenever the Qataris have a response, they know how to get it to us." Trump, at the White House Monday, confirmed U.S. officials had spoken with mediators and said: "We're going to win. It's going to go pretty quickly."

THE AXIOS REPORT AND TRUMP'S DENIAL
On Monday, Axios reported: "President Trump is willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release Iranian frozen funds in return for concrete Iranian steps regarding the nuclear program, U.S. officials say." A U.S. official told Axios the talks were "positive and constructive," that there would be no deal "unless the nuclear issues are addressed," and that "The sides still remain apart on the timing of the commitments and who takes which steps first." Monday evening, Trump posted on Truth Social, as quoted by The Hill: "Axios just released a story that 'Trump' offered Sanctions Relief and Frozen Funds to Iran. This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING! Axios' story, like most others, is a HOAX, used only for purposes of satisfying their Trump Derangement Syndrome. They should withdraw this fake story, IMMEDIATELY!" Axios updated its story with his statement. The same sanctions-for-nuclear-progress description was also given by a U.S. official to CNN and Al Jazeera.

THE AGENDA IN ONE LINE
Iran wants the blockade lifted, oil sanctions waived, frozen funds released and a ceasefire on all fronts before Hormuz reopens. Washington says there is no deal unless the nuclear issues are addressed. Axios frames the gap as Hormuz and the blockade versus nuclear concessions.

WHAT WE STILL DO NOT KNOW
Has Washington delivered its formal reply through Qatar? Did it arrive by Tuesday, as Araghchi hoped? Is there any written U.S. offer at all, given Trump's denial? No State Department or White House readout of Monday's mediator contacts has been published that ZB30 could find.

Debunking the Core Bullish Argument That Strong EPS Equates to Strong Price Gains

The investment mosaic is far more complicated than suggested by hosts, investment strategists, panelists and guests in the business media.First-Level Thinking Vs Second-Level Thinking

Specifically, many distill the bullish argument to this: Since 2026 S&P EPS is expected to be about +20% (well above consensus expectations at the beginning of the year), the S&P price gains in 2026 should be about in line with that profit growth (or better). Candidly, that sort of distillation is the essence of “first-level thinking.

”First-level thinking is lazy, simplistic and superficial — it looks for simple formulas and easy answers.  To paraphrase Howard Marks:First-level thinking says, “S&P EPS growth will be strong, let’s buy the market.”

Second-level thinking says, “S&P EPS growth will be strong, but everyone knows it. Stocks are fairly or overpriced, let’s sell the market.”

Most recent examples of when S&P EPS was better than expected and strong were in 2018 (+20.5% EPS growth, -6.6% decline in the S&P), 2006 (+16.7% EPS growth, +11.3% rise in the S&P), 2005 (+19.3% EPS growth, +8.8% rise in the S&P) and 2004 (+20.1% EPS growth, +4.2% rise in the S&P).
