text:
LETTERS FROM STOCKHOLM

THE MAN GOWON SENT TO WASHINGTON: MY FATHER’S SECRET DIPLOMATIC MISSION TO THE UNITED STATES

By Kio Amachree

There are pieces of one’s family history that begin as stories told around a dinner table and end, decades later, in government archives.

For much of my life, I knew that my father, Chief Godfrey Kio Jaja Amachree QC, had been entrusted with sensitive responsibilities by Nigeria’s leaders. I knew about his legal career. I knew about his years at the United Nations. I knew that during the Nigerian Civil War he had acted on behalf of General Yakubu Gowon’s Federal Military Government in its dealings with the United States.

But knowing something as a son and seeing it recorded in the confidential and secret diplomatic cables of another government are two entirely different things.

Today, declassified documents in the official Foreign Relations of the United States series allow us to reconstruct at least part of what happened.

And the documents are remarkable.

The United States Department of State did not describe my father merely as a Nigerian lawyer visiting Washington.

It described him as the “personal representative” of General Yakubu Gowon and Federal Commissioner for External Affairs Okoi Arikpo.

That distinction matters.

This was February 1969.

Nigeria was fighting for its survival as a single country. The Nigerian Civil War had become an international humanitarian and diplomatic crisis. Images of starving Biafran children had transformed Western public opinion. American politicians were demanding action. Relief policy had become entangled with diplomacy, military strategy and the question of whether the United States should become more deeply involved.

At precisely that moment, Nigeria needed to know what the new American administration intended to do.

Richard Nixon had entered the White House only weeks earlier.

Gowon wanted an answer.

And one of the men he sent to find it was my father.

THE MISSION BEGINS

A confidential State Department telegram dated 9 February 1969 carries an extraordinary subject line:

“Godfrey Amachree Mission to USG.”

USG meant the United States Government.

According to the American record, my father arrived in the United States on 4 February 1969 as the personal representative of General Gowon and Commissioner Arikpo.

The following day he met representatives of American oil companies in New York.

He then went to Washington.

There, on 6 February, he held what the State Department described as “lengthy discussions” with several members of the United States Congress: Charles Diggs, John Culver, John Brademas, Roger Morris and Donald Fraser, as well as staff members representing Senators Edward Brooke and James Pearson.

The following day he spent approximately ninety minutes with Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Joseph Palmer.

The cable also recorded his intention to make contact with Senator Edward Kennedy.

This was not ceremonial diplomacy.

My father had been dispatched into the political centre of Washington to determine what the incoming Nixon administration and influential members of Congress were thinking about Nigeria and Biafra. (Office of the Historian⁠￼)

WHY GOWON SENT HIM

The most revealing section of the American cable explains why he had been sent.

According to the State Department account, my father said that officials in Lagos were deeply worried about American attitudes toward the war.

The new Nixon administration was reviewing policy. Humanitarian pressure inside the United States was enormous. Some Nigerian officials apparently believed that Washington did not understand the realities confronting the Federal Military Government.

There were also concerns in Lagos about the information reaching the government through Nigeria’s normal diplomatic channels.

The American cable states that some Federal Military Government officials blamed Nigeria’s ambassador, Joseph Iyalla, for the problem.

It then records something extremely important:

Gowon and Arikpo asked Amachree to travel to America to obtain an independent assessment.

That tells us considerably more about his role.

He was not simply delivering a prepared message.

He was being used as an alternative channel of information.

In modern diplomatic language, one might describe this as a form of back-channel diplomacy — although the surviving documents do not establish that this was his formal title.

His value appears to have been precisely that he stood partly outside the conventional diplomatic machinery.

He had been Nigeria’s Solicitor-General and Permanent Secretary in the Federal Ministry of Justice. He had then entered the highest levels of the United Nations system. In February 1962, the United Nations announced that he had become Under-Secretary in charge of the UN Civilian Operation in the Congo. (Digital Library⁠￼)

He therefore arrived in Washington not as an unknown political messenger but as someone who already understood international diplomacy and had relationships within the American establishment.

The State Department itself called him a “prominent Nigerian lawyer and former UN Under Secretary.”

Gowon was evidently sending someone whom Washington would take seriously. (Office of the Historian⁠￼)

HE WAS ALSO LISTENING

Perhaps the most interesting aspect of the mission is that my father was not simply defending the Federal Government’s position.

He was listening.

After his congressional meetings, the State Department recorded that he had acquired a better understanding of the depth of American humanitarian concern.

The cable’s assessment was striking.

It reported his view that part of Nigeria’s difficulty was actually in Lagos: constructive suggestions from Ambassador Iyalla about improving the Federal Government’s image in America had apparently not been sufficiently acted upon.

That is important because it complicates any simplistic picture of an envoy sent merely to repeat government propaganda.

The documentary record suggests something subtler.

He was gathering intelligence about American political attitudes, testing arguments, discovering where Nigeria’s position was weak and considering what Lagos might have to change.

The Americans themselves remarked that he appeared to have been deeply influenced by what he heard during his congressional meetings. (Office of the Historian⁠￼)

THE HUMANITARIAN CRISIS

The great diplomatic problem was Biafran relief.

Whatever arguments existed about sovereignty, secession and responsibility for the war, the humanitarian catastrophe had become impossible for Washington to ignore.

Joseph Palmer made the American position unmistakable.

As long as children were dying from hunger, he told my father in substance, the American public would find it difficult to understand arguments about the political and military obstacles preventing relief.

My father explored possible compromises.

He discussed whether Nigerian officials should travel to America to explain federal relief and rehabilitation policies directly.

Among the proposed delegation were Arikpo, Rehabilitation Commissioner Anthony Omo-Bare and Ukpabi Asika, administrator of the East Central State.

My father also raised the possibility of additional airfields being made available for humanitarian relief.

The American record specifically notes that the airfield proposal was his own idea, rather than necessarily an already approved Federal Government position.

He promised to urge Lagos to consider further measures to facilitate humanitarian assistance.

That distinction deserves emphasis.

The archival evidence does not justify claiming that my father personally controlled Nigerian relief policy. He did not.

What it does show is that, as Gowon’s representative, he was discussing concrete ways of breaking the diplomatic deadlock and taking ideas back to the Federal Government. (Office of the Historian⁠￼)

CIVILIAN BOMBING

Another uncomfortable subject arose.

Palmer confronted my father about American concern over Federal Nigerian bombing that was killing civilians in Biafra.

My father did not dismiss the concern.

According to the American account, he agreed that civilian casualties were damaging both from humanitarian and political perspectives. He expressed the belief that they were not deliberate, while acknowledging the dangers inherent in wartime bombing accuracy.

The State Department nevertheless made clear to him how strongly Washington believed corrective measures were necessary.

This is one of those passages where history should be allowed to speak without embellishment.

The Nigerian Civil War remains deeply painful and contested. Any serious account of it must distinguish between documented events, contemporary claims and later interpretations.

The American diplomatic record shows that civilian casualties were explicitly raised with Gowon’s representative and that the concern was intended to be transmitted back to Lagos. (Office of the Historian⁠￼)

THE SOVIET QUESTION

There was another enormous strategic issue hanging over these conversations: the Soviet Union.

The Cold War was at its height.

Nigeria’s wartime relationships inevitably raised questions in Washington about Soviet influence.

My father raised American concern over increasing Soviet involvement in Nigeria.

Palmer’s response was revealing. According to the telegram, Washington did not regard communism as the overriding issue in its Nigerian policy, although American officials believed Moscow was exploiting the war and growing anti-American sentiment.

The Americans insisted that their principal concern remained humanitarian.

My father was therefore attempting to establish not simply what Washington was saying publicly, but what actually motivated American policy.

That was exactly the intelligence Gowon needed from his independent representative. (Office of the Historian⁠￼)

OIL AND AMERICAN BUSINESS

The mission also extended beyond the battlefield.

Before reaching Washington, my father had met senior American oil interests in New York.

Nigeria’s Companies Decree had created concern among foreign businesses, including Mobil.

The State Department record shows that he discussed the negotiations surrounding the decree and subsequently briefed Mobil officials.

Again, the significance is broader than one meeting.

Nigeria was fighting a civil war while simultaneously trying to preserve relationships with the foreign companies and governments upon which parts of its economy and international position depended.

My father’s assignment therefore appears to have crossed several overlapping areas: diplomacy, humanitarian policy, Congressional opinion, international business and Nigeria’s wider relationship with the United States. (Office of the Historian⁠￼)

THE MEETING HE HAD TO HAVE

There was, however, one person he had not initially managed to see.

The new American Secretary of State, William P. Rogers, had been unavailable.

That mattered.

A second State Department telegram, classified SECRET and dated 12 February 1969, records what happened next.

On 10 February my father telephoned Palmer.

According to the American record, Arikpo was unhappy that the meeting with Rogers had not taken place and asked that another attempt be made.

More significantly, the telegram states that Gowon and Arikpo attached importance to my father seeing the Secretary of State personally.

The meeting was arranged for 11 February.

My father told Rogers that considerable uncertainty remained in Lagos about American policy.

Rogers gave him the answer he had crossed the Atlantic to obtain.

The Nixon administration had not yet decided to overturn existing American policy toward Nigeria.

The policy review then underway was concentrated particularly on humanitarian relief.

Washington, Rogers indicated, did not want to become politically entangled in imposing a settlement; its immediate concern was getting food to people in need.

My father told Rogers that he now understood the depth of American humanitarian concern and would return to Lagos able to explain the real nature of Washington’s position. (Office of the Historian⁠￼)

That was the essence of the assignment.

Gowon wanted to know what America intended to do.

His representative went directly to the new Secretary of State and asked.

Then he carried the answer home.

AN EVEN MORE EXTRAORDINARY POSSIBILITY

The secret telegram contains another fascinating detail.

My father had been speaking with Senator Kennedy’s staff.

According to what was relayed to him, Biafran representatives had suggested that Biafra’s sovereignty might be negotiable.

My father’s reported response was immediate: if that were genuinely Biafra’s position, there might be a basis for ending the war.

He asked Kennedy’s office about arranging a meeting involving himself and Biafran representatives, with Kennedy present, in order to establish precisely what was being proposed.

He even offered to return to the United States whenever Senator Kennedy could arrange such a meeting. (Office of the Historian⁠￼)

We must be careful here.

The surviving cable does not establish that such a meeting eventually took place. Nor does it prove that a peace agreement was close.

It records a diplomatic possibility being explored.

But even that is historically significant.

My father’s role had moved beyond simply explaining Lagos’s position.

He was potentially exploring whether an American political intermediary could help clarify terms upon which the opposing sides might talk.

WASHINGTON’S VERDICT

Perhaps the most revealing sentence appears near the end of the first State Department telegram.

After assessing the mission, American officials wrote that the Department was pleased to have an:

“additional direct channel to FMG leadership.”

FMG meant the Federal Military Government. (Office of the Historian⁠￼)

That sentence may be the best description of my father’s function.

He was a direct channel.

Not the ambassador.

Not the Foreign Ministry bureaucracy.

A man whom Gowon and Arikpo trusted to go to Washington, speak with American officials and politicians, listen carefully, form his own assessment and report directly back to Nigeria’s leadership.

The U.S. government’s own published historical index later identified him simply as:

“Amachree, Godfrey, personal representative of Major General Gowon.” (Office of the Historian⁠￼)

THE MAN BEFORE THE MISSION

None of this happened by accident.

Before the Civil War, my father had already occupied positions almost unimaginable for a Nigerian of his generation.

The Nigerian Official Gazette records him as Solicitor-General of the Federation and Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Justice in 1961. (Gazettes Archive⁠￼)

The London Gazette records Queen Elizabeth II’s approval in 1960 of his appointment as Queen’s Counsel for the Federation of Nigeria. (The Gazette⁠￼)

Then came the United Nations.

On 15 February 1962, the UN announced that Chief Godfrey Kio Jaja Amachree had assumed office as Under-Secretary responsible for the United Nations Civilian Operation in the Congo.

The operation covered governmental administration, public finance, health, education, agriculture, aviation, transport, communications, the judiciary, labour, social affairs and public works.

The UN announcement also noted that U Thant had selected him as one of his principal advisers. (Digital Library⁠￼)

By the time Gowon needed someone who understood both Africa and the machinery of Western diplomacy, my father had already spent years inside that machinery.

HISTORY HIDDEN IN AN ARCHIVE

I write this not merely because he was my father.

I write it because Nigerian history has too often been reduced to presidents, generals, coups and elections.

Countries are also built — and sometimes held together — by people working in rooms that never appear in photographs.

Diplomats.

Civil servants.

Lawyers.

Negotiators.

People entrusted to carry messages when the message cannot safely be misunderstood.

In February 1969, with Nigeria at war and Washington reconsidering its position, General Yakubu Gowon and Okoi Arikpo wanted an independent assessment of the United States.

They chose Chief Godfrey Kio Jaja Amachree.

He flew to America.

He met oil executives in New York.

He went to Capitol Hill.

He talked with congressmen and senatorial staffs.

He spent ninety minutes with America’s senior African-affairs official.

He discussed famine, bombing, Soviet influence, American business interests, humanitarian airfields and possible negotiations.

And when the Nigerian leadership insisted that he obtain an answer from the very top of American diplomacy, he sat down with the Secretary of State.

The Americans themselves concluded that they now possessed an additional direct channel to Nigeria’s leadership.

Those are not family recollections.

They are contained in the diplomatic archives of the United States government.

More than half a century later, I can finally read the confidential reports written about my father’s mission while he was carrying it out.

For a son, that is profoundly personal.

For a political scientist, it is something else.

It is evidence.

And evidence allows us to put a forgotten Nigerian back into the historical record where he belongs.

Chief Godfrey Kio Jaja Amachree QC was not merely observing one of the most dangerous diplomatic moments in Nigeria’s history. The surviving American records establish that General Gowon’s government trusted him to enter Washington as its personal representative, discover what the United States intended to do, explore possible solutions and report back to Lagos.

Exactly how much influence his recommendations ultimately had on Gowon’s subsequent decisions would require further archival evidence before any responsible historian could say.

But the mission itself is no longer a matter of family legend.

Washington documented it.

And Washington remembered his name.

⸻

Historical note

This article relies primarily on declassified United States Department of State records published in the official Foreign Relations of the United States, 1969–1976 series, particularly Telegram 20875 of 9 February 1969 and Telegram 22400 of 12 February 1969, together with contemporary United Nations and Nigerian/British government records. Where those documents record American officials’ impressions or statements attributed to participants, they should be understood as contemporary diplomatic reporting rather than independent proof of every underlying assertion.

The company said this will not impact its ability to supply hot-rolled steel products.
"This is an unfortunate but necessary action to help ensure the survival of Stelco in what has become a challenging and unsustainable market for cold-rolled and coated products caused by the ongoing and sustained trade disruptions impacting the Canadian steel industry," Stelco vice-president of sales Frederic Fafard stated in the memo.
U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order in June applying up to 50 per cent tariffs to certain steel and aluminum imports from Canada.
"Stelco’s market for cold-rolled and galvanized products has contracted significantly, while import penetration for these products remains at heightened levels," Fafard said in the memo.
"While the measures taken by the federal government in Canada have served to reduce imports into Canada overall, import volumes remain at levels that prevent Stelco from being able to bridge the gap in the market created by the trade crisis."
Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs acquired Hamilton-based Stelco in a $3.4-billion Cdn cash-and-stock deal that closed in November 2024. In a news release announcing the deal, Stelco's then-CEO Alan Kestenbaum stated the transaction "keeps national interests at the forefront and recognizes the importance of the workforce."
"We're very disappointed," Wells said. "In particular, when Cliffs bought us in the fall of 2024, they made commitments. One of those commitments was to maintain the same number of unionized employees."
In an email to CBC News on Monday, a Cleveland-Cliffs spokesperson confirmed Joly has been in touch with chairman and CEO Lourenco Goncalves.
"Both Cliffs and the Canadian government have the interests of the Stelco workers in mind, and will continue to work together to minimize the impact of the current market situation on Canadian workers," wrote Pat Persico, the company's senior director of corporate communications.
She said that while Stelco is idling some of its operations in Hamilton, the company's total output of steel will not be impacted as it consolidates production at its Lake Erie Works.
"Very importantly, job opportunities at Lake Erie Works will be offered to Hamilton employees," Persico wrote in a previous email.
"We expect that a significant number of employees affected by the indefinite idle at Hamilton should be absorbed at Lake Erie Works."
Wells told CBC News on Tuesday that his union was informed that 46 positions would be offered.
Industry Minister 'extremely disappointed'
In a statement on Monday, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly slammed the decision to lay off workers, while noting Ottawa had offered to help Stelco weather the impact of U.S. tariffs.
"Our government has made clear to the company that we are ready and willing to provide financial support to sustain operations and protect jobs. Its decision to reject these practical proposals and continue with layoffs is extremely disappointing," she said.
"Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs have made significant commitments to Canadian steelworkers. We will use every lever possible to defend Canadian industry, protect jobs, and secure our supply chain."
Trump announces new steel plant in Iowa
On Monday, U.S. President Trump touted a new $15-billion US investment plan by Minnesota-based steelmaker Mesabi Metallics as evidence that American tariffs on imported steel are working as his administration intended.
The company announced plans to build a massive plant in Iowa, with production set to begin in 2030.
"I imposed powerful 50 per cent tariffs on all foreign steel, and now our steel industry is roaring back to life." Trump said at a news announcement in the Oval Office. "Everyone is building their plant here because they don't want to pay tariffs. It's really not that complicated."

The move is raising concerns north of the border, where Kevon Stewart, director of United Steelworkers District 6, said his phone has been lighting up with calls from distressed Canadian workers.

"Everything is timing right now," he told CBC News on Monday.

"This is not only a wake-up call, because the call for action has been there before. But we've got to come up with a game plan that ensures workers are protected if and when these measures are implemented."
He said such protections could include increased benefits, or removing the waiting time for benefits.

Colin Mang, an economist at McMaster University in Hamilton, said the layoffs announced Monday are "a consequence of our trade war with the United States." For Stelco, he said the situation is worsened by a steady flow of foreign products coming into Canada.

"The lack of access to the American market has meant that we have a surplus of steel production capacity here in Canada, and there just isn't enough domestic Canadian demand in order to absorb all of the output from the steelmakers here," Mang told CBC News.

"The Canadian government has worked to restrict the amount of steel coming into Canada, but when you look at a variety of steel products, particularly the kinds of flat products that Stelco manufactures, Canada has imported about 1.2 million tons from other trading partners around the world. That's because we continue to have free trade agreements with a variety of countries. So, it's very difficult to restrict imports from our other trading partners."

Blair Dickerson, president of the Canadian Steel Producers Association, said his thoughts are with the workers impacted by Monday's announcement. He also called upon Canada's federal government and the Trump to resolve their ongoing trade tension.

"Days like today demonstrate how challenging the tariff situation is, and provide a stark reminder as to the urgency of finding a solution," Dickerson said in an email.

"Recognizing the Government's support to date, Canada must continue and deepen the work of keeping unfairly traded steel out of our market, enforcing our measures at the border, and ensuring our producers can be competitive here at home."

text:
PLEASE WAKE UP.

Today there is ONE Saving GOSPEL: Paul’s gospel of the grace of God. Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again the third day (1 Corinthians 15:1–4). By grace through faith, not of works (Ephesians 2:8–9) KJV.

Gospel means good news. In English it is “god-spell”: good tidings. In Greek it is euangelion: a good message announced. 

The word itself is not Matthew–John and not a lifestyle. It is news that is preached, heard, and believed. 

Scripture names more than one gospel because God announced different good news in different programs. 

The gospel that saves today is Paul’s: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again. By grace through faith, not of works. Any other message offered as the way to be saved now is another gospel.

Anything else offered as the way to be saved now is another gospel.

Paul already settled the penalty for this age:
“But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.” (Galatians 1:8–9)

Read the words. “UNTO YOU.” The Galatians Had Already RECEIVED Paul’s gospel. What he cursed was a message preached to them in place of that gospel: circumcision, law, works mixed with Christ. “Another gospel, which is not another,” but a perversion of the one THEY HAD been given by Paul (Galatians 1:6–7).

That is not Paul saying God never gave any other good news. He did.

“The gospel of the uncircumcision was committed unto me, as the gospel of the circumcision was unto Peter.” (Galatians 2:7)

These were not all “fake or false” in their time. They are powerless to save TODAY, in this dispensation of Grace because they are not the revelation of the mystery given to Paul.

1. The Gospel of the Kingdom
 “Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” (Matthew 4:17, 23; 9:35; 24:14)
 That is Israel’s earthly kingdom, the Son of David on David’s throne. It demanded national repentance, righteousness, endurance to the end (Matthew 24:13). It is not “Christ died for your sins, believe and be sealed.”

2. The Gospel of the Circumcision
 “The gospel of the circumcision was unto Peter” (Galatians 2:7).
 Peter’s message to Israel: Jesus is Israel’s Messiah, repent, be baptized, remission of sins, the promise to Israel (Acts 2:36–38; 3:19–21). That is prophecy resumed, not the Body formed.

3. John the Baptist’s Gospel
 “The baptism of repentance for the remission of sins.” (Mark 1:4; Luke 3:3; Acts 19:4) Believe on Him that should come. Water to Israel. When Paul found men who knew only John’s baptism, he had to give them Christ (Acts 19:1–5).

4. The Gospel Jesus sent the twelve to preach
 Matthew 10:5–7: not to the Gentiles, not to the Samaritans, “The kingdom of heaven is at hand.” Heal the sick, cleanse lepers, raise the dead, cast out devils. That commission is not 1 Corinthians 15.

5. The “everlasting Gospel” of Revelation 14:6–7
 An angel preaches to them that dwell on the earth: “Fear God, and give glory to him… worship him that made heaven, and earth.” 

That is tribulation preaching to the nations after this age has closed. It is not how a sinner is justified today.

6. Law-keeping as the way of life
 “The man that doeth them shall live in them.” (Galatians 3:12; Leviticus 18:5) Do and live was the old covenant. 

Paul says that is not of faith. Mix it with Christ now and you have fallen from grace (Galatians 5:4) as a rule of standing, even if some of those preachers still believed 1 Corinthians 15 and are saved yet unprofitable.

-Gospels that were NEVER FROM God:

7. Another Jesus, another spirit, another gospel (2 Corinthians 11:4)
 A Jesus who is only a teacher, only an example, only a king you crown by works, only a healer you prove by tongues. Not the crucified and risen Lord who finished the work.

Cont..

There were three beautiful woman in my home... all had insane bodies. I was laying on the cushions that are under my living room stairs & I was doing my contemplation thing as I watched them. I caught a glimpse of one & she was bouncing on a hobby horse... enjoying my home. Why did I have a hobby horse in my spot? No f*ckin clue but she was ridin that thing like that scene in that 80s flick. Another one was enjoying my home while at the same time, playfully entertaining me with anecdotes. Sometimes... just laying beside me, telling me about her life. I remember how I was affectionately rubbing her back. Her voice was distant at first but slowly, as she spoke more, grew in volume & clarity. As for the third... she'd lay on my stomach or straddle my head in her arms as she spoke to me in whispered tones & breath. Never distant, always clear throughout. It felt peaceful & the only real way to describe her voice was... "nice". She told me encouraging things & while she spoke of her life, she'd compliment my heart & mind. When I think about it, it felt like laying with two elements... "water" & "fire". Both interchangeable depending on the circumstance they found themselves in & they found ease & comfort in my iterations of "earth" & "wind". Yeah, deep... but just go with me on this. What was so cool was that there was no need to make a "choice" because there was nothing to "keep" aside from the moments intention. We all understood that & had zero expectations for anything. It was all just a flow of love & chill. No competition & none to outdo the other as both knew they were at the pinnacle of their complementary uniqueness. It was free but unfortunately... short lived. I was dissapointed I had to wake but life demands it when you're constantly on-call. My saving grace was that I woke up with that "nice" voice in my head & the feeling of the other girls' lower back on my palm. I wanted to go back to sleep but I couldn't.

Friend: but what happened to the first girl? 

She left... she didnt get what this was. She thought I was looking for one thing & assumed the moment was just about gettin busy. Since it was all she had to offer... she bounced. Yo, hell yeah there are sexual "inevitables" but those things mean very little to me without connection. I can get that stuff on my own but what these offered was their heart... without stressing about what came next. That extra stuff sets it apart from the everyday. It was genuinely good people just being cool. Whether something happened or didnt wasnt the point. That first chick didnt get that.

Im gonna ruminate on this for the rest of the damn day..."

text:
"During the Irish Potato Famine (1845-1852), the Ottoman Empire offered humanitarian assistance to the people of Ireland, an act remembered today as a symbol of cross-cultural solidarity.

According to widely cited historical accounts, Sultan Abdülmecid I initially sought to donate £10,000 to famine relief. After learning that Queen Victoria had contributed £2,000, diplomatic sensitivities reportedly led the Ottoman donation to be reduced to £1,000. 

Beyond this official contribution, Ottoman ships carrying food supplies are said to have sailed to Irish ports, notably near Drogheda, where local memory preserves the story of their arrival.

While some details; especially regarding the ships, are discussed and debated by historians, the episode holds strong cultural significance. 

In Ireland, it is often cited as an example of unexpected compassion from a distant empire during one of the country's darkest periods. In Turkey, it is remembered as part of a broader Ottoman tradition of charitable diplomacy.

Today, this shared memory is reflected symbolically: the crescent and star appear on the crest of Drogheda United Football Club, commonly linked to gratitude for Ottoman aid."

text:
Cold email tools are racing to make outbound easier.

Apollo, Instantly, a dozen others are all building toward the same thing. Upload your website, they scrape some contacts, sequences go out.

The problem is none of it gets smarter. It’s a black box. Same angles, same positioning, same results until you turn it off.

What actually works looks different.

You start with an ICP and run it through a qualification gate. You do niche-level research to understand what that specific buyer cares about right now. You source contacts, A/B test copy and offers, and score the outputs so the system knows what a winner looks like vs. a loser.

Then you layer intent signals (events, Trigify, etc) and lookalike audiences on top of the campaigns that are already working.

The difference between those two approaches is the difference between a campaign and an engine. One runs. The other learns and compounds.

text:
Good. At last you have offered a thesis. You say the principal sources of instability are ethnonationalist extremism and Eritrean meddling. That claim has to survive the chronology. It does not.

In 2018 Eritrea was not Abiy Ahmed’s enemy. It was his principal partner in the rapprochement that bought him a Nobel Peace Prize. He was celebrated for reconciliation across the Horn, Eritrea, Djibouti, Somalia and Sudan included.

Now follow the sequence. Eritrea went from peace partner and wartime ally to adversary. Fano went from fighting beside federal forces to fighting the federal government. Ethiopia’s Somaliland memorandum produced a major rupture with Somalia. Former enemies inside the country have now built a seven organization alliance against Addis Ababa. The Sudan file cannot be wished away either. Yale’s Humanitarian Research Lab concluded with high confidence that activity consistent with military assistance to the Janjaweed, the RSF, was occurring from an active ENDF installation at Asosa. A UN investigation has documented the broader foreign support sustaining Sudan’s catastrophic war.

Inside Ethiopia the balance sheet is staggering. The Northern Ethiopian War killed hundreds of thousands. War then engulfed Amhara and Afar. Conflict in Oromia persisted. Displacement became massive. Fighting now stretches again across Amhara, Tigray, Oromia and Afar. Examine, as I have asked you more than once, the Ethiopian language testimony on Abiy’s own account of the origins and planning of the northern war. Some of the allegations from former insiders are grave. Treat them as testimony to be tested, not as inconveniences to be swept aside because they spoil the government story.

Your explanation still has a causal hole. Eritrea changed. Fano changed. The TPLF changed. Alliances changed. Ethiopia’s relations with its neighbours changed. The government at the centre did not. Ethnonationalism is a real structural force. Eritrean intervention, where it is demonstrated, deserves scrutiny. Remember what else is demonstrated. By the prime minister’s own admission Eritrea helped prevent a state collapse. It was not a distant meddler in 2018 and through the northern war. It was a major ally of the same government you now treat as the injured party, an ally that helped keep Abiy Ahmed’s regime standing. Scrutiny that begins after the rescue and forgets the rescue is not analysis. It is amnesia with a thesis attached. Neither proposition explains why so many former allies became adversaries, why former adversaries now cooperate, or why the extraordinary regional optimism of 2018 and 2019 collapsed into this degree of internal and regional confrontation.

That is why the question you first fled remains the only one that matters. Who is burning the house. If your theory requires almost every actor around the same government to become the principal cause at a different hour, it is time to look at the actor who has occupied the centre of the house throughout.

text:
"Both have rejected or undermined
proposals.

- **1937 Peel Commission:** Palestinian Arab leaders rejected partition, while the mainstream Zionist leadership accepted the principle, though not necessarily the proposed borders. Palestinians viewed partition as granting a large portion of their country to a relatively new Jewish immigrant community and violating the principle of self-determination of the Arab majority.

- **1947 UN Partition Plan:** The Jewish Agency accepted the plan; Palestinian Arab leaders and neighboring Arab states rejected it. Arabs objected that the Jewish community, then roughly one-third of the population and owning a smaller share of the land, was allocated a state covering a substantial portion of Palestine. They also rejected the legitimacy of creating a Jewish state and feared displacement. War followed, Israel was established, and hundreds of thousands of Palestinians became refugees. 

Those rejections were therefore not simply “they were offered a state and wanted none.” They reflected a combination of Palestinian nationalism, opposition to partition, rejection of Zionism, perceived unfairness, and the belief that accepting the plan would legitimize dispossession.

**After 1967, the position changed**

Following Israel’s capture of the West Bank, Gaza, and East Jerusalem in 1967, the Palestine Liberation Organization gradually moved toward accepting a state in those territories—about 22% of historic Palestine—alongside Israel. The PLO formally accepted this framework in stages, especially after the 1980s, and the Palestinian Authority has continued to support it, although Hamas has rejected Israel’s legitimacy and has not consistently accepted a negotiated two-state settlement.

**What about the famous 2000–2001 and 2008 negotiations?**

It is also too simple to say that Palestinians rejected generous offers:

- At **Camp David in 2000**, no final written agreement was presented for Palestinians to accept or reject. The parties disagreed over borders, Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, security, and sovereignty. The Clinton Parameters and the 2001 Taba talks came closer, but the parties still did not agree.

- In **2008**, Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert made a far-reaching proposal, according to his account, but negotiations ended before a signed agreement. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas says the map and terms remained unresolved and that he could not accept an offer without being able to study and negotiate it fully.

At the same time, Palestinian violence, rejectionist rhetoric, refusal by Hamas to recognize Israel, and the failure to accept or counter some proposals clearly contributed to the collapse of negotiations. Palestinian leaders have not been blameless.

**Israel has also rejected or constrained two-state proposals**

Israel accepted partition in principle in 1947, but later Israeli governments and movements rejected Palestinian statehood or supported policies that made it harder to establish one. Israel rejected or resisted several elements of Arab and Palestinian proposals, including the demand for a state based on the 1967 lines, a Palestinian capital in East Jerusalem, restrictions on settlement activity, and a solution to the refugee issue. Israeli settlement expansion in the West Bank, continuing occupation, and political opposition to Palestinian sovereignty have also undermined the possibility of two states. Israeli public and governmental support for the idea has fluctuated; it has never been a permanent consensus.

**Palestinian leaders rejected the original partition plans, largely because they regarded them as unjust and illegitimate. Later, the PLO accepted the principle of two states but disputed the terms, sovereignty, borders, Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, and security arrangements. Israeli leaders have sometimes supported two states, but other Israeli governments and influential political movements have rejected Palestinian statehood.

Since 2014, allegations of high-level corruption have continued to intensify and the deeper concern is the apparent political migration of accused leaders. When politicians facing corruption cases join the ruling party and investigations slow down or disappear from public attention, it creates the perception that political protection can buy legal immunity.

Electoral bonds further deepened this concern by enabling anonymous political funding. To many citizens, the message appeared brutally simple: pay for political protection, secure influence and carry on as usual.

Ordinary taxpayers are exhausted by corruption embedded across institutions and political parties, regardless of which party governs a state. The situation becomes even more disturbing when voters themselves are openly offered money and inducements to secure electoral victories.

India needs a Singapore-style zero-tolerance approach to corruption but that transformation cannot begin only with laws or governments. It must start with citizens rejecting cash-for-votes, civil servants refusing political pressure, IAS officers upholding integrity and political parties accepting genuine accountability. A nation cannot defeat corruption when those who enable it keep rewarding those who practise it.

text:
Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif held a series of meetings today with senior executives from leading global financial institutions — Barclays, J.P. Morgan, Citi, BlackRock and Rothschild & Co — during his visit to the United Kingdom. The engagements underscored growing international financial sector interest in Pakistan's economic reform trajectory and improving investment climate.

Meeting Mr. Mohammad Kamal Syed, Head of Private Bank and Wealth Management UK at Barclays, the Prime Minister welcomed the bank's interest in Pakistan and briefed him on the government's macroeconomic stabilization measures, encouraging Barclays to explore opportunities in the country's financial sector.

With a high-level J.P. Morgan delegation led by Mr. Matthieu Wiltz, Co-CEO for EMEA JP Morgan, the Prime Minister discussed deepening the partnership across capital markets, trade finance, and investment banking, and invited the firm to expand its footprint in Pakistan. The delegation reaffirmed its interest in sovereign debt capital markets and corporate banking opportunities.

The Prime Minister also met a group of senior officials of Citi, led by Mr. David Livingstone, Chief Client Officer. Prime Minister commended the bank's long-standing presence in Pakistan and encouraged an expansion of its corporate and institutional banking services in the country.

In a meeting with a BlackRock delegation comprising Gordon Fraser and Sam Vecht, Co-Heads of Emerging Markets and Frontiers, and Emily Fletcher, Portfolio Manager and Research Analyst, the Prime Minister invited increased allocations to Pakistani equities and fixed income within the firm's frontier markets strategy, with both sides emphasizing the importance of sustained policy consistency in building investor confidence.

In a meeting with Rothschild & Co, represented by Lord Mark Sedwill, Chair of Geostrategic Advisory and Mr. Majid Ishaq, Head of UK Investment Banking, discussions centered on Pakistan's geo-economic priorities and potential advisory collaboration on capital markets and investment strategy.
Across all engagements, the visiting executives expressed confidence in Pakistan's economic reform momentum and reaffirmed their institutions' commitment to deepening engagement with the country's financial sector. 

The meetings reflect the growing traction of Pakistan's economic reform program among the world's leading financial institutions, and mark a significant step in the government's broader effort to strengthen international investor confidence and attract sustained capital flows into the country.

Finance Minister Senator Muhammad Aurangzeb and Advisor to PM on Privatization and Chairman Privatization Commission Muhammad Ali were also present in the meetings.

text:
The word "sideburns" is named after a Civil War general. And the man behind it has an interesting story.

His name was Ambrose Burnside, and "sideburns" is just his last name flipped around. He wore these magnificent whiskers that ran down both cheeks and swept up into his mustache, and people started calling the look "burnsides." 

Somewhere along the way the syllables got switched, and we've said "sideburns" ever since.

But what about the man behind the whiskers?

Burnside was one of the few men in the army humble enough to admit he wasn't up to the top job.

Twice he was offered command of the entire Army of the Potomac. Twice he said no. He cautioned Congress he "was not competent to command such a large army." 

But they gave him the appointment. And at Fredericksburg it went as badly as he feared, a costly defeat that weighed on him for the rest of his life. 

But Burnside's story didn't end there. He continued to serve his country. As governor of Rhode Island and then a US senator.

Today many have forgotten the general. But his sideburns are immortal.

text:
Building more and more housing is certainly not THE solution to helping (and, clearing, frankly)  the thousands upon thousands of drug addicted and mentally ill people who reside in the streets and parks of my city, San Francisco. 
How do I know? Because if the bulk of these people were NOT addicted to drugs or NOT suffering from mental illness, they would live in far less degraded and far less unsanitary circumstances. They would not carelessly strew dirty syringes, or spread excrement, urine, vomit on the pavement in their immediate environment, or start fires in their encampments. Focusing on getting these individuals into permanent or even long term housing as the top and first priority is a huge mistake. MOST SIMPLY ARE NOT READY FOR IT: they either are too focused on getting their next high and/or are incapacitated by their poor mental health. 

These ARE approaches that should work in my city of San Francisco:

1) Many (if not most) living in the street are from other places: assign social workers to learn if they have a social network and programs  back home to help and house them. If they do, work with family members and friends to enable them to return home. Pay for transportation back home. 

2) For those who are mentally and physically-abled, and do not have a social network and resources elsewhere...particularly those who were long term residents of San Francisco, offer them space in 
2 year recovery and abstinence programs, strict programs that test regularly for drugs and alcohol and that guide them into gainful employment and affordable housing...in San Francisco and beyond. 

San Francisco has run a couple of abstinence and recovery programs over the past 10 - 20 years or so through the Salvation Army, and this model is now being funded more and more it's so successful. 

3) For those who are mentally or physically disabled, and/or who are so addicted to drugs and /or alcohol they simply cannot stay sober, offer them space in asylums with social services (medical & psychiatric care) and basic, but humane accommodations...outside of the city in more affordable areas.  

4) Do NOT provide incentives (stipends, welfare, free housing, free medical care, free supplies to make using illegal drugs in public as easy as possible, permissive laws that allow public inebriation to become normalized) to those who come to San Francisco primarily for the temperate weather, generous benefits, and "easy" (but, often short) life of constant inebriation.  

5) And, for those who refuse the above proferred services...for those who simply continue to abuse drugs.. sometimes overdosing again and again on fentynal..sometimes until they die, tell them to leave the city or they will be arrested and then forced to leave the city or be sent to prison. 

Harsh? I don't think so. 

A) The streets of San Francisco should never have become hospice central for those who no longer care whether they live or die. And, B) this approach recognizes that there are other stakeholders living in this same environment...working class families, tax payers, small business owners, recovering drug addicts...recovering alcoholics, and, last, but not least, children. 

Did you know that the Tenderloin neighborhood in San Francisco
...one of the neighborhoods with THE most homeless...also has more children per capita than any other neighborhood in our city? What about these stakeholders? Don't they matter? Shouldn't our compassion extend to these stakeholders as well? Why should so much of our public funding go to those who reside on our streets and our parks...often befouling...and making much less safe... their immediate surroundings? 

6) And, yes, build more housing...but not as an immediate antidote to solve the crisis of thousands upon thousands of drug or alcohol addicted people / mentally ill people living on our streets.

text:
September 29, 1011. A Danish army took Canterbury after a three week siege, and the archbishop they captured became the first Archbishop of Canterbury to be murdered.

England in 1011 was being systematically dismantled. Æthelred, remembered as the Unready, though his actual epithet means ill-counselled rather than unprepared, had spent twenty years paying Danish armies to go away. They kept coming back, because paying them worked.

That September a Danish force under Thorkell the Tall besieged Canterbury.

It held three weeks. Then it fell, and the sources say it fell through betrayal, by an abbot named Ælfmaer, whose life the archbishop had once saved.

The cathedral was ransacked and burned. Among the captives were the Bishop of Rochester, an abbess, the king's reeve, and the Archbishop of Canterbury, Ælfheah.

Ælfheah was about 58 and had led an unusual life for a churchman. He began as a hermit. As Bishop of Winchester he commissioned a famous organ reportedly audible more than a mile away. He had also been the man sent to confirm Olaf Tryggvason in the Christian faith after the raids of 994, which means he had negotiated with Vikings before and knew precisely what he was dealing with.

They held him seven months and demanded three thousand pounds for him personally.

He refused to let it be paid.

That is the whole point of the story and it needs the context to land properly. The Danegeld system worked because England paid. Paying for the archbishop meant more silver going into an army that would use it to come back for more. He was, deliberately, refusing to be a line item.

On April 19, 1012, at Greenwich, the Danish army was drunk after a delivery of wine, and they brought him out.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, which is close to contemporary and not given to embellishment, records it flatly. They seized the bishop, and pelted him there with bones and the heads of cattle, and one of them struck him on the head with the butt of an axe.

Some accounts say a Danish convert named Thrum, baptised by Ælfheah himself the day before, delivered that final blow to end it, and was killed by his own comrades for doing it.

Another source says Thorkell the Tall tried to stop the whole thing and offered everything he owned except his ship to buy the archbishop's life. The Chronicle does not mention that, so handle it carefully. But Thorkell did change sides shortly afterward and entered Æthelred's service with forty five ships, which is at least consistent with a man who had been disgusted by something.

Ælfheah was canonised in 1078. Cnut, who conquered England in 1016 and then spent his reign making himself an English king rather than a Danish conqueror, had the body moved to Canterbury with great ceremony in 1023. That was a deliberate act of reconciliation by a Dane for something Danes had done.

And there is one more thing.

In December 1170, in Canterbury Cathedral, another Archbishop of Canterbury heard four knights coming for him and, by the accounts of men who were present, commended himself to God and to Saint Ælfheah before they cut him down.

That was Thomas Becket, who understood exactly whose position he was standing in.

Once They Pick Up, Don’t Miss 📞

Episode 25 of my weekly recap as a team leader at REAL.

Last week my team committed to never quitting on a lead before touch eight. This week we focused on what happens when an online seller lead finally answers.

✅ Many online seller leads do not know why an agent is calling. They clicked a button to see what their home is worth. My team has to understand the process better than the seller does.

✅ The seven-step seller call:
1️⃣ Fast, friendly intro
2️⃣ No interrogation
3️⃣ One question
4️⃣ A value drop under 30 seconds
5️⃣ A 15-minute visit, no cost, no need to clean
6️⃣ Two specific appointment times
7️⃣ Clear expectations

✅ Offering two times is not pushy. The seller raised their hand. The appointment is the next step of what they already asked for.

✅ Three net sheets at every appointment: the instant cash offer, off-market offers from our investor network, and a traditional listing after repairs. The seller sees the full picture and chooses.

✅ Convenience is often a disguise for something harder in someone’s life. Sometimes the easier path is the right call, even if listing nets more. That is serving a client.

✅ On the buyer side, my team is auditing every lead from the last 90 days with no offer written. The missing conversion is in the leads we took a nap on.

✅ Q4 is one week away. Many agents coast through the holidays, then pay the piper in Q1 when MLS and association dues hit and the pipeline is empty. My team sharpens these skills every day now, so nobody has to leave the industry in Q1.

text:
I am plagued by a lifelong terror of being discovered as an outsider.

At an In-N-Out Burger in Glendale, the line was thirty people deep under neon palm trees.

The illuminated board on the wall offered only three stark items: Hamburger, Cheeseburger, Double-Double.

Yet the people ordering ahead of me were murmuring arcane incantations like high-ranking freemasons: "Four-by-four, animal style, well-done fries, neapolitan shake."

My turn arrived. My palms were slick with nervous sweat.

A kid in a crisp paper hat beamed at me with the unfiltered enthusiasm of a golden retriever.

"Hey man! What can we get cooking for you?"
"A Double-Double," I whispered. Then, gathering all my courage, I mumbled: "...Can I do that 'Animal Style'? Or do I need a special card for that?"

The kid’s eyes widened with pure, evangelical joy.

"A special card?! Bro! Did someone tell you that?!"
He slapped the stainless-steel counter with both hands, grinning ear to ear.

"Animal Style is for the people, my guy! Mustard-seared beef, grilled onions, extra thousand island. Is this your first time?"

"My first time," I confessed, shrinking back.

"Stop it right now," he shouted to the kitchen line.

"We got a first-timer on table four! Make this one beautiful!"

He handed me my plastic ticket and winked—a wink so utterly devoid of irony it disarmed my cynical heart.

"You're about to have a religious experience, brother. Welcome to California."

Sitting in that noisy booth, biting into the sharp, sweet tang of grilled caramelized onions, I felt a stupid grin spread across my face.

They didn’t invent secret menus to keep outsiders out; they made them so an eighteen-year-old cashier can hand a lonely stranger the keys to the kingdom.

text:
Waddy  
Who Must Explain Themselves

Dennis A. Waddy
Who holds power in America? The familiar answer names presidents, legislators, governors, and judges. Their authority matters, and the Constitution divides it. Yet a person can encounter consequential power without entering a capitol or courtroom. An insurer decides how to evaluate a claim. An employer controls a schedule. An agency determines whether an application meets its rules. To understand a power structure, we should ask who makes decisions, who controls the evidence and explanation, and who bears the cost of a challenge. Power is most revealing when one person must explain every detail of their conduct while the institution can simply announce a result.
The American constitutional design begins with a fear of concentrated authority. In Federalist No. 51, James Madison argued that government must be arranged so its departments can check one another. The legislative, executive, and judicial branches hold different responsibilities, and the courts describe checks and balances as part of their constitutional relationship. These safeguards matter because public officials are people with interests and ambitions, not disembodied rules. A division of authority creates opportunities to question a decision and limits any one office’s reach.1
But constitutional checks do not describe every relationship in which one party can shape another’s choices. A private company can set the procedure through which it reviews a customer’s complaint. A school can decide what counts as satisfactory evidence. A supervisor can assign work and assess performance. None of these powers is identical to a legislature’s power to make law. Their practical importance comes from the decisions they can make and the consequences people experience while trying to contest them.
Consider an insurance dispute. A policyholder may know what happened in an accident and still lack access to every document, image, or account used by the company. The company has staff, established procedures, and experience interpreting its policies. The policyholder may have to request records, compare explanations, and ask for reconsideration while continuing ordinary life. California’s Department of Insurance maintains a consumer services division that gathers and responds to inquiries and complaints about insurance companies and producers. That avenue offers a possible check, but invoking a check takes effort. The existence of a complaint process tells us little by itself about how easy it is for a person to use.2
The control of information is a second form of power. If the decision maker possesses the records and defines which facts are relevant, the affected person may struggle even to formulate an objection. The Freedom of Information Act gives people a way to request records from federal executive agencies, subject to statutory exemptions. That law concerns government records; it does not make a private insurer’s entire file public. Its broader lesson is that access to information can make accountability possible. An answer such as “we reviewed the evidence” carries less weight than an explanation identifying what was reviewed and how it supported the conclusion.3
A meaningful chance to answer also matters. In Goldberg v. Kelly, the Supreme Court held that certain public assistance benefits could not be terminated without a hearing beforehand. The case concerned a specific government benefit and constitutional due process; it does not establish the same procedure for every private dispute. It nevertheless clarifies a democratic principle: when a decision has serious consequences, the person affected should have an appropriate chance to understand and respond to the case against them. A process that permits an appeal only after an unexplained decision may leave the person guessing about what to contest.4
The third question is who can afford to challenge a decision. An appeal may require forms, records, calls, transportation, time away from work, or professional help. These burdens fall unevenly. The Legal Services Corporation’s 2022 Justice Gap study found that low-income Americans received no or insufficient legal help for 92 percent of their civil legal problems. That statistic describes the study’s population and its measure of legal help; it does not prove that every disputed decision is unjust. It does show why a formal right to seek a remedy cannot be treated as proof that everyone can pursue one on equal terms.5
Institutions have different purposes, rules, and people within them. A power imbalance does not prove that every adverse decision is wrong. A sound challenge requires care with facts, openness to contrary evidence, and willingness to correct one’s own account. We should examine whether both sides can be heard and their reasons tested.
Here moral agency belongs in the argument. People inherit procedures they did not design, but they make choices within them. An adjuster can identify the evidence supporting a finding. A supervisor can explain a decision. A public official can offer a fair chance to respond. A citizen can document events, ask precise questions, and acknowledge uncertainty. Responsibility is exercised through decisions made inside a system.
Power in America cannot be mapped only by drawing the three branches of government. We must follow decisions into the places where they affect a life. Who decided? What evidence could each party see? Was the reason clear? What did review cost? These questions neither assume guilt nor guarantee agreement. They make authority answerable. A society committed to accountable power should not leave the burden of explanation entirely on the person least able to compel an answer.
Notes
1. James Madison, “Federalist No. 51,” February 8, 1788, National Constitution Center, https://t.co/Nl4mQZegMW; United States Courts, “Court Role and Structure,” accessed September 29, 2026, https://t.co/Olx1F9rPfT.
2. California Department of Insurance, “Consumer Services Division,” accessed September 29, 2026, https://t.co/WSMFN7sUGs.
3. National Archives and Records Administration, “Freedom of Information Act (FOIA),” accessed September 29, 2026, https://t.co/2bDCkoh8LG.
4. Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254, 264–71 (1970), https://t.co/YGRTB4i8VI.
5. Legal Services Corporation, The Justice Gap: The Unmet Civil Legal Needs of Low-Income Americans (2022), https://t.co/DQg3dV7AFO.

text:
LEGACY — Part 4 — His Mind, and Who Knew (2/3)
The Ledger: Two Presidencies, One Reckoning
Voters had already priced the age question. In January 2024, 76% of registered voters had major or moderate concern about Biden’s health for a second term, including a majority of Democrats.
VI. THE POLL THE CAMPAIGN COULD NOT SPIN PAST
Long before the June 2024 debate, internal and external polling indicated that the electorate had already factored the President’s cognitive state into its political calculus. Six months before the debate, public confidence had already severely eroded. The January 2024 poll is the NBC News survey of 1,000 registered voters, January 26–30, 2024.
- Combined 76% had major or moderate concerns that Biden lacked the mental and physical health for a second term.
- 62% called it a major concern; 14% moderate.
- By party: 95% of Republicans, 81% of independents, and 54% of Democrats had major or moderate concerns. This skepticism was not strictly partisan.
- By comparison, 61% had major or moderate concerns about Trump’s criminal and civil cases.
Other winter-spring 2024 surveys rhymed. Quinnipiac in February: 67% said Biden was too old for another term; 64% said he lacked the mental fitness; 62% the physical fitness. Trump’s numbers on the same questions were better, not good. ABC in January had already found only 28% saying Biden had good mental sharpness and good physical health. After the debate, Morning Consult recorded mental-fitness attribution at 37% of voters, a series low; Democratic confidence dropped nine points in a week. CBS/YouGov after the debate: 72% said he lacked the mental and cognitive health necessary to serve.
The political meaning is blunt. This was not a Republican-only panic. Half or more of Democrats were already telling pollsters they were worried before Hur, and long before Atlanta. The inner circle’s public line — that the issue was a right-wing obsession — was false as a description of the electorate. It may have been useful as a description of the information the inner circle wanted the electorate to use.
VII. ATLANTA, JUNE 27, 2024
The first general-election debate was supposed to settle the age question by showing Biden in command. It did the opposite. In what became the fatal blow to his reelection campaign, Biden delivered a halting, raspy performance against Donald Trump, frequently losing his train of thought and staring blankly.
He could not land attacks that existed, in sharper form, in his briefing books. Trump lied frequently and rambled; the split-screen still made Biden’s fragility the story. White House aides said he had a cold. Then jet lag from June foreign travel. Then that it was one bad night. Democrats watching in green rooms did not talk like people who had seen one bad night. They talked like people who had seen a fear confirmed.
The debate did not create the concern. It nationalized it in a format no comms plan could crop. From that night until July 21, the presidency and the campaign were two different operations: one still insisting he was running, the other watching donors, members, and polling detach in sequence.
The first 2024 general-election debate was not a Commission on Presidential Debates event. Both campaigns bypassed the CPD and accepted CNN’s invitation for Thursday, June 27, 2024, at the network’s Midtown Atlanta studios, 9:00 p.m. to about 10:39 p.m. ET. A second debate was booked for September 10 on ABC. Biden exited the race on July 21; that second night never happened. Nielsen put the television audience at 51.3 million across measured networks — high for a June weeknight, down more than 30 percent from the 73 million who watched their first 2020 debate. CNN itself drew 9.53 million, the largest program in the network’s history. More than half the TV audience was 55 or older.
Rules both campaigns signed. Ninety minutes. No opening statements. Two commercial breaks; no staff contact during those breaks. No studio audience. Identical podiums; coin toss for position and closing order. Biden won the toss, took the viewer’s-right podium, and spoke first in closings; Trump got the last word. Two minutes per answer, one minute rebuttal, extra minute at the moderators’ discretion. No props, no pre-written notes; pen, pad, water only. Microphones muted except for the candidate whose time it was — a Biden-side request after the 2020 shouting match. Green podium lights meant the mic was live; yellow timing lights at 15 seconds, flashing red at five, solid red and cut. Moderators: Jake Tapper and Dana Bash. They enforced time more than they fact-checked. That choice later became its own fight: Democrats said Trump’s falsehoods skated; the format’s defenders said muted mics and an empty room were the point.
How he got there. Biden came off back-to-back Europe trips (D-Day in France, G7 in Italy) and a Los Angeles fundraiser, then spent roughly six days at Camp David. A movie theater and a hangar were built into mock stages. The tight circle was Ron Klain, Mike Donilon, and Bruce Reed; a larger list of aides rotated in. Prep did not start before 11 a.m.; an afternoon lie-down was built in. The White House said he exercised and worked earlier. Politico later reported he woke with a bad cold two days out, could barely speak, shortened that day’s mocks, and tried to pack the lost work into Wednesday and a Thursday session before flying to Atlanta. The campaign told the press during the debate that he had a cold and had tested negative for COVID. Some journalists asked why that had not been leaked before he walked out hoarse.
They did not shake hands.
What the country heard. Tapper opened on the economy and inflation. Biden’s first minutes set the night. The voice was raspy, low, hard to hear. He defended the recovery, then reached for a tax-and-billionaire riff and lost the sentence.
From the CNN rush transcript, the collapse is on the page: He said there were “a thousand trillionaires in America — I mean, billionaires,” that they pay 8.2 percent, that 24 or 25 percent would raise “$500 million — billion dollars.” Then: childcare, elder care, health care, “every single solitary person eligible for what I’ve been able to do with the COVID — excuse me, with dealing with everything we have to do with. Look, if — we finally beat Medicare.” Tapper cut him for time. Trump: “Well, he’s right. He did beat Medicaid. He beat it to death.” (Trump’s wording wobbles across transcripts between Medicare and Medicaid; the cut was the same.) Tapper later said he wrote “holy smokes” on his iPad. In the 2025 book Original Sin, Bash’s note to Tapper is rendered as: he just lost the election. That is the moderators’ after-action, not a contemporaneous chyron — but it matches what Democratic operatives were already texting, and what Democratic members said privately within hours.
Politico’s night-of description is the visual half of the same file: frozen at the podium when he was not speaking, mouth open, eyes wide and unblinking for long stretches. That split-screen — not any one policy answer — is what 51 million people took home.
Other documented stumbles, not a complete transcript:
- Abortion / Roe. Asked whether he supported restrictions, he tried to recap Roe’s trimester framework and could not hold it: first trimester “between a woman and a doctor”; second “between a doctor and an extreme situation”; third “between the doctor, I mean, between the women and the state.” For a campaign that had treated Dobbs as a central contrast, the explanation was the opposite of a close.
- Immigration non sequitur. In an abortion answer he veered to a murdered young woman and an immigrant perpetrator — an apparent reference to a Houston case — without landing the policy point he was supposed to be making.
- Afghanistan pivot. Critiquing Trump’s economy, he suddenly said Trump “didn’t do anything about” Afghanistan — the withdrawal that was one of Biden’s own worst nights.
- Border answer. He wandered; Trump said, “I really don’t know what he said at the end of that sentence. I don’t think he knows what he said either.”
- Age question becomes golf. Asked how they would handle the job at their ages, both men slid into a handicap argument instead of a fitness answer. That exchange is comic in isolation. On this night it read as two old men changing the subject.
- Closer. The campaign later claimed a “strong finish.” AP noted the closing statement was still hard to understand. Afterward he told a crowd, “We’re going to beat this guy.” Early Friday, asked if he should step aside: “No, it’s hard to debate a liar.” He said he thought they “did well,” and that he had a sore throat.
He also landed some intended punches — Trump’s tax cuts, January 6, “loser” and “sucker” language about service members, with Beau invoked. Those lines existed. They did not rearrange the night. Style ate substance because the style was the question the debate had been called to answer.
What Trump did on the same stage. A complete ledger does not treat Trump’s 90 minutes as a silent control group. He was louder, more fluent, and densely inaccurate. He restated the 2020-election fraud claim; on accepting 2024 results he said he would if it was a “good and fair election,” then returned to 2020. He offered false or inflated claims on abortion (that everyone wanted Roe gone; that Democrats support abortions after birth), immigration, and the economy. Moderators largely let the clock, not a referee, handle it. Viewers who already distrusted him heard a familiar Trump. Viewers who had been told Biden was sharp heard something they had not been prepared to see. Both things happened in one split screen. That is why Democratic panic and Trump’s “victory lap” could be simultaneous without either side inventing the tape.
Immediate political sequence (the 24 days, tightened).
Night of, June 27. Donors texting face-palms and worse. Kate Bedingfield, Biden’s former communications director, said on CNN it was “really disappointing.” Claire McCaskill: he had one job and did not do it; phones from high office were not mere hand-wringing. Schumer’s public post still framed a policy choice. Jeffries stood by him. Fetterman told the party to “chill” and compared morning-after pile-ons to his own 2022 debate. Pelosi on Friday: performance “wasn’t great,” values “far outshone the other guy,” and she knew of no one pushing him out — yet. House members in swing seats were already talking replacement in private.
June 28–30. Campaign: cold, one bad night. North Carolina rally the next day, more energy, intended as a reset. Party polling and donor calls through the weekend. Morning Consult and others showed mental-fitness numbers making new lows (covered in Section VI).
July 2–5. Pelosi on television: is this “an episode or a condition,” and the question is “legitimate” for both men. That phrasing, from the most important Democrat not then in elected leadership, licensed the revolt. Rep. Lloyd Doggett became the first sitting House Democrat to call for withdrawal. Biden’s July 5 ABC interview: he was staying, and he would “beat him again in 2020.”
July 10–11. Clooney op-ed. Pelosi treating the decision as still open. NATO “President Putin” / “Vice President Trump.”
July 21. Withdrawal letter.
The debate did not reveal a secret medical file. It removed the last staging advantage the White House had built: short clips, friendly rooms, no audience, a muted opponent. They got the muted opponent and the empty room. They still had to stand for 90 minutes with a live mic, a clock, and no aide at the elbow. That was the test they had asked for in May when they accepted an early debate to “reset” the age issue. The reset ran the other way.
The debate at a glance:
- Date / place / time: June 27, 2024; CNN Atlanta studio; 9:00–10:39 p.m. ET
- Audience: None in studio; 51.3 million on TV (Nielsen)
- Format owner: CNN, not the CPD
- Mic rule: Auto-mute except on a speaker’s clock (Biden ask)
- Staff during breaks: Forbidden
- Notes on stage: Forbidden
- Handshake: None
- Prep site: Camp David, about six days; 11 a.m. start, afternoon rest; cold two days out
- Declared illness: Cold; COVID-negative, per campaign mid-debate
- Signature clip: “We finally beat Medicare” after billion/million mix
- Age question: Became a golf-handicap argument
- Second debate: ABC, September 10 — cancelled by withdrawal
- Campaign line, June 28: Bad night, sore throat, still running
- Party line by mid-July: Episode-or-condition, then open revolt
The missing piece was never a hidden extra gaffe. It was the architecture: an early debate the incumbent sought, rules he helped write, and a week of closed prep that did not survive contact with a live hour-and-a-half. The tape is the primary source. Everything after it is people arguing about whether they had already known what the tape showed.
VIII. NATO, JULY 11: THE ENCORE NO CAMPAIGN WANTED
The Washington NATO summit was designed as a competence demonstration. Under immense pressure to prove his fitness, Biden got through prepared Ukraine remarks. Then, introducing Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a security-compact ceremony:
“Ladies and gentlemen, President Putin.”
Gasps. A correction: he was “so focused on beating Putin.” Zelenskyy: “I’m better.” Biden: “You’re a hell of a lot better.” European leaders offered the public courtesy that slips happen. Off-camera, The Telegraph quoted officials calling the optics a ruin of months of work. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the whole world had noticed.
Hours later, at a rare solo press conference, Biden said he “wouldn’t have picked Vice President Trump” if she were not qualified to be president. He meant Harris. Reuters treated the two slips as a set. They were a set: the same week the campaign needed a clean summit, the president named the enemy in the ally’s place and the opponent in the deputy’s place.
IX. THE INTERNAL REVOLT AND FINANCIAL FREEZE
Following the June 2024 debate, the Biden campaign attempted to contain the fallout, attributing the President’s performance to a cold and travel fatigue. However, this narrative quickly fractured under the weight of internal party anxiety and an unprecedented revolt from major donors. The public calls for Biden to step aside were initially a trickle that rapidly became a flood.
- July 10, 2024: Actor and major Democratic fundraiser George Clooney published an op-ed in the New York Times calling for a new nominee. Clooney, who had co-hosted the June 15 fundraiser for Biden (Section III), stated plainly: “the one battle he cannot win is the fight against time.” He claimed his assessment was shared privately by “every senator and Congress member and governor” he had spoken with. The op-ed landed the day before the NATO summit slips. Nancy Pelosi, on television, had already framed the choice as still open — an unmistakable signal from the party’s most important vote-counter that “I’m running” was no longer an order the caucus would obey.
- Mid-July 2024: The pressure mounted significantly. By July 12, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries met with Biden at the White House to convey the deep concerns of his caucus. Reports indicated that both Jeffries and Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer were privately pressing Biden to step aside.
- July 17, 2024: Representative Adam Schiff, a prominent California Democrat and close ally of Nancy Pelosi, publicly called for Biden to exit the race, citing “serious concerns” about his ability to defeat Donald Trump.
Behind the scenes, donors began freezing money. Major contributors signaled they would withhold funding down-ballot if Biden remained at the top of the ticket, fearing a landslide defeat that would cost Democrats both the House and the Senate, a fear explicitly voiced by Clooney.
The pressure culminated in a coordinated effort by party elders, notably former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, to present Biden with a stark choice: withdraw voluntarily or face an increasingly public and humiliating fight. By widely cited counts, more than 30 congressional Democrats had publicly called for him to step down by July 19.
Faced with an untenable political reality — plummeting polls, a frozen campaign war chest, and the loss of nearly all institutional support — Biden officially ended his re-election campaign on July 21, 2024.
