text:
The Cornell rape story -- which is starting to look much more complicated as new information comes out -- is not a "Duke Lacrosse" incident where an accuser has fabricated an incident.  

Rather, it's a "campus rape," or a "sexual misconduct" -- a gross and squalid sexual incident the experience of which the woman considers to be nonconsensual, at least in hindsight, but which in the eyes of the law, based on a third-party assessment of the facts as she alleges them was a consensual sex act.  However, there are numerous instances where men have been punished with social shunning, reputational destruction, job loss, university disciplinary penalties or other extra-legal sanctions for alleged acts that did not meet legal definitions of crimes or were not supported by sufficient evidence to sustain criminal prosecutions.

"Rape" is a concept with many definitions.  Traditionally, it was defined as "sex with an unwilling woman, obtained by force, overwhelming her resistance."  Since the 1970s, the laws surrounding this have changed.  

The first big reform was the requirement of resistance: You don't have to resist to be a victim of robbery or battery, why is the victim's resistance an element of sex crimes?  So, the requirement that the woman be resisting was removed. But when the woman is not resisting and does not have to be violently overwhelmed, what does it mean to obtain the sex by force? Clearly, whatever achieves sex with an unwilling woman is sufficient force to satisfy the element.  So we're left today with "Sex with an unwilling person" or "sex without consent."

But now, how do you define consent? How does a third party examining disputed facts after an incident determine its presence or absence? What if there was consent for one act but not for another? What if it was given at one point but revoked later? Is mere acquiescence consent, or must consent be enthusiastic? What if there is a spoken verbal agreement to participate in the act but the woman was intoxicated?

Several of these questions are implicated in this case. According to a statement the woman made, she drank ten drinks and then went to the fraternity house, likely with the intention of having sex with one of the accused men.  When she got there, the man offered her ketamine, which she voluntarily ingested. He then asked her if his friend could also have sex with her.  She -- in a state of intoxication -- verbally consented to the three-way and engaged in it.  

While this was going on, a third man came into the room and asked if he could join in.  According to her statement, the woman refused because she believed that having sex with three men would require her to have anal sex. 

The first man, who was heavily intoxicated, as all the participants were, could not maintain an erection and eventually lost consciousness, and at this point, the third man joined in.  At some point, the second man began dry heaving because he was so intoxicated.  

According to her statement, a total of seven men came into the room and she makes various allegations about their conduct. She says several of them snorted lines of ketamine off of her body. 

A couple of weeks after the incident, the woman went to the campus police and reported it as a rape. During an interview with detectives, she gave a sworn statement six single-spaced pages long detailing the incident.  The police sent the statement to the local prosecutor who determined that based on New York state law, the allegations the woman made did not constitute a crime.  

In New York, it is a crime to have sex with a person who is unconscious or so impaired as to be unable to speak or express consent or refusal, and it is also a crime to give someone drugs without their knowledge in order to obtain sex from them. In this case, the woman voluntarily consumed the drugs and alcohol, which does not invalidate her verbal consent to the sex acts she participated in.

The prosecutor sent his finding back to the police and told them that the complainant was welcome to speak with him further if she had any questions. He says she never contacted him.  The woman's statement and the Cornell University police investigation also formed the basis of the university disciplinary proceedings that arose out of these events. Cornell says it found some of the men responsible for wrongdoing under university disciplinary policies -- which have different elements and definitions than New York state criminal law -- and that the men were punished.  

The woman has now filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell, the men and other defendants, alleging facts that differ substantially from the sworn statement she gave to the police two weeks after the incident.  The prosecutor has agreed to reopen the investigation and present the facts to a grand jury, but in light of the fact that the woman's story has changed materially from her original sworn statement, it will be a very difficult case to prosecute.

Many people have personal ideas or definitions of what rape is that may differ from the offense that is codified in the law.  A lot of people believe that if several men have sex with a woman that is intoxicated on alcohol and ketamine, that is unquestionably rape, without regard to her acknowledged verbal agreement to the sex act or her active participation in it; they believe someone who is so impaired cannot meaningfully consent. That is not what the law says in New York.

As such, prosecutors in New York, disciplinary tribunals at Cornell University, and pundits on social media may reach different conclusions about whether this is rape or not. This was, by all accounts a squalid, disgusting and shameful event. The question is whether this is something that was done to this woman or whether it is something she was a willing participant in.

text:
The story Cornell's Jane Doe initially told police was not that seven fraternity brothers forcibly drugged and gang-raped her for hours.

She described going to the fraternity house to meet a man she was interested in, willingly participating in multiple sexual encounters, voluntarily taking Ketamine more than once, declining sexual advances at several points without apparent consequence, and ending the final threesome of the night when she said she was tired.

But in the civil case, voluntary Ketamine use becomes forced drugging, consensual threesomes become gang rape, and Doe repeatedly exercising her ability to say ‘yes’ and ‘no’ becomes seven men taking advantage of her inability to consent.

These are not minor differences in recollection. They go right to the heart of whether or not a rape actually occurred.

In the early 1870s, a family calling themselves the Benders settled beside the Osage Trail in Labette County, Kansas, and kept a cabin that served as a store and inn for travelers heading west. There were four of them: an older couple, John Bender and his wife, and a younger man and woman known as John Junior and Kate.

A canvas sheet divided the single room. Guests were seated at the table with their backs to it, and struck from behind. The bodies were dropped through a trap door into the cellar and buried in the orchard.

People had been disappearing along that stretch of road for months. In March 1873, a doctor, William York, vanished while searching for another missing traveler. His brother, a Kansas state senator, led armed parties along the trail and questioned the Benders.

In early May, neighbors noticed that the cabin stood abandoned and the livestock were starving. Searchers dug up the orchard and found the remains of at least eleven people.

The family had scattered. A reward was offered and never collected. Vigilantes later claimed to have caught and killed them, but no bodies were identified, and no Bender was ever tried.

text:
U.S. Homeland Drone Defense: Capability Exists, Coverage Does Not - The United States possesses credible counter-UAS technologies and has demonstrated operational defeat of hostile or unauthorized drones, including kinetic, non-kinetic and directed-energy effects, but the public official record does not establish a continuous national defensive architecture capable of reliably detecting, classifying, tracking and defeating a coordinated drone swarm across the geographically dispersed military, infrastructure and civilian targets that constitute the homeland attack surface. USNORTHCOM itself describes more than 350 homeland installations with varying degrees of defensive capability and criticality, while simultaneously developing deployable fly-away teams and additional detect-track-identify-defeat capacity. https://t.co/PRV2ueWG4N
The principal vulnerability is therefore architectural rather than technological: sensor coverage is incomplete, different agencies possess different statutory authorities, civilian airspace constraints complicate active mitigation, installations retain local defensive responsibilities, critical infrastructure is predominantly outside the military perimeter, and the economics of defending thousands of potential targets against inexpensive attritable aircraft remain unfavorable. The Department of Defense formally identified production capacity, technology innovation, authorities, policy, open architectures, system integration and force structure as outstanding Replicator 2 problems rather than solved conditions. Media Difesa
Material progress since 2024 is nevertheless evident. USNORTHCOM became the Defense Department’s homeland C-sUAS synchronizer; JIATF-401 subsequently became the principal organization for accelerating counter-drone delivery at scale; updated homeland policy expanded commander discretion; federal rules effective 1 July 2026 created a framework for qualified state, local, tribal and territorial agencies to exercise counter-UAS authorities; and operational forces have now used high-energy lasers against cartel-linked drones on the southern border. https://t.co/PRV2ueWG4N
These advances principally improve point and regional defense; they do not by themselves solve saturation. The December 2024 Defense Department counter-unmanned-systems strategy explicitly identifies future systems that will be more autonomous, more networked, capable of longer loiter, larger payloads and swarm behavior, while the department’s response emphasizes defenses able to confront larger numbers of increasingly capable autonomous systems. Media Difesa
The strategic requirement through 2031 is consequently a transition from isolated counter-drone equipment toward a distributed homeland air-surveillance and engagement ecosystem in which inexpensive sensors, Remote ID and other cooperative data, passive RF detection, radar, electro-optical/infrared systems and intelligence feeds are fused into common operational pictures, while commanders and law-enforcement authorities gain scalable low-collateral effectors suitable for dense civilian airspace. Current federal experimentation and procurement indicate that this transition has begun, but the verified public record does not demonstrate that it has reached nationwide operational maturity. Governo di Guerra
The five-year risk is asymmetric: commercial drone integration is simultaneously increasing legitimate traffic density while autonomy, alternative communications links and swarm coordination reduce the usefulness of defenses that depend disproportionately upon detecting conventional control signals; successful homeland defense will therefore require discrimination between legitimate and hostile traffic at machine speed, not merely additional interceptors. The FAA’s 2025 integration concept already described more than 800,000 registered drones, while federal research programs have explicitly tested threats using cellular communications, airborne detection and multisensor data fusion. Amministrazione Federale dell’Aviazione
The decisive uncertainty is not whether additional counter-UAS systems will be fielded—they already are—but whether the United States can scale sensors, authorities, trained personnel, command integration and economically sustainable effectors quickly enough that a sophisticated adversary cannot exploit the enormous difference between defending selected protected sites and protecting the broader homeland against simultaneous, geographically distributed attacks.

America’s drone problem is no longer detection. It is scale.
The United States has already demonstrated that it can detect, track and defeat unmanned aircraft over its own territory; what it has not yet demonstrated is that it can do so at the scale required by a coordinated, multi-axis and geographically distributed attack. That distinction now matters more than any individual counter-drone technology. By September 2026, USNORTHCOM was operating across a homeland environment containing more than 350 military installations with uneven defensive coverage, JIATF-401 had deployed more than $20 million in counter-UAS systems to priority southern-border sites in roughly four months, and Joint Task Force–Southern Border had reported more than 300 drone defeats during 2026. The fiscal, industrial and security stakes are therefore converging: the United States possesses functioning tools, but its defence will depend on whether sensors, authorities, command networks, interceptors and factories can be scaled before adversaries learn to saturate them.

The United States has crossed the technical threshold but not the systems threshold
The 2026 operational record is no longer one of prototypes alone. By 4 September, Joint Task Force–Southern Border had reported more than 300 UAS defeats during the calendar year, including more than 100 in August, while the Army Multipurpose High-Energy Laser had defeated 11 cartel-linked drones since its first operational employment on 24 August. These figures matter because they establish that kinetic, non-kinetic and directed-energy counter-UAS systems are no longer confined to demonstrations.

They do not establish swarm resilience. A system that can defeat repeated individual targets may still fail when track volume, engagement channels, operator workload, thermal margins or interceptor stocks are saturated simultaneously. No figure in the dossier establishes national simultaneous-track capacity, validated multi-wave engagement depth, average regeneration time or the number of sites capable of sustaining several attack waves without external reinforcement. The strategic gap is therefore not between “having” and “not having” counter-UAS capability, but between successful local engagements and sustainable system throughput.

That is why Replicator 2 is more important than any one interceptor contract. Its September 2024 direction did not define the problem narrowly as a procurement shortage; it identified production capacity, technology innovation, authorities, policy, open-system architecture, system integration and force structure as the barriers to protecting critical installations and force concentrations, with an objective of materially improved capability within 24 months of congressional funding approval. The programme is, in effect, an attempt to turn counter-drone defence from equipment acquisition into institutional scaling.

The numbers show a force that is moving quickly but still buying in small lots
The disparity between operational urgency and current procurement scale is visible in the numbers. JIATF-401 deployed more than $20 million in counter-UAS technology to priority southern-border locations within approximately four months, but the first Replicator 2 purchase announced in January 2026 involved only two DroneHunter F700 systems. In February, JIATF-401 announced a $5.2 million agreement for the Bumblebee V2 low-cost kinetic interceptor, with deliveries scheduled to begin in March.

Those purchases are meaningful because they open rapid-acquisition pathways and establish different effector classes, not because they yet amount to national mass. Project Flytrap 5.0 evaluated more than 20 counter-UAS systems under common standards, while Falcon Peak 26.2, conducted from 31 August to 25 September 2026 at Yuma Proving Ground, was designed to test emerging technologies under homeland-relevant conditions and increase emphasis on low-collateral defeat.

The pattern is clear. The United States is still in the stage of selecting, standardising and integrating a portfolio. The 2031 requirement is fundamentally different: serial production, regional inventories, common command interfaces and enough attritable systems to continue fighting after the first wave.

The cost-exchange ratio will decide whether success is sustainable
Counter-UAS economics are becoming as important as probability of kill. Electronic warfare can be repeatedly employed at low marginal cost where hostile aircraft still depend on exploitable control links; low-cost interceptor drones can defeat RF-independent targets but consume physical inventory; high-energy lasers offer deep electrical magazines but remain constrained by line of sight, dwell time, thermal management and environmental conditions; conventional projectile systems provide another layer but create ammunition and collateral-risk constraints.

The architecture therefore cannot be built around a single “best” weapon. It must push each target toward the cheapest adequate engagement method while preserving finite high-value effectors for threats that require them. The $5.2 million Bumblebee V2 agreement and the first Replicator 2 DroneHunter purchase point in this direction because both seek lower-cost, lower-collateral solutions rather than relying exclusively on missile-class interception.

Directed energy is the most visible attempt to change magazine economics. The 11 AMP-HEL defeats reported by 4 September 2026 demonstrate real operational use, but they do not answer the harder saturation question: how many targets can one system service consecutively before beam dwell time, heat dissipation or target transition becomes limiting? The dossier contains no public national figure for this. Until those throughput metrics exist, “deep magazine” should not be confused with “unlimited rate of fire”.

Swarm defence is becoming a command-and-control problem before it becomes a firepower problem
A coordinated swarm can overwhelm a defender without physically defeating every interceptor. It can saturate sensor processing, create false tracks, exploit classification delays, force expenditure on decoys, overload command networks or attack several sites simultaneously so that mobile reinforcement cannot concentrate.

This is why JIATF-401’s institutional role matters. By September 2026, its second interagency summit brought together more than 200 leaders and experts from 75 departments and agencies. That scale reflects the real problem: military services, FAA, DHS, law-enforcement bodies and infrastructure operators cannot operate separate tactical pictures during a high-tempo attack.

Project Flytrap’s assessment of the Integrated Battle Command System–Maneuver common tactical user interface is therefore more strategically important than it first appears. The requirement is to move beyond a shared display toward a network able to correlate tracks, assess target priority, identify which effectors can engage, check inventory and legal availability, allocate the least costly suitable response and immediately reassign another system if the first engagement fails.

The 2031 threshold is not merely a “common operating picture”. It is common resource allocation under saturation.

Industrial capacity is the hidden magazine behind every interceptor
The most serious long-term constraint may sit outside the operational system entirely. In August 2026, the U.S. government’s Section 232 action concluded that domestic UAS and component production remained insufficient to meet national-security needs reliably or support wartime surge at adequate scale. The identified dependencies included motors, electronic speed controllers, lithium-ion batteries and docking stations.

That matters directly to counter-UAS defence because many low-cost interceptors rely on the same commercial industrial base as the systems they are intended to destroy. An architecture built around attritable drone interceptors is sustainable only if motors, batteries, electronics and airframes can be produced faster than combat consumes them.

The policy response is substantial but slow by operational standards. The August 2026 measures imposed a 100 per cent ad valorem duty on certain larger or security-sensitive UAS, thermal-imager-equipped systems, docking stations and specified critical components, while smaller UAS and additional components received 25 per cent duties. A component tariff under Annex III is scheduled to take effect on 9 February 2027, while approved onshoring plans are expected to commit to construction before 20 January 2029.

Those dates define the industrial risk. Procurement demand is accelerating in 2026, but some of the manufacturing capacity intended to support it will not physically mature until later in the decade.

Point defence will fail if regional depth does not emerge
USNORTHCOM’s more than 350 homeland military installations already have varying defensive capability and criticality. That alone makes a nationally uniform point-defence model unrealistic. A thousand interceptors stored centrally do not protect a site that requires them within minutes, and a deployable counter-UAS team cannot reinforce several geographically separated attacks at once.

The emerging architecture therefore needs four levels of depth: site-level ready inventory for immediate engagements; regional reserves capable of reinforcing multiple facilities within hours; national reserves able to rebalance between regions; and an industrial replenishment pipeline replacing what operations consume.

Fly-away kits remain valuable within this structure. An 11-person USNORTHCOM team deployed to Minot Air Force Base in October 2025 and successfully engaged more than 100 targets of interest while obtaining operational certification. But the same fact demonstrates the limitation of mobile reinforcement: one team can close one gap at one time. Distributed attacks are specifically designed to exploit that scarcity.

By 2031, resilience will therefore be measured less by how many counter-drone systems exist nationally than by where they are positioned, how quickly they can be replenished, and whether one region can support another without exposing a second vulnerability.

The next 12–24 months will show whether Washington is building a network or another collection of programmes
The decisive evidence will arrive before 2031. Over the next 12–24 months, Replicator 2 must move beyond demonstration quantities into larger follow-on orders; JIATF-401’s common testing standards must influence procurement rather than remain an evaluation tool; industrial onshoring must begin producing measurable capacity rather than policy announcements; and interoperability exercises must prove that several geographically separated sites can share tracks, magazines and effector status during realistic multi-wave attacks.

The cost of failure will not fall on one institution. The Department of Defense will carry the operational burden of defending more than 350 homeland installations with uneven local capability; DHS and other federal agencies will face pressure to extend protection across borders and critical infrastructure; state and local authorities will inherit a larger role in distributed response; private infrastructure operators will bear the consequences where persistent active defence remains unavailable; and the industrial base will absorb the cost of accelerated procurement if foreign dependencies remain unresolved.

By 2027 and 2028, the relevant question will no longer be whether the United States has good counter-drone technologies. It will be whether those technologies have become a regionalised, interoperable and replenishable defensive system. If they have not, the attacker’s advantage will not come from superior engineering. It will come from forcing a fragmented defence to spend, decide and react faster than its institutions and factories can sustain.  -https://t.co/GanaLePoFY via @https://debuglies.com

text:
Why Is Trevor Lee Charged with Mortgage Fraud?

On paper, the answer is simple.

Trevor Lee is charged with mortgage fraud because prosecutors say he used false employment and income documents to obtain a $1 million home loan.

But that is not the whole story of how he got here.

Earlier this year, Lee spent the 2026 legislative session pushing immigration legislation over public benefits and lawful-presence requirements. His H.B. 88 sought to tighten eligibility rules for certain public assistance programs. After that bill stalled, immigration provisions were folded into H.B. 386, which passed the House but did not become law.

Lee made no secret of his frustration. He argued publicly that Utah needed to prioritize taxpayer-funded benefits for citizens and lawful residents, and he told voters the immigration fight was not over.

Then primary season arrived.

On April 15, just days before the Davis County Republican convention, two former business associates went public with allegations against Lee. One involved altered checks from 2013. The other came from Enevive CEO Trent Spafford, who accused Lee of seeking $93,000 in advances while promising to help the company obtain a government contract involving Hill Air Force Base.

Lee denied abusing his office and called the accusations a political “hit job.”

Three days later, Bob Stevenson defeated Lee among convention delegates, 55 percent to 45 percent. Stevenson later beat him in the June Republican primary, with early results showing roughly 66 percent to Lee’s 34 percent.

House Speaker Mike Schultz asked the Utah Attorney General’s Office to independently investigate the allegations.

And that is where the story takes an interesting turn.

According to the charging documents filed September 28, investigators were assigned to look into “allegations of public corruption” involving Lee.

But Lee is not charged with public corruption.

Instead, investigators obtained documents connected to his home financing. Prosecutors allege Lee submitted a forged Enevive employment contract, overstated his income, and used a Blue Logic offer letter he knew did not reflect income the company could actually pay.

The charging documents also say Lee admitted signing Spafford’s name on the Enevive contract.

Those are serious allegations. If prosecutors prove them, the fact that investigators originally started somewhere else does not make mortgage fraud any less criminal.

There is also a direct link between the two investigations. Spafford alleged that the $93,000 in advances was intended to help Lee show greater income while financing his house. Looking at the mortgage was therefore not a random detour.

But the original question remains.

What happened to the public-corruption allegation?

The investigation began with a claim that Lee abused his legislative office. It ended, at least so far, with charges involving private mortgage paperwork uncovered while investigators were examining his finances.

And the timing is difficult to ignore.

Lee pushed controversial immigration bills. Damaging allegations appeared days before his nominating convention. Those allegations triggered an Attorney General investigation. Lee lost renomination. Months later, prosecutors charged him with different crimes discovered during that investigation.

That chronology does not prove Lee was politically targeted.

But it does raise a fair question about whether he would have faced this level of investigative scrutiny if the political events earlier this year had unfolded differently.

text:
Where the Formless Becomes Form

Long ago, around the year 1200, a king asked a master stonecutter to make a special statue of the divine for a holy temple.

The stonecutter chose a fine, gray stone from the mountain. 
When the priests saw the smooth stone, they smiled and said, “The mountain has given us its heart.”

At first, the stonecutter shaped the stone into a tall, smooth, round pillar. It had no eyes, no mouth, and no human shape. 
This showed that the divine has no single form and is quiet, like the big sky. 

It reminded people that the holy presence is everywhere, even in places we cannot see.

But the chief priest told the stonecutter, “People also need a face to look at. They need to feel like the divine is looking back at them.”

So, the stonecutter took his tools and carefully carved four different faces on the sides of the pillar, one for each direction:

Facing East: He carved a calm and kind face. This showed the divine as a peaceful teacher, like the earth that feeds us.

Facing South: He carved a fierce face with angry eyes. 
This showed the divine as fire, destroying bad things so new things can grow.

Facing West: He carved a young, smiling face.
This showed the divine as water, full of joy and giving new life.

Facing North: He carved a soft, gentle face that looked like a woman. 
This showed love and kindness, joining both male and female energies together as one.

But the stonecutter did not carve a fifth face on top. He left the top of the stone empty and round.

He told the priest, “The fifth face is invisible. It is the sky, the open space, and the truth that our eyes cannot see. People must look up into their own hearts to find it.”

For hundreds of years, the holy stone stood in the temple. 
Families walked around it in a circle. 
They poured clean water over the top, offered green leaves, and put bright red and yellow powders on the faces. 
Each person would stop at the face they needed most that day, seeking peace, strength, a fresh start, or love.

Many years passed, and the statue traveled far away from its first home. Today, it sits quietly inside a museum

The divine is one, but comes to us in many ways, as a teacher, a protector, a creator, and a lover. 
And above all of them is the quiet, hidden presence that holds everything together.

​There is, however, a third response to consider: "Welcome home." As a Jewish follower of Yeshua, your spiritual journey has an incredibly rich destination in the Catholic Church. Rather than asking you to leave your Jewish heritage at the door, Catholicism offers the most direct, unbroken continuity with it, presenting itself not as a replacement of Judaism, but as its historical and sacramental fulfillment.

​Exploring the Catholic faith naturally completes your Jewish identity for several foundational reasons:

​The Fulfillment of the Passover: The Last Supper was a Passover Seder. Jesus did not abolish the Todah (thanksgiving) sacrifice or the Paschal Lamb; He became it. ​The Written and Oral Law: Just as Judaism relies on both the Torah (written law) and the Mishnah/Talmud (oral tradition and teaching authority), the Catholic Church operates with Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition, guided by a living teaching authority (the Magisterium).

​Embracing Catholicism does not mean abandoning your Jewishness. Stepping into a Catholic parish is stepping into the fulfillment of the covenants made with Abraham, Moses, and David. It is a space where Yeshua is not just recognized as Savior, but physically encountered in the Eucharist every single day.

text:
The Catholic funeral liturgy is not mainly a memorial of a life well lived. It is a public act of worship in which the Church proclaims that death has been transformed by Christ’s death and resurrection, commends the deceased to God’s mercy, and consoles the living with the hope of eternal life.⁠

Its purpose is threefold: to praise God for the gift of the life that has now returned to Him, to pray for the forgiveness of the deceased person’s sins, and to strengthen the mourners with the Word of God and the Eucharist.⁠

The three “stations”
The rites usually unfold in three movements, often over two days.

1. The Vigil for the Deceased (the wake)
The Christian community keeps watch with the family. Scripture is read, prayers of intercession are offered, and the assembly asks God to receive the deceased into “the kingdom of light and peace.” This is the usual place for words of remembrance or a eulogy. The focus is both on the person’s life and on the paschal mystery—Christ’s passage from death to life.⁠

2. The Funeral Mass (Mass of Christian Burial)
This is the heart of the liturgy. The community gathers in church to give thanks for Christ’s victory over death, to commend the deceased to God’s mercy, and to be strengthened by the Eucharist.⁠

Typical elements include:

Reception of the body at the church door. The coffin is sprinkled with holy water (a reminder of baptism) and covered with a white pall (the baptismal garment that clothes every Christian equally).

The Paschal candle stands nearby, the same candle lit at Easter, symbolizing the risen Christ who has conquered darkness.

Liturgy of the Word: readings chosen for their message of hope and resurrection, followed by a homily that explains the mystery of Christian death rather than delivering a eulogy.

Liturgy of the Eucharist: the Church offers the sacrifice of Christ and prays that the deceased may be purified of remaining sin and admitted to the banquet of heaven. The living and the dead remain one Body in Christ.

Final Commendation: incense honors the body as a temple of the Holy Spirit; the Song of Farewell is sung as the community entrusts the person to God.

3. The Rite of Committal

At the grave, tomb, or columbarium the body (or cremated remains) is committed to its resting place. The prayers ask that the deceased “sleep in peace until you awaken him/her to glory.” The grave itself becomes a sign of hope because Christ sanctified the tomb by lying in one for three days.⁠

Core theological meaning

Catholics believe baptism unites a person to Christ’s death and resurrection (Romans 6:3-5). The funeral therefore treats the body with reverence—it was a temple of the Holy Spirit and will be raised. Prayer for the dead is offered because most people still need purification after death; the Eucharist is the Church’s most powerful prayer for that mercy. At the same time the rites insist that death does not break the bonds of the Communion of Saints: the living continue to pray for the dead, and the dead intercede for the living.
In short, the liturgy looks simultaneously backward to baptism, forward to the resurrection of the body, and upward to the mercy of God. It refuses both despair and mere sentimental remembrance. It proclaims that the last word belongs to the risen Christ.

text:
In military fiction and defense marketing videos, combat lasers are often portrayed as the ultimate game-changer. Promoted as weapons with an infinite magazine, system developers highlight their low cost per shot, speed-of-light engagement times, and freedom from physical ammunition logistics. Against swarms of low-cost attack drones and anti-ship cruise missiles, high-energy laser systems like the U.S. Navy's HELIOS or the UK's DragonFire sound like an invincible defensive shield.

However, stripping away the sci-fi hype reveals a far more restrictive reality. While high-energy lasers do not use traditional physical shells, their operational magazine is strictly bounded by immovable engineering limits. From massive power spikes and extreme thermal buildup to atmospheric degradation, lasers face severe real-world constraints when deployed on active battlefields.

The Power Grid Bottleneck 

A laser weapon does not create energy out of thin air; it converts raw electrical current into a concentrated beam of coherent light. To burn through the metal skin of a fast-moving missile or melt the internal circuitry of a drone, a laser system requires massive amounts of power delivered in precise, high-voltage spikes.

On a naval vessel or ground vehicle, drawing hundreds of kilowatts of electricity places an immense burden on the ship's internal generators or mobile power banks. Firing a high-energy laser continuously can drop voltage across shipboard battle networks, interfere with radar arrays, or stall mechanical drive systems. To prevent system-wide power failure, laser operators rely on high-density capacitor banks or flywheel energy storage systems that act as electrical shock absorbers. Once those energy storage banks are depleted during an engagement, the laser cannot fire until the ship's generators recharge them. The infinite magazine is immediately capped by the speed at which the ship can generate and store raw electricity.

The Thermal Trap: Waste Heat and Cooldown Cycles

The second major bottleneck limiting laser operations is energy inefficiency. Modern solid-state and fiber lasers are notoriously inefficient at converting electrical input into usable optical output. Most military lasers operate at efficiency levels between 30 and 40 percent.

This means that for every 100 kilowatts of optical beam power fired at a target, the laser system generates roughly 200 kilowatts of internal waste heat. If that intense thermal load is not immediately dissipated, sensitive optical lenses expand, focal points distort, and internal electronics burn out.

Managing this thermal spike requires heavy liquid cooling units and massive heat exchangers. In high-intensity combat, where a laser must engage multiple incoming targets in rapid succession, internal temperatures rise quickly. Once thermal thresholds are reached, the system must enter a mandatory cooldown cycle, rendering the weapon completely offline. Far from firing continuously, a laser's engagement rate is strictly limited by how fast its cooling system can dump waste heat.

Atmospheric Degradation: Moisture, Dust, and Thermal Blooming

Even when a laser has full power and cool electronics, its effectiveness is dictated by environmental conditions. Unlike physical bullets or interceptor missiles, light beams are highly sensitive to the atmosphere they travel through.

Environmental Scattering: Cloud cover, sea fog, rain, dust storms, and smoke absorb and scatter laser light. In adverse weather, a 300-kilowatt laser beam can lose a massive percentage of its optical energy before ever reaching the target, turning a lethal thermal strike into a harmless flashlight beam.

Thermal Blooming: As a high-power laser passes through the air, it heats up the surrounding atmosphere. This superheated air acts like a defocusing lens, causing the laser beam to spread out, lose energy density, and miss its target's critical structural points.

The Realistic Future of Directed Energy 

High-energy lasers are not a magic cure-all that will replace traditional missiles and kinetic guns. Instead, systems like HELIOS and DragonFire are designed as valuable secondary layers within a larger, multi-tiered defensive system. They excel at destroying slow-moving, low-cost reconnaissance drones and unguided rockets, preserving expensive kinetic interceptors for high-speed, heavy threats.

Military lasers offer revolutionary point-defense capabilities, but their supply of firepower is far from infinite. Bounded by raw electrical generation, severe waste-heat buildup, and atmospheric scattering, laser weapons are governed by the same physical friction as traditional arms. Understanding these engineering limits is essential to building a grounded, realistic air-defense posture for modern warfare.

text:
U.S. Emergency Oil Reserve Falls to Its Lowest Level Since 1982

The United States is offering to lend up to 40 million barrels of oil from its emergency reserve, three months after companies borrowed only about 500,000 barrels when the same volume was offered in June.

The Energy Department announced the new offer on September 29. It covers the last part of the 172 million barrels Washington pledged in March toward a coordinated International Energy Agency release of 400 million barrels, the largest in the agency's history. About 30 countries joined that agreement. Proposals are due October 6, according to Reuters.

The barrels are loans. Companies that take crude from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve must later return it with additional barrels as a premium, an arrangement the department says restocks the reserve at no cost to taxpayers.

The reserve now holds about 284 million barrels. When the March program began, the department put the SPR at about 415 million barrels.

The administration is pressing other countries to do more. Alongside the new offer, Washington urged European governments to release oil from their own reserves, as fuel prices climb less than two months before the midterm elections, Bloomberg reported.

On the same day, IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said member countries may discuss further releases if needed, though he said that was not the agency's top priority at present. He said the IEA is watching diesel and other refined-product markets closely. Birol has said the March release amounted to 20% of members' total emergency stocks.

text:
Hormuz Didn't Lose Its Leverage. The Pressure Migrated.

Today I argued that Iran has traded a veto over Hormuz for a tax. The strongest objection is endurance: the US can sustain escorts longer than Iran can sustain lost oil revenue, so the tax erodes over time.

Start with what's true. Flows are genuinely improving. Middle East crude exports reached their highest level since the war began in September, though they remain well below February. Iran is also losing more per day than Washington. I don't dispute either point.

But the September data tells a more interesting story than "Iran is losing."

1. The adaptation worked, and adaptations have costs. In the spring, JPMorgan warned that OECD commercial inventories could approach operational floors by September under a prolonged Hormuz shutdown. September arrived without that outcome. Inventories still fell, but far less than feared, because demand dropped sharply, alternative routes expanded, and escorted volumes kept moving. Escorts are now part of that adaptation, while Washington is also keeping policy buffers available: today it offered another 40 million barrels in SPR loans. That is the difference between having a capability and depending on its continuous use.

2. The bypass network has its own vulnerabilities. Drones that Saudi Arabia says were launched from Iraq shut the East-West pipeline and halted Yanbu crude exports for more than a week. The Houthis have fired missiles at Yanbu while advancing toward Bab el-Mandeb. While Yanbu was down, Saudi Arabia shifted exports back to its Gulf terminals. Its Hormuz exports roughly quadrupled from August, and ship-to-ship transfers off Oman reached their limits. The pipeline is back, but at about half its pre-attack rate. Barrels are being redistributed across routes as individual corridors become constrained.

The problem is no longer a single chokepoint. It's a network.

3. Demand destruction bought time, but it isn't spare capacity. It is economic pain doing the balancing. With diesel exceptionally expensive and Brent around $100, asking demand to absorb another major disruption gets progressively harder.

The doctrine implication: a durable Phase 1 can't treat Hormuz in isolation. If traffic is displaced onto the East-West pipeline, Yanbu and the Red Sea while attacks on those routes remain permissible, the settlement relocates the vulnerability instead of resolving it. The interlock annex should bind each party against attacks on designated energy infrastructure and maritime corridors that it directs, coordinates or knowingly facilitates after entry into force, with attribution and dispute procedures before any snapback.

Neither Washington nor Tehran controls every armed group in the region. The architecture shouldn't pretend otherwise, and it shouldn't collapse because one of those groups fires.

Iran's leverage didn't simply disappear. The pressure moved to where the barrels went.

— @AndreDoctrine

text:
Iran didn't lose its leverage in Hormuz. It changed form.

CNN's latest piece argues that Iran has lost considerable leverage over the strait. The data doesn't support that. Iran has lost its veto over Gulf oil. It has not lost its leverage. It has converted it into something harder to negotiate away.

The numbers don't hold. The "80% of pre-war flows" claim rests on one strong week measured against a low 17.1 mb/d baseline. Most trackers put pre-war throughput near 20 mb/d. Kpler's own barrel-based measure has averaged 8.6 mb/d since mid-June, September crude is tracking about 7.4 mb/d, and last week Kpler's own blog put Hormuz at roughly 40% of 2025 flows. Barrels are moving on a few escorted, AIS-dark supertankers, not through a reopened strait: about 55 transits in a week versus roughly 910 before the war.

The article's "2 billion barrel" inventory draw doesn't match JPMorgan's published figure of about 555M, a third of the bank's forecast. The market held because demand fell by more than 4M b/d, not because Iran was outmaneuvered. That cushion is finite.

What Iran lost: the ability to stop flows entirely, most of its own exports under the US blockade, and the $150 oil scenario its strategy needed.

What it kept is a tax, not a veto. Every barrel moves escorted, dark and expensive, paid for with US naval endurance, and tankers are still being struck. Iran doesn't need to win at sea. It only needs to keep the system fragile.

What it expanded is the target list. The bypass routes are now under fire. Drones from Iraq, not the Houthis as CNN reported, took Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline offline. The Houthis are pushing toward Bab el-Mandeb and claiming strikes on Yanbu, and France is deploying air defenses to a Saudi port. Every workaround becomes a new pressure point.

The tell is Tehran's own terms. Iran's Sept 25 plan asks for the blockade and sanctions to be lifted first, the strait to reopen on day seven, and nuclear talks to follow. A party that believes it has run out of cards doesn't bargain like that.

The real picture is mutual depletion. Washington has improved its walk-away position, but it hasn't created pressure to settle. JPMorgan's economic redlines for forcing a deal have all been crossed, and there is still no deal.

The doctrine implication: Hormuz leverage now sits in Iraq, Yemen and the Red Sea. A Hormuz-only bargain leaves Iran's most effective pressure points untouched.

You can't end five wars with one deal.

— @AndreDoctrine

"Offer revives June plan that drew bids for only about 500,000 barrels
Release completes U.S. share of a March accord with 30 IEA countries
Routine drawdowns are restricted below 252.4 million barrels, ​though emergency releases remain allowed.

 The US Government said on Tuesday it is offering to loan ‌energy companies up to 40 million barrels of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the last US batch of crude from a global deal to unleash reserves in the wake of the war on Iran.
Washington agreed in March to loan 172 million barrels of oil from the SPR as part of a ​wider deal with about 30 countries in the International Energy Agency to release 400 million barrels from reserves around ​the world.

In June, the US offered to loan the last 40 million barrels from that agreement, ⁠but later that month revealed that companies only agreed to borrow about 500,000 barrels.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the US ​and Japan have delivered on their commitments under the agreement, but said "several European member countries have released only a fraction of ​the crude oil and petroleum products they pledged."

Reuters reported on Wednesday that the White House has urged the European Union to draw down emergency diesel inventories in a bid to lower prices. The EU has not disclosed the total volumes its members have so far ​released,, although the IEA has said EU countries' contributions will primarily take the form of refined products, rather than ​crude oil.

SPR LIMITS
The amount of oil in US SPR has sunk to less than 284 million barrels, the lowest level since 1982. ‌President ⁠Donald Trump released large amounts following the start of the war with Iran and former President Joe Biden made big releases after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.

Trump has felt pressure to lower fuel prices ahead of the November midterm elections in which his Republican party is campaigning to maintain thin majorities in Congress. Gasoline pump prices are about $4.45 a gallon, up ​almost 50% since the war ​began in late February, ⁠and diesel prices have surged about 70% and have hit record levels around $6.50 a gallon.

The latest release could temporarily take the SPR level below a point where draw down restrictions ​come into force.

US law prohibits the president from ordering routine, small draw downs if ​the SPR falls ⁠below 252.4 million barrels. The president could still order releases for major emergencies.
The US is loaning oil from the SPR to companies that will repay in crude, with premiums of up to 24%. The department says that system will help stabilize ⁠markets with ​no cost to US taxpayers. But the return of the oil is ​not slated to be completed until late 2028.
The department said companies have until October 6 to submit proposals on borrowing the oil."

text:
Adam is 23 and autistic. He saved all year for his first festival, and he almost didn't go.

He'd always put it off because he had no one to go with.

His dad, Andy, was so worried he made an emergency plan. If Adam wanted out, Andy would drive to Hampshire and bring him home.

Then, on the first day, a group of lads from Bristol asked to borrow his tent mallet.

That was all it took.

They didn't just give it back and leave. They noticed he was on his own, moved his tent into their circle, and kept him with them all weekend.

A few days in, Adam texted his dad: "Dad, I think I've found my people."

By the end, Adam was in tears. Happy ones. He didn't want to leave.

Andy posted a thank-you so the lads' parents would know what their sons had done. It blew up. Adam is an aspiring drum and bass DJ, and since then he's had bookings, an invite to the Pete Tong Academy, and an offer to play Boomtown 2027.

Nobody planned any of it. A few strangers just didn't let him sit alone.

Someone at the edge of your group is waiting for a small invitation. Ask them in.

It costs you almost nothing. For them, it can be the whole weekend.

text:
The clip Buzz Patterson shared is about Cole Schmidtknecht, a 22-year-old from Wisconsin who died in January 2024 after an asthma attack. His insurance (UnitedHealthcare via OptumRx, a pharmacy benefit manager) dropped coverage of his daily Advair inhaler. The price jumped from about $66 to $539 with no effective warning or easy alternative offered at the Walgreens he visited. He left without it because he couldn’t afford it, then suffered a fatal attack days later.

That specific event happened in early 2024, while Joe Biden was president. 

The broader problems, PBMs changing formularies for rebate deals, patients getting hit with sudden unaffordable prices for maintenance drugs, pharmacies not always helping find workarounds, are longstanding. They existed before 2024, continued after, and have drawn criticism from people across the political spectrum, including John Oliver in the segment Patterson posted. 

If the same thing happened today, it could still go badly for a lot of people. The big new federal rules on pharmacy middlemen were signed this year but most of them do not start until 2028 or 2029. In Wisconsin they are still working on a law named after Cole that would stop surprise price jumps in the middle of the year. Some pharmacies might try harder to help now because the story is well known. But a person could still walk into a drugstore, get told their inhaler suddenly costs five hundred dollars, and leave without it if they cannot pay that day. The system has not fully fixed that problem yet.

text:
🚨 JESSICA HAD 312,000 FOLLOWERS.

MARCUS HAD 34,000.

AMINA HAD JUST 7,400.

If I showed you only their social-media profiles and asked:

“WHO HAS THE STRONGEST BUSINESS?”

Most people would probably choose Jessica.

Huge mistake.

Because the numbers everyone could SEE told only a tiny part of the story.

Let me show you what was happening behind the scenes.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

👩 MEET JESSICA WALKER.

Jessica built a lifestyle and entrepreneurship page.

312,000 followers.

Her videos regularly received:

40,000 views.

80,000 views.

Sometimes 500,000+.

One video passed 2 million.

Her comments were full of:

“Love this!”

“Needed this today!”

“🔥🔥🔥”

“Where did you get that?”

From the outside?

Jessica looked incredibly successful.

Brands contacted her.

People recognized her.

Friends assumed she was making a fortune.

Then Jessica launched a £49 digital guide.

She had spent weeks creating it.

She posted:

“IT'S FINALLY HERE!”

The launch post received thousands of likes.

Hundreds of comments.

Massive reach.

Jessica refreshed her sales dashboard.

17 sales.

She refreshed again.

21. 

By the end of the launch?

Far fewer customers than she'd imagined.

Jessica couldn't understand it.

“How can hundreds of thousands of people follow me but hardly anyone is buying?”

Because Jessica had built something valuable...

ATTENTION.

But attention and purchase intent are not the same thing.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

👨 NOW MEET MARCUS REED.

Marcus owned a small marketing consultancy.

Followers?

34,000.

Nothing compared with Jessica.

Most of his posts received modest engagement.

No celebrity status.

No millions of views every week.

But Marcus had made one decision early:

He wasn't trying to attract everybody.

His business helped independent dental practices generate more qualified local enquiries.

Very specific.

When a dentist landed on Marcus's profile, it was immediately obvious:

WHO he helped.

WHAT problem he solved.

WHAT outcome he focused on.

WHAT the next step was.

Marcus didn't need 300,000 random people watching.

He needed dental-practice owners.

So his content answered questions THEY cared about.

“Why are people clicking your dental ads but not booking?”

“How much should a dental practice spend on local lead generation?”

“Why do potential patients abandon your booking page?”

“What should happen after someone requests an appointment?”

His posts weren't designed primarily to go viral.

They were designed to make the RIGHT person think:

“This guy understands my problem.”

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

👩 THEN THERE WAS AMINA HASSAN.

7,400 followers.

The smallest account by far.

But Amina had built an email-marketing consultancy for small e-commerce brands.

She knew many of her followers by name.

When someone asked a question?

She answered.

When she noticed the same problem appearing repeatedly?

She created content about it.

She offered a useful free checklist.

Interested people joined her email list.

Her emails taught.

Her case studies demonstrated her approach.

Her website explained her service.

Her follow-up answered common objections.

And when someone wasn't ready to buy?

Amina didn't disappear.

She continued helping.

Weeks later, sometimes months later, people came back.

“I've been reading your emails for three months.”

“We finally need help.”

“Can we book a call?”

Amina's 7,400 followers didn't LOOK as impressive as Jessica's 312,000.

But Amina wasn't trying to win a popularity contest.

She was building relationships with potential customers.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🚨 NOW LET ME ASK YOU AGAIN:

WHO HAS THE STRONGEST BUSINESS?

You still can't know from follower count.

Because I haven't told you enough.

You'd need to know things like:

💳 How many paying customers?

💰 Revenue?

💸 Expenses?

📊 Profit?

📧 Qualified leads?

🎯 Conversion rate?

💵 Customer acquisition cost?

🛒 Average order value?

🔄 Repeat purchases?

🤝 Retention?

📈 Customer lifetime value?

💰 Cash flow?

THOSE numbers begin telling you what the follower count cannot.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔥 THIS IS WHERE MANY ENTREPRENEURS GET DISTRACTED.

We obsess over the numbers everyone else can see.

100,000 FOLLOWERS.

1 MILLION VIEWS.

50,000 LIKES.

2 MILLION IMPRESSIONS.

Why?

Because they're public.

They make us feel like something is happening.

And don't misunderstand me:

ATTENTION MATTERS.

Reach matters.

Followers matter.

Views matter.

A large audience can be an extraordinary business advantage.

But only if you know what to DO with that attention.

Because:

1,000,000 views × no clear next step = attention.

50,000 followers × wrong audience = weak relevance.

10,000 likes × no offer = engagement.

500 qualified prospects × a strong offer = BUSINESS OPPORTUNITY.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🎯 LESSON #1: STOP TRYING TO ATTRACT EVERYONE.

Marcus understood this.

He didn't say:

“I HELP BUSINESSES GROW.”

That's so broad it could mean almost anything.

Instead:

“I help independent dental practices generate more qualified local patient enquiries.”

Immediately, the right person can recognize themselves.

That's the power of specificity.

Ask yourself:

WHO exactly am I helping?

WHAT problem am I solving?

WHY does that problem matter?

WHAT is it costing them?

WHAT have they already tried?

WHY hasn't that worked?

WHAT outcome are they trying to achieve?

CAN I genuinely help them achieve it?

Then build from there.

PERSON

↓

PROBLEM

↓

SOLUTION

↓

OFFER

↓

RESULT

Not:

PRODUCT

↓

POST

↓

CROSS FINGERS

↓

HOPE SOMEONE BUYS.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔥 LESSON #2: 5,000 RIGHT PEOPLE CAN MATTER MORE THAN 500,000 RANDOM PEOPLE.

Imagine you sell software designed specifically for independent restaurants.

Which audience would you prefer?

500,000 random social-media followers?

Or:

5,000 restaurant owners, managers and operators?

The larger audience gives you more potential reach.

But the smaller audience may have dramatically greater relevance.

That's the distinction.

You don't simply need:

MORE PEOPLE.

You need:

MORE OF THE RIGHT PEOPLE.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💡 LESSON #3: FOLLOWERS AREN'T CUSTOMERS.

Amina understood this better than anyone.

She didn't wake up every morning screaming:

“BUY MY SERVICE!”

Instead, she built trust.

She explained problems.

Answered questions.

Shared examples.

Showed her process.

Addressed objections.

Published useful information.

Collected emails.

Followed up.

And gradually people moved:

STRANGER

↓

CONTENT VIEWER

↓

FOLLOWER

↓

EMAIL SUBSCRIBER

↓

QUALIFIED LEAD

↓

CUSTOMER

↓

REPEAT CUSTOMER

↓

REFERRAL

That's completely different from:

POST

↓

GET LIKES

↓

POST AGAIN

↓

GET MORE LIKES

↓

WONDER WHY NOBODY BUYS.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

📧 LESSON #4: DON'T BUILD YOUR ENTIRE BUSINESS ON AN ALGORITHM YOU DON'T CONTROL.

Jessica eventually realized something uncomfortable.

She had 312,000 followers…

But she couldn't guarantee that 312,000 people would see tomorrow's post.

So she started building assets around the attention she'd created.

A website.

An email list.

Lead magnets.

Landing pages.

Follow-up emails.

Customer records.

Better offers.

Retention campaigns.

Now social media had a PURPOSE.

SOCIAL MEDIA

↓

ATTENTION

↓

CALL TO ACTION

↓

LANDING PAGE

↓

LEAD

↓

FOLLOW-UP

↓

OFFER

↓

CUSTOMER

↓

GREAT EXPERIENCE

↓

REPEAT PURCHASE

↓

REFERRAL

Suddenly Jessica wasn't simply collecting followers.

She was building infrastructure.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💰 LESSON #5: STOP BEING IMPRESSED BY REVENUE WITHOUT ASKING ABOUT COSTS.

You've probably seen posts like:

🚨 “WE DID $150,000 THIS MONTH!”

Great.

But that number alone doesn't tell you what the owner kept.

Suppose a hypothetical business generated:

$150,000 revenue.

But then paid for:

$48,000 advertising.

$24,000 inventory or fulfilment.

$15,000 staff and contractors.

$8,000 software and services.

$7,000 refunds and payment fees.

$12,000 other operating expenses.

Suddenly that $150,000 headline tells a very different story.

Revenue matters.

But so do costs and cash flow.

🔥 REVENUE CAN MAKE A GREAT SCREENSHOT.

HEALTHY ECONOMICS HELP KEEP THE BUSINESS ALIVE.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

📊 LESSON #6: KNOW WHAT'S HAPPENING BETWEEN THE VIEW AND THE SALE.

Imagine 100,000 people see your content.

5,000 visit your profile.

1,000 click your link.

250 become leads.

30 buy.

What happened to everyone else?

THAT'S where business owners should become curious.

Maybe the content attracted the wrong people.

Maybe the CTA was unclear.

Maybe the landing page was weak.

Maybe the offer didn't feel valuable enough.

Maybe there wasn't enough trust.

Maybe the checkout was confusing.

Maybe follow-up was nonexistent.

Instead of automatically saying:

“I NEED MORE FOLLOWERS!”

Ask:

“WHERE ARE WE LOSING THE PEOPLE WE ALREADY HAVE?”

That question can completely change how you approach growth.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⚙️ LESSON #7: BUILD A MACHINE, NOT A POSTING HABIT.

Posting every day can be useful.

But posting isn't the entire business.

Marcus built a system:

CONTENT

↓

RIGHT AUDIENCE

↓

ATTENTION

↓

CLEAR CTA

↓

LANDING PAGE

↓

LEAD

↓

FOLLOW-UP

↓

CONVERSATION

↓

OFFER

↓

SALE

↓

DELIVERY

↓

RESULT

↓

RETENTION

↓

REFERRAL

Now every piece has a job.

Content attracts.

The CTA directs.

The landing page captures.

Follow-up nurtures.

The offer converts.

Delivery creates value.

Customer experience builds trust.

Retention increases value.

Referrals create new opportunities.

🔥 THAT'S NOT JUST CONTENT.

THAT'S A BUSINESS SYSTEM.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🚨 AND HERE'S WHERE THIS GETS INTERESTING.

Jessica originally thought:

“I need MORE followers.”

Marcus thought:

“I need more QUALIFIED prospects.”

Amina thought:

“I need stronger RELATIONSHIPS with the people already paying attention.”

Three completely different approaches.

And this is why you should never judge a business from its social-media profile.

The person with 500,000 followers might have an extraordinary company.

Or a struggling one.

The person with 5,000 followers might barely be making sales.

Or quietly running a highly profitable niche business.

YOU DON'T KNOW.

Because follower count doesn't tell you.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔥 SO IF YOU'RE BUILDING AN ONLINE BUSINESS, STOP THINKING YOUR FIRST MILESTONE MUST BE:

100,000 FOLLOWERS.

Try this instead:

Get your FIRST customer.

Learn why they bought.

Improve your offer.

Get 10 customers.

Talk to them.

Understand what they value.

Improve delivery.

Collect genuine feedback.

Fix problems.

Improve your message.

Generate referrals.

Increase retention.

Then attract more qualified people.

And repeat.

Because 10 customers who LOVE what you provide can teach you more about building a business than 100,000 people who simply scroll past your content.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💥 THE REAL ONLINE-BUSINESS EQUATION ISN'T:

FOLLOWERS = MONEY.

It's closer to:

RIGHT PEOPLE

↓

REAL PROBLEM

↓

USEFUL SOLUTION

↓

CLEAR OFFER

↓

TRUST

↓

ACTION

↓

GOOD DELIVERY

↓

CUSTOMER SATISFACTION

↓

RETENTION

↓

REFERRALS

↓

SUSTAINABLE GROWTH

AI can accelerate parts of this.

Advertising can accelerate it.

Automation can improve it.

Social media can feed it.

Great content can amplify it.

But none of those replaces the fundamentals.

🔥 ATTENTION WITHOUT DIRECTION IS JUST ATTENTION.

🔥 TRAFFIC WITHOUT CONVERSION IS JUST TRAFFIC.

🔥 SALES WITHOUT GOOD DELIVERY ARE HARD TO SUSTAIN.

🔥 GROWTH WITHOUT HEALTHY ECONOMICS CAN BECOME EXPENSIVE CHAOS.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🚨 SO STOP ASKING ONLY:

“HOW DO I GET MORE FOLLOWERS?”

Start asking:

“Am I attracting the RIGHT people?”

“What problem am I solving?”

“Is the problem important enough?”

“Is my offer clear?”

“Why should someone trust me?”

“What happens after someone sees my content?”

“How do I capture interested prospects?”

“How do I follow up?”

“Where am I losing potential customers?”

“Do customers get enough value to return?”

“Would they recommend me?”

Those questions aren't as glamorous as:

“HOW DO I GO VIRAL?”

But they are the questions that help build businesses.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

I reposted this lovely shoutout on my WhatsApp Status. I have 2,000+ people from the fitness industry seeing my daily work.

In the picture attached: a first reaction from a former colleague. I saved his ass several times in the past…

German bros know what the word 
„nett“ means – it’s the little sister of sh*t.

Not a single word like: "Hey Marco, awesome that you support young builders for free with your time and knowledge."

Nope. Directly: "bUt oUr pRoDuCt iS bEtTeR." 

Dude, nobody even asked you.

So you post something good from a young builder – not even about yourself – and „normies“ start roasting you instantly. 

For what? Because an ambitious person from the US is trying something?

Long story short: 

His boys will see what Computer Vision next level really means...

Context: they are building a CV system solely for the free-weight area in a gym.
A 4-point corner-cam setup capturing everything and everyone in that area. 

Yeah, try that with German privacy laws. 

Try measuring exercises down to the millimeter while living obstacles constantly move in front of the lens. 

No, that’s not possible – not even with 3-second predictive CV models.

If they truly found the holy grail of CV calibration, occlusion handling, and camera drift in a shaking gym environment, well, I would go all in with my last penny. But their landing page hasn't shown a single working product video for over a year.

Once again: an isolated single solution with zero connectivity. Next-app fatigue. 

The 999th single-feature app.
Instead of working together, your own people fight against you. 

I even offered „his boys“ a free slot in our hub in the past. Response? Ghosting.

You might think politics, taxes, or [insert your favorite German rage topic here] is the real issue.

This mindset is burned deep into the German BIOS, and the wake-up call is going to be brutal.

Some people in the industry already call me the Uli Hoeneß (in his best times) of fitness with all my rants. 😂

It’s about two principles: support and demand (fördern und fordern).

text:
Frequent nighttime micro-awakenings between ages 50 and 69 are more than just poor sleep.
They are a specific signal of your polygenic risk for Alzheimer’s.

A polygenic risk score tallies thousands of small genetic variants to map inherited vulnerability. In midlife, subtle sleep fragmentation begins reflecting that underlying genetic load.

This pattern is uniquely age-dependent, appearing between 50 and 69 while remaining absent in younger decades. Two things follow from this.

First, nighttime fragmentation provides a direct window into early brainstem biology. The locus coeruleus, a small structure responsible for regulating wakefulness, is among the earliest brain regions where abnormal protein deposits accumulate.

When this regulatory center experiences early stress, it directly destabilizes the sleep-wake cycle. The result is repeated nighttime waking and altered REM sleep decades before daytime symptoms appear.

Second, sleep transforms from a passive symptom into an accessible screening marker. Because sleep patterns can be monitored continuously at home, subtle shifts offer an early signal of vulnerability long before standard brain imaging detects anything.

That timeline matters because it shifts the entire focus upstream. Identifying biological risk during midlife creates a practical window to protect sleep architecture and neurological health while cognition is completely intact.

Worth keeping in mind as sleep tracking becomes a standard part of health.

text:
“You’re close to a rotting cabin. You should sell it before it becomes a burden.”

That caught my attention.

At the table, she had m0:cked the property as worthless.

Now she was already suggesting a sale.

“I haven’t even seen it.”

“You don’t need to. Rural properties are expensive to maintain. I know people who can arrange an appraisal and handle the paperwork.”

“Why would you do that?”

“Because unlike you, I understand real estate.”

Her tone was dismissive, but something alert moved behind her eyes.

“For a worthless shack, you seem interested.”

Brooke gave a short laugh.

“I’m trying to save you from yourself.”

“I didn’t ask you to.”

“Fine. Let it collapse.”

I picked up my duffel bag and walked toward the front door.

Mom followed me onto the porch.

The rain had softened into a cold mist.

“Brooke didn’t mean it,” she said.

I had heard that sentence my entire life.

Brooke had not meant to destroy my birthday cake when we were children.

She had not meant to tell my first serious boyfriend that I had cheated on him.

She had not meant to borrow money and deny receiving it.

She had not meant to m0:ck me at Dad’s funeral.

Brooke never meant anything, yet everyone around her carried the consequences.

“She called me filthy in front of the family,” I said.

“She’s grieving.”

“So am I.”

“She’s under pressure.”

“She just inherited a Miami apartment.”

Mom flinched.

“This is not the time to fight.”

“I’m not fighting. I’m leaving.”

I walked down the steps.

Behind me, the door closed.

Over the next several days, Brooke continued making jokes about my inheritance.

On Monday, she sent me a photograph of the Miami skyline.

Enjoy the mosquitoes.

On Tuesday, she wrote:

Does the shack even have electricity?

On Wednesday, she called.

Her voice was unusually pleasant.

“I spoke to someone about the property,” she said. “He thinks it may be difficult to sell, but he might still make you an offer.”

“You contacted someone without asking me?”

“I was trying to help.”

“I don’t need help.”

“Tessa, you have no idea what rural land involves. Taxes, maintenance, liability, access rights. You’ll be back on duty soon. Let me handle it.”

“Why are you so interested?”

“I’m not interested. I’m being practical.”

“You m0:cked it at the funeral.”

“I was upset.”

I said nothing.

Brooke hated silence because it forced her to hear her own words.

She sighed.

“Fine. Keep it. I tried.”

That evening, I spread the documents across the kitchen table of my temporary apartment.

The property was larger than I had realized. Two hundred acres of forest, a creek, a narrow stretch of lakefront, and one private road crossing the southern boundary.

There was no mortgage.

The trust was modest but sufficient to prevent an immediate forced sale.

Nothing in the papers explained Brooke’s sudden interest.

On Friday evening, Mom called.

“At least visit the cabin once,” she said. “Your father wanted you to see it.”

Her voice was quieter than usual.

“Did Dad ever take Brooke there?”

“I don’t think so.”

“Did he take you?”

“No.”

“Then why did he own two hundred acres none of us knew anything about?”

There was a pause.

“He called it family land. He said the people connected to it valued privacy.”…

text:
Around 63,500 newly recorded cases of alcoholism and alcohol-related psychosis in Russia in 2024. Not an estimate from a Western blogger. Figures from Russia’s own statistics agency, Rosstat.

That is not everyone living with alcohol dependence in the country. Those are cases recorded for the first time in a single year. Yes, the figure fell compared with 2023. But tens of thousands of new diagnoses do not disappear because someone starts talking about the “decadent West.”

People in the comments argue that one video cannot represent an entire nation. Correct. Then they point to people struggling with addiction on the streets of Philadelphia—as though one American neighborhood suddenly represents the entire West.

So selective footage is misleading only when it damages Russia’s image?

America’s drug crisis is real. It demands investigation, treatment, and political accountability. But no death in Philadelphia excuses a life destroyed in a Russian provincial town. Someone else’s catastrophe is not proof that your own country is doing well.

The historical contradiction matters, too. The Soviet state collected revenue from alcohol sales while simultaneously campaigning against drunkenness. Gorbachev’s 1985 anti-alcohol campaign helped reduce mortality. Yet public opposition and lost government revenue were among the reasons it was dismantled. The state depended on income from a product whose addictive use was destroying its citizens’ lives.

That is what deserves scrutiny—not a competition to find the most disturbing footage, but the system, its incentives, and the price families pay.

My criticism is not directed at the person with missing teeth in the video. Their appearance does not make them less deserving of help. My criticism is directed at a state that claims the authority to lecture the world on morality, while answering questions about its own social failures with a guided tour of someone else’s poorest neighborhoods.

“Traditional values” should be measured by how families actually live, not by how solemnly television presenters talk about them. National greatness should be measured in the length and quality of human lives—not in the ability to explain why things are also bad across the Atlantic.

If Russia truly offers the world a better way of life, why is that claim so often defended with other countries’ failures rather than its own achievements?

Paxton’s office took over the case after the McLennan County district attorney recused himself due to a conflict (Hoffman had previously sought legal advice from him). The first trial in 2025 ended in a hung jury. The victim then made clear he did not want to testify again. ￼
Rather than retry the case, prosecutors from Paxton’s office offered a plea deal. Hoffman pleaded guilty to two misdemeanors—indecent assault and displaying harmful material to a minor. The plea documents did not specify the victim’s age, so Hoffman was not required to register as a sex offender in Texas. The original proposed sentence was time served plus one day in jail. ￼
The judge rejected the one-day term. The final agreement was 60 days in jail, surrender of Hoffman’s Texas law license, and a lifetime protective order.
