20. How One HCTGS Tower Works
The full derivation, the prior art and the engineering detail are spread across more than forty concept papers in the HCTGS archive, each adding a piece rather than repeating one. What follows is condensed to what a reader needs in order to trust the numbers.
Reference machine: HCTGS v26 Deutschland (doi:10.5281/zenodo.20630205) — the fullest description of the machine in the series: the cascade, the vortex, the pressure budget, the operating window and the eleven German contributions. Later editions refine single parts of it rather than replace it. The archive is at https://t.co/9Cb5wlNreG

The machine already exists in nature. A waterspout forms over warm water when the surface runs ten to fifteen degrees warmer than the air above it — photographed every summer, and nobody has to be persuaded it works. The tower gives that natural machine three conditions weather never holds steady: a hot core against an actively chilled cupola, a base held near 60 °C instead of 30, and a moisture supply the cascade produces on schedule rather than the sky delivering by chance.

Vortex power has a record, and it is worth reading. James T. Yen at Grumman presented the Tornado Wind Energy Conversion System in September 1975 and held US Patent 4,070,131 by 1978, with federal funding and a university evaluation programme behind it. Eric Jacobs closed the file in April 1983: the prospect of reaching a power coefficient above 0.2 was assessed as very low, against 0.375 for conventional machines. The reason was structural — fixed vanes create a low-pressure region at their trailing edge, and that back-pressure draws air out of the tower and weakens the vortex before it can form. Rechenberg at TU Berlin reached the same conclusion in 1984 by a different route: internal friction caps the amplification. Mamulashvili’s programme in St Petersburg ran on patents from 1984 and 1988 and ran until 1997; holding the vortex steady was the step it left open, and the chilled cupola and the fed base of the tower answer it.

Every one of these machines worked on air, and each of them established where the limit sits — which is why the limit is known at all. They worked with slide rules and modest budgets, and they published what they found, including the results that closed their own programmes. That is the lineage this architecture stands in.

The water version has been built at small scale, and it worked. John Piña Craven patented the Hurricane Tower in 1998 and ran a ten-metre prototype at the Natural Energy Laboratory on Kona from 2005: warm saline water at the base, evaporation, a propeller accelerating the rising vortex, and a heat exchanger at the top carrying 7–8 °C deep water to make the saturated air rain out as fresh water. That is the nearest prior art on the water side, and it belongs in the record.
And one entry complicates the claim, which is why it is named here rather than left for a reviewer to find. Yeh, US 4,935,639 (1990), discloses combustion heating at the foot of an air vortex tower. The easy version of a novelty statement — that this one drives the vortex rather than catching the weather — fails on contact with that patent. The distinction has to be drawn tighter.

The defensible claim is two sentences. Rotation is imparted by the hydrogen burner entering horizontally and tangentially below the waterline, while the magnesium flame works behind a ceramic wall — so angular momentum goes into the liquid, the steam leaves an already-turning surface, and the salts stay behind to crystallise. And condensation happens in flight against a chilled mist of the plant’s own distillate, which is what produces the collapse that pumps the column.

22. Two Seas, Two Designs
The Kingdom has two coasts, and they are different machines.
The Red Sea is deep, and the cold is close. Depths exceeding a thousand metres lie within reach of the shore along much of the coast, and the deep water sits near 21–22 °C year-round — cooler than the surface by a margin that matters, and cold enough that the chilled end of the cascade has geography working for it rather than refrigeration alone. The surface runs 26 to 30 °C. The span between them is free.

The Gulf is shallow, warm and saline. Average depth is on the order of thirty-five metres; summer surface temperatures run above 33 °C in places, and salinity exceeds 40 grams per litre in the western reaches — among the highest of any open sea. For a membrane process, every one of those conditions is a headwind: warmer feed, higher osmotic pressure, and a receiving basin that disperses slowly.

For a thermal cascade, two of the three are tailwinds. The warm feed is a head start. The high salinity means more mineral per cubic metre — the concentrate is richer before the first stage runs. And the third condition, the slow-exchanging basin, is answered by separating the intake on land.

And the Gulf takes its cold pole from the land. The Red Sea supplies one by geography — deep water close to shore. On the Gulf the cold end comes from the land — the salt pit and the desert night — because a cascade draws its driving pressure from its cold end.

The answer is the plant’s own salt. One tower crystallises roughly 27,000 tonnes of sodium chloride a day, and far beyond any salt market that stream has to go somewhere. Placed in lined cells beside the plant and grown cell by cell at the rhythm of production, it becomes a thermal mass — cooled by the plant’s own saturated brine, which stays liquid to about −21 °C, circulating in sealed salt-proof loops laid as the body grows, with a shallow day zone and a deep season zone. The disposal question and the storage body become one object, and the published fill level is the cumulative salt account.

•That is what carries a tower on a warm coast where no cold current runs, and it is published separately as NC-SPT-1, the Self-Grown Salt Pit (https://t.co/7r4gZzzCqU ). On the Gulf it is one of the enabling conditions rather than an option among several.

The design consequence: Red Sea sites lean on the natural cold pole and on the mountains behind them. Gulf sites lean on the existing industrial base, the grid connections, the ports, and on brine that neighbouring plants have already concentrated and are already permitted to handle. Pre-concentrated brine replaces the concentration step. Industrial waste heat replaces the upper rungs of the temperature ladder.
Four contracts from one structure — water, cooling, power, minerals — and on the Gulf coast the cooling contract is the one that signs first.

And the northwest corner deserves naming separately, because the groundwork is already down. Where the Gulf of Aqaba meets the Red Sea the water goes past eighteen hundred metres within sight of the shore — the shortest reach to deep cold water anywhere on either coast, and the best cold pole the Kingdom has. Behind it the relief rises fast, which is mountain-shaft geography. And the site is no longer raw ground: roads, port capacity, grid connection, water supply and workforce housing have been laid in over years of development, at a cost already spent, which the next project inherits.

For a tower cluster that is a decade of site preparation received as a gift. Two clusters there would carry an industrial estate of their own — factories buying power at generation cost, cooling at marginal cost and process water at specification, on ground where the access is already built.
And the position does something unique among Saudi sites. The northwest corner is closer to Aqaba, to the Sinai and to the eastern Mediterranean approaches than it is to Riyadh. A cluster there could supply water beyond the Kingdom’s own border if the Kingdom chose to, by pipeline over short distances rather than by tanker over long ones — and the mineral streams would leave through a port that already exists.

23. The Mountain That Carries the Cistern
This is the part that gives the article its title, and it is geography rather than metaphor.
The Sarawat range runs the length of the Red Sea coast, rising through the Hijaz and reaching nearly 3,000 metres in the Asir. It stands close behind the shoreline — in places the ground climbs from sea level to two thousand metres within forty kilometres.

Where a shaft runs inside rock, the mountain carries the height instead of the structure. A freestanding tower on flat coast must build every metre of its own elevation. A mountain shaft does not: the cupola and its cistern sit at the elevation the rock provides, and the condensate collects there without a pump ever lifting it. What a freestanding tower achieves at six hundred metres, a mountain shaft achieves higher, for the cost of boring rather than the cost of standing.

And from a cistern at that elevation, water leaves downhill. The gravity distribution that follows is the oldest part of this architecture and the least exotic: a chain of break-pressure cisterns, each twenty to fifty kilometres onward and slightly lower, each resetting the pressure line so that every reach runs at low pressure in cheap, safe pipe, and each drop able to turn a small turbine on the way.

The limit is elevation rather than distance. Gravity reaches everything below the cistern, at any pipe diameter. Everything below it is.
For the Kingdom this has a specific shape. The escarpment towns of the Asir and the Hijaz sit below a cistern line the Sarawat can carry. The coastal plain of the Tihamah sits far below it. The interior plateau climbs again, and where it climbs above the cistern, the water arrives by pumped stage, paid for by tower power — stated here so that the corridor maps are read correctly rather than optimistically.

The same geometry that guards a coastal plant guards a town below a wadi. Where an escarpment channel turns, momentum carries the flow toward the outer bank and a debris flow continues straight while the channel does not — and that is the point at which the settlement downstream is reached. A wedge set into the outer bank at the bend returns the flow to the channel rather than across the ground beside it, with an armour field of placed rock ahead of the apex to take the boulders and the timber, and expendable ground behind it under the same two conditions that govern the coastal version. On a peninsula where the rain arrives in hours rather than months, that is a use for the geometry with more working days in it than the coastal case.

 It is published separately as NC-TWV-1, the Aligned Twin V-Nose Coastal Defence Geometry (https://t.co/Gnw1Mul6Z6), which carries the freshwater case in full.

23b. Where the gradient stops, the tower pays for the climb
Gravity reaches everything below the cistern, and the peninsula has ground on both sides of that line. So the question is what it costs to lift the rest — and a tower is the rare water plant that can answer with its own product.
The arithmetic is short enough to check. Raising a cubic metre by one metre costs about 3.2 watt-hours with real pumps. A tower at warm-sea output generates 15.6 to 20.9 kilowatt-hours for every cubic metre it delivers. So:
DestinationLift from the coastCostShare of the tower’s own generation

Riyadh and the interior plateau~610 m2.0 kWh/m³10–13 %

Taif~1,880 m6.0 kWh/m³29–38 %

Abha and the high Asir~2,270 m7.3 kWh/m³35–47 %

Abha, from a 900 m mountain cistern~1,370 m4.4 kWh/m³21–28 %

The plateau is the case that matters most, and it is the cheapest one. Riyadh sits near six hundred metres. Lifting water to it costs about a tenth of what the tower generates delivering that same water, and nine tenths of the generation goes to the grid. Water for the capital is a rounding entry inside the energy case.

And the mountain shaft changes the high cases too, because the cistern starts where the rock put it. Water lifted from a cistern at nine hundred metres reaches the Asir escarpment for two thirds of what it would cost from sea level, and above a certain point on that escarpment the lift disappears entirely and the gradient does the work.

This is the inversion the architecture now offers. Every ancient system on this peninsula moved water downhill, because downhill was the only direction available without power. The falaj found the gradient. The birkat waited for the sky. The terraces at Taif caught what came down the mountain and held it. Each of them could choose only how well it kept what arrived; the lift and the direction lay beyond them.

A tower can lift, and it pays for the lift out of what it makes. The peninsula’s oldest constraint was the direction of the water. It was the direction.
And the direction is the part that requires a decision rather than an engineer.

The birkats along the Darb Zubaidah were endowed for pilgrims who would arrive generations later. The falaj holds its gradient because someone surveyed it for a village that did not yet exist. The terraces at Taif were cut by people who would see perhaps two harvests from them. Water infrastructure on this peninsula has always been ordered by someone accounting in a longer unit than a lifetime, because that unit is what makes building it possible at all.

That habit went quiet for a while, in the Kingdom as everywhere else, when the planning unit shortened to the budget cycle. Vision 2030, set out by His Royal Highness Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, reopened it — in what has been built since: a heritage economy at AlUla, Diriyah rebuilt around what was already there, a green initiative counted in trees rather than in announcements, an expanded rail and port network, and an industrial base that was a hydrocarbon export and is becoming something wider.

Those are decisions whose returns arrive after the term in which they were taken. A tower fleet with 2050 as its horizon asks for the same habit at a longer range — and it is the one kind of programme where the habit already exists here, in the stone, from the century before last and the one before that.

The direction was the one thing the ancients had to accept. A generation that can, and plans on their timescale, stands in a position new to this ground.

23c. A mountain that holds a season
The interior loses open water to the air at a rate few countries experience so directly, which is why every historic solution here went underground or under cover.
A sealed cavern in the Arabian Shield holds a city’s month, and more. There is no evaporation from a lined cavern in granite, no dust, no algae, no temperature swing, and no exposure to anything at the surface. Filled from a cistern above it and drawn down by gravity below it, a cavern store needs no pump in either direction — it sits in the line rather than beside it.

Which converts a daily supply into a seasonal one. A tower produces every day of the year at a steady rate, and demand on this peninsula follows the thermometer. A store that holds months rather than days lets the fleet run flat while the cities draw as they need, and it gives a national system a reserve measured in seasons rather than in days of tank capacity.

And the oldest rule on this peninsula carries straight into this century: hide the water from the sky. Open storage in this climate gives a share of its contents back to the air before anyone uses it, which is why the Nabataeans cut their chambers into sandstone rather than building basins on it. The Arabian Shield is ancient granite, among the oldest rock on earth, and a sealed cavern inside it stores water with no evaporation loss at all — protected from dust, from heat, and from every surface hazard. What Hegra did for a season, a cavern in the Shield does for a city’s month.

Excavation for any underground siting follows the pre-excavation tomography protocol this series published separately (PETP-STD-1.0), and the rock cavern work itself is existing prior art within the series — the Cold Frontier and Hot Frontier editions and the Great Salt Lake study — rather than a new claim.

24. Five Configurations, and the Floating Class
There is no universal tower. The cascade is a set of mechanisms; the site chooses the housing.
Mountain shaft — where rock close to deep water supplies height and containment. The Red Sea coast behind the Sarawat is this geography in its clearest form.

Mountain tower — where relief exists and the rock resists boring.
Hybrid — 300 metres below ground and 300 above, so drilling and concrete proceed in parallel.
Freestanding tower — 400 to 600 metres on flat coast where no relief is in reach. The Gulf coast at Jubail and Ras Al Khair.
Deep shaft — 600 metres at the waterline, where sixty bar of hydrostatic head drives the cascade with no pump at all.

And the floating class, a different delivery model rather than a sixth site. A semi-submersible under maritime law is a vessel rather than a building: it anchors without a construction permit, it can be bought or leased, and it can be moved when the need moves. It is the fastest route from decision to first cubic metre, and it is the right answer where a construction queue would otherwise run for years.

The unit of build is the cluster rather than the tower — two to ten HCTGS Towers, growing as the site, the demand and the grid connection allow. A programme of one hundred towers is a programme of ten to fifty clusters over twenty-five years, which is a different proposition from a single construction project and should be read as one.

Access and maintenance are their own design question. The shaft carries a rotating column at temperature and under partial vacuum, so anything reached through the column is reached at standstill. Turbine stages, heat exchangers, electrolyser cells and burner lances are wearing parts on a service interval.

In the deep shaft configuration the answer is already cut. A second service shaft of three metres, driven alongside the main bore, adds 0.36 percent to the excavation and gives permanent access at every level without entering the column.

For the other configurations, two arrangements answer it, and both put maintenance outside the process envelope. The first is what refineries and power stations already use: a separate access structure standing beside the column on its own foundation, with landings at the level of each stage, its own lift, its own escape route and a crane at the head, tied to the shaft only by bridges with movement allowance. The second sets the column inside a widening base — structural rather than solid — whose interior carries the stages that need no great heat: crystallisation, separation, storage, packing, and the reservoir that doubles as ballast at the foot. Which one is built is a decision for the contractor and the operator against the site, the seismic class and the price of ground.

Ilir Mehmetaj · Independent Concept Developer · Graz, Austria · CC BY-NC-ND 4.0

What this architecture states about the metal is its cost side: on the order of $200 a tonne in electrolysis energy from the tower’s own power, against magnesia at around $800 a tonne. The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve holds about 284 million barrels, its lowest level since 1982.

text:
You’re mixing three different things and treating them as one.

USMCA does not “expire in 2036, so leave it alone.” Article 34.7 required a joint review on July 1, 2026. The United States declined to rubber-stamp a 16-year extension in its current form. That is how the sunset/review clause was written. The pact stays in force until 2036 unless the parties extend it. Declining a 16-year lock-in is using the agreement, not ripping it up. 

“Both sides abided for decades” is also false. Softwood lumber, dairy supply management, and provincial alcohol rules were running fights under NAFTA and USMCA, under more than one U.S. president. Canada’s supply-managed dairy, poultry, and eggs still sit behind TRQs and over-quota tariffs in the 200–300% range. That is treaty-legal protectionism. It is not “treating the U.S. exactly as a captive customer shouldn’t notice.” Then Ottawa passed Bill C-202, which bars future concessions on dairy, poultry, and eggs. That shrinks the bargaining room before the last round is finished. 

On the walkout: Carney ended the August talks and recalled the team. USTR Greer said Canada declined to finalize terms that had been on the table. Carney said Washington asked too much and offered too little. You can pick a side on who moved last. You cannot say Canada “only retaliated” after a U.S. violation and leave out that Ottawa stood up and left the room while Mexico kept talking. After that walkout, the tariffs stayed and the next tranche of bans was already queued. That sequence is not “the treaty required us to leave.” 

If the argument is that Section 232 metals and auto tariffs sit on top of USMCA duty-free treatment, say that. That is a real fight. It is not the same claim as “USMCA expires in 2036, Trump violated it, Canada just answered.” One is a tariff overlay dispute. The other is a refusal to treat a scheduled review as a rubber stamp, plus a Canadian decision to walk instead of stay and bargain over trucks, autos, steel, and third-country rules.

Name-calling does not close that gap.

Iran says it is ready to negotiate and is discussing new proposals through Qatari mediators, including a possible path toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Washington, however, insists that Iran’s nuclear program must be addressed as part of any broader deal.

In March, Washington agreed to release 172 million barrels from the reserve following the outbreak of the war with Iran.

text:
WHITE HOUSE URGES EUROPE TO RELEASE EMERGENCY DIESEL STOCKS

Washington has asked the EU to tap emergency diesel inventories to ease global fuel prices, Reuters reports, citing two sources.

U.S. officials argue that several European countries have fallen short of earlier reserve-release commitments. Additional EU action remains undecided, while Washington is considering diesel export restrictions. No final U.S. decision has been announced. (https://t.co/uhYKzjvGEQ)

Separately, the U.S. is offering to loan up to 40 million barrels of SPR crude. Reuters now confirms this is the final tranche of the existing 172-million-barrel commitment, reviving an earlier offer that attracted limited uptake. (https://t.co/uhYKzjvGEQ)

MARKET PULSE VIEW

Releasing finished diesel can provide more direct relief to fuel users than releasing crude, which must first pass through refineries.

But European stock releases combined with restrictions on American exports could work against each other: one adds available supply, while the other reduces access to replacement cargoes.

For trucking, farming and manufacturing, sustained diesel shortages would raise operating costs and squeeze margins. Companies able to pass those costs through could prolong inflation pressure.

Emergency inventories provide temporary protection. Their effectiveness depends on release volumes, delivery speed and whether normal supply routes recover before those stocks need replenishing.

WATCH NEXT

• European release decisions and delivery schedules.
• The scope of any U.S. export restrictions.
• Diesel inventories, freight costs and refinery output.

Source: Reuters, September 29, 2026.

text:
Only 60 1967 Mercury Comets were built with Ford's 427 FE V8, making the combination one of the rarest factory performance cars of the era. The 427 was Ford's legendary Side-Oiler, and Mercury offered it in two forms: the R-code with dual four-barrel carburetors and a factory rating of 425 horsepower and the W-code with a single four-barrel rated at 410 horsepower. The 427 Comets were available across four body styles—the lightweight 202 two-door sedan, Capri hardtop, Caliente hardtop, and Cyclone hardtop. Production records generally break the 60 cars down into 22 202s, seven Capris, four Calientes, and 27 Cyclones. Of the total, 51 were R-code cars and nine were W-code cars.

The 202 sedan was the most stripped-down and purposeful version. Twenty-two were built with the R-code 427, and the cars were configured with drag racing very much in mind. Mercury removed much of the factory sound insulation, saving roughly 150 pounds, while some cars received a trunk-mounted battery to improve rear weight distribution. Every 427 Comet received a four-speed Toploader and a 9-inch rear axle with 3.89:1 gearing and Traction-Lok. The 427 itself used the FE's cross-bolted main-bearing structure, forged internals, solid lifters, and side-oiling system designed to maintain oil supply under sustained high-rpm loads.

What made the cars so effective was the combination of massive engine capacity and relatively compact Mercury bodywork. The 427's official ratings were 425 horsepower for the dual-quad R-code and 410 for the single-carb W-code, but race-prepared examples could produce substantially more. Period and surviving-car accounts document these Comets as factory-built performance machines rather than ordinary street cars that happened to receive a large engine. The 202 was particularly attractive to racers because its two-door post body was lighter and more rigid than the hardtops. One documented R-code 202, for example, was ordered with virtually no options beyond the equipment needed to turn it into a serious drag-racing platform.

The rarity becomes even more remarkable when the body-style numbers are examined. Only four Caliente hardtops received the R-code 427, while just one of the seven Capri hardtops received the W-code engine. That single W-code Capri is commonly described as the rarest Mercury ever produced. The 427 Comet program was clearly aimed at performance enthusiasts and drag racers, and its limited production gave Mercury a factory weapon capable of competing in the NHRA environment without looking anything like a purpose-built race car.

The 1967 Mercury Comet 427 therefore occupies a strange place in muscle-car history. It was not produced in large numbers, and it was never the mainstream face of Mercury performance. Instead, only 60 examples combined a relatively understated mid-size Mercury body with Ford's 427 FE Side-Oiler. The result was a car that could look almost ordinary from a distance while carrying one of the most serious racing engines Ford had available. That combination of anonymity, factory engineering, and extreme rarity is what makes the 427 Comet so fascinating—not because every surviving example was an 11-second car, but because Mercury quietly built a small batch of cars with the hardware to become formidable drag racers straight from the factory.

text:
The reason a Black man got into one of America's most closed trades in 1973 was that the airplanes were French. Nobody hired at Federal Express had ever worked on a Falcon, so for a few weeks the question that keeps people out, who has experience, had no answer at all.

James Coopwood walked through that gap on April 15, employee number 469, and understood exactly what had happened to him. He spent the next thirty years making sure the next man would not have to wait for an accident.

In July of 1974 Businessweek told its readers that Federal Express was taking a nosedive.

The magazine was not being cruel. The company was losing as much as a million dollars a month.

Paychecks were going out postdated. The founder had started asking people not to cash them.

Pilots were buying jet fuel on their own credit cards to keep the aircraft moving. Inside six months the company would lose almost a third of its start-up cash.

James Coopwood had been there fifteen months. He was twenty-six years old, he was from Memphis, and he was the first Black aviation maintenance technician the company had ever put in that hangar.

If the company went under, that job went with it. There was not a second one of those in Memphis.

He had been hired on April 15, 1973, employee number 469, the first Black aviation maintenance technician the company ever had. He had come out of the Air Force, where the military taught him engines.

Then he walked into the one civilian hangar in Memphis where the usual question did not work.

The usual question in aircraft maintenance is who has experience. It is the question that keeps the trade closed, because you cannot get experience unless somebody already inside lets you into the building.

In the spring of 1973 the question had no answer at Federal Express. The airplanes were French.

They were Dassault Falcon 20s, executive jets built to carry ten people in leather seats at five hundred and thirty-five miles an hour. The company had bought them and had them cut open.

The cutting was done at a shop in Little Rock. A cargo door was set into the left side of the forward fuselage, fifty-five inches by seventy-four and a half.

It ran on a closed hydraulic circuit of its own, so it would swing open even when the rest of the aircraft was dead on the ramp.

The floor was rebuilt to take concentrated weight. The passenger windows were plugged, one by one, until the thing had no way to see out.

Coopwood drove the hundred and thirty-odd miles between Memphis and Little Rock getting them ready to carry mail. He said later that after the Air Force, commercial aircraft turned out to be a whole different world.

"It was something that everybody had to get used to, because nobody hired at FedEx had any experience on those Falcons," he said. "But I never stopped because I had a drive, and my drive been in me ever since I was in high school."

Nobody hired there had worked on those Falcons. For one strange stretch, every man walking into that hangar had the same amount left to learn.

The company he joined had already failed once in public, five weeks before they hired him.

On March 12, 1973, Federal Express flew to eight cities. The sales team had hoped for as many as six hundred packages.

Six came.

They hired Coopwood on the fifteenth of April. They tried again on the seventeenth.

That night the executives and their families came out and stood on the ramp outside the sorting hangar at Memphis International to watch. Three hundred and eighty-nine people were working, and fourteen Falcons were waiting with their windowless sides turned to the light.

Coopwood was not watching. By the company's own account he was out there loading, putting boxes through the fifty-five inch door he had been preparing in Little Rock.

A hundred and eighty-six packages went out to twenty-five cities that night, from Rochester to Miami. The company had three hundred and eighty-nine people on its books to move them.

Then came the two years nobody puts in the anniversary posts.

The company lost around twenty-nine million dollars in those first years. Drivers were paying for gasoline out of their own pockets.

Fifteen months earlier this company had given a Black man in Memphis a job that no other hangar in the city had offered him. By that summer it was on the newsstand as a failure and its checks were dated forward.

Nobody would have blamed him for leaving. It had taken until 1973 for that hangar to hire its first Black technician, and there was no reason to believe a second chance was coming.

He stayed thirty years.

The record does not say what that cost at his kitchen table, and I am not going to invent it. It says the checks were postdated and it says he was there.

The company came out the other side. Coopwood became its first Black supervisor in aircraft maintenance, and he was honest about what that felt like.

There was a position open, he said, and they asked him if he would like it. He had to think about it for a while, because it came with a lot of responsibility.

It was a challenge, he said, and he took it. He had his ups and downs and he stood it out.

Then he did the thing that outlives him, and it was not a speech.

He started the company's first Apprentice Aircraft Maintenance Technician program, aimed at people already inside the building in entry-level jobs who had been told their whole lives that skilled aviation work belonged to somebody else. One of his colleagues later put the reason in a single line.

If you can see it, you can be it.

Here is what those people were actually up against. To sit for an aviation mechanic's certificate you need eighteen months of practical experience for one rating, thirty for both.

The FAA counts that time only if you are working under somebody else's certificate.

It has to be full time and it has to be eighteen actual months. The agency has told applicants that ten hours a day, six days a week for a single year does not count, even though the hours come out the same.

So a man sweeping that hangar could not study his way in.

Somebody had to put him on a payroll, under a supervisor, and keep him there for a year and a half.

An apprenticeship program is not encouragement. It is a paid job, a certificated supervisor and a paper trail, which are the only three things eighteen months of qualifying experience can be built out of.

He had gotten through a door that happened to be unguarded for a few weeks in 1973. What he built afterward was meant to open on purpose.

Two men stood on that ramp on the first night.

Fred Smith died on June 21, 2025, at eighty. He was buried at Arlington National Cemetery with military honors and a flyover, memorialized in front of a crowd at FedExForum, and written up at length in the national papers.

James Coopwood died on July 8, 2026, at seventy-eight. His celebration of life was held on July 24 at New Bethel Missionary Baptist Church in Germantown, Tennessee, and the Commercial Appeal ran an item.

The first Falcon delivered to the company is in the Smithsonian now, purple and white with orange trim, in the business aviation gallery at the Udvar-Hazy Center.

Federal Express named its aircraft after employees' children. The museum's own record notes that this first one is called Wendy, after the founder's daughter.

The cargo door is still in the side of it. Fifty-five inches by seventy-four and a half, the same measurement he was working to on the road to Little Rock in April of 1973.

In 2021 the Bureau of Labor Statistics counted Black workers as 5.7 percent of the aircraft mechanics and service technicians in the United States. Black workers were 12.3 percent of everybody employed in America that year, so the trade was running at under half its share.

Fifty-three years after a company had to hire men without experience because there was no such thing as experience yet, the trade is back to asking who has experience.

The answer still depends on who gets handed the job where experience is made.

The route he built is legal, it is open, and almost nobody who could use it has ever been told it is there. So tell somebody the numbers.

Eighteen months for one rating, thirty for both, and a job where somebody lets you put your hands on the aircraft.

He got in through an accident. He spent thirty years making sure nobody coming behind him would have to wait for one.

🇹🇭 Chaos at Thai Airport Brings Staff to Tears as Angry Passengers Vent Frustration

BANGKOK — Chaos has engulfed Bangkok’s Suvarnabhumi Airport after severe flooding crippled Thai Airways’ ground operations, leaving thousands of bags stranded, flights delayed or cancelled and exhausted passengers demanding answers.

The disruption became so severe that the Royal Thai Air Force was called in, deploying 69 personnel to help overwhelmed ground crews restore operations and tackle the mountain of delayed luggage.

Around 5,600 pieces of baggage were left unprocessed at the height of the crisis after flooding across Bangkok prevented large numbers of Thai Airways ground-handling employees from reaching work. Faulty baggage carts compounded the shortage, creating a bottleneck that spread rapidly through the airline’s operations.

Passengers reported waiting five or six hours for luggage, while others were forced to leave the airport without their bags. Some travellers complained that information from the airline was scarce, leaving passengers dependent on one another for updates.

The pressure also fell heavily on airport workers. Staff already stretched by shortages faced increasingly frustrated travellers as delays accumulated and departure times repeatedly slipped.

Thai Airways chief executive Chai Eamsiri has apologised and accepted responsibility for the disruption, saying the carrier offered “no excuses” for what happened. The airline has brought office employees into ground operations and arranged additional assistance to accelerate baggage processing and delivery.

Almost the entire Thai Airways schedule suffered disruption during the worst period. By Tuesday, the airline was still dealing with luggage associated with 52 flights, while reporting indicated dozens of services had been delayed and several cancelled.

The airline has also begun cutting flights to relieve pressure on its overwhelmed ground-handling system, with services linking Bangkok with destinations including Singapore, Hanoi, Phuket and Khon Kaen among those affected.

Suvarnabhumi itself remained operational throughout the crisis, highlighting that the breakdown was primarily within Thai Airways’ handling operation rather than a complete shutdown of Bangkok’s main international airport.

With soldiers now helping airline workers shift stranded luggage, Thai Airways faces the urgent task of clearing the backlog — and restoring passenger confidence after days of extraordinary disruption at one of Southeast Asia’s busiest aviation hubs.

text:
The United States government flew a ninety-one-year-old Black brickmaker to South America because nobody else in the country could still do it. George Black could not read a word until his wife taught him, and he ended up in the White House, on the evening news, and in the villages of Guyana showing people how to raise houses out of their own dirt.

He never called himself the last brickmaker in America. He said he was making a living for his family. Go look at the sidewalks in Old Salem.

There is a photograph of an old man holding a brick.

He is ninety-nine years old in it. The brick in his hands is one he made when he was forty-four.

It came out of the wreckage of Old Main, the original North Carolina Baptist Hospital building, which opened in 1923 and came down in 1978.

Every brick in that hospital was shaped by hand. The hands were his.

His name was George Henry Black.

By the time somebody put that brick back in his palm, the city of Winston-Salem was largely made out of him, and most of the country had never heard of him.

He was born in Randolph County on February 15, 1879, fourteen years after the war ended. His father had been born into slavery.

In 1889 the three of them walked.

George was ten. His brother was older, and their father led them the fifty miles from Liberty to Winston because word had come down that three men working together in the brickyards could earn a dollar and fifty cents a day.

They made it. They got the work.

Ten months later their father was dead.

The boys stayed, because there was no school for them and nothing to go back to. They hauled other men's bricks and took whatever else paid.

That is how George Black learned the trade. From the bottom of it, carrying what other men made.

The brickyard belonged to the Hedgecock family, and somewhere on that lot sat an old mud mill, broken.

A mud mill is not a delicate machine. It is a barrel with blades inside it that chews clay and water into mud a man can work with, and it turns because an animal walks in a circle all day pulling it.

They told him he could have it. They told him it would do for firewood.

He took it home and fixed it.

He tied a mule to it, and the mule started walking the circle, and the blades turned, and out came the mud. He dug his own clay, the red Carolina clay that lies under everything in that part of the state.

He worked with a wooden mold that held six bricks at a time.

He filled it with his hands, judging the amount by feel, six and six and six, and then he stacked what he had made and burned it in a kiln in his own back yard.

The machines came. Every other brickyard in America bought them, because a machine could do in an hour what a man could do in a day.

He kept the mule.

He was still doing it that way seventy years later. Thousands of bricks a day, by hand, out of a hole in his own ground.

His bricks came out rough on the face and a little irregular, which made them harder to lay. A bricklayer had to slow down and be careful with his mortar, and plenty of bricklayers hated him for it.

The people building the most expensive houses in Winston-Salem would not take anything else.

They did not crack. Forsyth County's own preservation record puts it flatly, that the bricks made today are nowhere near as good as the ones he made.

Look at what they hold up.

The 1923 North Carolina Baptist Hospital. Wachovia bank branches.

The mansions of Buena Vista, which is the neighborhood where the money lived.

Churches and businesses and sidewalks all over town.

The Salem College library, the old YWCA on Glade Street, the bank building at 916 West Fourth Street.

The Market Firehouse on Salem Square, and the brick walks of Old Salem that visitors photograph every single day without once asking whose hands the clay went through.

Charleston. Savannah.

And in 1931, at fifty-two years old, George Black went to Colonial Williamsburg to work as a brickmaker in the early years of the restoration.

America was rebuilding its colonial capital, and it wanted the place to look the way it looked in the seventeen hundreds, and the country could not find enough men who still knew how to make a brick that way.

The man who knew was the son of a man who had been owned.

They brought him back in the 1970s as a consultant and an instructor, so the restorers could learn it from him directly.

Emily Wilson, who sat with him for hours near the end of his life, put the money down in her book. Twenty-five cents for every thousand bricks.

He married Martha Jane Hampton in 1897, and they had eight children, and every one of those children came up working in the brick business.

He could not read when he married her.

She taught him. His granddaughter says Martha did it because she could see what kind of mathematician she had married, and that reading and figuring are the reason the family came through the Depression standing.

The yard on Dellabrook Road turned into something bigger than a business. Evelyn Terry, another granddaughter, describes it as the neighborhood's employment office, because anybody who needed work could climb that hill and find some.

There was a boy who lived across the street named Thomas Brabham. His grandfather came to George Black and said the rest of the boys around there were going astray, and asked him to take this one under his wing and put him to work.

He did. Remember that boy.

Sometime in the 1950s a car came up the drive at 111 Dellabrook Road, and the man who got out of it was one of the top men at Wachovia Bank.

He had come to check on his brick order.

Sit with the arithmetic of that. This is North Carolina under Jim Crow, a white bank executive standing in a Black man's yard, in a decade when a Black man was expected to drop his eyes and say yes sir and thank you for the business.

George Black was in his seventies.

He told the man he had given his word and the bricks would be ready. Then he told him to go away and do his banking.

The man left.

In 1970 a CBS crew came out to that same yard, because Charles Kuralt had heard there was somebody in Winston-Salem still making bricks with a mule.

Kuralt asked him how many bricks he thought he had made in his lifetime. Black would not even guess at the number.

The story ran on the evening news, and the next day a man from the United States Agency for International Development got on the phone.

Guyana was trying to rebuild itself, village by village, and did not want a factory. It wanted somebody who could teach ordinary people to make bricks with their own hands, and the American government had been unable to find a single man left in the country who still could.

Kuralt told him the brickmaker was in his nineties.

The official said he did not care.

So the State Department sent George Black to South America. He was ninety-one years old, and he stayed several months.

Under his direction the villagers went from nothing to turning out between ten thousand and twenty-four thousand bricks a day.

He came home a national story. Richard Nixon received him at the White House, and the following year the campaign put him in a re-election advertisement.

Then he went back out to the yard on Dellabrook Road and went back to work.

In 1978 the hospital came for Old Main.

The building was fifty-five years old and the medical center wanted something modern standing there instead. Two of the men running the place told a young development officer named Gary Fleming to save some of the bricks before they were hauled off as rubble.

The demolition crew carried them over to his office, which was in a basement. There was no room to keep them, so Fleming took them home and stacked them in the basement of his own house on Buena Vista Road.

Buena Vista. The same neighborhood whose front walls George Black had made.

And somewhere in all of that, somebody put one of those bricks into the hands of the ninety-nine-year-old man who had shaped it, and a photographer raised a camera.

That is the picture.

The next year a museum borrowed one of his six-brick molds for an exhibit, and he did not want to let it go.

He told them to bring it back, come warm weather, because he would be making brick when the weather turned.

He was one hundred years old and he was making plans for the spring.

George Henry Black died on October 9, 1980. He was a hundred and one.

His granddaughter Dolores Black McGee said he never understood the fuss anybody made over him. She said he told them the same thing every time, that he was just trying to make a living for his family.

Then the honors came, one after another, the way they always come once a man is safely gone.

His house and brickyard went on the National Register of Historic Places in 2000, listed as nationally significant, which fewer than four out of every hundred listed properties ever are.

In 2003 the General Assembly of North Carolina passed a resolution honoring him, and the county unveiled a bronze statue downtown at Second and Chestnut. In the statue he is holding a brick and a trowel.

A street marker went up in 2007. A local landmark designation followed in 2011.

The bricks out of Old Main sat in that Buena Vista basement for roughly forty-five years, until Fleming picked up the phone and offered them back to the hospital for its hundredth birthday.

One of them is going into a time capsule, to be opened in a hundred years. Another one is mounted on a plaque in a medical library.

His own house is still at 111 Dellabrook Road. He lived in it from 1934 until the day he died in it.

When a reporter walked up to it, the porch boards had buckled and rotted through, there was glass missing out of a front window, and what was left of the front steps was a pile of rubble.

Out back, where the kilns were, a tree had grown into one of the walls and swallowed it.

Evelyn Terry has spent more than twenty years trying to save that house.

She dug those kilns back out of the dirt between 2009 and 2011, and the man who helped her do it was Thomas Brabham, the boy from across the street.

He came back and put his hands in that yard one more time before he died in 2013.

So the ledger reads like this. His bricks are in a time capsule and on a plaque and in a hospital and in the banks and in Colonial Williamsburg, and under the shoes of every visitor who walks Old Salem.

The man himself is in bronze downtown, holding a brick he will never be allowed to set down.

And the last front steps in that city being built out of George Black bricks are the ones going in at George Black's own front door, laid by his own family, ninety years after he laid everybody else's.

He made theirs first.

Historical figures who were opposed, ignored, or destroyed in their own generation, then treated as foundational later.
1. Jesus of Nazareth
Tried and executed as a blasphemer and political threat by Jewish authorities and Rome. His followers were a small, persecuted sect. Within a few centuries Christianity became the dominant religion of the Roman world and, over two millennia, the largest religious tradition in history. His moral and theological claims still shape law, ethics, art, and politics across continents.​
2. Socrates
Athens convicted him of impiety and corrupting the youth and forced him to drink hemlock. Many citizens saw him as a dangerous gadfly who undermined traditional piety and democracy. Through Plato and later schools he became the starting point of Western philosophy; the “unexamined life” and the Socratic method remain core to education and political thought.​
3. Joan of Arc
A peasant girl who claimed divine voices, led French armies, and helped turn the Hundred Years’ War. The English and their Burgundian allies burned her as a heretic and witch. A generation later her conviction was overturned; in 1920 the Catholic Church canonized her. She became a national symbol of France and an enduring image of courage and conviction.​
4. Galileo Galilei
The Church placed him under house arrest for defending heliocentrism and treating Scripture as non-scientific on astronomy. He spent his last years silenced. Later centuries treated him as the emblem of modern science; the Vatican formally acknowledged the error of the 1633 condemnation in 1992. His method and discoveries helped set the scientific revolution in motion.​
5. Ignaz Semmelweis
A Hungarian physician who showed that doctors washing their hands slashed deaths from childbed fever. Colleagues mocked him, resisted the idea of invisible contagion, and drove him from practice; he died in an asylum. Once germ theory took hold he was recognized as a founder of antiseptic medicine. Countless lives have been saved by the practice he could not get accepted in his own hospital.​
6. Vincent van Gogh
Sold almost nothing, was viewed as unstable, and died by suicide believing himself a failure. His work was dismissed as crude and excessive. Within decades he became one of the most influential painters in history; his paintings now define modern art’s emotional intensity and are among the most valuable in the world.​
7. Nikola Tesla
Pioneered alternating current, radio principles, and much of the electrical infrastructure of the 20th century, yet died poor and relatively forgotten after losing business wars and public attention to Edison and others. Mid-20th-century reappraisal made him a symbol of visionary engineering; AC power and related technologies still run the modern world.​
8. Alan Turing
His code-breaking work shortened World War II and helped found computer science. Britain then prosecuted him for homosexuality, subjected him to chemical castration, and he died at 41. Decades later he received a royal pardon and is widely honored as a father of computing and artificial intelligence.

text:
Robert Anderson covert funds

Robert B. Anderson (1910–1989), Eisenhower’s Treasury Secretary (1957–1961) and earlier Navy Secretary, is the figure most closely tied to “covert funds.” After leaving office he worked as an international consultant, diplomat, and fixer with documented and alleged links to intelligence-related money and later ran an illegal offshore bank.
 
Documented CIA-related offer
A 1973 CIA “Family Jewels” memo (later released with JFK assassination files) records that Anderson, while serving as special ambassador on Panama Canal talks amid anti-U.S. riots, contacted the CIA and offered to inject about $300,000—described as coming from “American business interests”—to influence Panamanian elections. The Agency declined.
 
He acknowledged passing information to the CIA at times. Through his New York consulting practice he maintained a network of contacts and associates (including Ghassan Shaker) in the Middle East. In Oman after the 1970 palace coup, he assembled an advisory circle around Sultan Qaboos (sometimes called the “Muscat Mafia”) that included people with intelligence ties; he received oil and mineral concession authority and later said he was working to reduce British dominance there. British diplomats viewed him with suspicion and sometimes referred to him only indirectly in cables.
 
Unconfirmed “black gold” rumor
Some accounts (notably by Sterling and Peggy Seagrave) claim that shortly after World War II Anderson, then on the Secretary of War’s staff, was present when Japanese war loot (“Yamashita’s gold”) was found in the Philippines and proposed parking it in secret “black gold” accounts for future covert operations. This has never been confirmed. 

Later illegal banking and hidden money
In the 1980s Anderson and a partner operated the unregistered Commercial Exchange Bank and Trust of Anguilla (with a New York office). He used it to hide personal income (including Unification Church consulting fees routed through Uruguay) and handled client funds. Depositors lost at least $4.4 million, much of it funneled into failed oil-and-gas deals. Prosecutors said the bank also handled money for at least one drug dealer. In 1987 he pleaded guilty to tax evasion and operating an unregistered offshore bank; he received a short prison term, house arrest, probation, and was later disbarred. He died in 1989.
 
A 2026 Reason article by an Oxford researcher draws on newly released files, British archives, and other sources to portray Anderson as a Cold War-era fixer whose official résumé sat alongside a less official role as intelligence go-between and handler of discreet funds. Many details remain fragmentary or unproven. Other Robert Andersons (Ponzi-scheme operators, brokers, an FBI counterintelligence official, etc.) appear in searches but lack the same combination of high office, intelligence contacts, and hidden-money activity.

You tried to sound clever....but you fundamentally misunderstood ancient textual criticism and basic historical methodology.

You mixed up composition date with manuscript survival. I explicitly said we have fewer than 20 physical copies (manuscripts) of Alexander’s histories, preserved 1,000+ years after his death. Arrian and Plutarch wrote 400 years after Alexander, but the oldest physical manuscripts we actually possess date to the Middle Ages (10th century AD). Meanwhile, we have physical New Testament papyrus fragments dating within decades of the originals. Learn the difference between when a book was composed and when the physical manuscript survived.

The New Testament isn't "one claim." It’s an anthology of 27 distinct documents written by multiple independent authors across different geographic locations and of whom were divinely inspired by God when writing it. God Himself is the author. 

Early epistles like 1 Corinthians 15 preserve oral creeds that critical, non Christian scholars date to within 3 to 5 years of the crucifixion.

Tacitus was a Roman senator with access to imperial records. He explicitly recorded that Jesus Christ was executed under Pontius Pilate. Josephus was born in 37 AD in Jerusalem, a direct contemporary living alongside the primary eyewitnesses. In ancient history, sources writing within decades are considered breaking news.

Nobody uses archaeology to "prove miracles." We use it to prove the Gospel authors were real eyewitnesses who accurately knew 1st-century geography, rulers, and cultural details. Skeptics claimed Pontius Pilate was fictional until archaeologists unearthed the Pilate Stone in 1961. The historical setting isn't a myth, the accounts are grounded in reality.

1 Corinthians 15 documents over 500 witnesses who saw the resurrected Christ at one time, many of whom were still alive when it was written for anyone to verify. On the 25th anniversary of 9/11, the Archbishop of Canterbury Sarah Mullally became global meme fodder. Mullally conferred an interfaith award on Osama bin Laden apologist Maulana Hafiz Ashrafi. The photograph went viral. Mullally, an über-feminist who had pledged to wipe out misogyny in the Church, was caught on camera, grinning like a barracuda alongside Ashrafi and his wife, who was dressed like a sarcophagus. Ashrafi’s daughter, masked like a Ninja at a Halloween party, put the finishing touches on the comedy of the absurd. A week later, desperate to compete with his partner in interfaith suicidal empathy, Pope Leo XIV approved a declaration titled “A Journey of Hope” (...) it urges greater dialogue with Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and other religions. It elevates Islam to a key fraternal partner. It castigates perpetrators of “Islamophobia.” It does not preach Jesus’ uniqueness. And it reads the riot act to Christians who engage in the unforgivable sin of “proselytism.” In effect, the declaration is Pope Leo’s ultimatum to St. Paul. “Put your aggressive proselytizing on mute,” Leo is telling Paul. “Cool the sales pitch. Cut the converts. Quit cruising around the Mediterranean persuading Jews and Greeks to follow Jesus. It’s ruining the Vatican’s interreligious dialogue with devotees of Artemis, Zeus, and Hermes and killing our fraternity with disciples of Dionysus, Isis, and Mithras. Leo’s document does not define “proselytism,” leaving room for weaponized ambiguity. Not once does the document use the term “evangelism,” my preferred term for proselytism. One has to turn to the Oxford English Dictionary, which defines “proselytism” as “the making or seeking of converts.” The root word is proserkhesthai, ‘to approach.’ You’ve got to approach someone if you wish to convert them. It is striking that while the Vatican anathematizes proselytism, the European Court of Human Rights approves proselytism as a bona fide manifestation of religion. The ECHR recognized this in the landmark Kokkinakis v Greece case, wherein a Jehovah’s Witness challenged his conviction for attempting to convert a Greek Orthodox Christian on a home visit. Kokkinakis was arrested more than 60 times for proselytism. He was also imprisoned several times. The court based its verdict on the European Convention on Human Rights (Article 9), which asserts that the right to freedom of religion includes the right to change one’s religion (as does Article 18 of the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights). “Proselytism is linked to freedom of religion; a believer must be able to communicate his faith and his beliefs in the religious sphere as in the philosophical sphere,” Judge Pettiti stated. “Believers and agnostic philosophers have a right to expound their beliefs, to try to get other people to share them and even to try to convert those whom they are addressing.” According to the court, proselytism is valid since religious conversion, as permitted by Article 9, often involves being persuaded by others. “Indeed, without proselytism, the right to change religion ‘would be likely to remain a dead letter,’” Andrew Hambler, an expert in employment law, writes in his peer-reviewed article in the Industrial Law Journal. Hambler might as well have quoted the apostle Paul. Writing to the Romans, Paul strings together a series of rhetorical questions: “How then will they call on him [Jesus] in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching?” (Romans 10:14). In this sense, proselytism has the strongest claim to legitimacy, Hambler emphasizes. Sadly, “proselytism” bashing is now a staple of papal pontificating. During his visit to the Rimini Meeting of Friendships Among Peoples, Leo “recalled that his predecessors have repeated on several occasions, ‘the Church does not engage in proselytism,’” Vatican News reported. In a letter to the cardinals, Leo slammed “the temptation of proselytism.” Pope Francis frequently attacked proselytism. “Proselytism is solemn nonsense; it makes no sense,” he famously said. For Rome, “the view that proselytism is the only way to engage with the other no longer make[s] sense in a world that increasingly resembles an interconnected and constantly evolving global village.” So how does one preach Christ? Sure, Rome isn’t calling for “renouncing the truth” but “proclaiming it in a manner befitting the Gospel: with esteem, listening, and charity.” But the exaggerated emphasis on interreligious dialogue can lead to “grave confusion,” as Bishop Joseph Strickland warns. He contends that Leo’s document risks placing dialogue above evangelization, suggesting that non-Christian religions are authentic paths to God and raising doubts about the Church’s missionary mandate. The New Testament scholar Robert Gagnon observes that Leo’s document “at the very least depresses or discourages evangelism (what it calls ‘proselytism’), if not outright rejecting it.” Gagnon calls the document “utter nonsense,” adding: “It is heretical to discourage conversion to Christianity from other faiths. This Pope and his Vatican cohorts have made many missteps in a relatively short time, but this is the worst.” I would applaud if Leo warned against using coercion, cajolery, or crookery in proselytism. But Leo redefines evangelistic outreach as the supine expectation of a lover whose words “do not disturb others,” do not “make demands or oblige,” but “only lead others to marvel at such love.” Christians must not proactively seek to convert others but, like a lover, “simply wait[s] for them to inquire about the love that has filled his or her life.” This is pious humbug. No great love story would be penned, or no great romantic movie would find an audience if all the lover did was to “simply wait.” Even a peacock proactively opens his feathers and dances to attract a peahen. Jesus didn’t ask his disciples to “simply wait” but to go to the very ends of the earth to proclaim the gospel. Paul did the very opposite of “simply waiting.” He went around the Mediterranean on three missionary journeys. He preached to Jews and Gentiles. Jewish and Christian scholars agree that Paul wasn’t trying to “convert” Jews to “Christianity” or to “Roman Catholicism.” Saul the Jew never became Paul the Christian. He remained a Jew to his death. In the highly fraught sectarian context of Second Temple Judaism, where the Jesus Movement emerged as one of the many Jewish sects, Paul was preaching to the Jews that their Scriptures had been fulfilled and their Jewish Messiah had come in the person of Jesus. Paul is emphatic that the gospel is “to the Jew first.” Much of his preaching takes place in synagogues. The embryonic “churches” are actually synagogue sub-groups comprised of Jewish Jesus followers who keep Torah, Paul Treblico argues in his monograph Self-designations and Group Identity in the New Testament. Paul didn’t “simply wait” for Jews or Gentiles to enquire about Jesus. For example, in the synagogue at Thessalonica, “for three weeks he argued with them from the [Hebrew] scriptures, explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, ‘This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Messiah.’” Luke, the author of Acts, notes that “some of them were persuaded” (Acts 17:3-4). The five verbs: arguing, explaining, proving, proclaiming, and persuading, suggest that Paul was proactively proselytizing the Jews. In Athens, Paul “argued” in “the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the market place every day with those who chanced to be there” (17:17). Rather than “esteem” other religions, “his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols” (17:16). The Greek word for “provoked” is paroxyno, from which we get our English word “paroxysm.” In Corinth, he “argued in the synagogue every sabbath and persuaded Jews and Greeks” (18:4). In Ephesus, he “entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, arguing and pleading about the kingdom of God” and “argued daily in the hall of Tyrannus” for two years (19:8-10). Non-Jewish proselytes did indeed attend synagogues. In his magnum opus Jew and Gentile in the Ancient World, Jewish historian Louis Feldman argues that Judaism possessed a robust spirit of proselytism and attracted large numbers of converts and proselytes throughout the Greco-Roman world before the rise of early Christianity. Ironically, while Pope Leo is shying away from proselytism, Islam is making massive inroads with dawa. In July, Muslim organizations launched aggressive proselytization campaigns using the FIFA World Cup series to recruit new converts in 16 cities of the United States, Canada, and Mexico. The Muslim Ummah of North America (MUNA) kicked off its dawa at SoFi Stadium in California with banners inviting football fans to “discover Islam” as a “faith of peace, purpose, and submission to the Creator.” MUNA missionaries offered free copies of the Qur’an in English, Spanish, Bengali, and other languages, promoting the Islamic text as a book that “has inspired billions of people for over 1,400 years” and Islam as a religion “regardless of race, language, nationality, or background.” But scholars and ex-Muslims are warning the West that dawa is not simply the sharing of Islamic faith in the Christian sense of “evangelism.” “Dawa as practiced by radical Islamists employs a wide range of mechanisms to advance their goal of imposing Islamic law (sharia) on society,” Ayaan Hirsi Ali, a human rights activist and former Muslim, explains in her book The Challenge of Dawa: Political Islam as Ideology and Movement and How to Counter It. “The ultimate goal of dawa is to destroy the political institutions of a free society and replace them with the rule of sharialaw.” Like Catholics, many evangelicals are not only failing to understand the sinister aspects of Islamic dawa but, unlike Paul, are unwilling to confront it with robust argumentation and challenge. I find it difficult to comprehend why certain religious groups resent proselytizing others or having their members proselytized. If Jews tried to convert me, I’d feel honoured. In fact, I’d joyfully go with my Jewish proselytizers to the synagogue. Since I read Hebrew, I can join in the prayers. As a chaplain at a London university, I had excellent relations with hardline Muslim leaders. They’d tell me they respect me but loathe my liberal Anglican clergy colleagues. “We know you are trying to convert us and you know we are trying to convert you,” they’d say. In turn, I respected and loved them for their convictions and passion for dawa (Islamic proselytism). My Hindu students were candid: “You’re wasting your time. Britain is a post-Christian country. We are here to convert Britons to Hinduism,” they’d say. On campus, even Buddhists, Stoics, and atheists proselytized unapologetically. It was a playground of ideas. I am richer for my interactions with the evangelists of these religions and philosophies. Likewise, my mission was to preach the gospel and pray that they would come to faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. With Paul, I would remind myself daily: “For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Romans 1:16). While I was a student in Cambridge, Catholics and Orthodox unrelentingly tried to convert me to their “one, true church.” I felt flattered. A religion that doesn’t proselytize is essentially saying: “We are a closed club. We don’t want you. You are not good enough for us.” On my part, I’ve never missed an opportunity to evangelize. I did this for eight hours while I was flying back from India to England to defend my doctoral thesis, with a Briton who had left Christianity for Buddhism, even though I desperately needed the time to prepare for my viva voce. At the end of our conversation, the Buddhist promised to reconsider the claims of Christ. Leo doesn’t believe in proselytism because he doesn’t understand the transformative power of the gospel. In India, millions of Dalits (untouchables) have been liberated from three millennia of the caste system because missionaries proselytized them. In the Islamic world, millions of Muslims have been unshackled from the slavery of Islam because someone shared Christ with them—as my ex-Muslim colleagues at the Ideological Defense Institute would testify. Paul said: “I’m compelled to do it, and doomed if I don’t!” (1 Corinthians 9:16, The Message). He ends his life and ministry incarcerated in Rome, “expounding the gospel [to his fellow-Jews] from morning till evening, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the law of Moses and from the prophets” (Acts 28:23). In the landmark Mbuyi v Newpark Childcare Ltd employment tribunal case, Sarah Mbuyi, a Christian nursery worker, framed her workplace proselytism in these terms: “I believe what I have got is a gift and a desire to share.” That’s why I love the Sri Lankan theologian D.T. Niles’ definition of evangelism as “one beggar telling another beggar where to find bread.”

text:
Prayers go to God. They are offered in heaven.
The smoke rises “before God” from the angel’s hand. The destination is God, not the angel. The setting is the heavenly temple: golden altar, censer, incense—the same pattern as the earthly sanctuary, now seen from the other side. So: to heaven if you are speaking from earth; in heaven if you are watching the liturgy John sees.

Whose prayers?
“The prayers of all the holy ones / all God’s people / all the saints”—the same group named in Revelation 5:8, where the elders hold bowls of incense “which are the prayers of the saints.” John does not split the Church into “only the living” and “the dead do not count.” In this book the martyrs under the altar already cry out to God (Revelation 6:9–11). They are conscious, they know the earth is unfinished, and they speak to God about it.

Who do they go to?
God. The angel does not collect prayer as its own. It presents incense with the prayers. Heaven is not a wall. It is a liturgy. Someone in heaven is handling what the holy ones have prayed.

Scripture already assumes that those who belong to Christ are alive to God (Luke 20:38), that heaven is aware of earth (Luke 15:7, 10; Revelation 6:10), and that Christians ask other members of the Body to pray because “the prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective” (James 5:16). Paul begs the churches to pray for him. He never says, “Ask only people who still have a pulse.” The question is not whether prayer may be shared in the Body. It is whether death severs the Body. The New Testament’s answer is that it does not (Romans 8:38–39; Hebrews 12:22–24).

text:
The NCAA wanted to crush Michigan.

In the negotiated resolution phase, enforcement staff proposed a multi-year postseason ban to settle the case. They viewed that as a generous offer, one Michigan would be wise to accept.

The Committee on Infractions is a different story. None of its members were involved in those negotiations.

The COI has a few dozen members, but only a handful are assigned to any one case.

In Michigan's case, it was six. Six people decided Michigan's fate.

A different six might have ruled more harshly.

Financially, and at the staff level, Michigan got hammered. They shattered the NCAA records for fines and show causes. No bowl ban or vacated wins, though. Those are reserved for tattoos and text messages.

Their fans should feel grateful, not celebratory. There's a reason the school's leadership looked more relieved than joyous, and didn’t fight the ruling.

Lucky Michigan. They are the first and only school to reject an offer in the negotiated resolution phase and end up with a better outcome…sort of.

And it wasn't because they were exonerated or vindicated in any way.

Even that lenient panel found them guilty and wrote that a postseason ban was "required in this case." They got off easy.

To be fair, they were forced to keep employing Sherrone Moore as head coach.

Even I think that's harsh.

I’m half Mexican and half Japanese. I grew up in the United States, became a citizen, served in the Army, deployed four times, and I consider myself American without hesitation.

If the United States and Mexico were somehow at war, my loyalty would be to the United States. That does not mean I suddenly stop having Mexican roots, family traditions, food, music, language, or cultural influences.

That is the part I think gets lost when people say, “If you want to be American, then just be American.”

Being American has never required everyone to become culturally identical. Italian-Americans did not stop being Italian. Irish-Americans did not stop being Irish. Japanese-Americans did not stop being Japanese. Over time, those cultures became part of the larger American culture.

That is what assimilation actually looks like in practice: you adopt the country, its laws, its civic identity and its loyalties, while parts of the culture you came from become part of the American version of you.

A mariachi band playing The Star-Spangled Banner is a pretty good example of that. They are not rejecting America by using Mexican instrumentation. They are literally using their heritage to honor America.

So I understand the concern about national cohesion. I just think there is a major difference between refusing to integrate into a country and integrating while still remembering where you came from.

Americanization does not have to mean cultural erasure. It can mean cultural addition.

text:
As the #NHL #NHL 2027-2028 season begins, I want to offer up my team-by-team thoughts here:

Anaheim Ducks - Lost some players that may have made a difference but will still be ok. Will teeter between just missing the playoffs or just making it. Carlsson has a lot to prove now.

Boston Bruins - It depends which Jeremy Swayman shows up this season. Pasta will easily net 35-40 goals though.

Buffalo Sabres - Will not be as good as last season, so get ready for a rough ride.

Calgary Flames - Bottom of the barrel and will see last place overall.

Carolina Hurricanes - Defending Champs, though I can't predict a repeat but absolutely cup contenders. I do think Nikishin will get an offer from Carolina he can't refuse.

Chicago Blackhawks - They'll have another rough season. Bedard being out to start doesn't help matters. Kane's farewell tour will at least be the highlight.

Colorado Avalanche - I say this every year, but cup contender and could win it all. Goaltending may be the issue here though. Blackwood/Wedgewood played great last season but they aren't known to be great.

Columbus Blue Jackets - About the same as last year, maybe a tad worse. Nothing to write home about.

Dallas Stars - Another team that can be a cup contender and could win it all.

Detroit Red Wings - Larkin needs to get traded to start a rebuild for this team. It won't be easy for Detroit.

Edmonton Oilers - Could be McDavid's last go at it with Oilers. If they aren't in a playoff spot come trading deadline, he'll get traded to a contender to win before signing elsewhere in the offseason. If they are in a solid playoff spot and look competitive, then he'll stay. Goaltending is a problem again.

Florida Panthers - Looks like they are trying to buy a cup with all their moves. That may backfire on them, but we'll see. I see no reason why they won't make the playoffs again short of more injuries.

Los Angeles Kings - Solid team, playoff bound but will have to start thinking of the future soon.

Minnesota Wild - Absolutely underrated team and one that I tend to cheer for as the underdog come playoff time.

Montreal Canadiens - A team on the uprise. Expect exciting things from them. Dobes may end up winning the Vezina trophy this year.

Nashville Predators - Stamkos quietly scored over 40 goals last year and will do it again this year. This is an odd team because on paper, they are better than they have been on ice. 

New Jersey Devils - They need goaltending. Off-season moves have been minor. Will likely miss playoffs again (sorry to my friends who are Devils fans)

New York Islanders - Sorokin & Schaefer won't be able to save this team. At least they got new 3rd jerseys as per fan submissions!

New York Rangers - Dorofeyev was the big addition here, will score over 30 goals and maybe over 70pts. Will play well and the team will teeter between missing the playoffs or making it. As a Rangers fan, I think they will *just* squeeze into it but be eliminated first round. Drury will be done after that.

Ottawa Senators - May end up battling Calgary and Vancouver for last place overall.

Philadelphia Flyers - I predict they win their division. Martone will surprise folks and be rookie of the year.

Pitsburgh Penguins - Lots of players on their last legs here. If they make the playoffs, they may not make it far but we'll see. Team needs to start thinking of future franchise players and fast before they become the worst team in the next few years.

San Jose Sharks - Absolutely will make the playoffs this year. Celebrini will have another amazing year, and Stenberg will end up being the surprise of the draft with 25-30 goals and 70+ pts.

Seattle Krakken - Another team that will be fighting to not be a bottom dweller team.

St. Louis Blues - They'll back a little bounce back from some bad play last year. Let's see where it takes them.

Tampa Bay Lightning - Nothing major has changed and that's OK! Will remain competitive.

Toronto Maple Leafs - Gavin McKenna will be mostly hype but will improve a lot over time and that's expected. Team will make the playoffs and, as always, will lose quickly.

Utah Hockey Club - I'm happy Trocheck went here, they'll be exciting to watch again.

Vegas Golden Nights - Mitch Marner will have one of his best years this year. One of these teams that should be a cup contender as well.

Vancouver Canucks - Will see some slight improvement with Manny Malhotra as the coach. Need to avoid the injury bug here to at least keep competitive and not get last place overall.

Washington Capitals - This is Ovechkin's swan song year. He'll break some more records and pad a few stats.

Winnipeg Jets - Just please trade Connor Hellebuyck and get this over with and move on. He won't be playing here. I like the Jets, but they need help now. #NHLFaceoff
